    @Override                                   // compiler checks this really overrides
    public String generate()                    // wider access (protected -> public): OK
            throws FileNotFoundException {      // narrower checked exception: OK
        return "traffic stats";                 // covariant return: String is-a Object
    }
}

public class OverrideDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Report r = new TrafficReport();         // upcast
        r.print();                              // "Report: traffic stats" - runtime dispatch
    }
}

Rules

Rule Detail
Signature Same name and parameter types (after erasure for generics)
Return type Same, or a covariant subtype for reference types (Java 5+). Primitives must match exactly
Access modifier Same or wider (private < default < protected < public). Never narrower
Checked exceptions Same, narrower (subclass), fewer or none. Never new or broader checked exceptions
Unchecked exceptions Any. No restriction
Cannot override final, static (hidden instead), private (not inherited), constructors
Package-private Overridable only by subclasses in the same package
super.method() Calls the parent's implementation
@Override Optional but strongly recommended. It catches typos such as equals(Employee e) overloading instead of overriding
synchronized/strictfp Not part of the signature. They can be added or removed freely

Why the access and exception rules? Because of the Liskov Substitution Principle: code written against Report r must still work when r is a TrafficReport. If the override were less accessible, or threw a checked exception the caller isn't prepared for, substitution would break.

Classic trap: overloading disguised as overriding

class Point {
    int x;
    public boolean equals(Point p) { return p.x == x; }  // OVERLOAD, not override of equals(Object)
}
// HashSet / HashMap call equals(Object), so this method is never used. @Override would have caught it.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Can an overriding method throw a RuntimeException the parent doesn't declare? Yes. Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted.
  • What's a covariant return type? An overriding method returning a subtype of the original return type (e.g. clone() returning MyClass instead of Object).
  • Can we override with a generic parameter change? Only if the erasures match. void m(List<String>) and void m(List<Integer>) clash with the error "name clash: same erasure".
A23 Class A has a public method; class B overrides it as private. Will it work? Why?
  • No, it's a compile error: "attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public".
  • An overriding method can't reduce visibility. Otherwise A a = new B(); a.m(); would call a private method through a public reference, which breaks the Liskov substitution principle. Widening access (protected to public) is allowed.

No. It's a compile-time error.

class A {
    public void show() { System.out.println("A"); }
}
class B extends A {
    // private void show() { System.out.println("B"); }
    // error: show() in B cannot override show() in A
    //        attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public
}

Why

  • Overriding rule: the overriding method cannot reduce visibility. Java checks this because of substitutability (LSP):
    A ref = new B();
ref.show();   // the compiler allows this because A.show() is public...
              // ...so at runtime B's version MUST be callable from anywhere
  • If B could make it private, a perfectly legal call through an A reference would hit a method the caller isn't allowed to access, which breaks the type system.
  • Allowed directions: protected → public (widening) is fine, and public → public is fine. public → protected/default/private is an error.
  • The same applies to interface methods. Implementing an interface method (implicitly public) requires public in the class. Omitting public gives "attempting to assign weaker access privileges".

Contrast with the reverse (A23 vs A11): if A's method is private and B declares a public method with the same signature, it compiles. It's not an override, just a new method (A11).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Can B override it as protected? No, that's still weaker than public. Same error.
  • What if the method is static in both? Hiding follows the same rule: you can't hide with weaker access.
  • Why can overriding widen access? Widening never breaks existing callers. Anything callable before is still callable.
A24 Difference between HashMap and Hashtable. Co. 2
HashMap Hashtable
Thread safety Not synchronized Synchronized (every method locks the whole table)
Performance Faster Slower
Null 1 null key, many null values No null key or value (NPE)
Iteration Fail-fast iterator Enumerator (legacy) plus iterator
Since Java 1.2, Collections Framework Java 1.0, legacy

Use HashMap single-threaded and ConcurrentHashMap for concurrent access. Hashtable is effectively obsolete.

Aspect HashMap (Java 1.2) Hashtable (Java 1.0, legacy)
Thread safety Not synchronized Every public method is synchronized (one lock on the whole table)
Performance Fast Slow under contention (all threads serialize)
Null key/values One null key, any number of null values No nulls (NPE for key or value)
Superclass AbstractMap Dictionary (obsolete abstract class)
Iteration Iterator, fail-fast (ConcurrentModificationException) Enumeration (keys(), elements()) is not fail-fast; its Iterator views are fail-fast
Default capacity / growth 16, doubles (power of two) 11, grows to 2n + 1
Index calculation (n - 1) & hash with hash spreading h ^ (h >>> 16) (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length
Collision handling Linked list → red-black tree when the bucket has ≥ 8 entries (Java 8) Linked list only
Ordering None (use LinkedHashMap for insertion/access order) None
Java 8 extras compute, merge, forEach, getOrDefault (both have them via Map defaults, Hashtable overrides them synchronized) Same API through Map
Recommendation Single-threaded or confined use Don't use. For concurrency use ConcurrentHashMap 
import java.util.*;

public class MapCompare {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, String> hm = new HashMap<>();
        hm.put(null, "nullKey"); hm.put("k", null);           // fine
        System.out.println(hm);                               // {null=nullKey, k=null}

        Map<String, String> ht = new Hashtable<>();
        try { ht.put(null, "x"); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("Hashtable: no null key"); }
        try { ht.put("k", null); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("Hashtable: no null value"); }
    }
}

Gotcha: even Hashtable's per-method synchronization doesn't make compound operations atomic. if (!t.containsKey(k)) t.put(k, v) is still a race. Use ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent/computeIfAbsent.

Likely follow-ups:

  • HashMap vs Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>())? The latter wraps with a single mutex like Hashtable (and allows nulls). Iteration still needs manual synchronized(map).
  • Why is Hashtable's index a modulo while HashMap's is a mask? HashMap keeps the capacity a power of two, so & (n-1) equals % n and is cheaper.
  • Is Hashtable deprecated? Not formally, but it's considered legacy.
A25 Internal working of HashMap Co. 2Other rounds (Question List)
  • It is backed by an array of buckets (Node<K,V>[] table). The default capacity is 16 and is always a power of 2.
  • put(k, v):
    1. hash = h ^ (h >>> 16). This hash spreading mixes the high bits into the low bits.
    2. Bucket index = (n - 1) & hash.
    3. Empty bucket: insert the node. Otherwise walk the bucket: if a key matches by hash == and equals(), replace the value; if not, append a new node.
  • Load factor 0.75: when size > capacity * 0.75 (e.g. 12 for capacity 16), it resizes to double capacity. Each node either stays at its index or moves to index + oldCap.
  • Treeify: a bucket's list becomes a red-black tree when it reaches 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets. With a smaller table it resizes instead. A tree turns back into a list at 6 nodes. Worst-case lookup goes from O(n) to O(log n).
  • get(k) follows the same hash, then index, then equals path. Average time is O(1).

Structure (Java 8+): an array Node<K,V>[] table of buckets. Each bucket is null, a linked list of Nodes, or a red-black tree of TreeNodes.

static class Node<K,V> implements Map.Entry<K,V> {
    final int hash;   // cached spread hash
    final K key;
    V value;
    Node<K,V> next;
}

Key constants

Constant Value Meaning
DEFAULT_INITIAL_CAPACITY 16 Always a power of two (tableSizeFor rounds up)
DEFAULT_LOAD_FACTOR 0.75 Trade-off between space and collision probability
threshold capacity × loadFactor Resize when size > threshold (12 for the default)
TREEIFY_THRESHOLD 8 A bucket's list becomes a tree when it reaches 8 nodes...
MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY 64 ...but only if table.length >= 64. Otherwise the table resizes instead
UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD 6 A tree converts back to a list when it shrinks to ≤ 6 (during resize split)
MAXIMUM_CAPACITY 2^30

put(key, value) step by step

  1. Compute the hash with spreading:
    static final int hash(Object key) {
    int h;
    return (key == null) ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}
    XOR-ing the high 16 bits into the low 16 matters because the index uses only the low bits. Without it, hashCodes that differ only in their high bits (e.g. Float keys, or multiples of 2^16) would all collide.
  2. Lazy init: the table is allocated on the first put (resize()), not in the constructor.
  3. Find the bucket index: index = (n - 1) & hash. With n = 16, n - 1 = 0b1111, so it takes the low 4 bits. That equals hash % n for power-of-two n, but is faster and is never negative.
  4. Empty bucket → place a new Node.
  5. Non-empty bucket → walk the chain. For each node, check p.hash == hash && (p.key == key || key.equals(p.key)).
    • Match → replace the value (the key object stays the same) and return the old value.
    • No match → append at the tail (Java 8; Java 7 inserted at the head).
    • If the chain length reaches TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) → treeifyBin: treeify if table.length >= 64, else resize.
    • If the bucket is a TreeNode → putTreeVal (O(log n)).
  6. modCount++ (drives fail-fast iterators). If ++size > threshold, call resize().

resize()

  • Doubles the capacity (newCap = oldCap << 1) and the threshold.
  • Rehash is cheap: since n doubles, each node either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCap, depending on a single bit: (hash & oldCap) == 0. The bucket is split into "lo" and "hi" lists, preserving relative order.
  • Tree bins are split the same way. If a half has ≤ 6 nodes, it's untreeified.
  • Cost: O(n) when it happens, amortized O(1) per put. Pre-size when you know the count: new HashMap<>(expected / 0.75f + 1), or Java 19+ HashMap.newHashMap(expected).

get(key): compute the hash → index → check the first node → then traverse the list (O(k)) or the tree (O(log k)), using hash == then equals.

Tree bins: ordered by hash. On ties, by compareTo if keys are mutually Comparable, else tieBreakOrder (class name, then System.identityHashCode). Treeification is a defence against poor hash functions and hash-flooding attacks. With a good hash the probability of a bucket reaching 8 is ~0.00000006 (Poisson distribution, per the JDK source comments).

Complexity: average O(1) for get/put/remove. Worst case O(log n) in Java 8+ (O(n) in Java 7, or for non-Comparable keys with identical hashes).

Why Java 8 switched from head to tail insertion: in Java 7, concurrent resizes with head insertion could reverse a list and create a cycle, which made get() spin forever at 100% CPU. Tail insertion avoids the cycle, but HashMap is still not thread-safe (lost updates, corrupted size).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why is capacity a power of two? So that (n-1) & hash replaces the slow %, and so the resize split works with a single bit.
  • Why load factor 0.75? An empirical balance. Higher means more collisions. Lower means more memory and more frequent resizes.
  • Why treeify at 8 but untreeify at 6? The gap (hysteresis) stops a bucket flapping between list and tree around one threshold.
  • Is iteration order guaranteed? No. It can change after a resize. Use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap.
A26 How are HashMap collisions handled? Co. 2
  • A collision means different keys land in the same bucket. HashMap uses separate chaining: the bucket holds a linked list of nodes, with new nodes appended at the tail since Java 8.
  • Lookup inside a bucket compares the hash and then equals().
  • Since Java 8, a long chain (8 or more nodes, table of at least 64) is converted to a red-black tree. This keeps worst-case lookup at O(log n) and protects against hash-flooding attacks.
  • A good hashCode() and resizing keep chains short in the first place.

A collision happens when two different keys land in the same bucket index. That happens either because their hashCodes are equal, or because (n-1) & hash maps different hashes to the same slot.

HashMap uses separate chaining:

  1. Linked list in the bucket (Java 8 appends at the tail). Lookup walks the chain comparing hash first (a cheap int check), then ==, then equals().
  2. Treeification (Java 8): when a single bucket reaches 8 nodes and the table has ≥ 64 buckets, the list becomes a red-black tree (TreeNode), so lookups go from O(k) to O(log k). If the table is smaller than 64, HashMap resizes instead, because spreading entries is the better fix when the table is small.
  3. Untreeify back to a list when a bin drops to ≤ 6 nodes during a resize split.
  4. Resizing reduces collisions overall by doubling the bucket count and spreading the entries.
import java.util.*;

public class CollisionDemo {
    record BadKey(int id) {
        @Override public int hashCode() { return 42; }   // every key collides
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<BadKey, String> m = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) m.put(new BadKey(i), "v" + i);
        System.out.println(m.get(new BadKey(77)));   // v77 - still correct, just slower
        // All 100 entries are in one bucket -> treeified once table >= 64.
        // BadKey isn't Comparable, so the tree falls back to tieBreakOrder: lookups may degrade toward O(n).
    }
}

"Aa" and "BB" have the same String.hashCode() (2112). That's a classic interview example of a real collision. Keys still stay distinct because equals() distinguishes them.

Other collision strategies (for comparison)

Strategy Used by
Separate chaining (list/tree) HashMap, ConcurrentHashMap, Hashtable (list only)
Open addressing, linear probing IdentityHashMap, ThreadLocal.ThreadLocalMap
Open addressing, probing Set.of/Map.of immutable implementations (ImmutableCollections.SetN/MapN)

Reducing collisions in your code

  • Write a good hashCode() using all the significant fields (Objects.hash(...), or records/Lombok generate it).
  • Use immutable keys.
  • Implement Comparable on key classes that are likely to collide, so that tree bins can order them.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is a collision the same as a duplicate key? No. A duplicate is equals()-equal, and its value gets replaced. A collision is a different key in the same bucket, and both are kept.
  • Why compare hash before equals? An int comparison is cheap and filters out most non-matches before the potentially expensive equals.
  • What is hash flooding? An attacker sends many keys with identical hashes (e.g. crafted query params) to make the map degrade. Treeification limits the damage.
A27 hashCode(), equals(), toString() in the context of HashMap. Co. 2
  • hashCode() decides which bucket a key goes to.
  • equals() decides whether two keys in the same bucket are the same key, which means replace rather than add.
  • Contract: if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). The reverse need not hold, and that is what a collision is. Always override both together, using the same fields.
  • toString() has no effect on HashMap behaviour. It only controls how keys and values print (e.g. {Employee[name=Anshul]=103}). Without it you see Employee@1b6d3586.

Roles

Method Role in HashMap Default (Object)
hashCode() Chooses the bucket (after spreading and masking) Identity-based int (not the memory address on modern JVMs; often a random or thread-local generated value stored in the object header)
equals(Object) Finds the exact key within the bucket Reference equality ==
toString() Not used for storage or lookup. Only for printing (map.toString() calls each key's and value's toString()) and logging ClassName@hexHashCode, e.g. Employee@1b6d3586

The equals/hashCode contract (from Object Javadoc)

  1. Consistency: repeated hashCode() calls return the same value while the fields used in equals don't change.
  2. a.equals(b) ⇒ a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). This is mandatory.
  3. Equal hash codes do not imply equals (collisions are allowed).
  4. equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and x.equals(null) == false.

What breaks if you violate it

Override Effect in HashMap
Neither Identity semantics. Two "logically equal" objects are different keys
Only equals Equal objects usually land in different buckets. Duplicates are stored and get with an equal-but-different object returns null
Only hashCode Same bucket, but equals uses ==, so they are still treated as different keys (duplicates stay in one bucket)
Both, consistently Correct logical-key semantics

Correct implementation (Java 17)

import java.util.Objects;

public final class Employee {
    private final String name;
    public Employee(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public String getName() { return name; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Employee other)) return false;   // pattern matching (16+)
        return Objects.equals(name, other.name);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hashCode(name); }  // or Objects.hash(f1, f2...)
    @Override public String toString() { return "Employee[name=" + name + "]"; }
}
// Or simply: public record Employee(String name) {}  -> equals/hashCode/toString generated

Gotchas

  • Use the same fields in both equals and hashCode.
  • getClass() != o.getClass() vs instanceof: instanceof allows subclasses but can break symmetry if a subclass adds fields. Make value classes final.
  • JPA entities: don't base hashCode on a generated @Id that is null before persist. Use a business key, or a constant hashCode with id-based equals.
  • Lombok @Data on JPA entities with bidirectional relations → StackOverflowError in hashCode/toString.
  • Arrays as keys use identity equals. Wrap them, or use Arrays.hashCode/Arrays.equals in your own key class.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Can two unequal objects have the same hashCode? Yes. That's a collision, and it's legal.
  • Why must equal objects have equal hash codes? Otherwise HashMap looks in the wrong bucket and never calls equals.
  • Does HashMap use toString? No. It's only used in map.toString() and debugging output.
A28 What happens when custom objects are used as HashMap keys? Co. 2 
Employee e1 = new Employee("Anshul");
Employee e2 = new Employee("Ravi");
Employee e3 = new Employee("Anshul");
HashMap<Employee, Integer> empM = new HashMap<>();
empM.put(e1, 101);
empM.put(e2, 102);
empM.put(e3, 103);
System.out.println(empM.size());
  • WITHOUT overriding equals/hashCode: the Object versions use identity, so e1 and e3 are different keys. Size = 3 (Anshul->101, Ravi->102, Anshul->103). Also, empM.get(new Employee("Anshul")) returns null.
  • WITH both overridden on name: e3 has the same hash and equals(e1) is true, so its value replaces e1's. Size = 2: Anshul->103 (the original key object e1 is kept, only the value changes) and Ravi->102.
  • Overriding only one of the two breaks the contract and behaviour becomes unpredictable.
record Employee(String name) { }   // a record generates equals/hashCode/toString from 'name'
  • Mutable key pitfall: if a key's name changes after put, its hash changes. The entry stays in the old bucket, so get() and remove() can no longer find it (an effective memory leak). Use immutable keys such as String, wrapper types or records.
Employee e1 = new Employee("Anshul");
Employee e2 = new Employee("Ravi");
Employee e3 = new Employee("Anshul");
HashMap<Employee, Integer> empM = new HashMap<>();
empM.put(e1, 101);
empM.put(e2, 102);
empM.put(e3, 103);

Case 1: equals/hashCode NOT overridden

class Employee {
    private final String name;
    Employee(String name) { this.name = name; }
}
  • Object.hashCode() is identity-based, so e1, e2 and e3 (three distinct objects) almost certainly get different hashes. Object.equals uses ==, so even with a collision, e1 ≠ e3.
  • Result: empM.size() → 3. Both "Anshul" objects are separate keys.
  • empM.get(e1) → 101, empM.get(e3) → 103.
  • empM.get(new Employee("Anshul")) → null (a new identity). This is the common bug: you can't look up by value.
  • System.out.println(empM) → something like {Employee@1b6d3586=101, Employee@4554617c=102, Employee@74a14482=103} (order and hashes vary).

Case 2: equals/hashCode overridden on name (as in A27, or record Employee(String name))

  • e1.hashCode() == e3.hashCode() and e1.equals(e3) is true, so e3 is a duplicate key.
  • put(e3, 103) replaces the value of the existing entry and returns the old value 101. The key object stored remains e1. HashMap doesn't replace the key.
  • Result: empM.size() → 2.
  • empM.get(e1) → 103, empM.get(e3) → 103, empM.get(new Employee("Anshul")) → 103.
  • With the toString() override: {Employee[name=Ravi]=102, Employee[name=Anshul]=103} (iteration order isn't guaranteed).
  • empM.keySet().iterator() returns the e1 instance for Anshul. You can verify with ==.
Without overrides With overrides on name
size() 3 2
get(e1) 101 103
get(new Employee("Anshul")) null 103
Return of put(e3,103) null 101

Partial overrides: only equals → most likely size 3 (different buckets, equals never called). Only hashCode → size 3 (same bucket, but == comparison).

Mutable-key pitfall

import java.util.*;

class MutableKey {
    String name;
    MutableKey(String n) { name = n; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof MutableKey m && Objects.equals(name, m.name); }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hashCode(name); }
}

public class MutableKeyDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<MutableKey, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
        MutableKey k = new MutableKey("Anshul");
        map.put(k, 101);
        k.name = "Changed";                                  // hash changes, entry stays in old bucket
        System.out.println(map.get(k));                      // null  (looks in new bucket)
        System.out.println(map.get(new MutableKey("Anshul"))); // null  (old bucket, but equals fails)
        System.out.println(map.size());                      // 1     - entry is "lost" -> memory leak
        System.out.println(map.containsKey(k));              // false
    }
}

Rule: keys must be immutable, or at least the fields used in equals/hashCode must never change while the object is a key.

Records as keys (best practice, Java 16+)

record EmployeeKey(String name, String dept) {}       // final, immutable fields, auto equals/hashCode/toString
Map<EmployeeKey, Integer> ids = new HashMap<>();
ids.put(new EmployeeKey("Anshul", "IT"), 101);
ids.get(new EmployeeKey("Anshul", "IT"));             // 101

Caveat: a record is only shallowly immutable. A List component can still be mutated, so use List.copyOf in a compact constructor. Other good key types are String, Integer and enums (immutable, with cached hash in String's case).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Does put with an equal key replace the key? No. Only the value. The original key instance is kept.
  • What's the cost of a poor hashCode (e.g. constant)? Every entry goes into one bucket: O(log n) if the key is Comparable (tree), else it approaches O(n).
  • Why is String a good key? It's immutable, caches its hashCode, and has a well-distributed hash.
  • TreeMap with custom keys? It needs Comparable or a Comparator, and uses compareTo, not equals/hashCode. They should be consistent with each other.
A29 HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap. Other rounds (Question List)
HashMap ConcurrentHashMap
Thread safety No (concurrent puts can lose updates) Yes
Locking None Java 8+: CAS for an empty bucket, synchronized on the bucket's first node otherwise. Reads are lock-free. Java 7 used segments.
Null 1 null key and null values allowed No null keys or values (a null would be ambiguous with "absent")
Iterator Fail-fast (ConcurrentModificationException) Weakly consistent, never throws CME
Atomic operations None putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge

Use ConcurrentHashMap for shared caches and counters, e.g. map.merge(sensorId, 1, Integer::sum).

Aspect HashMap ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+)
Thread safety None. Concurrent writes cause lost updates or a corrupted size Thread-safe, highly concurrent
Locking — CAS to insert into an empty bin. synchronized on the bin's head node for non-empty bins. Reads are lock-free (volatile reads of Node.val/next)
Java 7 design — Segments (default 16, a ReentrantLock each), so concurrency was limited to the segment count
Null keys/values 1 null key, many null values Neither (NPE)
Iterators Fail-fast (ConcurrentModificationException) Weakly consistent: never throw CME, reflect some state at or after creation, may or may not show concurrent updates
size() Exact field Approximate under concurrency. Computed from baseCount + CounterCell[] (LongAdder-style striping). Use mappingCount() for a long
Atomic compound ops None (compute is not atomic across threads) putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, compute, merge, replace(k, old, new) are atomic
Resize Single thread Cooperative: multiple threads help transfer bins (ForwardingNode markers)
Treeify Yes (8 / 64) Yes (TreeBin with its own read-write lock)
Bulk ops — forEach, reduce, search with a parallelism threshold
Performance (single thread) Faster Slightly slower

Why no nulls? In a concurrent map, get(k) == null would be ambiguous: is the key absent, or mapped to null? You can't resolve it with a follow-up containsKey(k) because another thread may change the map in between. Doug Lea banned nulls to remove the ambiguity.

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;

public class ChmDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> hits = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
            String junction = "J" + (i % 5);
            pool.execute(() -> hits.computeIfAbsent(junction, k -> new LongAdder()).increment()); // atomic
        }
        pool.shutdown();
        pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        System.out.println(hits);   // each J0..J4 = 2000

        // WRONG (race) even on CHM - check-then-act across two calls:
        // if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);
        // RIGHT:
        // map.putIfAbsent(k, v);  or  map.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
}

Gotchas

  • Each CHM method is atomic, but a sequence of calls isn't. Use compute*/merge.
  • Keep the function passed to computeIfAbsent short, and never modify the same map inside it. It holds the bin lock, and recursive updates can deadlock or throw IllegalStateException("Recursive update").
  • ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() gives a concurrent Set.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not Collections.synchronizedMap? It uses one global lock, so readers block writers and each other. CHM has non-blocking reads and per-bin write locks.
  • What does "weakly consistent" mean? The iterator won't throw CME. It traverses elements as they existed at some point and may reflect later changes.
  • ConcurrentHashMap vs ConcurrentSkipListMap? CHM is unordered with O(1) average. The skip list map is sorted (a NavigableMap), O(log n), and lock-free.
A30 Java memory areas: Heap and Stack (plus Metaspace briefly). TCSCo. 2
Heap Stack
Stores Objects, instance variables, arrays, the String pool Method frames: local variables, primitives, object references, partial results
Scope Shared by all threads One per thread
Managed by Garbage collector (Young/Old generations) Pushed and popped automatically per method call (LIFO)
Error OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space StackOverflowError (e.g. deep recursion)
Size flags -Xms, -Xmx -Xss
  • Metaspace (Java 8+, replaced PermGen) holds class metadata in native memory. It is limited with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • Other areas: the PC register and the native method stack.

The JVM spec defines runtime data areas. Some are shared by all threads; others are per thread.

                 ┌───────────────────── JVM Process ─────────────────────┐
 Shared          │  HEAP (objects, arrays, String pool since Java 7)      │
 (all threads)   │    Young: Eden | S0 | S1      Old/Tenured              │
                 │  METASPACE (native memory): class metadata, method     │
                 │    bytecode, runtime constant pool (replaced PermGen)  │
                 │  CODE CACHE: JIT-compiled native code                   │
                 ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 Per thread      │  JVM STACK: frames {local vars, operand stack, frame   │
                 │    data / ref to constant pool, return address}        │
                 │  PC REGISTER: address of current bytecode instruction  │
                 │  NATIVE METHOD STACK: for JNI/native (C) calls         │
                 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Area Shared? Stores Size flags Error when exhausted
Heap Yes All objects and arrays, instance fields, interned strings, static field values (they live with the Class object in the heap on HotSpot since 8) -Xms, -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Stack Per thread One frame per method call: primitives, object references, partial results -Xss (e.g. 512k–1m) StackOverflowError (deep or infinite recursion). OOM: unable to create native thread when there's no room for new stacks
Metaspace Yes Class structures, method metadata, constant pools, annotations -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize (unbounded by default) OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
PC register Per thread Address of the current instruction (undefined for native methods) — None
Native method stack Per thread C frames for JNI calls Platform StackOverflowError/OOM
Code cache Yes JIT-compiled code -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize "CodeCache is full. Compiler has been disabled"
Direct memory Yes ByteBuffer.allocateDirect (Netty, NIO) -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize OOM: Direct buffer memory 
public class MemoryDemo {
    static int counter = 0;                 // class metadata in Metaspace; value stored with Class mirror on heap
    public static void main(String[] args) {     // frame for main pushed on main thread's stack
        int x = 10;                         // primitive in stack frame (local variable array)
        String s = new String("city");      // reference 's' on stack; object on heap; literal "city" in String pool (heap)
        int[] arr = new int[3];             // array object on heap
        compute(x);                         // new frame pushed; popped on return
    }
    static int compute(int n) { return n * 2; }
}

Key points

  • PermGen → Metaspace (Java 8): PermGen was a fixed-size part of the heap and caused frequent OOM: PermGen space. Metaspace uses native memory, grows automatically, and its classes are freed when their classloader is GC'd.
  • The String pool moved from PermGen to the heap in Java 7.
  • Escape analysis: the JIT may scalar-replace objects that don't escape a method, so in effect they are never allocated on the heap. The JVM spec still says "objects live on the heap".
  • Stack memory is thread-safe by nature. Heap objects shared between threads need synchronization.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Where are static variables stored? The variable metadata is in Metaspace. On HotSpot 8+, the values live in the java.lang.Class mirror object on the heap.
  • What causes StackOverflowError? Unbounded recursion, or very deep call chains (e.g. a bidirectional JPA toString).
  • Stack vs heap speed? Stack allocation is a pointer bump with LIFO freeing, which is very fast. Heap allocation also uses pointer-bump TLABs, but needs GC to reclaim.
A31 Explain the Java Collection Framework. TCS
  • It is a unified set of interfaces, implementations and algorithms for storing and processing groups of objects (in java.util).
  • Collection branches into:
    • List (ordered, duplicates allowed): ArrayList, LinkedList
    • Set (unique elements): HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet
    • Queue/Deque: PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque
  • Map (key-value) is a separate hierarchy: HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap.
  • Utility classes: Collections (sort, unmodifiable, synchronized wrappers) and Arrays. Iterator/ListIterator handle traversal, Comparable/Comparator handle ordering.
  • Concurrent implementations live in java.util.concurrent.

The Java Collections Framework (JCF), from Java 1.2, is a unified architecture of interfaces (contracts), implementations (data structures) and algorithms (Collections, Arrays utilities) for storing and manipulating groups of objects.

Hierarchy

                         Iterable<E>
                             │
                       Collection<E>
                             │
     ┌───────────────┬───────┴─────────────┬─────────────────────┐
  SequencedCollection (Java 21) ────────────┤                     │
     │               │                     │                     │
   List<E>         Set<E>               Queue<E>                 │
     │               │                     │                     │
 ├ ArrayList     ├ HashSet             ├ PriorityQueue           │
 ├ LinkedList*   │   └ LinkedHashSet   ├ Deque<E>                │
 ├ Vector        ├ SortedSet<E>        │   ├ ArrayDeque          │
 │  └ Stack      │   └ NavigableSet<E> │   └ LinkedList*         │
 └ CopyOnWrite-  │       └ TreeSet     └ BlockingQueue<E>        │
   ArrayList     └ EnumSet                 ├ ArrayBlockingQueue
                                           ├ LinkedBlockingQueue
                                           └ PriorityBlockingQueue ...
   (* LinkedList implements both List and Deque)

            Map<K,V>   (NOT a Collection)
               │
   ├ HashMap ── LinkedHashMap
   ├ Hashtable ── Properties
   ├ SortedMap ── NavigableMap ── TreeMap
   ├ WeakHashMap, IdentityHashMap, EnumMap
   └ ConcurrentMap ── ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentSkipListMap

Choosing an implementation

Need Use Complexity
Index access, mostly appends ArrayList get O(1), add amortized O(1), insert in middle O(n)
Queue/stack ArrayDeque (faster than Stack/LinkedList) O(1) at both ends
Unique elements, no order HashSet O(1) avg
Unique, insertion order LinkedHashSet O(1) avg
Sorted / range queries TreeSet/TreeMap (red-black tree) O(log n)
Key-value lookup HashMap O(1) avg
LRU cache LinkedHashMap(cap, 0.75f, true) + removeEldestEntry O(1)
Priority processing PriorityQueue (binary heap) offer/poll O(log n), peek O(1)
Enum keys EnumMap/EnumSet (array/bit-vector) Very fast
Concurrency See A32

Key concepts

  • Comparable vs Comparator: natural ordering (compareTo) vs external ordering (compare). Comparator.comparing(Emp::dept).thenComparing(Emp::name).
  • Fail-fast iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException when a structural change happens outside the iterator (based on modCount). Remove safely with iterator.remove() or list.removeIf(...).
  • Immutable vs unmodifiable: List.of() (Java 9) is truly immutable and null-hostile. Collections.unmodifiableList(x) is a read-only view, so changes to x show through.
  • Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view backed by the array: set works, add/remove throw UnsupportedOperationException.
  • Sequenced collections (Java 21): getFirst(), getLast(), reversed(), addFirst() on List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap.

Likely follow-ups:

  • ArrayList vs LinkedList? ArrayList almost always wins (cache locality, O(1) random access). LinkedList only helps for heavy insert/remove through an iterator.
  • Collection vs Collections? Collection is the root interface. Collections is a utility class (sort, unmodifiableList, synchronizedMap).
  • Why isn't Map a Collection? It stores pairs, and add(E) doesn't fit. It offers keySet(), values() and entrySet() collection views instead.
  • ArrayList growth? Default capacity 10 (allocated lazily on the first add), grows by 1.5x (old + (old >> 1)).
A32 Concurrent collections and concurrent access in Java. G2
  • Plain collections aren't thread-safe. Collections.synchronizedList/Map locks the whole collection, which makes it a bottleneck.
  • java.util.concurrent offers better options:
    • ConcurrentHashMap: fine-grained locking and atomic operations.
    • CopyOnWriteArrayList/Set: each write copies the array. Good when reads far outnumber writes (listener lists, config).
    • BlockingQueue (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue): producer-consumer with put/take.
    • ConcurrentLinkedQueue: lock-free, non-blocking.
    • ConcurrentSkipListMap/Set: sorted and concurrent.
  • Their iterators are weakly consistent (no ConcurrentModificationException).
  • For other shared state use synchronized, ReentrantLock, atomics (AtomicInteger, LongAdder) or volatile.

Problem: ordinary collections (ArrayList, HashMap) aren't thread-safe. Concurrent modification can cause lost updates, corrupted internal state, ConcurrentModificationException, or infinite loops (Java 7 HashMap).

Three generations of solutions

Approach Example Characteristics
Legacy synchronized Vector, Hashtable, Stack Every method synchronized. Slow, compound ops still racy
Synchronized wrappers Collections.synchronizedList/Map/Set(...) One mutex. You must manually synchronize when iterating
java.util.concurrent (Java 5+) ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, BlockingQueue... Fine-grained locking or lock-free (CAS), weakly consistent iterators, atomic compound ops 
List<String> sync = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
synchronized (sync) {                    // REQUIRED, otherwise CME / inconsistent reads
    for (String s : sync) System.out.println(s);
}

java.util.concurrent collections

Class Mechanism Best for
ConcurrentHashMap CAS + per-bin locks Shared caches, counters (A29)
ConcurrentSkipListMap / Set Lock-free skip list, sorted Concurrent sorted data, leaderboards
CopyOnWriteArrayList / Set Every write copies the array. Snapshot iterators Read-mostly lists: listeners, config, subscriber lists
ConcurrentLinkedQueue / Deque Lock-free (Michael-Scott queue) Non-blocking producer/consumer
ArrayBlockingQueue Bounded array, single lock + 2 conditions Bounded producer/consumer (back-pressure)
LinkedBlockingQueue Optionally bounded, two locks (put/take) Thread pool work queues (newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded one, a memory risk)
PriorityBlockingQueue Unbounded heap Priority task processing
DelayQueue Elements available after a delay Scheduling, retries, expiring cache entries
SynchronousQueue Zero capacity, direct hand-off newCachedThreadPool
LinkedTransferQueue transfer() waits for a consumer High-throughput hand-off

Producer–consumer with BlockingQueue (sensor ingestion)

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class SensorPipeline {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100);   // bounded = back-pressure

        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) queue.put("reading-" + i);  // blocks if full
                queue.put("EOF");
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                String r;
                while (!(r = queue.take()).equals("EOF")) System.out.println("processed " + r); // blocks if empty
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        producer.start(); consumer.start();
        producer.join(); consumer.join();
    }
}

Other concurrent-access tools: synchronized, ReentrantLock (tryLock, fairness, interruptible), ReadWriteLock/StampedLock (optimistic reads), Atomic* and LongAdder, volatile, CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Semaphore (rate-limiting connections), Phaser, ThreadLocal, and immutability (the simplest form of thread safety).

Gotchas

  • Check-then-act and read-modify-write sequences are races even on thread-safe collections.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList is terrible for write-heavy workloads (O(n) copy per write).
  • ConcurrentLinkedQueue.size() is O(n) and approximate.
  • In a microservices deployment, in-JVM concurrency doesn't protect against multiple instances. Use DB locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, optimistic @Version), Redis locks (Redisson), or ShedLock for schedulers.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators? Fail-fast throws CME (ArrayList, HashMap). Fail-safe/weakly consistent iterators work on a snapshot or tolerate changes (CopyOnWriteArrayList, CHM).
  • put/take vs offer/poll on a BlockingQueue? put/take block. offer/poll return immediately (false/null) or wait with a timeout.
  • How do you make a thread-safe Set? ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(), CopyOnWriteArraySet (read-mostly), or ConcurrentSkipListSet (sorted).
A33 wait() vs sleep(). G2
wait() sleep()
Class Object Thread (static)
Lock Releases the monitor Keeps any locks it holds
Where Must be inside synchronized, otherwise IllegalMonitorStateException Anywhere
Wakes up notify()/notifyAll(), a timeout, or an interrupt When the time elapses, or on interrupt
Purpose Communication between threads Pausing execution

Always call wait() in a while (condition) loop because of spurious wakeups.

Aspect wait() Thread.sleep()
Defined in java.lang.Object (instance method) java.lang.Thread (static method)
Purpose Inter-thread communication: wait for a condition signalled by another thread Pause the current thread for a duration
Lock (monitor) Releases the monitor of the object it's called on Keeps all locks it holds
Must be in synchronized Yes, on the same object, else IllegalMonitorStateException No
Wakes up when notify()/notifyAll(), a timeout (wait(ms)), interrupt, or spurious wakeup The time elapses or it's interrupted
After waking Must re-acquire the monitor before continuing Continues immediately (and still holds its locks)
Thread state WAITING / TIMED_WAITING TIMED_WAITING
Exception InterruptedException InterruptedException

Correct wait/notify pattern: always loop on the condition

public class SignalBoard {
    private String message;                      // shared state guarded by 'this'

    public synchronized void publish(String msg) {
        message = msg;
        notifyAll();                             // wake waiting threads (prefer notifyAll)
    }

    public synchronized String awaitMessage() throws InterruptedException {
        while (message == null) {                // while, NOT if: guards against spurious wakeups
            wait();                              // releases 'this' monitor while waiting
        }
        String m = message;
        message = null;
        return m;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        SignalBoard board = new SignalBoard();
        Thread reader = new Thread(() -> {
            try { System.out.println("Got: " + board.awaitMessage()); }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        reader.start();
        Thread.sleep(500);                       // sleep keeps no lock here; just pauses main
        board.publish("Signal J12 green");
        reader.join();
    }
}

Gotchas

  • sleep() inside a synchronized block holds the lock the whole time. Other threads are blocked. That's a common performance bug.
  • notify() wakes one arbitrary waiting thread and can cause missed signals or deadlock-like stalls if several conditions share one monitor. Prefer notifyAll(), or Condition objects from ReentrantLock (await/signal).
  • On InterruptedException, restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() rather than swallowing it.
  • In modern code, prefer higher-level tools: BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, CompletableFuture. TimeUnit.SECONDS.sleep(1) is more readable than Thread.sleep(1000).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why is wait() in Object and not Thread? Every object can be a monitor or lock, and a thread waits on a specific object's condition.
  • What is a spurious wakeup? A thread returns from wait() without a notify (allowed by the spec and the OS). That's why you check the condition in a while loop.
  • sleep(0) / yield? Both are scheduler hints. yield() suggests giving up the CPU, but there are no guarantees.
A34 The Callable interface. Co. 2
  • Introduced in Java 5 (java.util.concurrent). It is like Runnable, but call() returns a value and can throw checked exceptions.
  • Submit it to an ExecutorService and get back a Future<V>. Then use get() (blocking), isDone() and cancel().
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
Callable<Integer> task = () -> sensorRepo.countActive();
Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(task);
Integer count = f.get();   // blocks; throws ExecutionException if the task failed
pool.shutdown();

java.util.concurrent.Callable<V> (Java 5) is a task that returns a result and can throw checked exceptions, unlike Runnable.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Callable<V> { V call() throws Exception; }
Runnable Callable<V>
Method void run() V call() throws Exception
Returns value No Yes
Checked exceptions Can't throw Can throw
Usable with Thread, execute(), submit() submit(), invokeAll(), invokeAny() (not new Thread(...) directly; wrap it in a FutureTask)

With ExecutorService + Future

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class CallableDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3);
        Callable<Integer> trafficCount = () -> { Thread.sleep(300); return 1240; };
        Callable<Integer> aqi = () -> 182;

        Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(trafficCount);         // returns immediately
        try {
            Integer v = f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);            // blocks up to 2s
            System.out.println("traffic = " + v);
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {                       // exception thrown inside call()
            System.out.println("task failed: " + e.getCause());
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            f.cancel(true);                                    // interrupt the running task
        }

        List<Future<Integer>> all = pool.invokeAll(List.of(trafficCount, aqi)); // wait for all
        for (Future<Integer> r : all) {
            try { System.out.println(r.get()); } catch (ExecutionException e) { e.printStackTrace(); }
        }
        pool.shutdown();
    }
}

Future API: get(), get(timeout, unit), isDone(), cancel(mayInterrupt), isCancelled(), plus resultNow()/exceptionNow()/state() in Java 19+. Limitations: get() blocks, you can't chain or combine results, you can't complete it manually, and there are no callbacks.

CompletableFuture (Java 8): non-blocking composition

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class CfDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);   // don't block the common pool with I/O

        CompletableFuture<Integer> traffic = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 1240, io);
        CompletableFuture<Integer> aqi     = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 182, io);

        CompletableFuture<String> dashboard = traffic
            .thenCombine(aqi, (t, a) -> "Traffic=" + t + ", AQI=" + a)   // combine two independent tasks
            .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)                              // transform
            .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)                              // Java 9
            .exceptionally(ex -> "DATA UNAVAILABLE: " + ex.getMessage()); // fallback

        System.out.println(dashboard.join());   // join(): unchecked CompletionException instead of checked
        io.shutdown();
    }
}

Key methods: supplyAsync/runAsync, thenApply (map), thenCompose (flatMap, chains dependent async calls), thenCombine, allOf/anyOf, thenAccept, handle/whenComplete, exceptionally, completeOnTimeout. Without an executor argument, the async methods use ForkJoinPool.commonPool().

In Spring: @Async methods returning CompletableFuture<T>, which is useful for fanning out calls to several microservices in parallel.

Likely follow-ups:

  • get() vs join()? get throws the checked ExecutionException/InterruptedException. join throws the unchecked CompletionException.
  • thenApply vs thenCompose? thenApply(T→U) maps the result. thenCompose(T→CompletableFuture<U>) flattens nested futures.
  • How do you run a Callable on a raw Thread? new Thread(new FutureTask<>(callable)).start(). FutureTask is both a Runnable and a Future.
A35 execute() vs submit(). Other rounds (Question List)
execute(Runnable) submit(Runnable/Callable)
Defined in Executor ExecutorService
Returns void Future<?> / Future<T>
Accepts Only Runnable Runnable or Callable
Exceptions Thrown on the worker thread (goes to the UncaughtExceptionHandler) Captured in the Future and only rethrown as ExecutionException on get(), so they are silently lost if you never call get()
Aspect Executor.execute(Runnable) ExecutorService.submit(...)
Declared in Executor ExecutorService
Accepts Runnable only Runnable, Runnable + result, Callable<T>
Returns void Future<?> / Future<T>
Exception in task Propagates out of run(). The worker thread dies, the exception goes to the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler (the default prints the stack trace to stderr), and the pool replaces the worker Captured in the Future (FutureTask catches it). Nothing is printed. It only surfaces as ExecutionException when you call future.get()
Cancellation / result Not possible future.cancel(), future.get()
afterExecute(r, t) hook t = the exception t = null. You must inspect the Future yourself 
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ExecVsSubmit {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();

        pool.execute(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("boom-execute"); });
        // -> stack trace printed: Exception in thread "pool-1-thread-1" java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom-execute

        Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("boom-submit"); });
        // -> SILENT. Nothing printed.

        try { f.get(); }
        catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("caught: " + e.getCause()); } // caught: java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom-submit

        pool.shutdown();
    }
}

The production gotcha: "fire-and-forget" submit() calls whose Future is never checked silently swallow exceptions. Background jobs then fail with zero logs. Fixes:

  • Use execute() for fire-and-forget tasks, with a configured UncaughtExceptionHandler via a custom ThreadFactory.
  • Wrap the task body in try/catch and log inside it.
  • Override ThreadPoolExecutor.afterExecute and unwrap the Future.
  • Use CompletableFuture.runAsync(...).exceptionally(...) / whenComplete(...).
  • In Spring, configure an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler for @Async void methods.

ScheduledExecutorService.scheduleAtFixedRate: if one run throws, all future runs are silently suppressed. Always catch exceptions inside scheduled tasks.

Likely follow-ups:

  • What does submit(Runnable) return from get()? null on success, or the given result for submit(runnable, result).
  • shutdown() vs shutdownNow()? shutdown stops accepting tasks and lets queued ones finish. shutdownNow interrupts running tasks and returns the queued ones.
  • Why not Executors.newFixedThreadPool in production? Its unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue risks OOM. Build a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and a rejection policy.
A36 How do you create a thread? Extending Thread vs implementing Runnable. Other rounds (Question List)
  • Ways to create one: extend Thread, implement Runnable or Callable, use an ExecutorService (preferred in real code), use CompletableFuture, or in Java 21 use virtual threads (Thread.ofVirtual()).
Extend Thread Implement Runnable
Uses up your only superclass Class can still extend something else
Task and thread are tightly coupled Task is separate from the execution mechanism, so it can be reused with executors
Each object is its own thread One Runnable can be shared by many threads 
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("Running in " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
new Thread(task).start();          // start(), not run(); run() executes on the current thread

Ways to create and run concurrent work

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ThreadWays {
    // 1. Extend Thread
    static class Worker extends Thread {
        @Override public void run() { System.out.println("1. " + getName()); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        new Worker().start();

        // 2. Implement Runnable (or lambda) and pass it to Thread
        Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("2. " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
        new Thread(task, "sensor-poller").start();

        // 3. Callable + FutureTask (result-bearing)
        FutureTask<Integer> ft = new FutureTask<>(() -> 42);
        new Thread(ft).start();
        System.out.println("3. " + ft.get());

        // 4. ExecutorService (preferred in real apps: pooling, lifecycle, futures)
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
        pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("4. pooled"));
        pool.shutdown();

        // 5. CompletableFuture
        CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("5. async")).join();
    }
}

Extending Thread vs implementing Runnable

extends Thread implements Runnable
Inheritance Uses up your only superclass Class can still extend another
Design Mixes the task with the execution mechanism Separates the task (what) from the thread (how). Follows SRP
Reuse One Thread object = one run The same Runnable can be shared by many threads or submitted to executors
Executor compatibility Awkward Works directly with ExecutorService, CompletableFuture
Lambdas No Yes (Runnable is functional)
When to use Rarely. Only when customising Thread behaviour itself Almost always

start() vs run(): start() creates a new OS/JVM thread, which then calls run(). Calling run() directly executes it on the current thread, like a normal method. Calling start() twice → IllegalThreadStateException.

Virtual threads (Java 21, JEP 444)

Lightweight threads managed by the JVM and mounted on a small pool of carrier (platform) threads. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, it unmounts, so millions of concurrent blocking tasks become cheap. The thread-per-request style scales again without reactive code.

// Java 21+
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

public class VirtualThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-1").start(() -> System.out.println("hello from " + Thread.currentThread()));
        Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> System.out.println("another"));

        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {   // AutoCloseable since 19
            IntStream.range(0, 10_000).forEach(i -> ex.submit(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(100);              // blocking is fine: VT unmounts
                return i;
            }));
        }   // close() waits for all tasks
    }
}
  • Spring Boot 3.2+: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true.
  • Don't pool virtual threads. Create one per task.
  • Use a Semaphore to limit access to scarce resources (such as DB connections).
  • Pinning: in Java 21, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier thread. Prefer ReentrantLock there. JEP 491 (Java 24) removed most synchronized pinning.
  • Virtual threads help I/O-bound work, not CPU-bound work.
  • Be careful with ThreadLocal-heavy code (memory per thread). Scoped values are the future replacement.

Thread lifecycle: NEW → RUNNABLE → (BLOCKED | WAITING | TIMED_WAITING) → TERMINATED.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Daemon vs user thread? The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain (setDaemon(true) before start()). GC threads are daemons.
  • How do you stop a thread? Cooperatively: interrupt() plus checking isInterrupted(), or a volatile flag. Thread.stop() is deprecated, unsafe, and throws UnsupportedOperationException since Java 20.
  • Platform vs virtual threads? A platform thread is a 1:1 OS thread (~1 MB stack, thousands max). A virtual thread is M:N, a few hundred bytes to KBs, and you can have millions.
A37 How did you connect Java with Python?
  • Main answer (REST): "The Python ML model (e.g. traffic or crowd prediction) ran as a Flask/FastAPI microservice. Our Spring Boot service called it over REST using WebClient/RestTemplate (or Feign), with JSON request and response, timeouts, and retry/circuit breaker (Resilience4j). The two sides were decoupled and deployed as separate Docker containers."
  • Other options:
    • Kafka / message queue: Java publishes events and the Python consumer processes them and publishes results. Good for asynchronous, high-volume streams such as sensor data.
    • ProcessBuilder: run a Python script from Java and read its stdout. Fine for batch jobs, but fragile and not scalable.
    • gRPC: a typed, fast RPC contract between the two services.
    • Jython / GraalPy: run Python inside the JVM. Jython only supports Python 2.7, so it is rarely used.
PredictionResponse res = webClient.post().uri("http://ml-service:8000/predict")
        .bodyValue(request).retrieve().bodyToMono(PredictionResponse.class).block();

(A sample answer for a Smart City platform. Adapt it to your real experience.)

Main answer: Python as a separate microservice over REST (FastAPI)

"In our Smart City platform, the core services (incident management, traffic, dashboards) are Spring Boot. The data science team built Python models, for example traffic-congestion prediction and ANPR/video-analytics post-processing, using pandas, scikit-learn and PyTorch. Rather than embedding Python into the JVM, we deployed the models as a FastAPI microservice in its own Docker container, and the Java services call it over HTTP/JSON."

# predict_service.py (Python side)
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class TrafficInput(BaseModel):
    junction_id: str
    hour: int
    vehicle_count: int

@app.post("/predict/congestion")
def predict(inp: TrafficInput):
    score = min(1.0, inp.vehicle_count / 2000)   # model.predict(...) in reality
    return {"junction_id": inp.junction_id, "congestion_score": score}
# run: uvicorn predict_service:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
// Java side (Spring Boot 3.2+, RestClient)
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

record TrafficInput(String junction_id, int hour, int vehicle_count) {}
record Prediction(String junction_id, double congestion_score) {}

@Service
class CongestionClient {
    private final RestClient client;
    CongestionClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
        this.client = builder.baseUrl("http://ml-service:8000").build();  // K8s/compose service name
    }
    // annotate with Resilience4j @CircuitBreaker(name = "ml", fallbackMethod = "fallback") + @Retry
    Prediction predict(TrafficInput in) {
        return client.post().uri("/predict/congestion").body(in).retrieve().body(Prediction.class);
    }
    Prediction fallback(TrafficInput in, Throwable t) { return new Prediction(in.junction_id(), -1); }
}

What I'd emphasise:

  • Timeouts: connect and read timeouts on the HTTP client.
  • Resilience4j: circuit breaker, retry with backoff, bulkhead.
  • Contract: an OpenAPI spec (FastAPI generates /docs automatically).
  • Auth: a JWT/service token via the API gateway.
  • Observability: correlation IDs, Micrometer/Prometheus metrics on latency.
  • Scaling: the Python service scales independently (GPU nodes), with its own release cycle.

Alternatives and trade-offs

Approach How Pros Cons Use when
REST (FastAPI/Flask) HTTP + JSON Simple, language-agnostic, independent scaling and deployment, easy to debug Network latency (ms), JSON overhead Default for synchronous request/response
Kafka / RabbitMQ Java publishes an event (camera-frames, sensor-readings). Python consumes and publishes results to another topic Async, decoupled, buffers bursts, replayable Eventual consistency, more infrastructure Streaming sensor/video analytics, long-running jobs
gRPC Protobuf contract, HTTP/2 Fast binary protocol, strong typing, streaming, code generation for both languages Harder to debug, needs proto tooling High-throughput internal calls
ProcessBuilder Spawn python script.py, pass args/stdin, read stdout No extra service, quick Process startup per call (slow), fragile parsing, error handling, security (command injection), hard to scale Batch scripts, one-off report generation
GraalPy (GraalVM Polyglot) Run Python inside the JVM via Context.create("python") In-process, no network Limited native-extension support (NumPy etc. improving), GraalVM dependency Lightweight embedded scripting
Jython Python on the JVM — Python 2.7 only, effectively dead Avoid
Py4J / JEP Bridge to CPython Access to native libs Complex, coupled lifecycle Niche
Shared DB / files One writes, the other reads Simple Tight coupling via schema, polling Batch ETL

ProcessBuilder example (if asked)

import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

public class PythonRunner {
    public static String run(String junction) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("python3", "predict.py", junction); // args list: no shell injection
        pb.redirectErrorStream(true);
        Process p = pb.start();
        String out;
        try (var r = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(p.getInputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
            out = r.lines().reduce("", (a, b) -> a + b);
        }
        if (!p.waitFor(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { p.destroyForcibly(); throw new IllegalStateException("timeout"); }
        if (p.exitValue() != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("python failed: " + out);
        return out;   // e.g. JSON parsed with Jackson
    }
}

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you handle the Python service being slow or down? Timeouts, a circuit breaker with fallback (cached/last-known value), retries with exponential backoff, and async via Kafka for non-critical paths.
  • Why not ProcessBuilder in production? Per-call process overhead, no pooling, stdout parsing fragility, and difficulty scaling and monitoring.
  • How do you keep the contract in sync? Use the OpenAPI spec from FastAPI to generate Java client DTOs (openapi-generator), or protobuf for gRPC.
  • Sync vs async integration? Sync REST when the user waits for the answer. Kafka when the result can arrive later (e.g. analytics on camera feeds).
A38 What is the SOLID principle? Co. 2
  • S, Single Responsibility: a class should have one reason to change. For example, ReportService shouldn't also send emails.
  • O, Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification. Add a new AlertChannel implementation instead of editing a big if/else.
  • L, Liskov Substitution: subtypes must work wherever their base type is used, without breaking behaviour.
  • I, Interface Segregation: prefer many small, focused interfaces over one large interface.
  • D, Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete classes. Spring dependency injection with interface-typed constructor parameters is a direct example.

S – Single Responsibility Principle: a class should have one reason to change.

// BAD: one class validates, persists, and emails
// GOOD: split responsibilities
record Complaint(String id, String text, String email) {}
class ComplaintValidator  { void validate(Complaint c) { if (c.text().isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); } }
class ComplaintRepository { void save(Complaint c) { /* JDBC/JPA */ } }
class ComplaintNotifier   { void acknowledge(Complaint c) { /* send email */ } }
class ComplaintService {
    private final ComplaintValidator v = new ComplaintValidator();
    private final ComplaintRepository r = new ComplaintRepository();
    private final ComplaintNotifier n = new ComplaintNotifier();
    void register(Complaint c) { v.validate(c); r.save(c); n.acknowledge(c); } // orchestrates only
}

O – Open/Closed Principle: open for extension, closed for modification.

// BAD: if (type.equals("BUS")) ... else if ("METRO") ... edited for every new type
interface FarePolicy { double fare(double km); }
class BusFare   implements FarePolicy { public double fare(double km) { return 10 + km * 1.5; } }
class MetroFare implements FarePolicy { public double fare(double km) { return 20 + km * 2.0; } }
// New mode (e.g. e-bike)? Add a class; FareCalculator is untouched.
class FareCalculator { double calc(FarePolicy p, double km) { return p.fare(km); } }

L – Liskov Substitution Principle: subtypes must be usable anywhere the base type is, without breaking expectations.

// BAD: class Square extends Rectangle - setWidth also changes height, breaking Rectangle's contract.
// BAD: class ReadOnlyList extends ArrayList { add() throws UnsupportedOperationException }
// GOOD: model capabilities separately
interface Shape { double area(); }
record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape { public double area() { return w * h; } }
record Sq(double side)          implements Shape { public double area() { return side * side; } }

Signs of a violation: overrides that throw UnsupportedOperationException, strengthen preconditions, or weaken postconditions, and instanceof checks in client code.

I – Interface Segregation Principle: clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. Prefer small, focused interfaces.

// BAD: interface Device { void readData(); void rotateCamera(); void changeSignal(); }
interface Readable  { String readData(); }
interface Rotatable { void rotate(int degrees); }
class AirSensor implements Readable { public String readData() { return "AQI=182"; } }
class PtzCamera implements Readable, Rotatable {
    public String readData() { return "frame"; }
    public void rotate(int d) { System.out.println("rotate " + d); }
}

D – Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete classes. Both depend on interfaces. (Spring DI is the classic enabler.)

interface MessageSender { void send(String to, String body); }
class SmsSender   implements MessageSender { public void send(String to, String b) { /* SMS gateway */ } }
class EmailSender implements MessageSender { public void send(String to, String b) { /* SMTP */ } }

class AlertService {                            // high-level policy
    private final MessageSender sender;         // depends on abstraction
    AlertService(MessageSender sender) { this.sender = sender; } // injected (Spring @Service + constructor)
    void alert(String citizen) { sender.send(citizen, "Waterlogging reported near you"); }
}
// new AlertService(new SmsSender()); tests: new AlertService(mockSender)
Principle One-liner Smell when violated
SRP One reason to change God classes, 2000-line services
OCP Extend, don't edit Growing if/else/switch on types
LSP Subtypes are substitutable UnsupportedOperationException, instanceof checks
ISP Small, specific interfaces Empty or no-op method implementations
DIP Depend on abstractions new ConcreteDao() inside business logic; untestable code

Likely follow-ups:

  • DIP vs DI? DIP is the design principle (depend on abstractions). DI is a technique (supply dependencies from outside). IoC containers like Spring automate DI.
  • Which design patterns support OCP? Strategy, Template Method, Decorator, Observer.
  • Can you over-apply SOLID? Yes. Too many tiny interfaces and indirection (YAGNI) hurt readability. Apply it where change is likely.
A39 Monolithic vs microservice architecture. Other rounds (Question List)
  • Monolith: the whole application (UI, business logic, data access) is built and deployed as one unit with one shared database.
  • Microservices: the application is split into small, independently deployable services, each built around a business capability with its own database. They communicate over REST, gRPC or messaging, typically behind an API gateway with service discovery.
Monolith Microservices
Deployment Everything redeployed together Each service deployed independently
Scaling Scale the whole app Scale only the busy service
Tech stack One stack Can differ per service
Failure One bug can bring everything down Faults isolated (circuit breakers)
Data One shared database Database per service, eventual consistency
Complexity Simple to start, test and debug Distributed-system overhead: network, tracing, transactions (Saga)
Best for Small teams, MVPs Large, evolving systems (e.g. Smart City modules)

Monolith: the whole application (UI, business logic, data access for every module) is built, deployed and scaled as one unit, usually backed by one shared database. Example: a single Spring Boot WAR/JAR with incident, traffic, billing and user packages.

Microservices: the application is a set of small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability (bounded context, DDD) and its own data store. They communicate over the network (REST/gRPC synchronously, Kafka/RabbitMQ asynchronously). Example: incident-service, traffic-service, notification-service, identity-service, behind an API Gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway), with service discovery (Eureka/K8s DNS), a config server, and centralized logging and tracing.

Aspect Monolith Microservices
Deployment One artifact. Any change redeploys everything Each service deployed independently
Scaling Scale the whole app (vertical, or clone everything) Scale hot services only (e.g. traffic ingestion ×10)
Database Usually one shared DB, ACID transactions are easy DB per service. Distributed transactions → Saga, outbox pattern, eventual consistency
Technology One stack Polyglot possible (Java + Python ML service)
Fault isolation One memory leak can take down the whole app Failures contained (with circuit breakers, bulkheads)
Development speed Fast at first, slows as the codebase grows Slower start, scales across many teams (Conway's law)
Testing Simple end-to-end Contract tests, integration environments, harder E2E
Communication In-process method calls (ns) Network calls (ms), with latency, partial failure, retries
Operations Simple: one app, one log Complex: K8s, CI/CD per service, distributed tracing (Zipkin/OTel), centralized logs (ELK), monitoring
Consistency Strong Eventual (mostly)
Debugging Stack traces in one process Correlation IDs across services
Team ownership Shared codebase, merge conflicts Team per service, clear ownership

When to choose which

Choose a monolith (often a modular monolith) when:

  • The team is small (fewer than ~10 developers), the domain is new or unclear, or you're building an MVP or startup product.
  • Strong transactional consistency matters, or the ops/DevOps maturity is low.
  • You don't have heavy differential-scaling needs.

Choose microservices when:

  • Several teams need to deploy independently and the domain boundaries are well understood.
  • Modules have very different scaling or availability requirements. In a Smart City platform, for example: IoT sensor ingestion vs reporting vs citizen portal.
  • You need polyglot tech, and you have mature CI/CD, containers/Kubernetes and observability.

Migration path: Strangler Fig pattern. Put a gateway in front of the monolith and carve out one bounded context at a time (e.g. extract notification-service first, because it's loosely coupled).

Anti-pattern to mention: the distributed monolith. These are services that share a database or must be deployed together. You get all the costs of microservices with none of the benefits.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you handle transactions across services? The Saga pattern (choreography via events, or orchestration), with compensating actions plus a transactional outbox for reliable publishing.
  • How do services find each other? Service discovery: Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes Services/DNS, with client- or server-side load balancing.
  • How do you prevent cascading failures? Timeouts, circuit breakers (Resilience4j), bulkheads, retries with backoff, and fallbacks.
  • What is a modular monolith? One deployable unit with strictly separated internal modules (e.g. Spring Modulith). It's the easiest to split later.
A40 Which declarations are correct and why? Co. 2 
interface I { }  class A implements I { }  class B extends A { }  class C extends B { }
Statement Result Reason
A a = new I(); Compile error An interface can't be instantiated
I b = new B(); OK B IS-A A IS-A I (upcast)
C c = new B(); Compile error A parent object can't be assigned to a child reference without a cast. (C) new B() would compile but throw ClassCastException at runtime
C c2 = new A(); Compile error Same reason: A is not a C
B b = new C(); Valid type-wise (C IS-A B, upcast), but b was already declared as I b in the same scope, so this is a duplicate variable compile error. Renamed (e.g. B b2 = new C();) it is fine

Rule: a reference of a parent type can hold a child object (upcast). The reverse needs an explicit downcast, which is only safe if the actual object really is that type.

interface I { }
class A implements I { }
class B extends A { }
class C extends B { }

Hierarchy: I ← A ← B ← C. So C is-a B, is-an A, is-an I. The reverse is not true.

A a  = new I();   // (1)
I b  = new B();   // (2)
C c  = new B();   // (3)
C c2 = new A();   // (4)
B b  = new C();   // (5)
# Statement Verdict Reason
1 A a = new I(); Compile error "I is abstract; cannot be instantiated". Interfaces can't be instantiated. (Even new I(){} as an anonymous class would give type I, which can't be assigned to A without a cast. That cast would compile but throw ClassCastException, since the anonymous class isn't an A.)
2 I b = new B(); Valid Upcasting: B extends A, which implements I, so B is-an I. Implicit widening reference conversion. Only I's members are accessible via b.
3 C c = new B(); Compile error "incompatible types: B cannot be converted to C". That's downcasting without a cast: not every B is a C. With an explicit cast, C c = (C) new B(); compiles (B and C are related) but throws ClassCastException at runtime, because the actual object is a B, not a C.
4 C c2 = new A(); Compile error "incompatible types: A cannot be converted to C". Same reason: an A is not a C. (C) new A() → compiles, then ClassCastException.
5 B b = new C(); Type-wise valid (upcast C → B), but a compile error here "variable b is already defined in method main(String[])". Statement (2) already declared b (as I) in the same scope. Java doesn't allow redeclaring a local in the same scope, even with a different type. Renamed, e.g. B b3 = new C();, it's perfectly fine. 
public class CastDemo {
    interface I { }
    static class A implements I { }
    static class B extends A { }
    static class C extends B { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        I b  = new B();                 // OK
        B b3 = new C();                 // OK - upcast
        I anon = new I() { };           // OK - anonymous class implementing I (not "new I()")
        try {
            C c = (C) new B();          // compiles, fails at runtime
        } catch (ClassCastException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage()); // class CastDemo$B cannot be cast to class CastDemo$C ...
        }
        if (b instanceof C c) { /* safe downcast via pattern matching (16+) */ } else {
            System.out.println("b is not a C");
        }
    }
}

Rules to state in the interview

  • Upcasting (subtype → supertype) is implicit and always safe.
  • Downcasting (supertype → subtype) needs an explicit cast. It compiles only when the types are related (could possibly succeed), and it's checked at runtime (checkcast bytecode) → ClassCastException if wrong.
  • Casting between unrelated classes (e.g. (String) new A()) is a compile error ("incompatible types"). Casting to an interface from a non-final class compiles, because a subclass might implement it.
  • Use instanceof (with pattern matching) before downcasting.

Likely follow-ups:

  • What can you call on I b = new B()? Only members declared in I (and Object), even though the object is a B. Overridden methods still dispatch to B's implementation.
  • Why does (C) new B() compile at all? B and C are in the same hierarchy, so a B reference could point to a C. The compiler defers the check to runtime.
  • Would I i = (I) new String("x") compile? No. String is final and doesn't implement I, so the compiler knows the cast can never succeed.
A41 Which array declarations are valid and why? Co. 2
Declaration Result Reason
int[] n1 = new int[0]; Valid A zero-length array is legal (length 0). Useful for returning "empty" instead of null
boolean[] n2 = new boolean[-200]; Compiles, but throws NegativeArraySizeException at runtime The size is only checked at runtime
double[] n3 = new double[2241423798]; Compile error: "integer number too large" The literal exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE (2147483647). Adding L still fails, because the array size must be an int (lossy conversion from long)
char[] ch = new char[20]; Valid 20 elements, each defaulting to '\u0000' 
int[]     n1 = new int[0];
boolean[] n2 = new boolean[-200];
double[]  n3 = new double[2241423798];
char[]    ch = new char[20];
Declaration Compiles? Runtime Explanation
new int[0] Yes OK A zero-length array is legal: n1.length == 0. Useful as an empty return value instead of null (Effective Java), and as toArray(new String[0]). Accessing n1[0] → ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
new boolean[-200] Yes NegativeArraySizeException The size expression only has to be of type int. The compiler does not check the sign, even for constants. The JVM checks at runtime in the newarray instruction.
new double[2241423798] No — Compile error: "integer number too large: 2241423798". The literal exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647) and has no L suffix, so it isn't even a valid int literal. With 2241423798L you'd get "incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from long to int", because array sizes must be int (after unary promotion from byte/short/char; long is not allowed).
new char[20] Yes OK 20 chars, each defaulting to '\u0000' (the NUL character, numeric 0), not a space. Printing shows invisible characters.

Default values of array elements

Type Default
byte, short, int, long 0 / 0L
float, double 0.0f / 0.0
char '\u0000'
boolean false
Any reference (String, Integer, objects) null

Maximum array size

  • Theoretically Integer.MAX_VALUE elements, because the index is an int.
  • In practice, HotSpot reserves some header words, so the safe maximum is about Integer.MAX_VALUE - 8 (the JDK's ArrayList/ArraysSupport.SOFT_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH uses that limit).
