  • Managed: in the persistence context; changes are auto-flushed.
  • Detached: has an id but the persistence context is closed, so changes are not tracked. A typical example is an entity returned from a service after the transaction ended.
  • Removed: scheduled for deletion.

persist() makes the same instance managed. merge() copies state onto a managed instance and returns that instance; the argument stays detached. Spring Data's save() calls persist if entityInformation.isNew(entity) (the id is null, or @Version is null, or Persistable.isNew()), and merge otherwise.

Gotcha: if you assign ids manually (e.g. a UUID set in the constructor), save() thinks the entity isn't new. It calls merge, which costs an extra SELECT. Implement Persistable<ID> or use @Version to fix that.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is EntityManager thread-safe? The real one isn't. Spring's injected shared proxy is, because it binds a real one per transaction/thread.
  • What is the 2nd-level cache? A Hibernate SessionFactory-level cache shared across sessions (Ehcache/JCache/Infinispan). It is opt-in, using @Cacheable plus @org.hibernate.annotations.Cache.
  • Do you need repo.save() after modifying a managed entity? No. Dirty checking flushes it at commit.
C12 @GeneratedValue (strategies). Co. 2
Strategy How Notes
IDENTITY DB auto-increment column (MySQL) Simple, but disables JDBC batch inserts because the ID is known only after the insert
SEQUENCE DB sequence (PostgreSQL, Oracle) Best performance. allocationSize pre-allocates IDs, and batching works
TABLE A separate table simulates a sequence Portable but slow (row locks). Avoid
AUTO (default) Provider picks one (Hibernate 6 usually picks SEQUENCE) Not explicit
UUID (JPA 3.1) Generates a UUID Good for distributed systems 
@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "emp_seq")
@SequenceGenerator(name = "emp_seq", sequenceName = "emp_seq", allocationSize = 50)
private Long id;
Strategy How the id is produced Batch inserts DBs
IDENTITY DB auto-increment column; the id is known only after the INSERT Disabled. Hibernate must run each INSERT immediately to learn the id, so hibernate.jdbc.batch_size is ignored for inserts MySQL, SQL Server, Postgres (serial/identity)
SEQUENCE DB sequence; allocationSize (default 50) with the pooled optimizer gives 50 ids per DB round trip Works Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server 2012+, H2
TABLE A separate table emulates a sequence, using row locks Works, but slow and contended Any (portable)
AUTO (default) The provider chooses. Hibernate 6: SequenceStyleGenerator with a sequence per entity (<entity>_SEQ, allocation 50). On DBs without sequences (older MySQL), it falls back to a table Depends —
UUID (JPA 3.1 / Hibernate 6.2+) A UUID generated in Java Works (no DB round trip) Any 
@Entity
@Table(name = "challan")
public class Challan {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "challan_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "challan_seq", sequenceName = "challan_seq", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long id;
    // DB: CREATE SEQUENCE challan_seq START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 50;   <- INCREMENT must match allocationSize
}

@Entity
public class Device {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)   // or @UuidGenerator(style = UuidGenerator.Style.TIME)
    private UUID id;
}

@Entity
public class Ward {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)   // MySQL: AUTO_INCREMENT
    private Long id;
}

Batching config:

spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc.batch_size: 50
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true

(On MySQL, also add rewriteBatchedStatements=true to the JDBC URL.)

Gotchas

  • If the sequence's INCREMENT BY doesn't match allocationSize, you get duplicate-key errors, or Hibernate 6 fails schema validation. Keep them aligned (Flyway: INCREMENT BY 50).
  • Gaps in ids are normal: allocated blocks are lost on restart. Never use ids as business-visible sequential numbers such as challan numbers. Use a separate generator for those.
  • Random UUIDv4 primary keys cause B-tree index fragmentation (random inserts). Prefer time-ordered UUIDv7 or Style.TIME, or a Long PK with a UUID public id.
  • On MySQL, prefer IDENTITY over the TABLE strategy, and accept that inserts aren't batched (or use a UUID).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why does IDENTITY kill batching? The id is needed to put the entity in the persistence context, and it is only known after each INSERT executes.
  • What does allocationSize = 50 mean? One sequence call reserves 50 ids, which Hibernate hands out in memory.
  • Which would you pick for Postgres? SEQUENCE with a pooled allocation size.
C13 @RequestParam, @RequestBody, @PathVariable; handling request parameters. Co. 2G2
Annotation Source Example URL / body Typical use
@PathVariable URI path segment /employees/42 Identify a resource
@RequestParam Query string or form field /employees?dept=IT&page=0 Filtering, paging, optional values
@RequestBody HTTP body (JSON via Jackson) {"name":"Asha"} Create or update payloads 
@GetMapping("/employees/{id}")
public EmployeeDto get(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

@GetMapping("/employees")
public List<EmployeeDto> search(@RequestParam(required = false) String dept,
                                @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                                @RequestParam Map<String, String> allParams) { ... }

@PostMapping("/employees")
public ResponseEntity<EmployeeDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody EmployeeRequest req) { ... }

@GetMapping("/employees/filter")
public List<EmployeeDto> filter(@ModelAttribute EmployeeFilter filter) { ... } // binds ?dept=&city= to a POJO

Other details:

  • @RequestParam is required=true by default, and a missing value returns 400. Use defaultValue or Optional<T> for optional values.
  • @Valid plus Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @Email) throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which returns 400.
  • Also available: @RequestHeader and @CookieValue.
Annotation Source Example
@PathVariable URI template segment /api/v1/junctions/{id}
@RequestParam Query string or form field (application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart) ?status=OPEN&page=0
@RequestBody Request body, deserialised by an HttpMessageConverter (JSON through Jackson) POST/PUT/PATCH payloads
@RequestHeader HTTP header X-Tenant-Id
@CookieValue Cookie SESSION
@ModelAttribute Query and form params bound onto an object (setters or constructor) search filters
@RequestPart A multipart part (file + JSON) uploads
@MatrixVariable ;key=value path parameters (disabled by default) rare 
package com.trinity.citypulse.incident;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Max;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.util.MultiValueMap;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.web.multipart.MultipartFile;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/incidents")
public class IncidentController {

    private final IncidentService service;
    public IncidentController(IncidentService service) { this.service = service; }

    // /api/v1/incidents/42
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public IncidentDto get(@PathVariable Long id) { return service.get(id); }

    // /api/v1/incidents?status=OPEN&page=1&size=20&ward=W12
    @GetMapping
    public List<IncidentDto> search(
            @RequestParam(required = false) IncidentStatus status,              // enum converted; null if missing
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") @Min(0) int page,                 // defaultValue implies required=false
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") @Min(1) @Max(100) int size,
            @RequestParam Optional<String> ward,                                // Optional = not required
            @RequestParam(name = "tag", required = false) List<String> tags,    // ?tag=a&tag=b
            @RequestHeader(name = "X-Tenant-Id") String tenantId) {
        return service.search(tenantId, status, ward.orElse(null), tags, page, size);
    }

    // all query params at once
    @GetMapping("/raw")
    public Map<String, String> raw(@RequestParam Map<String, String> all,
                                   @RequestParam MultiValueMap<String, String> multi) { return all; }

    // bind query params onto an object (no annotation needed for non-simple types: @ModelAttribute implied)
    @GetMapping("/filter")
    public List<IncidentDto> filter(@Valid @ModelAttribute IncidentFilter filter) { return service.filter(filter); }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<IncidentDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateIncidentRequest req) {
        IncidentDto created = service.create(req);
        return ResponseEntity.created(java.net.URI.create("/api/v1/incidents/" + created.id())).body(created);
    }

    @PostMapping(path = "/{id}/evidence", consumes = "multipart/form-data")
    public void upload(@PathVariable Long id,
                       @RequestPart("file") MultipartFile file,
                       @RequestPart("meta") @Valid EvidenceMeta meta) { service.attach(id, file, meta); }
}

record IncidentFilter(IncidentStatus status, String ward, @Min(0) Integer minSeverity) { }

record CreateIncidentRequest(
        @jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank String title,
        @jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull IncidentStatus status,
        @jakarta.validation.constraints.Size(max = 500) String description) { }

Internals: RequestMappingHandlerAdapter holds a list of HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers: RequestParamMethodArgumentResolver, PathVariableMethodArgumentResolver, RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor (for @RequestBody, using HttpMessageConverters chosen by Content-Type), ServletModelAttributeMethodProcessor, and others. Simple types are converted by the ConversionService (String → Long, enum, LocalDate with @DateTimeFormat).

Errors you'll see (all 400 unless noted)

Situation Exception
Required @RequestParam missing MissingServletRequestParameterException
?page=abc MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException
Missing header MissingRequestHeaderException
Malformed JSON body HttpMessageNotReadableException
@Valid @RequestBody fails MethodArgumentNotValidException
Constraints directly on parameters (@Min on @RequestParam) Spring 6.1+ built-in method validation → HandlerMethodValidationException (previously ConstraintViolationException with @Validated on the class)
Wrong Content-Type HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException → 415

Gotchas

  • Since Spring 6.1, parameter names come only from -parameters compilation (the LocalVariableTableParameterNameDiscoverer was removed). Without the flag, @RequestParam with no name fails. Boot's parent POM sets the flag; otherwise use @RequestParam("status") explicitly.
  • @RequestBody can be read only once (it's a stream). Filters that log bodies must use ContentCachingRequestWrapper.
  • Don't use @RequestBody on GET. Use query params or @ModelAttribute.
  • Never bind request bodies straight to JPA entities (mass-assignment risk). Use DTOs or records.

Likely follow-ups:

  • @RequestParam vs @PathVariable? A path variable identifies a resource (/vehicles/{id}). Query params filter, sort or page.
  • How do you make a path variable optional? Map two paths ({"/x", "/x/{id}"}) with @PathVariable(required = false) or Optional.
  • How do you validate a @RequestParam? Put constraint annotations on it. Spring 6.1+ validates them automatically (or add @Validated on the class for older versions).
C14 What are REST controllers used for? (@RestController vs @Controller) TCS

REST controllers expose HTTP endpoints that return data (JSON/XML) to clients such as an Angular/React UI, mobile apps or other microservices.

@Controller @RestController
Return value is a view name (Thymeleaf/JSP) Return value is serialised to the response body
Needs @ResponseBody per method to return data = @Controller + @ResponseBody on every method
Server-side MVC pages REST APIs

@Controller vs @RestController

  • @Controller: return values are view names resolved by a ViewResolver (Thymeleaf/JSP). Add @ResponseBody per method to write the return value to the body.
  • @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody on every method. The return value goes through HttpMessageConverters (Jackson for JSON).
@RestController
@RequestMapping(path = "/api/v1/vehicles", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
public class VehicleController {

    private final VehicleService service;
    public VehicleController(VehicleService service) { this.service = service; }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<VehicleDto> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
                .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
                .eTag("\"" + service.version(id) + "\"")
                .body(service.get(id));
    }

    @PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    public ResponseEntity<VehicleDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateVehicleRequest req,
                                             UriComponentsBuilder uriBuilder) {
        VehicleDto dto = service.create(req);
        URI location = uriBuilder.path("/api/v1/vehicles/{id}").buildAndExpand(dto.id()).toUri();
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(dto);         // 201 + Location
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)                          // alternative to ResponseEntity
    public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) { service.delete(id); }
}

ResponseEntity<T> gives full control over the status, headers and body: ok(), created(uri), accepted(), noContent(), notFound(), badRequest(), status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT). Returning a plain DTO gives 200 (or the @ResponseStatus value).

Content negotiation

The ContentNegotiationManager determines the requested media types:

  1. the Accept header (default strategy);
  2. optionally a query parameter (?format=xml) via spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.favor-parameter=true;
  3. path extensions (.json). This is disabled by default since Spring 5.3 and removed from suffix pattern matching in 6.

Then AbstractMessageConverterMethodProcessor intersects the requested types with the produces types and the types the registered converters can write, and picks the best match. If nothing matches, the client gets 406 Not Acceptable (HttpMediaTypeNotAcceptableException). On the request side, consumes mismatches give 415.

To support XML, add jackson-dataformat-xml. Boot then auto-registers MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter, and Accept: application/xml works.

@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", produces = { MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE })
public VehicleDto getNegotiated(@PathVariable Long id) { return service.get(id); }

REST design checklist: plural nouns (/vehicles), HTTP verbs for actions, proper status codes, versioning (/api/v1 or a header; Spring 7 adds first-class API versioning), pagination (Pageable with page/size/sort), idempotency keys for POST, HATEOAS only if needed, OpenAPI docs via springdoc.

Likely follow-ups:

  • What happens if a @RestController method returns null? An empty body with 200. Prefer 404 or 204 explicitly.
  • How does Jackson get configured? JacksonAutoConfiguration provides an ObjectMapper (customise it with spring.jackson.* or a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer).
  • ResponseEntity vs @ResponseStatus? ResponseEntity is dynamic per request (headers, status). @ResponseStatus is static.
C15 Skeleton for getEmployeeById. TCS 
@Entity
public class Employee {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;
    private String name;
    // getters/setters
}

public interface EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository<Employee, Long> { }

public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public ResourceNotFoundException(String msg) { super(msg); }
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class EmployeeService {
    private final EmployeeRepository repo;
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public Employee getById(Long id) {
        return repo.findById(id)
                   .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Employee " + id + " not found"));
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/employees")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class EmployeeController {
    private final EmployeeService service;
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Employee> getEmployeeById(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(service.getById(id));
    }
}

A @RestControllerAdvice (see C20) maps ResourceNotFoundException to 404. An alternative without exceptions is return repo.findById(id).map(ResponseEntity::ok).orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());. In real code, return a DTO rather than the entity.

The layers: Controller (HTTP) → Service (business + transactions) → Repository (data) → Entity. A DTO crosses the HTTP boundary, and a global handler maps exceptions to responses.

Entity

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;

@Entity
@Table(name = "employee", uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(name = "uk_employee_email", columnNames = "email"))
public class Employee {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "employee_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "employee_seq", sequenceName = "employee_seq", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 150)
    private String email;

    @Column(length = 50)
    private String department;

    @Column(precision = 12, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal salary;

    private LocalDate joiningDate;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    protected Employee() { }                 // JPA needs a no-arg constructor

    public Employee(String name, String email, String department, BigDecimal salary, LocalDate joiningDate) {
        this.name = name; this.email = email; this.department = department;
        this.salary = salary; this.joiningDate = joiningDate;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public String getEmail() { return email; }
    public String getDepartment() { return department; }
    public BigDecimal getSalary() { return salary; }
    public LocalDate getJoiningDate() { return joiningDate; }
    public Long getVersion() { return version; }
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public void setEmail(String email) { this.email = email; }
    public void setDepartment(String department) { this.department = department; }
    public void setSalary(BigDecimal salary) { this.salary = salary; }
}

Repository

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import java.util.Optional;

public interface EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository<Employee, Long> {
    Optional<Employee> findByEmail(String email);
}

DTO (record) and mapper

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import java.time.LocalDate;

public record EmployeeDto(Long id, String name, String email, String department, LocalDate joiningDate) {
    // salary intentionally NOT exposed
    static EmployeeDto from(Employee e) {
        return new EmployeeDto(e.getId(), e.getName(), e.getEmail(), e.getDepartment(), e.getJoiningDate());
    }
}

Custom exception

package com.trinity.hr.common;

public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String resource;
    private final Object id;

    public ResourceNotFoundException(String resource, Object id) {
        super("%s not found with id %s".formatted(resource, id));
        this.resource = resource;
        this.id = id;
    }
    public String getResource() { return resource; }
    public Object getId() { return id; }
}

Service

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import com.trinity.hr.common.ResourceNotFoundException;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public class EmployeeService {

    private final EmployeeRepository repository;

    public EmployeeService(EmployeeRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; }

    public EmployeeDto getEmployeeById(Long id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
                .map(EmployeeDto::from)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Employee", id));
    }
}

Controller

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.Positive;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/employees")
public class EmployeeController {

    private final EmployeeService service;

    public EmployeeController(EmployeeService service) { this.service = service; }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<EmployeeDto> getEmployeeById(@PathVariable @Positive Long id) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(service.getEmployeeById(id));
    }
}

Global exception handler (RFC 9457/7807 ProblemDetail)

package com.trinity.hr.common;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice;

import java.net.URI;
import java.time.Instant;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(GlobalExceptionHandler.class);

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setTitle("Resource Not Found");
        pd.setType(URI.create("https://api.trinity.com/errors/not-found"));
        pd.setInstance(URI.create(req.getRequestURI()));
        pd.setProperty("resource", ex.getResource());
        pd.setProperty("timestamp", Instant.now());
        return pd;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleGeneric(Exception ex) {
        log.error("Unhandled error", ex);
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Unexpected error");
    }
}

A response for GET /api/v1/employees/99 (Content-Type: application/problem+json):

{
  "type": "https://api.trinity.com/errors/not-found",
  "title": "Resource Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "Employee not found with id 99",
  "instance": "/api/v1/employees/99",
  "resource": "Employee",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-02T06:15:30Z"
}

Design points to say aloud

  • Return a DTO, not the entity. That avoids lazy-loading serialisation errors, leaking fields (salary), and coupling the API to the schema.
  • findById returns Optional, so there is no null handling. Throwing from the service keeps the controller thin.
  • The read-only transaction lets Hibernate skip dirty-checking snapshots.
  • Avoid getReferenceById here: it returns a lazy proxy and fails late with EntityNotFoundException.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not return Optional from the controller? HTTP semantics belong in one place, and the advice handles 404 consistently.
  • Where do you map entity to DTO at scale? MapStruct (compile-time, no reflection).
  • How would you test this? @WebMvcTest with a mocked service for 200/404, @DataJpaTest for the repository, and a Mockito unit test for the service (C33–C35).
C16 PUT vs PATCH.
PUT PATCH
Semantics Replace the whole resource Partial update (only the fields sent)
Missing fields Set to null/default Left unchanged
Idempotent Yes Not guaranteed (usually is if implemented as "set field")
Body Full representation Changed fields only, or JSON Patch / Merge Patch

PUT can also create a resource at a known URI. PATCH is used for things like PATCH /devices/7 {"status":"OFFLINE"}.

PUT PATCH
Semantics Replace the whole resource with the payload (RFC 9110) Partially modify the resource (RFC 5789)
Missing fields Treated as "set to default/null" Left unchanged
Idempotent? Yes: N identical requests produce the same state Not guaranteed. Merge patch with absolute values is effectively idempotent; {"op":"add"} on arrays or "increment" ops are not
Safe? No No
Create if absent Allowed (client-chosen id) → 201 Usually not
Formats Full representation application/merge-patch+json (RFC 7396), application/json-patch+json (RFC 6902), or an ad-hoc partial DTO

PUT implementation

@PutMapping("/{id}")
@Transactional
public EmployeeDto replace(@PathVariable Long id, @Valid @RequestBody EmployeeUpdateRequest req) {
    Employee e = repository.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Employee", id));
    e.setName(req.name());
    e.setEmail(req.email());
    e.setDepartment(req.department());     // null in request => null in DB (full replacement)
    e.setSalary(req.salary());
    return EmployeeDto.from(e);            // dirty checking flushes
}

(In real code, move the @Transactional logic into the service.)

PATCH option 1: nullable DTO ("null means don't change")

public record EmployeePatchRequest(String name, @Email String email, String department) { }

@Transactional
public EmployeeDto patch(Long id, EmployeePatchRequest req) {
    Employee e = repository.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Employee", id));
    if (req.name() != null)       e.setName(req.name());
    if (req.email() != null)      e.setEmail(req.email());
    if (req.department() != null) e.setDepartment(req.department());
    return EmployeeDto.from(e);
}

The problem: it can't express "set this field to null". Fixes are JsonNullable<T> (openapitools jackson-databind-nullable), Optional<T> fields (absent = null field, explicit null = Optional.empty()), or the next option.

PATCH option 2: JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) with Jackson Rules: fields present overwrite, null removes or clears the field, absent fields are untouched, and arrays are replaced wholesale.

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import jakarta.validation.ConstraintViolationException;
import jakarta.validation.Validator;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

import java.io.IOException;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/employees")
public class EmployeePatchController {

    private final EmployeeService service;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;
    private final Validator validator;

    public EmployeePatchController(EmployeeService service, ObjectMapper objectMapper, Validator validator) {
        this.service = service; this.objectMapper = objectMapper; this.validator = validator;
    }

    @PatchMapping(path = "/{id}", consumes = "application/merge-patch+json")
    public EmployeeDto mergePatch(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody JsonNode patch) throws IOException {
        EmployeeUpdateRequest current = service.getForUpdate(id);                 // current state as DTO
        EmployeeUpdateRequest patched = objectMapper.readerForUpdating(current)  // apply only present fields
                .readValue(patch);
        var violations = validator.validate(patched);                             // validate the RESULT
        if (!violations.isEmpty()) throw new ConstraintViolationException(violations);
        return service.replace(id, patched);
    }
}

Note: readerForUpdating works on mutable objects (POJOs with setters). Records are immutable, so with record DTOs, merge at the JsonNode level instead: ObjectNode base = objectMapper.valueToTree(current); merge(base, patch); objectMapper.treeToValue(base, Dto.class).

JSON Patch (RFC 6902) is an array of operations:

[ { "op": "replace", "path": "/department", "value": "Traffic" },
  { "op": "remove",  "path": "/phone" } ]

Libraries: com.github.java-json-tools:json-patch, or jakarta.json.JsonPatch.

Concurrency: both PUT and PATCH should use optimistic locking. The client sends If-Match: "<version>" (ETag), and the server returns 412 Precondition Failed on a mismatch, or 409 when @Version throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is PATCH ever idempotent? It can be, for example merge patch with absolute values, but the spec doesn't require it.
  • Why validate after patching? Each field may be valid on its own while the merged object isn't. Validate the final state.
  • Which status should PUT/PATCH return? 200 with the updated body, or 204 with no body. PUT that creates returns 201.
C17 HTTP 204. Co. 2

204 No Content means the request succeeded and there is no response body. It is typical for DELETE, or for a PUT/PATCH that does not return the updated resource.

@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    service.delete(id);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}

Compare with 200 (success, with a body) and 201 Created (with a Location header).

204 No Content means the request succeeded and the server is intentionally sending no body. The response must not have a body. Headers (e.g. ETag) may still be present.

When to use it

  • DELETE /vehicles/42 succeeded.
  • PUT/PATCH succeeded and the client doesn't need the updated representation.
  • Fire-and-forget actions that completed synchronously (POST /devices/7/reboot when done inline).
  • CORS preflight OPTIONS responses (often 204).
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    service.delete(id);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}

// or
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
public void delete2(@PathVariable Long id) { service.delete(id); }

Compared with other codes

Code Meaning Body Typical use
200 OK Success Yes GET; PUT/PATCH returning the updated entity
201 Created A resource was created Usually yes, plus a Location header POST create
202 Accepted Accepted for async processing, not done yet Often a status URL Bulk import, report generation through Kafka
204 No Content Success with no body No DELETE, update without echo
404 Not Found The resource doesn't exist Error body (ProblemDetail) GET/DELETE of an unknown id

Debated cases

  • An empty search result (GET /incidents?ward=W99): return 200 with [] (or an empty page), not 204. The collection resource exists; it just has no items. Clients can iterate without special-casing.
  • DELETE of a missing id: either 404 (strict), or 204 (idempotent: "the end state is the same"). Pick one and document it.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Can a 204 have a body? No. Clients and proxies ignore or strip it, and some HTTP clients misbehave.
  • 204 vs 202 for async? 202 means "accepted, not done". 204 means "done, nothing to return".
  • What does a browser do with 204 on a form submit? It stays on the current page.
C18 Spring Boot Actuator.

Actuator provides production-ready endpoints for monitoring and managing the app. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator. Key endpoints:

  • /actuator/health: liveness and readiness probes for Kubernetes.
  • /info, /metrics (Micrometer), /prometheus.
  • /env, /beans, /mappings, /loggers (change log level at runtime), /threaddump, /heapdump.

Only health is exposed over HTTP by default. Expose more carefully and secure them with Spring Security.

management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,metrics,prometheus
  endpoint.health.show-details: when-authorized

You can add custom checks by implementing HealthIndicator (for example, a check for an external CCTV/VMS system).

spring-boot-starter-actuator adds production-ready endpoints for health, metrics, info, and diagnostics.

Endpoint Purpose
/actuator/health UP/DOWN, aggregated from HealthIndicators (db, diskSpace, redis, kafka...)
/actuator/health/liveness, /readiness K8s probes (auto-enabled on K8s, or via management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true)
/actuator/info Build, git and custom info
/actuator/metrics, /metrics/{name} Micrometer meters
/actuator/prometheus Prometheus scrape format (needs micrometer-registry-prometheus)
/actuator/loggers View or change log levels at runtime (POST)
/actuator/env, /configprops Properties (values are sanitised/masked)
/actuator/beans, /conditions, /mappings Context introspection
/actuator/threaddump, /heapdump Diagnostics (sensitive!)
/actuator/httpexchanges Recent requests (needs an HttpExchangeRepository bean)
/actuator/scheduledtasks, /caches, /flyway, /liquibase Feature-specific
/actuator/shutdown Graceful shutdown. Disabled by default

Exposure: by default, only health is exposed over HTTP. All endpoints are available over JMX if JMX is enabled.

management:
  server:
    port: 8081                       # separate port, not exposed through the public ingress
  endpoints:
    web:
      base-path: /actuator
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus,metrics,loggers
        exclude: env,beans
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized  # never | when-authorized | always
      probes:
        enabled: true
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState,db,redis
  info:
    env:
      enabled: true                  # info.* properties are hidden by default since Boot 2.6
    git:
      mode: simple
  metrics:
    tags:
      application: ${spring.application.name}
info:
  app:
    name: citypulse-incident-service
    team: smart-city

(Boot 3.4+ uses management.endpoint.<id>.access: read-only|unrestricted|none instead of the older .enabled property for enabling and restricting endpoints.)

Securing it

import org.springframework.boot.actuate.autoconfigure.security.servlet.EndpointRequest;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.health.HealthEndpoint;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.info.InfoEndpoint;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class ActuatorSecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    @Order(1)
    SecurityFilterChain actuatorChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to(HealthEndpoint.class, InfoEndpoint.class)).permitAll()
                .anyRequest().hasRole("OPS"))
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());
        return http.build();
    }
}

Other defences: a separate management port plus network policy, and never exposing heapdump/env publicly (they leak secrets).

Custom health indicator

package com.trinity.citypulse.health;

import org.springframework.boot.actuate.health.Health;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.health.HealthIndicator;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component("cctvGateway")                  // shows as "cctvGateway" in /health
public class CctvGatewayHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final CctvGatewayClient client;
    public CctvGatewayHealthIndicator(CctvGatewayClient client) { this.client = client; }

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try {
            long latencyMs = client.ping();
            return latencyMs < 500
                    ? Health.up().withDetail("latencyMs", latencyMs).build()
                    : Health.status("DEGRADED").withDetail("latencyMs", latencyMs).build();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return Health.down(e).withDetail("gateway", "unreachable").build();
        }
    }
}

Don't put external dependencies in the liveness group. If they are there, a downstream outage makes K8s restart every pod (a cascading failure). Readiness is the right place for them.

Micrometer and Prometheus

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Counter;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Timer;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class ChallanMetricsService {
    private final Counter challansIssued;
    private final Timer anprLatency;

    public ChallanMetricsService(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.challansIssued = Counter.builder("challan.issued").tag("source", "anpr")
                .description("Challans issued").register(registry);
        this.anprLatency = Timer.builder("anpr.recognition.latency").publishPercentiles(0.95, 0.99)
                .register(registry);
    }

    public void issue(Runnable work) {
        anprLatency.record(work);
        challansIssued.increment();
    }
}

Boot auto-instruments http.server.requests, JVM, HikariCP, Tomcat, cache, Kafka and logback metrics. Prometheus scrapes /actuator/prometheus, and Grafana dashboards and alerts sit on top. @Timed needs a TimedAspect bean, and @Observed (Micrometer Observation API) also gives tracing (Micrometer Tracing with OTel/Zipkin).

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you change a log level in prod without restarting? POST /actuator/loggers/com.trinity {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}.
  • Liveness vs readiness? Liveness means "restart me if I'm broken". Readiness means "don't route traffic to me yet".
  • How do you add custom info? info.* properties (with management.info.env.enabled), or an InfoContributor bean.
C19 Front Controller design pattern (DispatcherServlet).

A single entry point handles every request and delegates it to the right handler. Cross-cutting concerns (routing, security, i18n, error handling) therefore live in one place. In Spring MVC, that entry point is the DispatcherServlet:

  1. A request arrives at DispatcherServlet.
  2. HandlerMapping finds the controller method.
  3. HandlerAdapter invokes it, using argument resolvers for @PathVariable, @RequestBody and so on.
  4. The return value is written by an HttpMessageConverter (Jackson to JSON) or resolved by a ViewResolver.
  5. Exceptions go to a HandlerExceptionResolver (@ControllerAdvice).
  6. The response is sent.

Spring Boot auto-registers DispatcherServlet at /.

Front Controller means a single entry point handles every request and delegates to specific handlers. Cross-cutting concerns (routing, security, conversion, errors) live in one place. In Spring MVC that entry point is DispatcherServlet, which Boot registers at / through DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration.

The flow

Client
  -> Servlet container (Tomcat) -> Filter chain (Security, CORS, logging, ...)
  -> DispatcherServlet.doService() -> doDispatch()
       1. checkMultipart()
       2. getHandler(): iterate HandlerMappings
            RequestMappingHandlerMapping (@RequestMapping), RouterFunctionMapping, SimpleUrlHandlerMapping (static)
            -> HandlerExecutionChain (HandlerMethod + HandlerInterceptors)        [none -> 404 NoHandlerFoundException / NoResourceFoundException]
       3. getHandlerAdapter(): RequestMappingHandlerAdapter
       4. interceptors.preHandle()        (false -> stop)
       5. ha.handle():
            - HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers build arguments
              (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody -> HttpMessageConverter read, validation)
            - invoke the controller method (via the AOP proxy if any)
            - HandlerMethodReturnValueHandlers:
              @ResponseBody/ResponseEntity -> RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor -> content negotiation
              -> HttpMessageConverter.write() (Jackson)  => response committed, no view
              String/ModelAndView -> view name
       6. interceptors.postHandle()       (not called if an exception occurred; too late to change a @ResponseBody response)
       7. processDispatchResult():
            exception? -> HandlerExceptionResolvers:
                ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver (@ExceptionHandler / @ControllerAdvice)
                ResponseStatusExceptionResolver (@ResponseStatus, ResponseStatusException)
                DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver (Spring MVC exceptions -> 4xx/5xx)
            view?      -> ViewResolver (ThymeleafViewResolver/InternalResourceViewResolver) -> View.render(model)
       8. interceptors.afterCompletion()  (always, even on exception)
  <- Filters (post-processing) <- Client

DispatcherServlet's strategy beans are all auto-configured and replaceable: HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter, HandlerExceptionResolver, ViewResolver, LocaleResolver, MultipartResolver, FlashMapManager.

Custom interceptor

package com.trinity.citypulse.web;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.HandlerInterceptor;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.InterceptorRegistry;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.WebMvcConfigurer;

import java.util.UUID;

class CorrelationIdInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
    @Override
    public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, Object handler) {
        String cid = req.getHeader("X-Correlation-Id");
        if (cid == null) cid = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        MDC.put("correlationId", cid);
        res.setHeader("X-Correlation-Id", cid);
        req.setAttribute("startNanos", System.nanoTime());
        return true;
    }

    @Override
    public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, Object handler, Exception ex) {
        MDC.remove("correlationId");
    }
}

@Configuration
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    @Override
    public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
        registry.addInterceptor(new CorrelationIdInterceptor())
                .addPathPatterns("/api/**")
                .excludePathPatterns("/api/public/**");
    }
}

Filter vs interceptor

Filter (Servlet API) HandlerInterceptor (Spring MVC)
Runs before DispatcherServlet and for every request, including static resources Runs only for requests that map to a handler
Can wrap or replace the request and response Knows the HandlerMethod (can read annotations)
Spring Security lives here Auth checks per handler, logging, locale
Exceptions are not handled by @ControllerAdvice Exceptions go through HandlerExceptionResolvers

Likely follow-ups:

  • Who converts the object to JSON? An HttpMessageConverter (MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter) chosen through content negotiation.
  • Can there be multiple DispatcherServlets? Yes, each with its own child WebApplicationContext and mapping, but that's rarely needed in Boot.
  • What is WebFlux's equivalent? DispatcherHandler (reactive, non-blocking).
C20 Exception handling in Spring Boot. Co. 2G2
  • @ExceptionHandler works for one controller only.
  • @RestControllerAdvice (= @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody) is global, so you get a consistent error format.
  • Throw a custom exception from the service layer and map it to a status in the advice.
  • Spring 6 adds ProblemDetail (RFC 7807/9457, application/problem+json). Enable it for framework exceptions with spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true.
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setTitle("Resource Not Found");
        return pd;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
        pd.setProperty("errors", ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(FieldError::getField,
                        fe -> String.valueOf(fe.getDefaultMessage()), (a, b) -> a)));
        return pd;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleGeneric(Exception ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Unexpected error");
    }
}

Alternatives are @ResponseStatus on the exception class, or throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).

Options, from local to global

  1. try/catch in the controller (avoid, because it scatters logic).
  2. @ExceptionHandler methods inside one controller, which apply only to that controller.
  3. @RestControllerAdvice (= @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody): global handlers. Scope them with basePackages, assignableTypes or annotations, and order several advices with @Order.
  4. @ResponseStatus on a custom exception class: maps it to a status, with no body control.
  5. ResponseStatusException: throw it with a status and reason directly (throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Junction not found")). Good for quick cases.
  6. ErrorController/BasicErrorController at /error: the fallback for anything not handled, including filter errors.

Resolution internals: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver looks first at @ExceptionHandler methods in the controller, then in the advices. It picks the closest match in the exception hierarchy (ExceptionDepthComparator). It also matches causes for wrapped exceptions.

ProblemDetail (RFC 7807, now RFC 9457): Spring 6 supports it natively. ProblemDetail, ErrorResponse and ErrorResponseException produce application/problem+json.

  • spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true makes Boot register a ResponseEntityExceptionHandler advice that renders Spring MVC's built-in exceptions (400/404/405/415...) as ProblemDetail.
  • To customise, extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler yourself:
package com.trinity.citypulse.web;

import jakarta.validation.ConstraintViolationException;
import org.springframework.dao.DataIntegrityViolationException;
import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.lang.NonNull;
import org.springframework.orm.ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice;
import org.springframework.web.context.request.WebRequest;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.ResponseEntityExceptionHandler;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    // validation of @Valid @RequestBody -> 400 with field errors
    @Override
    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(@NonNull MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,
            @NonNull HttpHeaders headers, @NonNull HttpStatusCode status, @NonNull WebRequest request) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ex.getBody();                         // already a ProblemDetail
        pd.setTitle("Validation failed");
        List<Map<String, Object>> errors = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
                .map(fe -> Map.<String, Object>of(
                        "field", fe.getField(),
                        "message", String.valueOf(fe.getDefaultMessage()),
                        "rejected", String.valueOf(fe.getRejectedValue())))
                .toList();
        pd.setProperty("errors", errors);
        return ResponseEntity.status(status).headers(headers).body(pd);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail notFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ConstraintViolationException.class)        // @Validated method-level (service layer)
    ProblemDetail constraint(ConstraintViolationException ex) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Constraint violation");
        pd.setProperty("violations", ex.getConstraintViolations().stream()
                .map(v -> v.getPropertyPath() + ": " + v.getMessage()).toList());
        return pd;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(DataIntegrityViolationException.class)
    ProblemDetail conflict(DataIntegrityViolationException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Duplicate or invalid reference");
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
    ProblemDetail optimistic(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Resource was modified by another user");
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    ProblemDetail fallback(Exception ex) {
        logger.error("Unhandled", ex);                            // never leak stack traces to clients
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Internal error");
    }
}

You can also make domain exceptions extend ErrorResponseException, so they carry their own ProblemDetail.

Validation errors summary

  • @Valid @RequestBody → MethodArgumentNotValidException
  • @Valid @ModelAttribute → MethodArgumentNotValidException (a BindException subtype)
  • constraints on @RequestParam/@PathVariable (6.1+) → HandlerMethodValidationException
  • @Validated service methods → ConstraintViolationException

Exceptions not caught by @ControllerAdvice

  • Exceptions thrown in servlet filters, including Spring Security's filter chain, happen before DispatcherServlet. The advice never sees them, and they go to the container's /error (BasicErrorController).
  • For Security: implement AuthenticationEntryPoint (401) and AccessDeniedHandler (403).
  • For custom filters: catch the exception in the filter and either write the response directly, or delegate to the MVC resolvers:
import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.HandlerExceptionResolver;

import java.io.IOException;

@Component
public class TenantFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    private final HandlerExceptionResolver resolver;

    public TenantFilter(@Qualifier("handlerExceptionResolver") HandlerExceptionResolver resolver) {
        this.resolver = resolver;
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        try {
            if (req.getHeader("X-Tenant-Id") == null) throw new MissingTenantException();
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } catch (MissingTenantException ex) {
            resolver.resolveException(req, res, null, ex);   // routes to @RestControllerAdvice
        }
    }
}
  • Other cases the advice doesn't cover: exceptions in @Async methods (use an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler), @Scheduled jobs, Kafka listeners (DefaultErrorHandler/DLT), and errors after the response is already committed.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Two handlers match: which wins? The most specific exception type. Across advices, @Order, and controller-local handlers beat advices.
  • ResponseStatusException vs custom exception plus advice? RSE is quick but couples the service to HTTP. Domain exceptions plus advice are cleaner.
  • How do you hide stack traces in /error? server.error.include-stacktrace=never (the default) and include-message.
C21 @ConfigurationProperties; creating custom configuration properties. G2

@ConfigurationProperties binds a group of properties under a prefix to a type-safe object. Compared with many @Value annotations, it supports relaxed binding, nested objects and lists, and validation.

smartcity:
  vms:
    base-url: https://vms.local/api
    timeout: 5s
    cameras: [CAM-01, CAM-02]
@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "smartcity.vms")
public record VmsProperties(@NotBlank String baseUrl,
                            @DefaultValue("3s") Duration timeout,
                            List<String> cameras) { }

@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan            // or @EnableConfigurationProperties(VmsProperties.class) on a @Configuration
public class CityApp { ... }

@Service
public class VmsClient {
    private final VmsProperties props;
    public VmsClient(VmsProperties props) { this.props = props; }
}

Records give immutable constructor binding. Add spring-boot-configuration-processor to get IDE auto-completion through metadata.

@ConfigurationProperties binds a group of externalised properties (a prefix) onto a type-safe object. Compared with scattered @Values it gives relaxed binding, nested objects, lists and maps, type conversion (Duration, DataSize), validation and IDE metadata.

1. Record (immutable, constructor binding; preferred in Boot 3)

package com.trinity.citypulse.config;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotEmpty;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.bind.DefaultValue;
import org.springframework.boot.convert.DurationUnit;
import org.springframework.util.unit.DataSize;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "citypulse.anpr")
public record AnprProperties(
        @NotBlank String baseUrl,
        @DefaultValue("5s") Duration connectTimeout,
        @DurationUnit(ChronoUnit.SECONDS) @DefaultValue("30") Duration readTimeout,
        @DefaultValue("10MB") DataSize maxImageSize,
        @Min(1) @DefaultValue("3") int maxRetries,
        @NotEmpty List<String> cameraZones,
        Map<String, String> headers,
        @Valid @DefaultValue Retry retry) {

    public record Retry(@DefaultValue("200ms") Duration backoff, @DefaultValue("2.0") double multiplier) { }
}
  • Boot 3 uses constructor binding automatically when there is a single parameterised constructor. @ConstructorBinding is needed only when there are several constructors, and in Boot 3 it lives in org.springframework.boot.context.properties.bind.
  • @DefaultValue on a nested record makes Boot create an instance with defaults even when no properties are set.

2. JavaBean style (mutable; setters required)

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "citypulse.notify")
public class NotifyProperties {
    @NotBlank private String smsProvider = "msg91";
    private boolean enabled = true;
    // getters + setters (binding uses setters)
}

Registering them (one of these):

@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan("com.trinity.citypulse.config")     // scans for @ConfigurationProperties types
public class CityPulseApplication { }

// or
@Configuration
@EnableConfigurationProperties({AnprProperties.class, NotifyProperties.class})
class PropsConfig { }

// or, for third-party classes, on a @Bean
@Bean
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "citypulse.pool")
HikariDataSource reportingDataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(); }

YAML

citypulse:
  anpr:
    base-url: https://anpr.internal.trinity.com
    connect-timeout: 3s
    read-timeout: 45            # seconds because of @DurationUnit
    max-image-size: 5MB
    max-retries: 5
    camera-zones: [north, south, central]
    headers:
      X-Api-Version: "2"
    retry:
      backoff: 500ms
      multiplier: 1.5

Usage: inject it like any bean.

@Service
public class AnprClient {
    private final RestClient restClient;
    public AnprClient(RestClient.Builder builder, AnprProperties props) {
        this.restClient = builder.baseUrl(props.baseUrl()).build();
    }
}

Validation: with @Validated and spring-boot-starter-validation, invalid config fails startup with a clear BindValidationException report. This is fail-fast on bad deployments. Use @Valid on nested objects so they are validated too.

Relaxed binding: all of these bind to baseUrl: citypulse.anpr.base-url (recommended kebab-case in files), citypulse.anpr.baseUrl, citypulse.anpr.base_url, and the env var CITYPULSE_ANPR_BASEURL (uppercase, . → _, dashes removed). List index from an env var: CITYPULSE_ANPR_CAMERAZONES_0_=north. The prefix itself must be kebab-case, lowercase.

Metadata processor (IDE auto-complete and docs):

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-configuration-processor</artifactId>
  <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

This generates META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json at compile time, using Javadoc as descriptions. Add additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json for hints.

@ConfigurationProperties vs @Value

@ConfigurationProperties @Value
Relaxed binding full limited (kebab-case only)
Grouping/nesting, lists, maps yes awkward
Validation @Validated no
SpEL no yes (#{...})
IDE metadata yes no

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you reload properties at runtime? Spring Cloud @RefreshScope plus /actuator/refresh. @ConfigurationProperties beans are rebound on an EnvironmentChangeEvent.
  • Why records? Immutability and thread safety, and nobody can mutate config at runtime.
  • How do you test properties binding? Use ApplicationContextRunner().withPropertyValues(...), or @SpringBootTest(properties=...).
C22 Configuring different environments. TCS
  • Profile files: application.yml holds common settings. application-dev.yml, application-qa.yml and application-prod.yml override them.
  • Activate a profile with spring.profiles.active=prod, the SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod env var, --spring.profiles.active=prod, or -Dspring.profiles.active=prod.
  • Profile-specific beans: @Profile("dev") or @Profile("!prod") on beans or config classes.
  • Multi-document YAML: use --- with spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod.
  • Secrets and environment values: environment variables (relaxed binding: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL), Kubernetes ConfigMaps/Secrets, Vault.
  • Microservices: centralise config with Spring Cloud Config Server (Git-backed) via spring.config.import=configserver:, and refresh with @RefreshScope.
  • Precedence (high to low): command-line args, env vars, profile-specific files, application.yml.

Profiles are named sets of configuration and beans: dev, qa, uat, prod, or per city, e.g. blr, pune.

1. Profile-specific files

src/main/resources/
  application.yml          # common defaults
  application-dev.yml
  application-qa.yml
  application-prod.yml

Activate one with --spring.profiles.active=prod, the env var SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod, or -Dspring.profiles.active=prod. Profile-specific files override application.yml. If several profiles are active, the last one wins for conflicting keys.

2. Multi-document YAML with spring.config.activate.on-profile (Boot 2.4+; replaces the deprecated spring.profiles key)

spring:
  application:
    name: citypulse-incident
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/citypulse
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://prod-db.internal:5432/citypulse
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 30
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: "dev | qa"       # profile expressions: !, &, |
logging:
  level:
    com.trinity: DEBUG

3. Profile groups (Boot 2.4+): one name activates several profiles.

spring:
  profiles:
    group:
      prod: [proddb, prodkafka, monitoring]
      dev:  [h2, localkafka]

4. Profile-conditional beans

@Bean @Profile("!prod") SmsSender fakeSmsSender() { return new LoggingSmsSender(); }
@Bean @Profile("prod")  SmsSender realSmsSender(Msg91Client c) { return new Msg91SmsSender(c); }

spring.profiles.default sets the profile used when none is active. Don't use spring.profiles.active inside a profile-specific document; Boot rejects that.

Externalized config precedence (later overrides earlier: lowest → highest)

  1. Default properties (SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties)
  2. @PropertySource on @Configuration classes
  3. Config data files, in this order: a. application.yml inside the jar b. application-{profile}.yml inside the jar c. application.yml outside the jar (./config/, ./) d. application-{profile}.yml outside the jar
  4. RandomValuePropertySource (${random.uuid})
  5. OS environment variables
  6. Java system properties (-D)
  7. JNDI, then ServletContext and ServletConfig init params
  8. SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON
  9. Command-line arguments (--server.port=9090)
  10. Test properties: @SpringBootTest(properties=…), @TestPropertySource, @DynamicPropertySource (highest)

The rule of thumb: command line > system props > env vars > external files > packaged files > defaults. /actuator/env shows which property source each value came from.

Importing extra config:

spring:
  config:
    import:
      - optional:file:./secrets.yml
      - optional:configtree:/run/secrets/        # K8s secret volume: each file = one property
      - optional:configserver:http://config-server:8888

Spring Cloud Config

  • A central Config Server (@EnableConfigServer) is backed by Git, Vault, JDBC or the filesystem. It serves /{application}/{profile}/{label}, e.g. /citypulse-incident/prod/main.
  • Clients use spring-cloud-starter-config plus spring.config.import=configserver:http://config-server:8888, with spring.application.name and the profile selecting files.
  • Refresh: @RefreshScope beans and @ConfigurationProperties get rebound after POST /actuator/refresh. Spring Cloud Bus (Kafka/RabbitMQ) broadcasts the refresh to all instances (/actuator/busrefresh).
  • Encrypted values use {cipher}..., decrypted by the server (symmetric key or keystore).
  • On Kubernetes, ConfigMaps (plus Spring Cloud Kubernetes or configtree) are a common alternative.

Secrets handling

  • Never commit secrets to Git (application-prod.yml should contain no passwords). Scan with git-secrets or gitleaks in CI.
  • Inject them at runtime:
    • Env vars from K8s Secrets: SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD
    • Mounted secret files with configtree:
    • HashiCorp Vault (spring-cloud-starter-vault-config, dynamic DB credentials), AWS Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault
    • Jasypt ENC(...) for encrypted values in files (the key comes from an env var)
  • Use placeholders with no default for secrets: password: ${DB_PASSWORD}. Startup then fails if the value is missing.
  • Actuator /env masks keys like password, secret and key (management.endpoint.env.show-values=never|when-authorized, Boot 3).

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you see which profile is active? The startup log line ("The following 1 profile is active: prod"), Environment.getActiveProfiles(), or /actuator/env.
  • Env var vs application-prod.yml: which wins? The env var.
  • Should you build different jars per environment? No. Build once and configure per environment (12-factor). The same artifact is promoted through dev → qa → prod.
C23 SessionFactory: what it is and how to configure it.

SessionFactory is Hibernate's heavyweight, thread-safe, one-per-database factory that creates Session objects. A Session is lightweight and not thread-safe, and you use one per unit of work. The factory holds the mapping metadata, the connection provider and the second-level cache. The JPA equivalent is EntityManagerFactory → EntityManager.

In plain Hibernate you build it with new Configuration().configure("hibernate.cfg.xml").buildSessionFactory(). In Spring Boot you do not configure it. Boot auto-configures an EntityManagerFactory (Hibernate's SessionFactoryImpl implements it) from spring.datasource.* and spring.jpa.*. If you need native Hibernate APIs, unwrap it:

@Bean
public SessionFactory sessionFactory(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
    return emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class);
}
// or per-operation: Session session = entityManager.unwrap(Session.class);

SessionFactory (Hibernate native API):

  • It is a heavyweight, thread-safe, immutable factory, created once per database at startup. It holds the compiled mappings, metadata, the connection provider, the 2nd-level cache and the statistics.
  • It produces Sessions, which are lightweight, not thread-safe, and one per unit of work or transaction. Each Session wraps the persistence context (first-level cache).
  • JPA equivalents: SessionFactory ↔ EntityManagerFactory, and Session ↔ EntityManager. Since Hibernate 5.2, SessionFactory extends EntityManagerFactory and Session extends EntityManager.

Plain Spring (no Boot): LocalSessionFactoryBean

package com.trinity.legacy.config;

import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.orm.hibernate5.HibernateTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.orm.hibernate5.LocalSessionFactoryBean;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.EnableTransactionManagement;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.util.Properties;

@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
public class HibernateConfig {

    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource();
        ds.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/citypulse");
        ds.setUsername("app");
        ds.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));
        return ds;
    }

    @Bean
    public LocalSessionFactoryBean sessionFactory(DataSource dataSource) {
        LocalSessionFactoryBean sf = new LocalSessionFactoryBean();
        sf.setDataSource(dataSource);
        sf.setPackagesToScan("com.trinity.legacy.domain");
        Properties props = new Properties();
        props.put("hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto", "validate");
        props.put("hibernate.show_sql", "false");
        props.put("hibernate.jdbc.batch_size", "50");
        sf.setHibernateProperties(props);
        return sf;                               // FactoryBean -> exposes SessionFactory
    }

    @Bean
    public HibernateTransactionManager transactionManager(SessionFactory sessionFactory) {
        return new HibernateTransactionManager(sessionFactory);
    }
}

(The package org.springframework.orm.hibernate5 is still the one Spring 6.x uses for Hibernate 5.2+ and 6.x native support. A DAO then uses sessionFactory.getCurrentSession() inside @Transactional.)

Spring Boot: there is no SessionFactory bean by default. HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration creates a LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean (an EntityManagerFactory) and a JpaTransactionManager. Configure it through properties:

spring:
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate              # none | validate | update | create | create-drop (use Flyway/Liquibase in prod)
    open-in-view: false
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc.batch_size: 50
        default_batch_fetch_size: 50
        generate_statistics: false

When you need the native API, unwrap it:

@Service
public class BulkSensorIngestService {

    private final EntityManagerFactory emf;
    @PersistenceContext private EntityManager em;

    public BulkSensorIngestService(EntityManagerFactory emf) { this.emf = emf; }

    public SessionFactory sessionFactory() {
        return emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class);          // e.g. for Statistics, StatelessSession
    }

    @Transactional
    public void useNativeSession() {
        Session session = em.unwrap(Session.class);       // the transaction-bound Session
        session.setJdbcBatchSize(100);
    }

    public void statelessInsert(List<SensorReading> readings) {   // high-volume IoT ingest, no persistence context
        try (StatelessSession ss = sessionFactory().openStatelessSession()) {
            Transaction tx = ss.beginTransaction();
            readings.forEach(ss::insert);
            tx.commit();
        }
    }
}

Likely follow-ups:

  • getCurrentSession vs openSession? getCurrentSession is bound to the current transaction and closed automatically. openSession is a new one that you must close.
  • Why is SessionFactory expensive? It parses all mappings, builds metamodels and SQL, and initialises caches. Do it once.
  • What is a StatelessSession? It has no first-level cache, dirty checking or cascades. It suits bulk inserts.
C24 Configuring multiple data sources.

Steps:

  1. Define a separate property prefix for each data source.
  2. Create a DataSource, an EntityManagerFactory and a TransactionManager per DB. Mark one set @Primary.
  3. Point each @EnableJpaRepositories at its own repository package and entity package.
@Configuration
@EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages = "com.trinity.citizen.repo",
        entityManagerFactoryRef = "citizenEmf", transactionManagerRef = "citizenTx")
public class CitizenDbConfig {

    @Bean @Primary
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.citizen")
    public DataSourceProperties citizenDsProps() { return new DataSourceProperties(); }

    @Bean @Primary
    public DataSource citizenDataSource() {
        return citizenDsProps().initializeDataSourceBuilder().build();
    }

    @Bean @Primary
    public LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean citizenEmf(EntityManagerFactoryBuilder builder) {
        return builder.dataSource(citizenDataSource())
                      .packages("com.trinity.citizen.entity")
                      .persistenceUnit("citizen").build();
    }

    @Bean @Primary
    public PlatformTransactionManager citizenTx(@Qualifier("citizenEmf") EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return new JpaTransactionManager(emf);
    }
}
// A second class, e.g. IotDbConfig, repeats this without @Primary, using "app.datasource.iot" and other packages.

For the non-primary DB, use @Transactional("iotTx"). Use AbstractRoutingDataSource for read/write splitting or multi-tenancy.

Scenario: the primary DB (Postgres, citizen incidents) plus a reporting DB (a MySQL warehouse). Each needs its own DataSource → EntityManagerFactory → TransactionManager, and the repositories and entities go in separate packages.

com.trinity.citypulse
 ├── primary/   entity/Incident.java     repository/IncidentRepository.java
 └── reporting/ entity/DailyStat.java    repository/DailyStatRepository.java
app:
  datasource:
    primary:
      url: jdbc:postgresql://pg:5432/citypulse
      username: app
      password: ${PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD}
      driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver
      hikari:
        maximum-pool-size: 20
        pool-name: primary-pool
    reporting:
      url: jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/reporting
      username: report
      password: ${REPORT_DB_PASSWORD}
      driver-class-name: com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
      hikari:
        maximum-pool-size: 5
        pool-name: reporting-pool
        read-only: true
spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false

Primary config

package com.trinity.citypulse.config;

import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import jakarta.persistence.EntityManagerFactory;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.orm.jpa.EntityManagerFactoryBuilder;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.JpaTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean;
import org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.EnableTransactionManagement;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.util.Map;

@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
@EnableJpaRepositories(
        basePackages = "com.trinity.citypulse.primary.repository",
        entityManagerFactoryRef = "primaryEntityManagerFactory",
        transactionManagerRef = "primaryTransactionManager")
public class PrimaryDataSourceConfig {

    @Bean
    @Primary
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.primary")
    public DataSourceProperties primaryDataSourceProperties() { return new DataSourceProperties(); }

    @Bean
    @Primary
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.primary.hikari")       // binds pool settings onto HikariDataSource
    public HikariDataSource primaryDataSource(
            @Qualifier("primaryDataSourceProperties") DataSourceProperties props) {
        return props.initializeDataSourceBuilder().type(HikariDataSource.class).build();
    }

    @Bean
    @Primary
    public LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean primaryEntityManagerFactory(
            EntityManagerFactoryBuilder builder, @Qualifier("primaryDataSource") DataSource dataSource) {
        return builder.dataSource(dataSource)
                .packages("com.trinity.citypulse.primary.entity")
                .persistenceUnit("primary")
                .properties(Map.of(
                        "hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto", "validate",
                        "hibernate.physical_naming_strategy",
                        "org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy"))
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    @Primary
    public PlatformTransactionManager primaryTransactionManager(
            @Qualifier("primaryEntityManagerFactory") EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return new JpaTransactionManager(emf);
    }
}

Reporting config (same shape, no @Primary)

package com.trinity.citypulse.config;

import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import jakarta.persistence.EntityManagerFactory;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.orm.jpa.EntityManagerFactoryBuilder;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.JpaTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean;
import org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.util.Map;

@Configuration
@EnableJpaRepositories(
        basePackages = "com.trinity.citypulse.reporting.repository",
        entityManagerFactoryRef = "reportingEntityManagerFactory",
        transactionManagerRef = "reportingTransactionManager")
public class ReportingDataSourceConfig {

    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.reporting")
    public DataSourceProperties reportingDataSourceProperties() { return new DataSourceProperties(); }

    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.reporting.hikari")
    public HikariDataSource reportingDataSource(
            @Qualifier("reportingDataSourceProperties") DataSourceProperties props) {
        return props.initializeDataSourceBuilder().type(HikariDataSource.class).build();
    }

    @Bean
    public LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean reportingEntityManagerFactory(
            EntityManagerFactoryBuilder builder, @Qualifier("reportingDataSource") DataSource dataSource) {
        return builder.dataSource(dataSource)
                .packages("com.trinity.citypulse.reporting.entity")
                .persistenceUnit("reporting")
                .properties(Map.of("hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto", "none"))
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    public PlatformTransactionManager reportingTransactionManager(
            @Qualifier("reportingEntityManagerFactory") EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return new JpaTransactionManager(emf);
    }
}

Usage

@Service
public class DashboardService {
    private final IncidentRepository incidents;   // primary
    private final DailyStatRepository stats;      // reporting

    public DashboardService(IncidentRepository incidents, DailyStatRepository stats) {
        this.incidents = incidents; this.stats = stats;
    }

    @Transactional("primaryTransactionManager")                       // default anyway (@Primary)
    public void closeIncident(Long id) { incidents.findById(id).ifPresent(Incident::close); }

    @Transactional(transactionManager = "reportingTransactionManager", readOnly = true)
    public List<DailyStat> lastWeek() { return stats.findTop7ByOrderByDayDesc(); }
}

Gotchas

  • @Primary is required on one set. Otherwise auto-configured consumers (JdbcTemplate, Flyway, Actuator health) hit NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.
  • Boot's spring.jpa.* naming strategy and ddl-auto are applied to the EMF built by EntityManagerFactoryBuilder only partially. Pass Hibernate settings explicitly in properties(...), as above, for consistent naming.
  • With DataSourceProperties, use url (it is converted to Hikari's jdbcUrl). If you bind HikariDataSource directly with @ConfigurationProperties, the property must be jdbc-url.
  • A @Transactional spanning both DBs is NOT atomic. Each transaction manager handles only its own DB. Options: JTA/XA (Atomikos/Narayana, heavy), or more commonly an outbox/saga with eventual consistency.
  • Flyway migrates only the primary DataSource unless you configure a second Flyway bean.
  • For read/write splitting of the same schema (primary + replica), use AbstractRoutingDataSource with readOnly-based routing (wrapped in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy) rather than two EMFs.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How does a repository know which EMF to use? Through entityManagerFactoryRef in its package's @EnableJpaRepositories.
  • How do you inject an EntityManager for the second DB? @PersistenceContext(unitName = "reporting").
  • Multi-tenant DB per city? Hibernate multi-tenancy (MultiTenantConnectionProvider + CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver) or a routing DataSource.
C25 Lazy vs eager loading in Hibernate.
Relationship Default fetch
@ManyToOne, @OneToOne EAGER
@OneToMany, @ManyToMany LAZY
  • Lazy loads a proxy and runs the query only when the association is accessed. Eager loads it immediately. Best practice: make everything LAZY (@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)) and fetch what each use case needs.
  • LazyInitializationException: you accessed a lazy association after the session or transaction closed, for example in the controller or during JSON serialisation. Fix it by fetching inside a transaction, using a fetch join or entity graph, or mapping to a DTO. Do not rely on Open-Session-In-View; Boot enables it by default, so set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false.
  • N+1 problem: 1 query loads N parents, then N more queries load each child collection.

Fixes:

@Query("select d from Department d join fetch d.employees where d.id = :id")
Optional<Department> findWithEmployees(@Param("id") Long id);

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "employees")
List<Department> findAll();

Other options are @BatchSize(size = 50) or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size, and DTO projections.

Defaults (JPA)

Association Default fetch
