@ManyToOne, @OneToOne EAGER
@OneToMany, @ManyToMany LAZY
@ElementCollection LAZY
@Basic fields EAGER (lazy basics need bytecode enhancement)

Best practice: make everything LAZY (@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)) and fetch explicitly per use case. EAGER can't be turned off per query, and it causes hidden extra queries (eager @ManyToOne under JPQL triggers N+1).

How lazy works

  • For to-one: Hibernate puts a proxy (a ByteBuddy subclass, Employee$HibernateProxy$...) holding only the id. The first call to a non-id getter initialises it with a SELECT.
  • For collections: a PersistentBag/PersistentSet wrapper loads on first access (size(), iteration).
  • Initialisation needs an open Session/persistence context.

LazyInitializationException

@Service
public class DeptService {
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public Department get(Long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); }
}
// controller:
dept.getEmployees().size();   // tx closed -> LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session
// Also triggered by Jackson serialising the entity outside the transaction.

Fixes:

  • fetch what you need inside the transaction (JOIN FETCH or an entity graph);
  • map to a DTO inside the service;
  • Hibernate.initialize(dept.getEmployees()) (crude).

Anti-fixes: making things EAGER, hibernate.enable_lazy_load_no_trans=true (opens a new session per lazy load), or relying on OSIV.

Open Session in View (spring.jpa.open-in-view)

  • Boot sets it to true by default and logs a warning. OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor keeps the EntityManager open for the whole web request, so lazy loads in the controller or Jackson "work".
  • The cost: DB connections are held for the entire request, including slow serialisation and remote calls, which can exhaust the pool under load. Queries also fire from the view layer (hidden N+1), and the transaction boundary is blurred.
  • Set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false in services and fetch deliberately.

The N+1 problem

List<Department> depts = deptRepo.findAll();                // 1 query
depts.forEach(d -> d.getEmployees().size());                // N queries (one per dept)

Solutions:

public interface DepartmentRepository extends JpaRepository<Department, Long> {

    // 1. JOIN FETCH (DISTINCT is implicit for entity results in Hibernate 6)
    @Query("select d from Department d left join fetch d.employees where d.city = :city")
    List<Department> findWithEmployees(@Param("city") String city);

    // 2. Entity graph
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"employees", "head"})
    List<Department> findByCity(String city);

    // 3. DTO projection: no entities, no lazy problems
    @Query("""
           select new com.trinity.hr.dept.DeptSummary(d.id, d.name, count(e))
           from Department d left join d.employees e group by d.id, d.name
           """)
    List<DeptSummary> summaries();
}
# 4. Batch fetching: N queries -> N/50 queries using IN (...)
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size: 50
  1. @BatchSize(size = 50) on the collection or entity class, or @Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT).

Pagination gotcha: JOIN FETCH of a collection combined with Pageable makes Hibernate warn HHH90003004 ("firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory"). It loads every row and paginates in memory. The fix: page the ids first (select d.id from Department d ...), then fetch those ids with JOIN FETCH. Or use batch fetching.

Fetching two bags (two List collections) in one query throws MultipleBagFetchException. Use Set, or fetch them in separate queries (Hibernate dedupes them in the persistence context).

How to detect N+1: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true, logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG, datasource-proxy or p6spy, and asserting query counts in tests (e.g. hypersistence-utils / SQLStatementCountValidator).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is FetchType.LAZY guaranteed? No. It is a hint. Lazy @OneToOne on the non-owning side needs bytecode enhancement or @MapsId.
  • Why is getReferenceById lazy? It returns an uninitialised proxy without hitting the DB. That is handy for setting FKs.
  • JOIN FETCH vs EntityGraph? They are equivalent SQL-wise. Entity graphs are declarative and reusable on derived queries.
C26 One-to-Many relationship across multiple tables.

For a bidirectional mapping, the child (@ManyToOne) owns the foreign key, and the parent uses mappedBy.

@Entity
public class Department {
    @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "department", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<Employee> employees = new ArrayList<>();

    public void addEmployee(Employee e) { employees.add(e); e.setDepartment(this); } // keep both sides in sync
    public void removeEmployee(Employee e) { employees.remove(e); e.setDepartment(null); }
}

@Entity
public class Employee {
    @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "department_id")       // FK column in employee table
    private Department department;
}
  • cascade = ALL: saving or deleting the department cascades to its employees.
  • orphanRemoval = true: removing an employee from the list deletes its row.
  • Join table option (unidirectional, no FK in the child table): @OneToMany @JoinTable(name="dept_emp", joinColumns=@JoinColumn(name="dept_id"), inverseJoinColumns=@JoinColumn(name="emp_id")). A unidirectional @OneToMany without @JoinColumn creates a join table by default.
  • Chains across tables (City → Zone → Device) are just repeated one-to-many mappings. Fetch the levels you need with join fetch or an entity graph.
  • Avoid toString/equals that touch both sides, because that causes infinite recursion. In JSON, use DTOs or @JsonManagedReference.

Bidirectional Department (1) → Employee (N)

  • The owning side is the side with the foreign key: Employee.department (@ManyToOne + @JoinColumn). Only the owning side's changes are written to the FK column.
  • The inverse side is Department.employees (@OneToMany(mappedBy = "department")). It is a mirror for navigation.

Multi-level: Department → Employee → Address

package com.trinity.hr.domain;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

@Entity
@Table(name = "department")
public class Department {

    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String name;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "department", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<Employee> employees = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Department() { }
    public Department(String name) { this.name = name; }

    // helper methods keep BOTH sides in sync (in-memory consistency + correct FK)
    public void addEmployee(Employee e) {
        employees.add(e);
        e.setDepartment(this);
    }
    public void removeEmployee(Employee e) {
        employees.remove(e);
        e.setDepartment(null);          // with orphanRemoval -> DELETE employee
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public List<Employee> getEmployees() { return List.copyOf(employees); }   // don't expose the mutable list
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "employee", indexes = @Index(name = "idx_employee_department", columnList = "department_id"))
class Employee {

    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
    private Long id;

    private String name;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "department_id", nullable = false, foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_employee_department"))
    private Department department;                          // OWNING side (has the FK)

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "employee", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<Address> addresses = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Employee() { }
    public Employee(String name) { this.name = name; }

    public void addAddress(Address a) { addresses.add(a); a.setEmployee(this); }
    public void removeAddress(Address a) { addresses.remove(a); a.setEmployee(null); }

    void setDepartment(Department d) { this.department = d; }
    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public Department getDepartment() { return department; }
    public List<Address> getAddresses() { return addresses; }

    // equals/hashCode on id with a constant hashCode: safe across transient -> managed transition
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Employee other)) return false;
        return id != null && Objects.equals(id, other.id);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return getClass().hashCode(); }
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "address")
class Address {

    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
    private Long id;

    private String line1;
    private String city;
    private String pincode;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private AddressType type;           // HOME, OFFICE

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "employee_id", nullable = false)
    private Employee employee;

    protected Address() { }
    public Address(String line1, String city, String pincode, AddressType type) {
        this.line1 = line1; this.city = city; this.pincode = pincode; this.type = type;
    }
    void setEmployee(Employee e) { this.employee = e; }
}

enum AddressType { HOME, OFFICE }

Persisting the whole graph with one save (cascade):

@Transactional
public Long createDept() {
    Department d = new Department("Traffic Ops");
    Employee e = new Employee("Ravi");
    e.addAddress(new Address("12 MG Road", "Bengaluru", "560001", AddressType.HOME));
    d.addEmployee(e);
    return departmentRepository.save(d).getId();   // cascades to employees and addresses
}

Cascade and orphanRemoval

  • cascade = ALL (PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH) belongs only on parent → child (composition). Never cascade from @ManyToOne (removing an employee would delete the department) or on @ManyToMany REMOVE.
  • orphanRemoval = true deletes a child removed from the collection. CascadeType.REMOVE deletes children only when the parent is deleted.
  • Don't replace the collection (setEmployees(new ArrayList<>())) when orphanRemoval is on. Hibernate throws "A collection with cascade=all-delete-orphan was no longer referenced". Call clear() and then addAll() instead.

Unidirectional @OneToMany and join tables

@OneToMany                     // no mappedBy, no @JoinColumn -> Hibernate creates JOIN TABLE department_employees
private List<Employee> employees;

@OneToMany
@JoinColumn(name = "department_id")   // unidirectional with FK in child: extra UPDATE statements to set FK
private List<Employee> employees;

@ManyToMany
@JoinTable(name = "employee_project",
        joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "employee_id"),
        inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "project_id"))
private Set<Project> projects = new HashSet<>();

A unidirectional @OneToMany without @JoinColumn produces an unexpected join table and inefficient SQL. Prefer bidirectional, or plain @ManyToOne alone. For a join table with extra columns (e.g. assigned_on), model it as an entity (EmployeeProject) with two @ManyToOnes.

Fetching multi-level data

@Query("select distinct d from Department d left join fetch d.employees where d.id = :id")
Optional<Department> findWithEmployees(Long id);
// then addresses via default_batch_fetch_size, or a 2nd query:
@Query("select distinct e from Employee e left join fetch e.addresses where e.department.id = :deptId")
List<Employee> findWithAddresses(Long deptId);

Fetching employees and addresses (two List bags) in one query gives MultipleBagFetchException and a Cartesian product. Use two queries.

Gotchas

  • Lombok @Data/@ToString/@EqualsAndHashCode on bidirectional entities cause StackOverflowError (recursive toString/hashCode) and trigger lazy loads.
  • Jackson on bidirectional entities recurses infinitely. Use DTOs, or @JsonManagedReference/@JsonBackReference (or @JsonIgnore).
  • Index FK columns. Postgres doesn't index them automatically.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Who owns the relationship? The side with @JoinColumn (the FK). mappedBy marks the inverse side.
  • Why helper methods? So both sides stay consistent in memory. Setting only the inverse side writes no FK.
  • List vs Set for collections? A Set avoids MultipleBagFetchException and duplicates, but needs correct equals/hashCode. A List keeps order (@OrderColumn/@OrderBy).
C27 Implementing audit logs.

1. Spring Data JPA auditing records who created or changed a row and when:

@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef = "auditorAware")
public class AuditConfig {
    @Bean
    public AuditorAware<String> auditorAware() {
        return () -> Optional.ofNullable(SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication())
                             .map(Authentication::getName);
    }
}

@MappedSuperclass
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
public abstract class Auditable {
    @CreatedBy      private String createdBy;
    @CreatedDate    private Instant createdAt;
    @LastModifiedBy private String updatedBy;
    @LastModifiedDate private Instant updatedAt;
}

2. Hibernate Envers keeps the full history of changes. Add @Audited on the entity, and Envers writes every revision to <table>_AUD plus REVINFO. Query old versions with AuditReader.

3. AOP-based audit table records business actions (who did what, on which resource, from which IP). Use a custom @AuditLog(action="DELETE_DEVICE") annotation with an @Aspect @Around advice that saves an audit_log row. Save it asynchronously, or publish to Kafka, so the main flow is not slowed down.

Other options are DB triggers and CDC (Debezium). Audit tables should be append-only.

There are four levels of auditing, from simple to enterprise.

1. Spring Data JPA auditing ("who and when" columns)

package com.trinity.citypulse.audit;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.domain.support.AuditingEntityListener;

import java.time.Instant;

@MappedSuperclass
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
public abstract class Auditable {

    @CreatedBy      @Column(updatable = false) protected String createdBy;
    @CreatedDate    @Column(updatable = false) protected Instant createdAt;
    @LastModifiedBy                            protected String updatedBy;
    @LastModifiedDate                          protected Instant updatedAt;
}
package com.trinity.citypulse.audit;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.data.domain.AuditorAware;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaAuditing;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.AnonymousAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;

import java.util.Optional;

@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef = "auditorAware")
public class AuditConfig {

    @Bean
    public AuditorAware<String> auditorAware() {
        return () -> Optional.ofNullable(SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication())
                .filter(Authentication::isAuthenticated)
                .filter(a -> !(a instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken))
                .map(Authentication::getName)            // JWT "sub"/preferred_username
                .or(() -> Optional.of("system"));        // schedulers, Kafka consumers
    }
}

@Entity public class Incident extends Auditable { ... }. The AuditingEntityListener fills the fields in @PrePersist/@PreUpdate. Limit: this tells you only the latest modifier. There is no history of values.

2. Hibernate Envers (full row history)

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
  <artifactId>hibernate-envers</artifactId>
</dependency>
@Entity
@Audited                                   // creates incident_aud table: all columns + rev + revtype (0 add,1 mod,2 del)
public class Incident extends Auditable {
    @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;
    private String status;
    @NotAudited private String transientNote;
}

@Entity
@RevisionEntity(UserRevisionListener.class)
@Table(name = "revinfo")
public class UserRevision extends DefaultRevisionEntity {   // add "who" to each revision
    private String username;
    public void setUsername(String u) { this.username = u; }
}

public class UserRevisionListener implements RevisionListener {
    @Override public void newRevision(Object rev) {
        var auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
        ((UserRevision) rev).setUsername(auth != null ? auth.getName() : "system");
    }
}

(Envers types are in org.hibernate.envers.*.) To query history, use AuditReaderFactory.get(em).createQuery().forRevisionsOfEntity(Incident.class, false, true), or Spring Data Envers' RevisionRepository<Incident, Long, Integer> (findRevisions(id)). Envers writes in the same transaction, so it is consistent, but it adds write overhead.

3. AOP plus an async audit table (business-action audit: "who did what, through which API")

@Target(ElementType.METHOD) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface AuditAction { String value(); }       // e.g. "CHALLAN_CANCELLED"
package com.trinity.citypulse.audit;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.slf4j.MDC;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.time.Instant;

@Aspect
@Component
public class AuditAspect {

    private final AuditWriter writer;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public AuditAspect(AuditWriter writer, ObjectMapper mapper) { this.writer = writer; this.mapper = mapper; }

    @Around("@annotation(audit)")
    public Object around(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, AuditAction audit) throws Throwable {
        // capture context ON the request thread (SecurityContext/MDC are ThreadLocal)
        var auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
        String user = auth != null ? auth.getName() : "system";
        String correlationId = MDC.get("correlationId");
        String args = safeJson(pjp.getArgs());
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        try {
            Object result = pjp.proceed();
            writer.write(new AuditEvent(audit.value(), user, args, "SUCCESS", null,
                    correlationId, Instant.now(), System.currentTimeMillis() - start));
            return result;
        } catch (Throwable ex) {
            writer.write(new AuditEvent(audit.value(), user, args, "FAILURE", ex.getMessage(),
                    correlationId, Instant.now(), System.currentTimeMillis() - start));
            throw ex;
        }
    }

    private String safeJson(Object[] args) {
        try { return mapper.writeValueAsString(args); } catch (Exception e) { return "[unserializable]"; }
    }
}
public record AuditEvent(String action, String username, String payload, String outcome, String error,
                         String correlationId, Instant at, long durationMs) { }

@Component
public class AuditWriter {
    private final AuditLogRepository repo;
    public AuditWriter(AuditLogRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    @Async("auditExecutor")                                       // needs @EnableAsync + a bounded executor
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)        // audit survives business rollback
    public void write(AuditEvent e) { repo.save(AuditLog.from(e)); }
}

Points to mention:

  • Mask PII in the payload (Aadhaar, phone numbers).
  • Capture the user before going async. Otherwise use DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor.
  • Use a bounded queue and a rejection policy so audit can't take the app down.
  • Make the audit table append-only (no UPDATE/DELETE grants) and partition it by month.

4. Kafka-based audit events (microservices / Smart City scale)

  • Every service publishes AuditEvents to an audit-events topic, keyed by entity id for ordering. A dedicated audit service consumes them into Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (search) or cold storage (S3/Parquet) for retention.
  • Consistency: publish only after commit.
    • @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) sends to Kafka: simple, but the event is lost if the app crashes after commit.
    • Or use the Transactional Outbox: write an outbox row in the same DB transaction, and let a relay or Debezium CDC publish to Kafka. This gives at-least-once delivery, and the consumer must be idempotent (dedupe by event id).
  • Benefits: decoupled, cross-service view, replayable, and no write latency on the business path.
@Component
public class AuditEventPublisher {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, AuditEvent> kafka;
    public AuditEventPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, AuditEvent> kafka) { this.kafka = kafka; }

    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    public void on(AuditEvent e) { kafka.send("audit-events", e.correlationId(), e); }
}
// in service: applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new AuditEvent(...));

Likely follow-ups:

  • JPA auditing vs Envers? JPA auditing gives the latest who/when columns. Envers gives a full versioned history per row.
  • How is the user captured in Kafka consumers or schedulers? There's no SecurityContext, so fall back to "system", or carry the user id in the message headers.
  • How do you make audit tamper-evident? Append-only storage, a hash chain or signed records, WORM storage, and separate DB credentials.
C28 URL shortener in Java/Spring Boot.

Design:

  • POST /api/shorten {longUrl} returns {shortUrl}.
  • GET /{code} looks up the original and redirects:
    • 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache it, so there is less load but no analytics.
    • 302/307 makes every hit go through the service, so you can track clicks.

Code generation:

  • Base62 of an auto-increment or sequence ID ([0-9a-zA-Z]). Seven characters give about 3.5 trillion codes. It is unique by construction, so there are no collisions.
  • Distributed: use a Snowflake ID or pre-allocated ID ranges per instance.
  • Alternative: a hash (MD5/SHA-256 of the URL, first 7 characters). Collisions are possible, so check and retry with a salt.

Duplicates and conflicts:

  • Put a UNIQUE constraint on short_code. On DataIntegrityViolationException, regenerate.
  • To return the same code for the same long URL, add a unique index on a long_url_hash and look it up first.
  • For custom aliases, check availability and return 409 Conflict if it is taken.

Storage:

  • Table url_mapping(id, short_code UNIQUE, long_url, created_at, expires_at, click_count) in an RDBMS or a key-value/NoSQL store.
  • Hot lookups go through a Redis cache-aside (code → longUrl, with a TTL).
  • Record analytics asynchronously (Kafka).
  • Add rate limiting, and validate URLs to block malicious links.
private static final String BASE62 = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
static String encode(long id) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    do { sb.append(BASE62.charAt((int) (id % 62))); id /= 62; } while (id > 0);
    return sb.reverse().toString();
}

@GetMapping("/{code}")
public ResponseEntity<Void> redirect(@PathVariable String code) {
    String longUrl = service.resolve(code);   // Redis -> DB, throws NotFound
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.FOUND).location(URI.create(longUrl)).build();
}

Requirements

  • Functional: shorten a long URL, redirect a short URL to the long one, optional custom alias, expiry, click analytics.
  • Non-functional: read-heavy (about 100:1 redirect vs create), low-latency redirects (under 10 ms at p99 from cache), high availability, unguessable or short codes.
  • Rough scale: 100M new URLs a month is about 40 writes/s, and about 4,000 redirects/s. Over 5 years that is about 6B rows at ~500 B each, roughly 3 TB.

API

POST /api/v1/urls            {"longUrl": "...", "customAlias": "blr-traffic", "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z"}
  -> 201 {"shortUrl": "https://tmy.ly/aZ3kQ9", "code": "aZ3kQ9", "expiresAt": ...}
GET  /{code}                 -> 302 Location: <longUrl>   (404 if unknown, 410 Gone if expired)
GET  /api/v1/urls/{code}/stats -> clicks, by day/country/referrer
DELETE /api/v1/urls/{code}   -> 204

Code generation: option A, Base62 of a DB sequence or ID (recommended)

  • Characters [0-9a-zA-Z]. 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, so 7 characters is plenty.
  • id → Base62 is a bijection, so there are no collisions by construction.
  • Downside: sequential codes are guessable/enumerable. Fixes: start at a large offset, apply a reversible permutation or obfuscation of the id (Feistel cipher, Hashids/Sqids), or use a random 64-bit id.
  • To scale writes: give each app instance a range of ids (e.g. reserve 10,000 at a time from the DB or Redis INCRBY), or use Snowflake ids. Then no DB round trip is needed per create.
public final class Base62 {
    private static final char[] ALPHABET =
            "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ".toCharArray();
    private Base62() { }

    public static String encode(long value) {
        if (value == 0) return "0";
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        while (value > 0) {
            sb.append(ALPHABET[(int) (value % 62)]);
            value /= 62;
        }
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }

    public static long decode(String s) {
        long result = 0;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            int d;
            if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') d = c - '0';
            else if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') d = c - 'a' + 10;
            else if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') d = c - 'A' + 36;
            else throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid char " + c);
            result = result * 62 + d;
        }
        return result;
    }
}

Option B: hash the long URL (MD5/SHA-256/MurmurHash, Base62-encoded, first 7 characters)

  • It is deterministic: the same URL gives the same code, so dedupe comes for free.
  • Truncation causes collisions. Seven Base62 characters carry only about 41.7 bits. By the birthday paradox, there is about a 50% chance of at least one collision after roughly 2 million URLs, and at billions of URLs collisions happen constantly. On collision, append a salt or counter and rehash, then retry.
  • Every create needs a DB check.

Collision and duplicate handling

  • A unique index on short_code is the final arbiter. Insert, and on DataIntegrityViolationException regenerate and retry (bounded, e.g. 3 times). Never "check then insert", which is a race.
  • Same long URL submitted again: keep a long_url_hash column (SHA-256) with a unique index (per user/tenant if needed), and return the existing code instead of creating a new one. Hash it because long URLs exceed index-length limits.
  • Custom aliases go through the same unique index. A conflict returns 409 Conflict.
@Transactional
public ShortUrl shorten(String longUrl, String alias, Instant expiresAt) {
    String hash = sha256(normalize(longUrl));
    if (alias == null) {
        Optional<ShortUrl> existing = repo.findByLongUrlHash(hash);
        if (existing.isPresent()) return existing.get();                       // idempotent create
    }
    long id = idGenerator.next();                                            // range-allocated
    String code = alias != null ? alias : Base62.encode(obfuscate(id));
    try {
        return repo.saveAndFlush(new ShortUrl(id, code, longUrl, hash, expiresAt));
    } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
        if (alias != null) throw new AliasTakenException(alias);              // -> 409
        return repo.findByLongUrlHash(hash).orElseThrow(() -> e);             // concurrent same-URL insert
    }
}

(In production, do the retry outside the failed transaction. After a constraint violation the persistence context is unusable, so the retry or lookup should run in a new transaction.)

Storage schema

CREATE TABLE short_url (
  id             BIGINT       PRIMARY KEY,
  short_code     VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,
  long_url       TEXT         NOT NULL,
  long_url_hash  CHAR(64)     NOT NULL,
  owner_id       BIGINT,
  created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
  is_active      BOOLEAN      NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  CONSTRAINT uk_short_code UNIQUE (short_code),
  CONSTRAINT uk_long_hash  UNIQUE (long_url_hash)        -- or (owner_id, long_url_hash)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_short_url_expires ON short_url (expires_at) WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL;
  • It is a pure key-value access pattern, so you can also use Cassandra or DynamoDB at large scale (partition key = short_code). SQL is fine up to billions of rows with sharding by code.
  • Redis cache: GET url:{code} → longUrl, using cache-aside with a TTL equal to min(expiry, 24h). Hot links follow a Zipf distribution, so an 80–90%+ hit ratio is realistic. Cache negative lookups ("NULL" for 1 minute) to stop penetration attacks with random codes, or put a Bloom filter of existing codes in front.

Redirect: 301 vs 302

301 Moved Permanently 302 Found / 307 Temporary
Browser caches it Yes, so later clicks never reach you No, every click hits the server
Load lower higher
Analytics lost after the first click accurate
Changing the target or expiring impossible for clients that cached it works

Pick 302 (or 307) when you need analytics, expiry or editable links, which covers most products. Pick 301 for pure, permanent redirects where you want minimum load and SEO link equity.

Expiry: check expires_at on read (return 410 Gone), set the Redis TTL to the expiry, and have a nightly batch job delete or archive expired rows. Recycling codes is risky, so avoid it.

Analytics: don't write to the DB on the redirect path. Publish a click event (code, timestamp, IP → geo, user agent, referrer) asynchronously to Kafka. Stream-process it (Kafka Streams/Flink) into aggregates in ClickHouse, Druid or a time-series store. Use a Redis INCR for a real-time counter.

Scale and architecture

Client -> CDN/edge (optionally caches 301s) -> LB -> stateless redirect service (N pods, HPA)
          -> Redis Cluster (cache) -> DB (primary + read replicas / sharded by code)
       -> Kafka (click events) -> analytics consumers -> OLAP store
Create path: API service -> ID range allocator -> DB (unique indexes) -> warm cache
  • Split the read (redirect) and write (create) services, and scale them independently.
  • Add rate limiting per API key/IP on create (Redis token bucket), malicious URL scanning (Safe Browsing API), and abuse protection.
  • Multi-region: the cache is regional and the DB has global replication. Ids should be region-prefixed or Snowflake to avoid coordination.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not UUIDs as codes? Too long (22+ characters in Base62). Short codes are the whole point.
  • How do you avoid a single point of failure for the counter? Hand out id ranges per node, or use Snowflake (timestamp + node id + sequence).
  • How do you handle a viral link? The Redis hot key plus a local Caffeine near-cache on each pod, and CDN caching for 301s.
C29 What does LOC mean?

LOC = Lines of Code. It is a size metric for a codebase or a change, sometimes used for effort or productivity estimates and code-quality ratios (defects per KLOC). Variants are SLOC (source lines, excluding blanks and comments) and KLOC (thousands). It is a weak productivity measure, because fewer, cleaner lines are often better. In a banking/trade-finance context, LOC can also mean Letter of Credit: a bank's guarantee of payment to a seller on behalf of a buyer.

It depends on the context, so clarify it in the interview ("Do you mean lines of code?").

  1. Lines of Code (software engineering): a size metric for a codebase or a change.
    • Variants: physical LOC (all lines), SLOC/NCLOC (source lines excluding blanks and comments; SonarQube reports "Lines of Code" as NCLOC), and logical LOC (statements).
    • Uses: rough size and effort estimation (COCOMO), normalising defect density (bugs per KLOC), and tracking code growth or PR size (small PRs, roughly under 400 LOC, review better).
    • Limits: it measures volume, not value or quality. Fewer lines often means better code, and LOC varies by language and style. Never use it as a productivity metric. Better signals: cyclomatic or cognitive complexity, coverage, DORA metrics, and story or cycle-time throughput.
    • Tools: cloc, tokei, SonarQube, git diff --stat.
  2. Letter of Credit (banking/trade finance): a bank's guarantee to pay a seller on behalf of a buyer once documents meeting the terms are presented (governed by UCP 600). Types include sight/usance, revocable/irrevocable, confirmed, standby LC (SBLC) and back-to-back. This matters if the interviewer's domain is BFSI. Messages travel over SWIFT (MT700 for issuance).
  3. Others: Line of Control (geography), and Locus of Control (psychology).

In a Smart City context it is almost always lines of code, e.g. "The incident service is about 25K LOC across 6 modules, with 80% coverage."

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is a higher LOC count good? No. It means more to maintain. Value is delivered features at good quality.
  • What does SonarQube count as LOC? Non-comment, non-blank lines (NCLOC).
  • KLOC? Thousands of lines of code, e.g. defects per KLOC.
C30 @Transactional and why transaction management is used. Hexaware

Transactions guarantee ACID for a unit of work. Either all DB operations commit or all roll back, for example "debit + credit" or "save incident + save assignment". @Transactional is declarative. Spring wraps the bean in an AOP proxy that begins, commits or rolls back through the PlatformTransactionManager.

Key attributes:

Attribute Key points
propagation REQUIRED (default: join the existing transaction or create one), REQUIRES_NEW (suspend the outer one and start a new one, e.g. for an audit log), NESTED (savepoint), SUPPORTS, MANDATORY, NEVER, NOT_SUPPORTED
rollbackFor By default, rollback happens only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error). Checked exceptions commit unless you set rollbackFor = Exception.class
readOnly = true Flush and dirty-checking optimisations for queries
isolation, timeout Isolation level and timeout

Pitfalls:

  • Self-invocation. Calling a @Transactional method from another method of the same class bypasses the proxy, so no transaction is applied. Fix it by moving the method to another bean or injecting self/TransactionTemplate.
  • @Transactional has no effect on private methods; it applies only to proxied, public methods.
  • Catching the exception inside the method prevents rollback.

How it works (proxy-based AOP)

  • @EnableTransactionManagement (auto-enabled by Boot) registers BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor with TransactionInterceptor.
  • At bean creation, the auto-proxy creator wraps @Transactional beans in a CGLIB proxy (C4).
  • A call through the proxy goes to TransactionInterceptor.invoke → TransactionAspectSupport.invokeWithinTransaction:
    1. read the TransactionAttribute (propagation, isolation, timeout, readOnly, rollback rules);
    2. PlatformTransactionManager.getTransaction(def). JpaTransactionManager begins the JPA transaction, takes a JDBC connection, and binds the EntityManagerHolder/ConnectionHolder to the thread through TransactionSynchronizationManager (ThreadLocal);
    3. invoke the target method;
    4. on success, commit (flush, then commit). On an exception, check rollbackOn(ex) and roll back, or commit if the rule says so;
    5. clean up and unbind.

Propagation

Propagation Existing tx present No tx present
REQUIRED (default) join it create a new one
REQUIRES_NEW suspend it and create an independent new one (a new connection!) create a new one
NESTED savepoint inside the existing tx (rolls back to the savepoint only). Supported with JDBC DataSourceTransactionManager; limited with JPA create a new one
SUPPORTS join it run non-transactionally
NOT_SUPPORTED suspend it, run non-transactionally run non-transactionally
MANDATORY join it throw IllegalTransactionStateException
NEVER throw run non-transactionally

The use case for REQUIRES_NEW is audit or failure logging that must persist even when the outer transaction rolls back. The cost: it holds 2 connections per thread, so under load you risk pool exhaustion or deadlock.

Isolation levels

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom
READ_UNCOMMITTED possible possible possible
READ_COMMITTED (Postgres/Oracle/SQL Server default) no possible possible
REPEATABLE_READ (MySQL InnoDB default) no no possible (InnoDB prevents most with next-key locks)
SERIALIZABLE no no no

Isolation.DEFAULT uses the DB default. For counters and inventory (e.g. parking slot booking), prefer optimistic locking (@Version) or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)) over raising the isolation level globally. Note: JpaTransactionManager supports a custom isolation level only through HibernateJpaDialect.

Rollback rules

  • By default it rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException) and Error, and commits on checked exceptions (an EJB heritage).
  • @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) or noRollbackFor = BusinessWarningException.class.
  • Catching the exception inside the method means no rollback, unless you rethrow or call TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly().
  • UnexpectedRollbackException: an inner REQUIRED method throws, so the shared transaction is marked rollback-only. The outer method catches the exception and tries to commit, and Spring throws "Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only". Fix it with REQUIRES_NEW for the inner call, by not catching, or by redesigning.

readOnly = true

  • Hibernate sets the session to FlushMode.MANUAL and read-only, so no dirty-checking snapshots are kept (less memory and CPU).
  • It calls Connection.setReadOnly(true) as a hint to the driver or DB, which can route to a replica with a routing DataSource.
  • It does not prevent writes in all DBs. Native queries may still write.

The self-invocation pitfall

@Service
public class ChallanService {
    public void processBatch(List<Long> ids) {
        ids.forEach(this::processOne);       // 'this' = target, NOT the proxy -> no transaction!
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void processOne(Long id) { ... }
}

Fixes:

  1. Move processOne to another bean (the cleanest fix).
  2. Self-injection: @Lazy @Autowired private ChallanService self; then self.processOne(id).
  3. TransactionTemplate (programmatic):
    private final TransactionTemplate txTemplate;   // inject PlatformTransactionManager, then new TransactionTemplate(tm)
public void processBatch(List<Long> ids) {
    ids.forEach(id -> txTemplate.executeWithoutResult(status -> processOneInternal(id)));
}
  4. AspectJ weaving mode (@EnableTransactionManagement(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ)), which has no proxy limitations but needs build or load-time weaving.

Method visibility

  • Private methods are never transactional. The proxy can't override them, and Spring silently ignores the annotation.
  • Since Spring 6.0, protected and package-private methods work with CGLIB class proxies. Before 6.0, only public methods worked.
  • final methods can't be overridden either, so no transaction. The same goes for static methods.

Other gotchas

  • @Transactional on a @PostConstruct method has no effect (C5).
  • @Async plus @Transactional: the transaction is on the async thread. ThreadLocal transactions don't cross threads.
  • A long transaction holding a DB connection while calling remote APIs: do the HTTP calls outside the transaction.
  • timeout = 5 (seconds) sets the query timeout.
  • In tests, @Transactional on a test class rolls back after each test by default.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Class-level vs method-level @Transactional? The method-level annotation overrides the class-level one. Class level applies to all methods the proxy can intercept.
  • Does @Transactional work on interfaces? Yes, since Spring 5, also with class proxies. Annotating the concrete class is still recommended.
  • How do you run code after a commit? @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT), or TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization.
C31 @Cacheable, caching for DB performance, and cache consistency across instances. Hexaware

Enable caching with @EnableCaching. With @Cacheable, the first call runs the method and stores the result. Later calls with the same key return the cached value without hitting the DB, which reduces latency and DB load for read-heavy data such as master data or device configs.

@Cacheable(value = "employees", key = "#id", unless = "#result == null")
public EmployeeDto getById(Long id) { ... }

@CachePut(value = "employees", key = "#result.id")
public EmployeeDto update(EmployeeDto dto) { ... }

@CacheEvict(value = "employees", key = "#id")
public void delete(Long id) { ... }

Preventing DB problems:

Problem Fix
Stale or unbounded memory TTL plus size-based eviction (Caffeine maximumSize, Redis time-to-live)
Cache stampede (a hot key expires and many requests hit the DB) @Cacheable(sync = true), a lock or single-flight, jittered TTLs, refresh-ahead
Cache penetration (repeated lookups for non-existent keys) Cache null or empty results with a short TTL, a Bloom filter, input validation
Avalanche (many keys expire together) Randomised TTLs

Consistency across instances and microservices:

  • A local in-process cache (Caffeine) on each pod drifts, so use a distributed cache (Redis) shared by all instances.
  • Use the cache-aside pattern: read from cache, fall back to the DB and populate the cache. On write, update the DB, then evict (@CacheEvict) instead of updating the cache.
  • When another service owns the data, publish a domain event (Kafka) or Redis pub/sub on change, and consumers evict their entries.
  • Short TTLs are the safety net. For a two-level cache (local + Redis), broadcast invalidations.

Spring Cache abstraction: @EnableCaching plus a CacheManager (Caffeine, Redis, JCache/Ehcache, Hazelcast). It is proxy-based like @Transactional, so it has the same self-invocation and private-method pitfalls.

@Service
public class JunctionService {

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "junction", key = "#id", unless = "#result == null")
    public JunctionDto get(Long id) { return mapper.toDto(repo.findById(id).orElseThrow()); }

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "junctionsByWard", key = "#wardId", sync = true)   // sync: one loader per key per JVM
    public List<JunctionDto> byWard(String wardId) { ... }

    @CachePut(cacheNames = "junction", key = "#result.id()")                    // always executes, updates cache
    public JunctionDto update(Long id, UpdateJunction cmd) { ... }

    @Caching(evict = {
        @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "junction", key = "#id"),
        @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "junctionsByWard", allEntries = true) })
    public void delete(Long id) { ... }
}

Attributes:

  • key (SpEL; the default is SimpleKeyGenerator over all args), keyGenerator
  • condition (evaluated before the call), unless (evaluated after, on #result)
  • sync
  • beforeInvocation on evict (evict even if the method throws)

Local cache: Caffeine (single instance, or data that is OK to diverge)

spring:
  cache:
    type: caffeine
    cache-names: junction,junctionsByWard
    caffeine:
      spec: maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=10m,recordStats

Distributed cache: Redis, with per-cache TTL and JSON serialisation

package com.trinity.citypulse.config;

import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.cache.RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer;
import org.springframework.cache.annotation.EnableCaching;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.data.redis.cache.RedisCacheConfiguration;
import org.springframework.data.redis.serializer.GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer;
import org.springframework.data.redis.serializer.RedisSerializationContext.SerializationPair;

import java.time.Duration;

@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig {

    @Bean
    public RedisCacheConfiguration defaultCacheConfig() {
        return RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
                .entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
                .disableCachingNullValues()
                .prefixCacheNameWith("citypulse:v1:")          // versioned key prefix
                .serializeValuesWith(SerializationPair.fromSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer()));
    }

    @Bean
    public RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer perCacheTtl(RedisCacheConfiguration base) {
        return builder -> builder
                .withCacheConfiguration("junction", base.entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(30)))
                .withCacheConfiguration("liveSignalState", base.entryTtl(Duration.ofSeconds(15)))
                .transactionAware();                           // put/evict only after the tx commits
    }
}

Avoiding DB performance problems with a cache, and the classic failure modes

Problem What happens Mitigation
Stampede / thundering herd / dog-piling A hot key expires, and 1,000 concurrent requests all hit the DB sync = true (per JVM); a distributed lock (Redisson) so one rebuilds while others wait or serve stale data; early probabilistic refresh; Caffeine refreshAfterWrite
Penetration Requests for non-existent keys always miss and hit the DB (attacks, bad ids) Cache nulls briefly; a Bloom filter of valid ids; input validation and rate limits
Avalanche Many keys expire at the same moment, or Redis goes down, and load spikes TTL jitter (ttl + random(0..60s)); a multi-level cache (Caffeine + Redis); circuit breaker or fallback; Redis HA (Sentinel/Cluster)
Hot key One key overloads one Redis shard A local near-cache; replicate the key under suffixes
Big values Slow serialisation, network saturation Cache DTOs not entities, compress, paginate
Sizing Unbounded caches lead to OOM maximumSize/maximumWeight, Redis maxmemory + allkeys-lru/lfu, and monitoring hit ratio and evictions via Actuator cache.* metrics

What to cache: read-mostly reference data (wards, junction metadata, device configs), expensive aggregations, and remote API responses. Don't cache highly volatile or per-user sensitive data without careful keys and TTLs. Never cache JPA entities (lazy proxies, detached state).

Cache consistency across multiple instances and microservices

The problem: with a local cache, instance A updates the DB and evicts its own cache, but instances B and C keep serving stale data until their TTL expires.

Strategies:

  1. A centralised distributed cache (Redis): every instance reads and evicts the same entry, so instance divergence goes away.
  2. Cache-aside with evict-on-write: write to the DB, then delete the cache key (@CacheEvict). Don't update the cache: concurrent writers can leave a stale value. Do it after commit (transactionAware() or @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)). Otherwise a reader can re-populate the old value between the eviction and the commit.
    • Remaining race: a reader misses, loads the old value, the writer commits and evicts, then the reader writes the old value. This is rare. Mitigations are a delayed double delete (evict again after ~500 ms) and short TTLs.
  3. Write-through / write-behind: the cache layer writes to the DB synchronously (through) or asynchronously (behind, which risks data loss). It suits cache-first systems (Hazelcast/Redis Gears) and is less common with Spring's annotations.
  4. Two-level (Caffeine + Redis) with broadcast invalidation: on write, publish {cache, key} on Redis Pub/Sub or a Kafka topic. Every instance subscribes and evicts its local L1 entry.
  5. Cross-microservice ownership: service X caches data owned by service Y. Y publishes domain events (JunctionUpdated) to Kafka, and X's consumer evicts or refreshes its cache. Even better is CDC (Debezium) from Y's DB, which catches every change including manual SQL fixes.
  6. Versioning: keys include a version (junction:{id}:v{version}) or a namespace version (citypulse:v2:). Bumping it invalidates everything at once, which helps with schema changes in DTOs. You can also compare @Version before serving.
  7. Short TTL as a safety net: even with explicit invalidation, always set a TTL so missed events self-heal.

Here is an example of Kafka-driven eviction:

@Component
public class JunctionCacheInvalidator {
    private final CacheManager cacheManager;
    public JunctionCacheInvalidator(CacheManager cacheManager) { this.cacheManager = cacheManager; }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "junction-events", groupId = "#{T(java.util.UUID).randomUUID().toString()}") // every instance gets it
    public void onEvent(JunctionChangedEvent event) {
        var cache = cacheManager.getCache("junction");
        if (cache != null) cache.evict(event.junctionId());
    }
}

(A unique group id per instance gives broadcast semantics. An alternative is a static group per pod name.)

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why delete instead of update on write? Concurrent updates can write values in the wrong order. A delete plus a lazy reload converges.
  • Is sync = true enough for stampede protection? Only within one JVM. Across pods you need a distributed lock or stale-while-revalidate.
  • How do you monitor the cache? Actuator /actuator/caches, and the Micrometer metrics cache.gets{result=hit|miss}, cache.evictions, plus Redis INFO.
C32 JUnit annotations.
Annotation Purpose
@Test Marks a test method
@BeforeEach / @AfterEach Run before or after each test (setup and cleanup)
@BeforeAll / @AfterAll Run once per class (must be static unless @TestInstance(PER_CLASS))
@DisplayName Readable test name
@Disabled Skip a test
@ParameterizedTest + @ValueSource/@CsvSource/@MethodSource Run one test with many inputs
@Nested Group related tests in an inner class
@ExtendWith Register extensions (MockitoExtension, SpringExtension)
@Tag, @Timeout, @RepeatedTest Filtering, time limits, repetition
Mockito @Mock Create a mock
Mockito @InjectMocks Create the class under test and inject the mocks into it
@Spy, @Captor Partial mock, argument captor 
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({"2,3,5", "10,-1,9"})
void adds(int a, int b, int expected) { assertEquals(expected, a + b); }

JUnit 5 = Platform (launcher) + Jupiter (the new programming and extension model) + Vintage (runs JUnit 3/4). Imports come from org.junit.jupiter.api.*.

Core and lifecycle

Annotation Purpose
@Test A test method (no public needed)
@BeforeEach / @AfterEach Before and after each test (JUnit 4: @Before/@After)
@BeforeAll / @AfterAll Once per class. Must be static unless @TestInstance(PER_CLASS) (JUnit 4: @BeforeClass)
@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) One instance for all tests (the default is PER_METHOD, a new instance per test)
@DisplayName("..."), @DisplayNameGeneration(ReplaceUnderscores.class) Readable names
@Nested Inner (non-static) class for grouping, e.g. "when junction is offline"
@Tag("integration") Filter in Maven Surefire/Failsafe (groups)
@Disabled("reason") Skip
@Timeout(value = 2, unit = SECONDS) Fail if too slow
@RepeatedTest(5) Repeat
@TestFactory Dynamic tests (returns a Stream<DynamicTest>)
@TestTemplate Template invoked by providers (the base of parameterized and repeated tests)
@TestMethodOrder(OrderAnnotation.class) + @Order(1) Ordering (avoid order dependence)
@TestClassOrder Order nested classes
@ExtendWith(X.class) Register an extension (MockitoExtension, SpringExtension)
@RegisterExtension A programmatic extension instance on a field (e.g. WireMock)
@TempDir Inject a temp directory (Path)
@AutoClose (5.11+) Close a field after the test
@EnabledOnOs, @DisabledOnJre, @EnabledIfSystemProperty, @EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable, @EnabledIf("method") Conditional execution

Execution order for one test: constructor → @BeforeAll (once) → @BeforeEach → @Test → @AfterEach → … → @AfterAll. Inside @Nested classes, the outer @BeforeEach runs before the inner one.

Parameterized tests (junit-jupiter-params)

import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class FineCalculatorTest {

    private final FineCalculator calc = new FineCalculator();

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} km/h over -> Rs {1}")
    @CsvSource({ "5, 0", "15, 1000", "35, 2000", "60, 4000" })
    void speedingFine(int kmhOver, int expected) {
        assertThat(calc.speeding(kmhOver)).isEqualTo(expected);
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = { "KA01AB1234", "MH12DE4567" })
    void validPlates(String plate) { assertThat(PlateValidator.isValid(plate)).isTrue(); }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @NullAndEmptySource
    @ValueSource(strings = { "  ", "123" })
    void invalidPlates(String plate) { assertThat(PlateValidator.isValid(plate)).isFalse(); }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @EnumSource(value = ViolationType.class, names = { "RED_LIGHT", "WRONG_WAY" })
    void severeViolations(ViolationType type) { assertThat(type.isSevere()).isTrue(); }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @MethodSource("fineCases")
    void fines(ViolationType type, int repeat, int expected) {
        assertThat(calc.fine(type, repeat)).isEqualTo(expected);
    }

    static Stream<Arguments> fineCases() {
        return Stream.of(Arguments.of(ViolationType.RED_LIGHT, 1, 1000),
                         Arguments.of(ViolationType.RED_LIGHT, 2, 2000));
    }
}

Other sources: @NullSource, @EmptySource, @CsvFileSource(resources = "/fines.csv", numLinesToSkip = 1), @ArgumentsSource(MyProvider.class) and @FieldSource (5.11+). Arguments can be aggregated with ArgumentsAccessor or @AggregateWith.

Assertions: assertEquals, assertTrue, assertNull, assertThrows, assertDoesNotThrow, assertTimeout, and assertAll (grouped; reports every failure). Most teams use AssertJ (assertThat(...), fluent, ships with spring-boot-starter-test). Assumptions.assumeTrue(...) skips a test when an assumption doesn't hold.

Mockito annotations (org.mockito.*, with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class))

Annotation Purpose
@Mock A mock: all methods return defaults (null/0/empty) unless stubbed
@Spy Wraps a real object; real methods run unless stubbed (use doReturn().when(spy) for stubbing)
@InjectMocks Creates the class under test and injects @Mock/@Spy (constructor → setter → field)
@Captor ArgumentCaptor<T> to inspect arguments passed to mocks
@MockitoSettings(strictness = Strictness.LENIENT) Relax strict stubs (the default STRICT_STUBS fails on unused stubs with UnnecessaryStubbingException)

Key APIs: when(...).thenReturn/thenThrow/thenAnswer, doThrow/doNothing/doReturn().when(mock).method() (for void methods and spies), verify(mock, times(1)/never()/atLeastOnce()).method(...), verifyNoMoreInteractions, InOrder, argument matchers any(), eq(), argThat() (if you use one matcher, use matchers for every argument), mockStatic (inline mock maker, the default since Mockito 5), and BDD style given(...).willReturn(...) / then(mock).should().

Likely follow-ups:

  • @BeforeAll must be static, why? With PER_METHOD lifecycle there is no instance yet. Use @TestInstance(PER_CLASS) to make it non-static.
  • @Mock vs @Spy? A mock is entirely fake. A spy is a real object with selective stubbing.
  • JUnit 4 to 5 differences? @Before→@BeforeEach, @RunWith→@ExtendWith, @Ignore→@Disabled, @Test(expected=…)→assertThrows, and the new modular architecture with nested and parameterized tests.
C33 Writing test cases for Spring Boot applications.
Level Tool Loads Use for
Unit JUnit 5 + Mockito (@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)) No Spring Service logic, fast
Web slice @WebMvcTest(EmployeeController.class) + MockMvc MVC layer only Controllers, validation, JSON, advice
JPA slice @DataJpaTest JPA + embedded/Testcontainers DB, rollback per test Repositories, custom queries
Integration @SpringBootTest (+ webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) Full context End-to-end flows
Real infra Testcontainers (@Testcontainers, @Container, @ServiceConnection) Real Postgres/Kafka/Redis in Docker Prod-like integration tests

Mock Spring beans with @MockBean up to Boot 3.3. It is deprecated from Boot 3.4; use @MockitoBean instead.

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class EmployeeServiceTest {
    @Mock EmployeeRepository repo;
    @InjectMocks EmployeeService service;

    @Test
    void returnsEmployee() {
        Employee e = new Employee(); e.setName("Asha");
        when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(e));
        assertEquals("Asha", service.getById(1L).getName());
        verify(repo).findById(1L);
    }
}

Follow Arrange-Act-Assert (Given-When-Then), keep one behaviour per test, and use JaCoCo for coverage.

The test pyramid

        /  E2E / UI (few)      \      Postman/Newman, Selenium/Cypress against deployed env
       /  Integration (some)    \     @SpringBootTest + Testcontainers, contract tests
      /  Slice tests             \    @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest, @RestClientTest
     /  Unit tests (many, fast)   \   JUnit 5 + Mockito, no Spring context

Aim for fast feedback: most logic gets plain unit tests, and Spring contexts load only where wiring, serialisation or SQL matters. Spring's context cache reuses an identical configuration across test classes. Every distinct @MockitoBean set or property set creates a new context, which slows the suite.

1. Service unit test (Mockito, no Spring): the full example

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import com.trinity.hr.common.ResourceNotFoundException;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.DisplayName;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Nested;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.ArgumentCaptor;
import org.mockito.Captor;
import org.mockito.InjectMocks;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Optional;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.then;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.never;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class EmployeeServiceTest {

    @Mock EmployeeRepository repository;
    @InjectMocks EmployeeService service;
    @Captor ArgumentCaptor<Employee> employeeCaptor;

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("getEmployeeById")
    class GetById {

        @Test
        void returnsDto_whenEmployeeExists() {
            Employee e = new Employee("Asha", "asha@trinity.com", "Traffic", new BigDecimal("90000"),
                    LocalDate.of(2022, 1, 10));
            given(repository.findById(1L)).willReturn(Optional.of(e));

            EmployeeDto dto = service.getEmployeeById(1L);

            assertThat(dto.name()).isEqualTo("Asha");
            assertThat(dto.department()).isEqualTo("Traffic");
            then(repository).should().findById(1L);
        }

        @Test
        void throwsNotFound_whenMissing() {
            given(repository.findById(99L)).willReturn(Optional.empty());

            assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.getEmployeeById(99L))
                    .isInstanceOf(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
                    .hasMessage("Employee not found with id 99");

            then(repository).should(never()).save(any());
        }
    }
}

(When the service has a create method, employeeCaptor verifies what was saved: then(repository).should().save(employeeCaptor.capture()); assertThat(employeeCaptor.getValue().getEmail()).isEqualTo(...).)

2. Web slice: @WebMvcTest. This loads only the MVC infrastructure (controllers, advice, converters, filters, WebMvcConfigurer). Services are mocked. See C34 for the full MockMvc example.

@WebMvcTest(EmployeeController.class)
class EmployeeControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mockMvc;
    @MockitoBean EmployeeService service;     // Boot 3.4+/Spring 6.2: org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean
}
  • @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean (Spring Framework 6.2, Boot 3.4+) replace Boot's @MockBean/@SpyBean (org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito), which are deprecated in 3.4 and removed in Boot 4.
  • With Spring Security on the classpath, @WebMvcTest applies security. Use @WithMockUser or .with(jwt()), or exclude it.

3. JPA slice: @DataJpaTest. This loads entities, repositories, EntityManager, TestEntityManager and Flyway/Liquibase. Each test is transactional and rolled back. By default it replaces the DataSource with an embedded DB (H2). To test against the real engine, use Testcontainers:

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.jdbc.AutoConfigureTestDatabase;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.TestEntityManager;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@DataJpaTest
@Testcontainers
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)   // keep the container DB
class EmployeeRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection                                   // Boot 3.1+: wires spring.datasource.* automatically
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired EmployeeRepository repository;
    @Autowired TestEntityManager em;

    @Test
    void findByEmail_returnsEmployee() {
        em.persistAndFlush(new Employee("Ravi", "ravi@trinity.com", "Ops", new BigDecimal("50000"),
                LocalDate.now()));
        em.clear();                                      // force a real SELECT, not the 1st-level cache

        assertThat(repository.findByEmail("ravi@trinity.com"))
                .get().extracting(Employee::getName).isEqualTo("Ravi");
    }
}

(Testcontainers 2.x moves the class to org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer, which is non-generic. Before Boot 3.1, use @DynamicPropertySource to register spring.datasource.url and the other properties.)

4. Full integration: @SpringBootTest. This loads the whole context. Use webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT for a real server, or MOCK (the default) with @AutoConfigureMockMvc. Combine it with Testcontainers for Postgres, Kafka (KafkaContainer) and Redis, with WireMock for external HTTP, and with Awaitility for async assertions.

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@Testcontainers
class IncidentFlowIT {
    @Container @ServiceConnection static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");
    @Container @ServiceConnection static KafkaContainer kafka =
            new KafkaContainer(DockerImageName.parse("apache/kafka:3.8.0"));   // org.testcontainers.kafka.KafkaContainer
    @Autowired TestRestTemplate rest;
    // POST incident -> assert DB row -> assert Kafka event consumed (Awaitility)
}

Tip: put the containers in a shared abstract base class, or a @TestConfiguration with @Bean @ServiceConnection methods, so the context is reused. Spring Boot 3.1+ also supports TestApplication with SpringApplication.from(App::main).with(TestcontainersConfig.class) for local dev.

Other slices: @JsonTest (Jackson mapping), @RestClientTest (RestTemplate/RestClient with MockRestServiceServer), @WebFluxTest, @DataRedisTest, @DataMongoTest, @JdbcTest. Use ApplicationContextRunner for auto-config and conditional tests.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not use H2 for repository tests? Dialect differences (JSONB, sequences, native queries) hide bugs. Testcontainers matches production.
  • Why is my test suite slow? Too many unique contexts (different @MockitoBean sets or properties). Standardise base classes and prefer slices or unit tests.
  • Unit vs integration test in Maven? Surefire runs *Test, Failsafe runs *IT in the integration-test/verify phase.
C34 Testing REST APIs.

MockMvc (no real server; usually with @WebMvcTest):

@WebMvcTest(EmployeeController.class)
class EmployeeControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mockMvc;
    @MockitoBean EmployeeService service;   // @MockBean on Boot < 3.4

    @Test
    void getById_returns200() throws Exception {
        Employee e = new Employee(); e.setId(1L); e.setName("Asha");
        when(service.getById(1L)).thenReturn(e);

        mockMvc.perform(get("/api/employees/1").accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
               .andExpect(status().isOk())
               .andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("Asha"));
    }

    @Test
    void create_invalidBody_returns400() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(post("/api/employees").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content("{}"))
               .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());
    }
}

Other tools:

  • TestRestTemplate/WebTestClient with @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) for real HTTP calls.
  • RestAssured for fluent BDD-style API tests: given().when().get("/api/employees/1").then().statusCode(200).
  • Postman/Newman for manual and collection-based testing in CI.
  • WireMock to stub downstream services.

1. MockMvc (server-side, no real HTTP, fast): the full example

package com.trinity.hr.employee;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.trinity.hr.common.GlobalExceptionHandler;
import com.trinity.hr.common.ResourceNotFoundException;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Import;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.hamcrest.Matchers.is;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.eq;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.verifyNoInteractions;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.*;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultHandlers.print;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.*;

@WebMvcTest(EmployeeController.class)
@Import(GlobalExceptionHandler.class)             // advice is picked up by the slice anyway; explicit for clarity
class EmployeeControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mockMvc;
    @Autowired ObjectMapper objectMapper;
    @MockitoBean EmployeeService service;

    @Test
    void getById_returns200AndBody() throws Exception {
        given(service.getEmployeeById(1L)).willReturn(
                new EmployeeDto(1L, "Asha", "asha@trinity.com", "Traffic", LocalDate.of(2022, 1, 10)));

        mockMvc.perform(get("/api/v1/employees/{id}", 1L).accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
                .andDo(print())
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andExpect(content().contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id", is(1)))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("Asha"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.joiningDate").value("2022-01-10"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.salary").doesNotExist());
    }

    @Test
    void getById_returns404ProblemDetail_whenMissing() throws Exception {
        given(service.getEmployeeById(99L)).willThrow(new ResourceNotFoundException("Employee", 99L));

        mockMvc.perform(get("/api/v1/employees/99"))
                .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
                .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Resource Not Found"))
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.detail").value("Employee not found with id 99"));
    }

    @Test
    void create_returns400_whenBodyInvalid() throws Exception {
        String body = objectMapper.writeValueAsString(Map.of("name", "", "email", "not-an-email"));

        mockMvc.perform(post("/api/v1/employees")
                        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                        .content(body))
                .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());

        verifyNoInteractions(service);
    }

    @Test
    void update_returns200() throws Exception {
        given(service.update(eq(1L), any())).willReturn(
                new EmployeeDto(1L, "Asha K", "asha@trinity.com", "Traffic", LocalDate.of(2022, 1, 10)));

        mockMvc.perform(put("/api/v1/employees/1")
                        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                        .content("""
                                {"name":"Asha K","email":"asha@trinity.com","department":"Traffic"}
                                """))
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("Asha K"));
    }
}

(The create and update tests assume the controller also exposes POST and PUT mapped to the service, with a validated request record.) For secured APIs, add spring-security-test, then use @WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN"), .with(jwt().authorities(...)) and .with(csrf()).

Spring Framework 6.2 also adds MockMvcTester, which uses AssertJ-style assertions: assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/v1/employees/1")).hasStatusOk().bodyJson()....

2. WebTestClient (fluent; for WebFlux, or for MVC against a running server)

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureWebTestClient
class EmployeeApiWebClientIT {
    @Autowired WebTestClient client;   // needs spring-webflux on the test classpath for MVC apps

    @Test
    void getEmployee() {
        client.get().uri("/api/v1/employees/{id}", 1)
              .exchange()
              .expectStatus().isOk()
              .expectBody()
              .jsonPath("$.name").isEqualTo("Asha");
    }
}

You can also bind it to MockMvc with MockMvcWebTestClient.bindTo(mockMvc). TestRestTemplate is the classic blocking option with RANDOM_PORT.

3. RestAssured (BDD DSL, black-box against a running app or environment)

import static io.restassured.RestAssured.given;
import static org.hamcrest.Matchers.equalTo;

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class EmployeeRestAssuredIT {
    @LocalServerPort int port;

    @Test
    void getEmployee() {
        given().port(port).accept("application/json")
        .when().get("/api/v1/employees/{id}", 1)
        .then().statusCode(200).body("name", equalTo("Asha"));
    }
}

(spring-mock-mvc RestAssured module: RestAssuredMockMvc for the MockMvc mode.)

4. Postman / Newman (manual, exploratory and environment-level regression)

  • Collections with environments (dev/qa/uat variables), pre-request scripts (fetch a token from Keycloak), and test scripts: pm.test("200", () => pm.response.to.have.status(200)); pm.expect(pm.response.json().name).to.eql("Asha");
  • CI: newman run citypulse.postman_collection.json -e qa.postman_environment.json --reporters cli,junit,htmlextra in a Jenkins or GitLab stage after deployment (smoke tests).

Also mention: contract testing (Spring Cloud Contract, Pact) between microservices, and API docs/schema validation through springdoc OpenAPI.

Likely follow-ups:

  • MockMvc vs a real HTTP client? MockMvc has no network or servlet container, so it is faster but misses server-level behaviour (real filters/ports, HTTP/2, compression). Use RANDOM_PORT tests for those.
  • How do you test file upload? multipart("/api/...").file(new MockMultipartFile("file", "a.jpg", "image/jpeg", bytes)).
  • How do you mock an external API the service calls? WireMock (@EnableWireMock or WireMockExtension) or MockRestServiceServer.
C35 Handling exceptions in test cases. 
@Test
void getById_notFound_throws() {
    when(repo.findById(99L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());

    ResourceNotFoundException ex = assertThrows(ResourceNotFoundException.class,
            () -> service.getById(99L));
    assertEquals("Employee 99 not found", ex.getMessage());
}

@Test
void validInput_doesNotThrow() {
    when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(new Employee()));
    assertDoesNotThrow(() -> service.getById(1L));
}

// Mocking a dependency to throw
when(repo.save(any())).thenThrow(new DataIntegrityViolationException("dup"));

// Controller layer: exception mapped to HTTP status by @RestControllerAdvice
@Test
void getById_notFound_returns404() throws Exception {
    when(service.getById(99L)).thenThrow(new ResourceNotFoundException("Employee 99 not found"));
    mockMvc.perform(get("/api/employees/99"))
           .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.detail").value("Employee 99 not found"));
}

Notes:

  • Prefer assertThrows over @Test(expected=...) (JUnit 4), because it lets you assert on the message.
  • With AssertJ: assertThatThrownBy(() -> ...).isInstanceOf(X.class).hasMessageContaining("99").

1. JUnit 5 assertThrows. It returns the exception so you can assert on its details.

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

@Test
void throwsNotFound() {
    given(repository.findById(99L)).willReturn(Optional.empty());

    ResourceNotFoundException ex = assertThrows(ResourceNotFoundException.class,
            () -> service.getEmployeeById(99L));

    assertEquals("Employee not found with id 99", ex.getMessage());
    assertEquals("Employee", ex.getResource());
    assertEquals(99L, ex.getId());
}
  • assertThrows accepts subclasses too. Use assertThrowsExactly (5.8+) for an exact type match.
  • assertDoesNotThrow(() -> ...) asserts the happy path explicitly.
  • JUnit 4's @Test(expected = X.class) and ExpectedException rule are gone. expected couldn't check messages and passed if any line threw.

2. AssertJ (more fluent, and checks causes and fields)

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;

assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.getEmployeeById(99L))
        .isInstanceOf(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
        .hasMessageContaining("99")
        .hasFieldOrPropertyWithValue("resource", "Employee")
        .hasNoCause();

assertThatExceptionOfType(IllegalArgumentException.class)
        .isThrownBy(() -> Base62.decode("ab$"))
        .withMessage("Invalid char $");

Throwable thrown = catchThrowable(() -> service.process(badInput));    // given/when/then style
assertThat(thrown).isInstanceOf(ValidationException.class).hasRootCauseInstanceOf(DateTimeParseException.class);

assertThatNoException().isThrownBy(() -> service.getEmployeeById(1L));

3. Mockito: make dependencies throw

// non-void methods
given(repository.findById(1L)).willThrow(new DataAccessResourceFailureException("DB down"));
when(client.ping()).thenThrow(new ResourceAccessException("timeout"));

// void methods -> doThrow form
doThrow(new IllegalStateException("Kafka unavailable")).when(publisher).publish(any());
willThrow(new IllegalStateException("Kafka unavailable")).given(publisher).publish(any());   // BDD

// first call fails, second succeeds -> test retry logic
when(smsGateway.send(any(), any()))
        .thenThrow(new ResourceAccessException("timeout"))
        .thenReturn("MSG-123");

assertThat(alertService.notifyCitizen("9999999999", "Signal down")).isEqualTo("MSG-123");
verify(smsGateway, times(2)).send(any(), any());

Also test the code's reaction to exceptions: is it translated, does it roll back, is a fallback used, and is an error metric incremented?

@Test
void wrapsDbErrorInServiceException() {
    given(repository.findById(1L)).willThrow(new DataAccessResourceFailureException("DB down"));

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.getEmployeeById(1L))
            .isInstanceOf(ServiceUnavailableException.class)
            .hasCauseInstanceOf(DataAccessResourceFailureException.class);
}

4. MockMvc for advice-mapped exceptions (verifies the HTTP contract of the @RestControllerAdvice)

@Test
void notFoundIsMappedTo404() throws Exception {
    given(service.getEmployeeById(99L)).willThrow(new ResourceNotFoundException("Employee", 99L));

    mockMvc.perform(get("/api/v1/employees/99"))
            .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.detail").value("Employee not found with id 99"))
            .andExpect(result -> assertThat(result.getResolvedException())
                    .isInstanceOf(ResourceNotFoundException.class));
}

@Test
void typeMismatchIs400() throws Exception {
    mockMvc.perform(get("/api/v1/employees/abc"))
            .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());          // MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException
}

MvcResult.getResolvedException() lets you assert which exception the resolver handled.

5. Integration-level checks

  • @DataJpaTest with duplicate data: assertThatThrownBy(() -> repo.saveAndFlush(dup)).isInstanceOf(DataIntegrityViolationException.class). You need saveAndFlush, because the constraint only fires on flush.
  • Transaction rollback: call the service in a non-transactional test, force an exception, then assert the DB row count is unchanged.
  • Async or Kafka error paths: use Awaitility to assert that the message landed in the DLT.

Gotchas

  • Put only the throwing call inside the lambda. If the setup is inside it, a setup failure can satisfy the assertion and give a false pass.
  • With Mockito strict stubs, an unused willThrow stub fails the test (UnnecessaryStubbingException). That's good, because it flags dead setup.
  • Don't catch and swallow exceptions in tests (try { ... } catch (Exception e) { }). Use fail() if you must use try/catch.
  • Checked exceptions: test methods can declare throws Exception. That is better than wrapping.

Likely follow-ups:

  • assertThrows vs assertThatThrownBy? Both work. assertThrows returns a typed exception, while AssertJ chains assertions fluently (message, cause, fields).
  • How do you test that a void method throws? assertThrows(X.class, () -> service.voidMethod()). To make a mock's void method throw, use doThrow(...).when(mock).voidMethod().
  • How do you verify nothing was saved after an exception? verify(repository, never()).save(any()), or verifyNoMoreInteractions.
D

Security, Microservices & System Design

D1 Authentication vs authorization in Java/Spring Boot. Hexaware
  • Authentication checks who you are (username/password, JWT, OAuth2 login). If it fails you get 401 Unauthorized.
  • Authorization checks what you are allowed to do (roles/authorities such as ROLE_ADMIN or incident:write). If it fails you get 403 Forbidden.
  • Authentication always comes first. In Spring Security, the AuthenticationManager authenticates the user and puts an Authentication object in the SecurityContextHolder. Authorization (authorizeHttpRequests, @PreAuthorize) then reads that object's getAuthorities().
