Example components a Smart City dashboard would have (talking points with code)

These are illustrations of typical components. Describe only the ones you actually built, in your own project's terms.

1. Map view (incidents and sensors on a map)

@Component({
  selector: 'app-city-map',
  standalone: true,
  template: `<div #mapEl class="map"></div>`,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
})
export class CityMapComponent {
  incidents = input<Incident[]>([]);
  private mapEl = viewChild.required<ElementRef<HTMLDivElement>>('mapEl');
  private map?: L.Map;
  private layer = L.layerGroup();

  constructor() {
    afterNextRender(() => {                       // DOM is ready (SSR-safe)
      this.map = L.map(this.mapEl().nativeElement).setView([12.97, 77.59], 12);
      L.tileLayer('https://{s}.tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png').addTo(this.map);
      this.layer.addTo(this.map);
    });
    effect(() => {                                // re-draw markers when the input signal changes
      const list = this.incidents();
      this.layer.clearLayers();
      list.forEach(i => L.marker([i.lat, i.lng]).bindPopup(i.title).addTo(this.layer));
    });
    inject(DestroyRef).onDestroy(() => this.map?.remove());
  }
}

Talking points: marker clustering for thousands of devices, GeoJSON layers for zones/wards, a bounding-box query to fetch only the visible area, and running the map outside Angular's zone (NgZone.runOutsideAngular) to avoid excessive change detection.

2. Live alert feed over WebSocket (STOMP with Spring)

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class AlertStreamService {
  private auth = inject(AuthService);                    // inject() must run in an injection context (field initialiser)
  private client = new Client({                          // @stomp/stompjs
    brokerURL: 'wss://[host]/ws',
    reconnectDelay: 5000,
    beforeConnect: () => { this.client.connectHeaders = { Authorization: `Bearer ${this.auth.token()}` }; }
  });
  private _alerts = signal<Alert[]>([]);
  readonly alerts = this._alerts.asReadonly();
  readonly highCount = computed(() => this._alerts().filter(a => a.severity === 'HIGH').length);

  connect() {
    this.client.onConnect = () =>
      this.client.subscribe('/topic/alerts', msg => {
        const alert: Alert = JSON.parse(msg.body);
        this._alerts.update(list => [alert, ...list].slice(0, 200));   // cap the list size
      });
    this.client.activate();
  }
  disconnect() { this.client.deactivate(); }
}

Back-end side: Spring @EnableWebSocketMessageBroker, with SimpMessagingTemplate.convertAndSend("/topic/alerts", alert) fed by a Kafka consumer. Talking points: reconnect and backoff, deduplication by alert ID, throttling UI updates, audible or visual escalation for HIGH severity, and acknowledging alerts through REST.

3. Charts (KPI widgets)

These show incidents per hour, average response time, and sensor values over time, built with [ngx-charts / Chart.js via ng2-charts / ECharts / Highcharts]. Talking points: time-window selectors, server-side aggregation (do not send raw readings to the browser), and @defer (on viewport) for heavy charts.

4. Role-based menus

export const MENU: MenuItem[] = [
  { label: 'Dashboard', route: '/dashboard', roles: ['OPERATOR', 'SUPERVISOR', 'ADMIN'] },
  { label: 'Incidents', route: '/incidents', roles: ['OPERATOR', 'SUPERVISOR'] },
  { label: 'Reports',   route: '/reports',   roles: ['SUPERVISOR', 'ADMIN'] },
  { label: 'User Admin', route: '/admin',    roles: ['ADMIN'] },
];

@Component({
  selector: 'app-side-nav', standalone: true, imports: [RouterLink, RouterLinkActive],
  template: `
    @for (item of visibleMenu(); track item.route) {
      <a [routerLink]="item.route" routerLinkActive="active">{{ item.label }}</a>
    }`
})
export class SideNavComponent {
  private auth = inject(AuthService);
  visibleMenu = computed(() => MENU.filter(m => m.roles.some(r => this.auth.roles().includes(r))));
}

Roles come from JWT claims. The same roles protect routes (canMatch) and, most importantly, the APIs (Spring Security).

5. JWT interceptor: see E11 §7. Mention attaching the token, handling 401 with a refresh token (queueing concurrent requests during the refresh), and logging out on refresh failure.

Other typical components: a paginated and filterable incident grid (server-side paging, see E8), an incident detail and workflow timeline, SOP checklists, a CCTV camera tile grid, a device health/status board, a notifications bell, and dark/light themes for control-room screens.

Delivery tips

  • Lead with business context, then the components, then one hard problem you solved.
  • Quantify: "[N] screens", "[N] reusable components", "load time from [X]s to [Y]s", "[N] alerts per minute rendered smoothly".
  • Expect deep-dive follow-ups on anything you mention: OnPush, the interceptor order, how you unsubscribe, how token refresh works.

What interviewers look for: real ownership (not "we did"), understanding of why a choice was made, awareness of performance and security, and the ability to connect the UI to back-end APIs end to end.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you avoid memory leaks? Use the async pipe or signals, takeUntilDestroyed(), close WebSockets and clear intervals in ngOnDestroy/DestroyRef.
  • How do you handle thousands of map markers? Clustering, viewport-based fetching, canvas renderers, and updating outside the zone.
  • Where do you keep the JWT? In memory or a short-lived store, with a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie if the backend supports it. Avoid localStorage for long-lived tokens because of XSS risk.
  • How do you test a component? TestBed with provideHttpClientTesting()/HttpTestingController, plus mocked services and harnesses for Material components.
E13 Basic JavaScript concepts
  • Types: the primitives are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Everything else is an object, including arrays and functions. typeof null === 'object' is a historical quirk.
  • Closures: a function remembers the variables of the scope where it was defined, even after that scope has returned. Closures are used for private state, factories and memoisation.
  • this: set by how a function is called. As an object method it is the object. In a plain call it is undefined in strict mode, or window otherwise. call/apply/bind set it explicitly. Arrow functions don't have their own this and inherit it lexically.
  • Promises / async-await: a Promise is a future value that is pending, fulfilled or rejected. async/await is syntactic sugar over promises; use try/catch for errors and Promise.all to run work in parallel.
  • Event loop: JS runs on a single thread with a call stack. When the stack is empty, all microtasks run first (promise callbacks), then the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O). So setTimeout(fn,0) runs after Promise.resolve().then(fn).
  • == vs ===: == coerces types ('5' == 5 is true, null == undefined is true). === compares value and type with no coercion. Default to ===.

1. Data types

  • Primitives (7): string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null. They are immutable and copied by value.
  • Object (reference) types: objects, arrays, functions, Date, Map, Set and so on. They are copied by reference.
typeof 42          // "number"
typeof 10n         // "bigint"
typeof 'hi'        // "string"
typeof undefined   // "undefined"
typeof null        // "object"   ← a historical bug
typeof []          // "object"   → use Array.isArray([]) === true
typeof function(){}// "function"
typeof Symbol()    // "symbol"

let a = { x: 1 }; let b = a; b.x = 2;
console.log(a.x);  // 2 (same reference)
let c = structuredClone(a);   // deep copy; { ...a } is only a shallow copy

Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including [], {} and '0'.

2. Scope

  • Global, function and block scope. let and const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped (see E14).
  • Lexical scope: a function sees variables where it is defined, not where it is called.
const city = 'Bengaluru';
function outer() {
  const zone = 'North';
  function inner() { return `${city}-${zone}`; }   // looks up the scope chain
  return inner();
}
outer(); // "Bengaluru-North"

3. Closures

A closure is a function bundled with references to its outer variables, which stay alive after the outer function returns.

function createCounter() {
  let count = 0;                       // private state
  return {
    inc: () => ++count,
    get: () => count
  };
}
const c1 = createCounter();
c1.inc(); c1.inc();
console.log(c1.get());   // 2
console.log(c1.count);   // undefined (truly private)

Uses: data privacy and the module pattern, function factories, memoization, debounce, event handlers, and RxJS operators.

function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let t;
  return (...args) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); };
}

4. this binding (determined by how a function is called)

Call style this is
obj.method() obj (implicit binding)
fn() plain call undefined in strict mode or modules; globalThis in sloppy mode
fn.call(o, a) / fn.apply(o, [a]) / fn.bind(o) o (explicit binding)
new Fn() The newly created object
Arrow function Lexical: inherited from the enclosing scope; cannot be rebound 
const sensor = {
  name: 'AQI-01',
  regular() { return this.name; },
  arrow: () => this?.name,                        // `this` comes from module scope, so undefined
  delayed() { setTimeout(() => console.log(this.name), 0); }   // the arrow keeps the outer `this`
};
sensor.regular();          // "AQI-01"
sensor.arrow();            // undefined
const f = sensor.regular;
f();                       // TypeError in strict mode (this is undefined); undefined in sloppy mode
f.call({ name: 'X' });     // "X"
sensor.delayed();          // "AQI-01"

This is why Angular templates and RxJS callbacks commonly use arrow functions: they keep the component's this.

5. Prototypes and inheritance

Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] link. Property lookup walks the prototype chain. class is syntactic sugar over prototypes.

function Device(id) { this.id = id; }
Device.prototype.describe = function () { return `Device ${this.id}`; };

const d = new Device(7);
d.describe();                                     // "Device 7" (found on Device.prototype)
Object.getPrototypeOf(d) === Device.prototype;    // true
d.hasOwnProperty('describe');                     // false

class Camera extends Device {
  constructor(id, url) { super(id); this.url = url; }
  describe() { return `${super.describe()} (camera)`; }
}
new Camera(9, 'rtsp://...').describe();           // "Device 9 (camera)"

6. Promises and async/await

function fetchSensor(id) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => (id > 0 ? resolve({ id, value: 42 }) : reject(new Error('bad id'))), 100));
}

fetchSensor(1)
  .then(s => s.value)
  .then(v => console.log(v))       // 42
  .catch(e => console.error(e))
  .finally(() => console.log('done'));

async function load() {
  try {
    const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchSensor(1), fetchSensor(2)]);   // parallel
    return a.value + b.value;
  } catch (e) {
    console.error(e.message);
  }
}
Combinator Resolves when Rejects when
Promise.all All fulfil Any rejects (fails fast)
Promise.allSettled All settle Never; returns {status, value/reason} for each
Promise.race The first one settles The first one settles with a rejection
Promise.any The first one fulfils All reject (AggregateError)

Pitfall: await inside a for loop runs requests sequentially. Use Promise.all(items.map(fetch)) for parallel calls.

7. The event loop: microtasks vs macrotasks

JavaScript runs on a single thread. The event loop works like this:

  1. Run the current synchronous code (the call stack).
  2. Drain all microtasks: Promise .then/catch/finally, await continuations, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver.
  3. Render (in browsers), if needed.
  4. Take one macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events, MessageChannel), then go back to step 2.
console.log('1: sync');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2: timeout (macrotask)'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3: promise (microtask)'));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('4: queueMicrotask'));
(async () => {
  console.log('5: async fn body runs sync');
  await null;
  console.log('6: after await (microtask)');
})();
console.log('7: sync');

Output:

1: sync
5: async fn body runs sync
7: sync
3: promise (microtask)
4: queueMicrotask
6: after await (microtask)
2: timeout (macrotask)

Why: the synchronous lines run first (1, 5, 7). Then all microtasks run in the order they were queued (3, 4, 6). Then the macrotask runs (2). An endless stream of microtasks can starve rendering and timers. Node.js also has process.nextTick, which runs before promise microtasks.

8. == vs ===

  • === is strict equality: no type coercion. Use it by default.
  • == is loose equality: it coerces types first.
0 == ''            // true   ('' → 0)
0 === ''           // false
'5' == 5           // true
null == undefined  // true   (the one useful case: x == null checks both)
null === undefined // false
null == 0          // false
[] == false        // true   ([] → '' → 0, false → 0)
NaN == NaN         // false  → use Number.isNaN(x)
Object.is(NaN, NaN)// true;  Object.is(0, -0) → false
{} === {}          // false  (different references)

9. Spread, rest and destructuring

// Spread: expand
const base = { severity: 'LOW', status: 'OPEN' };
const incident = { ...base, id: 1, severity: 'HIGH' };   // later keys win → severity 'HIGH'
const all = [...[1, 2], ...[3, 4]];                      // [1,2,3,4]
Math.max(...[3, 9, 2]);                                   // 9

// Rest: collect
function log(level, ...msgs) { console.log(level, msgs); }
log('INFO', 'a', 'b');                                    // INFO ['a','b']
const { id, ...rest } = incident;                         // rest = {severity:'HIGH', status:'OPEN'}

// Destructuring with defaults and renaming
const { status: st = 'NEW', location: { lat = 0 } = {} } = incident;   // st='OPEN', lat=0
const [first, , third = 'x'] = ['a', 'b'];                // first='a', third='x'
[a1, b1] = [b1, a1];                                      // swap

// Optional chaining and nullish coalescing
const zone = incident.location?.zone ?? 'Unknown';        // ?? replaces only null/undefined, not 0 or ''

Other quick ones: map/filter/reduce; template literals; modules (import/export); Map/Set; immutability with Object.freeze (shallow); JSON.parse/JSON.stringify.

Likely follow-ups:

  • What does [1,2,3].map(parseInt) return? [1, NaN, NaN], because map passes (value, index) and parseInt treats the index as the radix.
  • Shallow vs deep copy? Spread and Object.assign copy only the top level. structuredClone copies deeply (but not functions).
  • Arrow vs regular function? An arrow has no own this, arguments or prototype, and cannot be used with new.
  • What is event delegation? One listener on a parent handles events from its children via bubbling and event.target.
E14 var, let, const and hoisting (TDZ)
Scope Re-declare Re-assign Hoisted
var function yes yes yes, initialised to undefined
let block no yes yes, but stays in the TDZ until its declaration line
const block no no (object contents can still change) yes, but stays in the TDZ 
console.log(a);   // undefined   (var is hoisted and initialised)
var a = 1;

console.log(b);   // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization (TDZ)
let b = 2;

const c = { x: 1 };
c.x = 2;          // OK: the object itself is mutable
// c = {};        // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));  // 3 3 3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j));  // 0 1 2 (new binding per iteration)

sayHi();          // "hi": function declarations are fully hoisted
function sayHi() { console.log('hi'); }

Comparison

var let const
Scope Function (or global) Block {} Block
Hoisted? Yes, initialised to undefined Yes, but uninitialised (TDZ) Yes, uninitialised (TDZ)
Access before declaration undefined ReferenceError ReferenceError
Redeclare in the same scope Allowed SyntaxError SyntaxError
Reassign Yes Yes No (TypeError)
Must initialise at declaration No No Yes
Creates a property on window (global scope) Yes No No

Hoisting

During the creation phase of each scope, JavaScript registers declarations before running code. The code is not physically moved.

console.log(a);   // undefined   (var is hoisted and initialised to undefined)
var a = 10;
console.log(a);   // 10

console.log(b);   // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
let b = 20;

console.log(c);   // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'c' before initialization
const c = 30;

console.log(d);   // ReferenceError: d is not defined   (never declared, a different message)

Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)

The TDZ is the period from the start of the block until the let/const declaration line runs.

let x = 'outer';
{
  // TDZ for the inner x starts here. It shadows the outer x even before its declaration.
  console.log(x);    // ReferenceError (not 'outer'!)
  let x = 'inner';
}

typeof undeclaredVar;   // "undefined" (safe)
typeof y;               // ReferenceError: y is in its TDZ
let y = 1;

function f(p = q, q = 1) {}   // f() → ReferenceError: q is accessed in its TDZ (default params are evaluated left to right)

Function scope vs block scope

function test() {
  if (true) {
    var v = 'var';
    let l = 'let';
    const k = 'const';
  }
  console.log(v);   // "var"  (var ignores the block)
  console.log(l);   // ReferenceError: l is not defined
}

Redeclaration

var n = 1;
var n = 2;        // fine, silently overwrites (a source of bugs)

let m = 1;
let m = 2;        // SyntaxError: Identifier 'm' has already been declared

let s = 1;
{ let s = 2; }    // fine: a different block, so this is shadowing, not redeclaration

const with objects and arrays

const makes the binding immutable, not the value.

const cfg = { refreshMs: 5000 };
cfg.refreshMs = 1000;      // allowed (mutating the object)
cfg = {};                  // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

const ids = [1, 2];
ids.push(3);               // allowed → [1,2,3]

const frozen = Object.freeze({ a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } });
frozen.a = 99;             // ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
frozen.nested.b = 99;      // allowed: freeze is SHALLOW

The classic loop closure question

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log('var:', i), 0);
}
// var: 3
// var: 3
// var: 3

for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log('let:', j), 0);
}
// let: 0
// let: 1
// let: 2

Why: var i is one function-scoped variable shared by all callbacks. By the time the timeouts run (macrotasks, after the loop finishes), i is 3. let j creates a new binding for each iteration, so each closure captures its own value.

Pre-ES6 fixes, which interviewers sometimes ask for:

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  (function (k) { setTimeout(() => console.log(k), 0); })(i);   // IIFE captures a copy
}
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(console.log, 0, i);                                 // pass it as a setTimeout argument
}

Function declarations vs function expressions

greet();                         // "hello": declarations are fully hoisted (name AND body)
function greet() { console.log('hello'); }

sayHi();                         // TypeError: sayHi is not a function (var hoisted as undefined)
var sayHi = function () { console.log('hi'); };

sayBye();                        // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'sayBye' before initialization (TDZ)
const sayBye = () => console.log('bye');

// Classes are hoisted like let (TDZ)
new Foo();                       // ReferenceError
class Foo {}

Precedence quiz:

console.log(typeof foo);   // "function"
var foo = 1;
function foo() {}
console.log(typeof foo);   // "number"

Why: during creation, the function declaration initialises foo, and the var foo declaration is ignored because the name already exists. At runtime, foo = 1 reassigns it.

Best practice

Use const by default, let when you must reassign, and never var in modern code. ESLint has the no-var and prefer-const rules for this, and they are commonly enabled in Angular projects.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Are let and const hoisted? Yes, they are hoisted but not initialised. That is exactly what the TDZ is.
  • What does this print: let a = 1; { console.log(a); let a = 2; }? A ReferenceError, because the inner a is in its TDZ and shadows the outer one.
  • Why does global var matter? var x at the top level becomes window.x and can clash with other scripts. let and const live in a separate declarative scope.

It is not a statement of what you did. Keep only what is true for you, and use numbers you can defend. Interviewers routinely ask "how exactly?" about any claim.

Tips

  • Don't recite your résumé or your personal history (hometown, hobbies) unless asked. Keep it professional.
  • End with a hook. Your last sentence should invite the interviewer to ask about your strongest project.
  • Tailor the proof points to the job description. If they stress microservices, lead with that achievement.
  • Practise out loud with a timer. Aim for about 90 seconds and avoid filler words.
  • Say "I" for your own contributions and "we" for team outcomes. Be honest about which is which.
  • Do not disclose confidential client names, city contracts or internal metrics if your NDA forbids it. Say "a large Indian city deployment" instead.

What interviewers look for: clarity, relevance to the role, evidence of ownership and growth, communication skill, and whether your story matches your résumé.

Typical Spring Boot service layout

incident-service/
 └─ src/main/java/com/trinity/incident/
     ├─ controller/     REST endpoints (@RestController)
     ├─ service/        business logic (interfaces + impl)
     ├─ repository/     Spring Data JPA repositories
     ├─ entity/         JPA entities
     ├─ dto/            request/response DTOs, mapper/ (MapStruct)
     ├─ config/         security, Kafka, Swagger, CORS config
     ├─ client/         Feign/WebClient clients to other services
     ├─ messaging/      Kafka producers/consumers
     ├─ exception/      custom exceptions + @RestControllerAdvice
     └─ util/
 └─ src/main/resources/ application.yml, db/migration (Flyway)
 └─ src/test/java/       unit + integration tests

Typical Angular layout

src/app/
 ├─ core/        singleton services, interceptors, guards, auth
 ├─ shared/      reusable components, pipes, directives, models
 ├─ features/    incident/, devices/, dashboard/, reports/ (lazy-loaded)
 ├─ layout/      header, sidebar, shell
 └─ app.routes.ts / app.config.ts
src/environments/  environment.ts, environment.prod.ts

Template answer

"At a high level we follow [microservices / a modular monolith moving to microservices]. The Angular SPA talks to an API gateway ([Spring Cloud Gateway / Nginx / Kong]), which routes to the Spring Boot services. Services register in [Eureka / Kubernetes service discovery] and pull configuration from [Spring Cloud Config / ConfigMaps]. Synchronous calls use [REST with OpenFeign/WebClient]. Asynchronous flows use [Kafka]. Each service owns its database/schema. Cross-cutting pieces include [Keycloak/auth-service] for auth, [ELK/EFK] for logs, [Prometheus + Grafana] for metrics, and [Zipkin/Jaeger/OpenTelemetry] for tracing. Inside each service we use a layered architecture: controller → service → repository, with DTOs and mappers at the boundaries."

 [Angular SPA] ──HTTPS/WSS──► [API Gateway] ──► [auth-service]
                                   │
               ┌───────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
               ▼                   ▼                     ▼
       [incident-service]  [device-service]     [notification-service]
               │   ▲               │                     ▲
               ▼   │               ▼                     │
             [DB]  └──────── [Kafka topics] ─────────────┘
                                   ▲
                       [integration/adapters] ◄── IoT gateways / vendor APIs

Typical Spring Boot service layout (layered, package-by-layer within a feature)

incident-service/
├── pom.xml (or build.gradle)
├── Dockerfile
├── src/main/java/com/[company]/[product]/incident/
│   ├── IncidentServiceApplication.java
│   ├── config/                 # SecurityConfig, KafkaConfig, OpenApiConfig, WebSocketConfig, CorsConfig
│   ├── controller/             # @RestController: IncidentController (thin; validation + mapping only)
│   ├── dto/                    # request/response records: CreateIncidentRequest, IncidentResponse
│   ├── mapper/                 # MapStruct mappers: IncidentMapper
│   ├── service/                # interfaces + impl: IncidentService, IncidentServiceImpl (business logic, @Transactional)
│   ├── repository/             # Spring Data JPA: IncidentRepository, specifications/custom queries
│   ├── entity/  (or domain/)   # @Entity classes: Incident, IncidentStatus (enum), AuditableEntity (base)
│   ├── messaging/              # Kafka producers/consumers: IncidentEventPublisher, SensorAlertListener
│   ├── client/                 # Feign/WebClient clients to other services or third parties
│   ├── exception/              # custom exceptions + GlobalExceptionHandler (@RestControllerAdvice)
│   ├── security/               # JWT filter, permission evaluators
│   ├── scheduler/              # @Scheduled jobs (SLA breach checks, data pulls)
│   └── util/                   # small helpers/constants (keep minimal)
├── src/main/resources/
│   ├── application.yml         # + application-dev.yml / -qa.yml / -prod.yml (profiles)
│   ├── db/migration/           # Flyway: V1__init.sql, V2__add_incident_priority.sql
│   └── logback-spring.xml
└── src/test/java/...           # unit tests (Mockito), slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest), Testcontainers ITs

Alternatives to mention: package-by-feature (incident/, assignment/, sop/, each with its own controller, service and repository), or hexagonal / ports & adapters (domain/, application/, adapters/in/web, adapters/out/persistence). Say which one your project uses and why. Shared code (common DTOs, exception model, security utilities) usually lives in a common library JAR, which should be kept small to avoid coupling.

Typical Angular layout (feature-folder, standalone)

src/
├── main.ts                      # bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig)
├── app/
│   ├── app.config.ts            # provideRouter, provideHttpClient(withInterceptors(...))
│   ├── app.routes.ts            # top-level lazy routes
│   ├── core/                    # singletons, loaded once
│   │   ├── auth/                # auth.service.ts, auth.guard.ts, role.guard.ts
│   │   ├── interceptors/        # jwt.interceptor.ts, error.interceptor.ts, loading.interceptor.ts
│   │   ├── services/            # websocket.service.ts, notification.service.ts
│   │   └── layout/              # shell, header, side-nav (role-based menu)
│   ├── shared/                  # reusable, stateless building blocks
│   │   ├── components/          # data-table, confirm-dialog, map-widget, kpi-card
│   │   ├── directives/          # has-role.directive.ts, severity.directive.ts
│   │   ├── pipes/               # time-ago.pipe.ts
│   │   └── models/              # shared interfaces / enums
│   └── features/                # one folder per business feature, lazy loaded
│       ├── dashboard/
│       ├── incidents/
│       │   ├── incident.routes.ts
│       │   ├── incident-list/   # .ts / .html / .scss / .spec.ts
│       │   ├── incident-detail/
│       │   ├── incident-form/
│       │   └── data-access/     # incident.service.ts, incident.store.ts (signals/NgRx)
│       ├── devices/
│       ├── reports/
│       └── admin/
├── environments/                # environment.ts, environment.prod.ts (API base URLs; no secrets!)
└── assets/                      # icons, map styles, i18n json

Classic NgModule apps follow the same idea with CoreModule (imported once), SharedModule, and lazy-loaded FeatureModules using loadChildren.

Delivery tips

  • Explain why: "Each service owns its data so teams can deploy independently", "Kafka decouples the device ingestion rate from processing", "a thin controller keeps business logic testable".
  • Mention conventions: DTOs never expose entities, a global exception handler, consistent API error format, and versioned APIs (/api/v1).
  • Be ready to discuss trade-offs and pain points: distributed transactions, shared libraries, and the cost of local development with many services.

What interviewers look for: whether you know the structure beyond your own folder, separation of concerns, the reasoning behind decisions, and familiarity with cross-cutting concerns (security, configuration, observability).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why use DTOs instead of returning entities? To decouple the API contract from the schema, avoid lazy-loading and serialisation issues, prevent over-posting, and allow API versioning.
  • Package-by-layer vs package-by-feature? By-layer is simple for small services. By-feature scales better, keeps related code together, and allows package-private encapsulation.
  • Where does validation happen? Format and required checks use Bean Validation on DTOs at the controller. Business rules belong in the service layer. Integrity is enforced by DB constraints.
  • How do the services share code? Through a small versioned common library for DTOs and errors. Avoid sharing domain entities between services.

E20 Coding standards, best practices and precautions G2
  • Clean code: meaningful names, small single-purpose methods, SOLID, DRY, no magic numbers, consistent formatting (Checkstyle/Prettier/ESLint).
  • Layering: Controller, then Service, then Repository. Use DTOs, never expose entities, and use constructor injection.
  • Validation and errors: Bean Validation (@Valid), a global @RestControllerAdvice, meaningful HTTP status codes, and no swallowed exceptions.
  • Security: parameterised queries (no SQL injection), no secrets in code (use Vault/env/K8s secrets), input sanitisation, least privilege, OWASP Top 10, keep dependencies updated.
  • Performance: avoid N+1 (fetch joins / @EntityGraph), paginate, add indexes, cache where it makes sense, use connection pools, and set timeouts on external calls.
  • Transactions and concurrency: keep @Transactional boundaries correct, use optimistic locking (@Version), prefer immutable or thread-safe objects.
  • Logging: SLF4J at the right levels, correlation/trace IDs, never log PII or passwords.
  • Testing and review: unit tests for business logic, a [≥X%] coverage gate in SonarQube, PR reviews, and passing CI before merge.
  • Angular: OnPush, trackBy, unsubscribe (async pipe / takeUntilDestroyed), strict TypeScript, lazy loading, no business logic in templates.
  • Git: small focused commits, a branch per feature, meaningful messages, and no direct pushes to main.

Template opening

"Our team follows [a documented coding guideline / Google Java Style / an internal checklist], enforced through [SonarQube quality gates, Checkstyle, ESLint] in CI and through mandatory peer review. Personally, I focus on readability, testability, security and observability. Concretely:"

1. Naming and readability

  • Classes are PascalCase nouns (IncidentService). Methods are camelCase verbs (assignOperator). Constants are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Packages are lowercase.
  • Use meaningful names, not data, temp or obj. Booleans read as questions: isActive, hasPermission.
  • Keep methods small with one level of abstraction. Avoid deep nesting by using guard clauses or early returns.
  • Avoid magic numbers: private static final Duration SLA_BREACH = Duration.ofMinutes(15);
  • Comments should explain why, not what. Use Javadoc for public APIs.

2. SOLID and design

Principle Practical example
Single Responsibility Controller handles only HTTP, service holds business logic, repository handles data access
Open/Closed A NotificationSender interface with SmsSender and EmailSender implementations. Add a channel without editing existing code.
Liskov Substitution Subclasses must not break the parent's contract (no UnsupportedOperationException overrides)
Interface Segregation Small, focused interfaces, not one GodService
Dependency Inversion Depend on interfaces; use constructor injection (@RequiredArgsConstructor), not field @Autowired

Also: DRY (without premature abstraction), KISS, YAGNI, composition over inheritance, and design patterns where they genuinely help (Strategy, Factory, Builder, Adapter for vendor integrations).

3. Exception handling

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {
    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ApiError> notFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                .body(new ApiError("NOT_FOUND", ex.getMessage(), req.getRequestURI(), Instant.now()));
    }
    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ApiError> validation(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex, HttpServletRequest req) { /* field errors */ }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    ResponseEntity<ApiError> generic(Exception ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        log.error("Unhandled error at {}", req.getRequestURI(), ex);           // log the stack trace server-side
        return ResponseEntity.internalServerError()
                .body(new ApiError("INTERNAL_ERROR", "Something went wrong", req.getRequestURI(), Instant.now())); // no stack trace to the client
    }
}
  • Never swallow exceptions (catch (Exception e) {}). Never use e.printStackTrace().
  • Throw specific custom exceptions, keep the cause (new XException(msg, e)), and use try-with-resources.
  • Return a consistent error format with correct HTTP status codes (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 500). Spring 6 also offers ProblemDetail (RFC 7807/9457).

4. Logging

  • Use SLF4J with parameterised messages: log.info("Incident {} assigned to {}", id, userId), not string concatenation.
  • Use the right level: ERROR for failures needing action, WARN for recoverable problems, INFO for business events, DEBUG for diagnostics (off in production).
  • Never log secrets or PII: passwords, tokens, full phone numbers or Aadhaar-like IDs. Mask them.
  • Add a correlation/trace ID with MDC so requests can be followed across microservices. Use structured (JSON) logs for ELK.

5. Null safety

  • Return Optional<T> from finders, and use orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException(...)). Don't use Optional for fields or parameters.
  • Return empty collections, never null.
  • Use Objects.requireNonNull, Bean Validation (@NotNull, @NotBlank, @Valid), and "CONST".equals(var) ordering.
  • In TypeScript, enable strict mode and use optional chaining ?. and ??.

6. Security precautions (OWASP Top 10 mindset)

  • Never hardcode secrets (passwords, API keys, JWT signing keys) in code or application.yml in Git. Use environment variables, [Vault / Kubernetes Secrets / a cloud secret manager], and Jasypt if required. Add .gitignore rules and secret scanning (for example gitleaks).
  • SQL injection: use parameterised queries, JPA parameters and PreparedStatement. Never concatenate user input into SQL.
  • Validate input on the server (never trust the UI), and encode output (Angular escapes interpolation by default; avoid bypassSecurityTrust*).
  • AuthN/AuthZ: method-level @PreAuthorize, and check ownership to prevent IDOR. Apply least privilege for DB users.
  • Use HTTPS only, a CORS allow-list (not * with credentials), and rate limiting at the gateway.
  • Dependencies: OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk or Dependabot, and keep libraries patched.
  • Do not expose entities directly (mass-assignment risk). Use DTOs.

7. Testing

  • Write unit tests for business logic (JUnit 5 + Mockito), following Arrange-Act-Assert with one behaviour per test and descriptive names (shouldEscalateWhenSlaBreached).
  • Use slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) and integration tests with Testcontainers (a real Postgres or Kafka).
  • Follow the coverage gate ([e.g. 80% on new code]), but focus on meaningful assertions, not just coverage numbers.
  • Every bug fix gets a regression test first: reproduce, fix, verify.

8. Code reviews and static analysis

  • Use small, focused PRs with a clear description and linked ticket. Self-review before requesting review.
  • The reviewer checklist covers correctness, edge cases, naming, tests, security, performance (N+1, missing indexes, unbounded queries), logging and backward compatibility.
  • Enforce a SonarQube quality gate in CI: no new blocker or critical issues, no new code smells above the threshold, and minimum coverage on new code. Use SonarLint in the IDE.
  • Use formatting and lint tools (Checkstyle/Spotless, ESLint/Prettier) so style is automatic, not debated.

9. Git branching and commits

  • Branching follows [GitFlow (main, develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*) / trunk-based with short-lived feature branches].
  • Use meaningful commits, for example Conventional Commits: feat(incident): add SLA escalation, or fix: handle null device location.
  • Never commit directly to main. Branch protection requires approvals and green CI. Rebase or squash according to team policy.
  • Tag releases and keep a changelog.

10. Performance and database precautions

  • Avoid N+1 queries (JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph). Paginate all list APIs. Select only the columns you need.
  • Index on filter and join columns, and check plans with EXPLAIN.
  • Keep transactions short. Avoid remote calls inside @Transactional.
  • Close resources, use timeouts on all HTTP clients, and use connection pool sizing (HikariCP).
  • Use backward-compatible DB migrations (expand then contract) for zero-downtime deployments.

11. Angular-specific standards

  • Follow the Angular style guide (one component per file, feature folders), use OnPush or signals, use the async pipe and takeUntilDestroyed, and use typed forms and strict TypeScript.
  • Use track in @for, avoid function calls in templates (use computed or pure pipes), and avoid any.

Delivery tips

Pick 5–6 points and give a real example for each ("In one review I caught a query without pagination that would have loaded [N] records"). Mention automation: standards that are enforced by tools are more credible than standards that depend on memory.

What interviewers look for: professional maturity, a security and quality mindset, team practices (reviews, CI gates), and concrete habits rather than buzzwords.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why constructor injection over field injection? It allows immutable (final) dependencies, makes dependencies explicit, works in tests without Spring, and fails fast on circular dependencies.
  • What does a SonarQube quality gate check? Conditions on new code: bugs, vulnerabilities, security hotspots reviewed, code smells, coverage percentage and duplication. CI fails if the gate fails.
  • Checked vs unchecked exceptions? Checked exceptions are for recoverable conditions the caller must handle. Unchecked exceptions are for programming errors or business violations. Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default.
  • How do you store secrets in Kubernetes? In Secrets, ideally synced from Vault or a cloud secret manager through an external secrets operator, mounted as environment variables or files, and never committed in manifests.
E21 Challenges faced (STAR template + examples)

STAR: Situation (context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what you did, technically), Result (measurable outcome plus what you learned). Keep it to 60–90 s.

The two scenarios below are examples only. Replace them with your own real experience.

Example 1: slow dashboard API. S: The [incident dashboard] API took [8 s] under load as data grew. T: I was asked to bring it under [1 s]. A: I profiled it with [logs / Hibernate statistics] and found N+1 queries plus a missing index. I added a fetch join with DTO projections, a composite index on (status, created_at), pagination, and a [Redis] cache for reference data. R: Response time dropped to [600 ms], and the team adopted query reviews.

Example 2: lost or duplicate sensor events. S: During peak hours some [IoT alerts] were duplicated and others were missed. T: I had to make ingestion reliable. A: I made the [Kafka] consumer idempotent with a unique event-ID check, used manual offset commits after a successful DB write, added retries with a dead-letter topic, and added alerting on consumer lag. R: No duplicate alerts after release, and failed events became traceable in the DLT.

Use the STAR method (aim for about 2 minutes)

Step Share What to say
Situation 15% Context: product, module, when, why it mattered
Task 10% Your responsibility or goal
Action 50–60% The steps you took: analysis, options considered, the decision, the implementation
Result 15–20% A measurable outcome, plus what you learned or changed to prevent a repeat

Blank template:

"S: In [month/year], on [module] of [product], we faced [problem], which was affecting [users/SLA/business]. T: I was responsible for [diagnosing / fixing / delivering] [X] by [deadline]. A: First I [investigated with tools/data]. I found [root cause]. I considered [option A] and [option B], and chose [B] because [reason]. I implemented [specifics], tested it with [how], and rolled it out [how, safely]. R: [Metric before → after]. We also [added monitoring / a test / a runbook] so it doesn't recur. I learned [lesson]."

The three scenarios below are EXAMPLES ONLY. They are plausible situations for a Smart City full-stack developer, written to show the structure. Do not narrate them as your own unless they actually happened. Replace them with your real stories, borrowing only the structure and the technical vocabulary.

Example 1 (illustrative): performance issue on the incident dashboard

  • S: "The operator dashboard's incident list API took [~8 s] at peak once a city crossed [N lakh] incident records. Operators complained that the screen froze during [festival / heavy-rain] events."
  • T: "I was asked to bring the p95 under [1 s] without a schema redesign."
  • A: "I enabled SQL logging and used EXPLAIN. I found (1) an N+1 problem loading assignedOfficer and location lazily for every row, (2) a missing composite index on (city_id, status, created_at), and (3) the API returning all records with client-side paging. I added @EntityGraph/JOIN FETCH, created the index through a Flyway migration (built concurrently in Postgres to avoid locking), switched to server-side pagination with a projection DTO, and cached reference data (incident types, zones) in Redis. On the Angular side I moved the list to OnPush with virtual scrolling."
  • R: "p95 dropped from [8 s] to [~400 ms], DB CPU fell [X]%, and I added a Grafana alert on API latency. Lesson: always paginate and profile queries with production-sized data."

Example 2 (illustrative): production bug with duplicate alerts

  • S: "After a release, operators saw duplicate alerts for the same sensor event, sometimes 3–4 copies, which caused confusion in the control room."
  • T: "As the owner of the alert consumer, I had to find the root cause quickly and fix it without losing alerts."
  • A: "I correlated logs by event ID in [Kibana] and saw the same Kafka offset processed several times. A slow downstream call had pushed processing past max.poll.interval.ms, so the consumer group rebalanced and the messages were redelivered (Kafka's at-least-once delivery). As an immediate mitigation, I raised the poll interval and reduced max.poll.records. For the permanent fix, I made the consumer idempotent, using a unique constraint on (source_id, event_id) with insert-if-absent, and moved the slow call to an async step. I added a regression test with Testcontainers Kafka."
  • R: "Duplicates went to zero. We documented 'every consumer must be idempotent' in our review checklist. Lesson: design for at-least-once delivery from day one."

Example 3 (illustrative): integrating a third-party IoT data source

  • S: "We had to onboard [a vendor's air-quality / parking / GPS] devices. The vendor API was poorly documented, rate-limited ([N] calls/min]), returned inconsistent units and timestamps in local time without a zone, and was down intermittently."
  • T: "Deliver a reliable integration in [2 sprints] that feeds the dashboard and alert engine."
  • A: "I built an adapter service: a scheduled poller using WebClient with timeouts, retries with exponential backoff, and a Resilience4j circuit breaker, plus a token-bucket limiter to respect the rate limit. I stored the raw payload for audit and replay, then normalised it into our canonical schema (UTC timestamps, SI units, a validated range). Invalid records went to a dead-letter table with the reason. Normalised events were published to Kafka. I wrote contract tests with WireMock using recorded vendor responses, and agreed a field-mapping document with the vendor."
  • R: "We went live on schedule and reached [99.x]% data completeness. Vendor outages no longer affected other services, and the same adapter pattern was reused for [N] more vendors. Lesson: treat external data as untrusted and build in observability for it."

Other challenge types to prepare: a tight deadline or changing requirements, learning a new technology quickly, a legacy code refactor, a difficult deployment or rollback, and working with an onsite or client team.

Delivery tips

  • Prepare 3–4 stories that can be adapted to many questions (challenge, failure, conflict, leadership, learning).
  • Pick challenges that were technical and impactful, where you drove the solution.
  • Be honest about mistakes. "I caused it, here is how I fixed it, and here is the process we changed" is a strong answer.
  • Avoid blaming people. Focus on the system and process.

What interviewers look for: structured thinking, debugging methodology, ownership, technical depth, measurable outcomes and learning.

E22 How do you handle conflicts? (STAR template)

Core message: listen first, focus on facts and goals rather than people, find common ground, and escalate only when needed.

"S: In [sprint/project], a [teammate / QA / frontend dev] and I disagreed about [e.g. API contract design / whether to refactor or patch / an estimate]. T: We had to agree quickly to stay on schedule. A: I set up a short one-to-one call and listened to their concerns first. I laid out the trade-offs using data ([e.g. performance numbers, a quick PoC]) and suggested [a compromise, e.g. patch now and refactor in the next sprint as a tech-debt ticket]. Where we couldn't agree, we took it to [the tech lead] with both options written down. R: We delivered on time, the [decision] was documented, and the working relationship got better. I learned to [discuss trade-offs early and in writing]."

Principles to mention

  • Separate the person from the problem. Listen first and restate the other view.
  • Use data and shared goals (customer impact, SLA, deadline), not opinions or seniority.
  • Try to resolve it 1:1 first. Escalate only with options and data, never as a complaint.
  • Disagree and commit once a decision is made, and document the decision (for example in an ADR).

STAR template

"S: On [project], [colleague/role] and I disagreed about [topic]. T: We needed to [decide/deliver] by [deadline] without hurting [quality/relationship]. A: I set up a short discussion to understand their reasoning, which was [their concern]. I explained mine: [my concern]. We listed the criteria that mattered ([e.g. delivery time, performance, maintainability]). I [built a quick POC / gathered metrics / asked the architect for input]. We agreed on [decision / compromise]. R: [Outcome]. Our working relationship [improved]. I learned [lesson]."

The two scenarios below are EXAMPLES showing the structure. Use your own real situation.

Example A (illustrative): technical disagreement

  • S: "A senior colleague wanted the new alert-notification feature to call the notification service synchronously over REST. I preferred publishing an event to Kafka."
  • T: "We had to finalise the design in the sprint's first week."
  • A: "I asked what worried him. It was mainly the extra complexity and harder debugging of async flows. I acknowledged that, then showed the risk of the synchronous approach: if the SMS gateway slows down, incident creation slows down too. I built a one-day POC and measured both under a simulated slow gateway. Sync incident creation went from [150 ms] to [3 s]; async stayed at [150 ms]. To address his concern, I proposed adding a correlation ID, a dead-letter topic, and a dashboard for consumer lag."
  • R: "We went with Kafka plus the observability additions he asked for. The design held up during a later SMS-gateway outage with no impact on incident creation. Lesson: the other person's concern often improves the final design."

Example B (illustrative): team or process conflict

  • S: "QA and development kept clashing over late-reported bugs. QA felt builds came too late; developers felt requirements kept changing."
  • T: "As [the module owner / a developer on the team], I wanted to reduce friction before a major city go-live."
  • A: "I talked to the QA lead one-on-one, then suggested three changes in the retro: (1) QA joins story refinement to add acceptance criteria up front, (2) we deploy to the QA environment daily from CI instead of at sprint end, and (3) we agree a definition of done that includes unit tests and a passing API test collection."
  • R: "Late-sprint defects dropped by [X]%, and go-live went smoothly. Lesson: most people conflicts are really process gaps."

Other variants to prepare: disagreeing with your manager about an estimate, a teammate not delivering their part, and a client or stakeholder pushing scope late.

Delivery tips

  • Never paint the other person as the villain. Show empathy and respect.
  • Make sure the story ends in a resolution, not "I was right".
  • Keep it professional. Avoid personal or emotional conflicts.

What interviewers look for: emotional maturity, communication, collaboration, a data-driven approach to decisions, and the ability to commit to a team decision.

E23 How do you integrate third-party data?
  • Pull (REST): WebClient (reactive) or OpenFeign/RestClient calling the vendor APIs. For periodic sync use @Scheduled or Quartz/ShedLock in a cluster. Track a lastSyncedAt value or cursor to do incremental pulls.
  • Push: expose webhook endpoints. Verify the signature or API key, acknowledge quickly (2xx), and process asynchronously.
  • Streaming: consume from Kafka/MQTT for high-volume IoT and sensor feeds, and scale with consumer groups.
  • Mapping and validation: use an adapter/anti-corruption layer to translate vendor DTOs into the internal model (MapStruct), validate the schema, and reject or quarantine bad records.
  • Resilience: timeouts, retries with exponential backoff, circuit breaker (Resilience4j), rate limiting, fallbacks, and a dead-letter queue for failures.
  • Idempotency: dedupe on the vendor event ID or a hash, and use upserts, so retries never create duplicates.
  • Storage: keep the raw payload (for audit and replay) separately from the normalised tables used by the app.
  • Security and ops: keep credentials in a vault or secrets store, use OAuth2 client-credentials where supported, and log or monitor sync failures with alerts.

Template: "In our project we integrate [e.g. traffic signal controllers / weather API / GPS vehicle tracking] using [mechanism]. My part was [building the adapter / scheduler / consumer, plus retry and idempotency handling]."

Integration patterns

Pattern When Spring tools
REST pull (polling) Vendor exposes an API; data changes periodically WebClient / RestClient / OpenFeign + @Scheduled (+ ShedLock when running several instances)
Webhooks (push) Vendor calls us on events A @RestController endpoint with HMAC signature verification, returning 2xx fast and processing asynchronously
Message/stream ingestion High-volume events, IoT Kafka (@KafkaListener), MQTT (Spring Integration MQTT / Paho) → Kafka bridge
File / SFTP / batch Daily dumps (CSV, XML, Excel) Spring Batch, Spring Integration SFTP, @Scheduled
Database / CDC Partner database or legacy system Debezium CDC → Kafka, or read replicas / views
Real-time streams Vendor WebSocket or SSE Reactor Netty WebSocketClient / WebClient SSE

Pipeline (whatever the transport)

 Source ─► Adapter (auth, rate limit, retry, circuit breaker)
        ─► Store RAW (audit/replay)  ─► Validate ─► Map/Normalise (canonical model)
        ─► Deduplicate (idempotency key) ─► Persist normalised + publish event (Kafka)
        ─► Invalid → dead-letter (table/topic) + alert
        ─► Metrics: fetched/accepted/rejected counts, lag, last-success timestamp

Key concerns to discuss

  • Authentication: API keys, OAuth2 client credentials, mutual TLS. Store secrets in a vault, never in code.
  • Mapping: an anti-corruption layer that translates vendor fields into our canonical domain model. Use MapStruct or a dedicated mapper. Make field mappings configurable per vendor where possible.
  • Validation: mandatory fields, value ranges (for example, AQI from 0 to 500), timestamps (convert to UTC, reject future-dated readings), units, and enums. Use Bean Validation plus custom rules.
  • Retries: exponential backoff with jitter. Retry only idempotent calls and transient errors (timeouts, 5xx, 429). Do not retry 4xx validation errors.
  • Rate limits: a client-side limiter (Resilience4j RateLimiter), respect Retry-After, batch requests, and use incremental fetches (since=lastSyncTime, cursor or ETag).
  • Circuit breaker and bulkhead: stop hammering a failing vendor, and isolate thread pools so one vendor cannot take down the service.
  • Idempotency: use a natural key (vendor + externalId + timestamp) with a unique constraint and upsert. Webhooks are redelivered and Kafka is at-least-once, so duplicates will happen.
  • Store raw and normalised: raw JSON (in a JSONB column, object storage or a Kafka topic) for audit, debugging, and reprocessing when mapping logic changes. The normalised tables serve queries and the UI.
  • Ordering and late data: use event time rather than processing time. Handle out-of-order data with last-write-wins on event_ts.
  • Schema evolution: a tolerant reader (@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)), version adapters, and contract tests.
  • Monitoring: Micrometer counters (fetched, accepted, rejected), a "last successful sync" gauge, an alert when data is stale for more than N minutes, and a correlation ID in logs. Show data health on an ops dashboard.
  • Testing: WireMock with recorded vendor responses, Testcontainers, and a sandbox vendor environment.

Code sketch

// 1) Client with timeouts, retry, circuit breaker and rate limiter
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class AqiVendorClient {
    private final WebClient vendorWebClient;   // built with base URL, auth filter, connect/read timeouts

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "aqiVendor", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
    @RateLimiter(name = "aqiVendor")
    @Retry(name = "aqiVendor")                 // backoff configured in application.yml; retries on IOException/5xx/429
    public List<VendorReading> fetchSince(Instant since) {
        return vendorWebClient.get()
                .uri(uri -> uri.path("/v1/readings").queryParam("since", since.toString()).build())
                .retrieve()
                .bodyToFlux(VendorReading.class)
                .collectList()
                .block(Duration.ofSeconds(30));   // blocking is fine inside a scheduler thread
    }

    private List<VendorReading> fallback(Instant since, Throwable t) {
        log.warn("AQI vendor unavailable since={}, cause={}", since, t.toString());
        return List.of();                       // skip this cycle; the watermark is not advanced
    }
}

// 2) Scheduled poller with a watermark (incremental sync), safe across instances
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class AqiSyncJob {
    private final AqiVendorClient client;
    private final IngestionService ingestion;
    private final SyncStateRepository syncState;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${integration.aqi.poll-ms:60000}")
    @SchedulerLock(name = "aqiSync", lockAtMostFor = "PT5M")   // ShedLock: only one instance runs it
    public void sync() {
        Instant since = syncState.getWatermark("AQI").orElse(Instant.now().minus(Duration.ofHours(1)));
        List<VendorReading> batch = client.fetchSince(since);
        if (batch.isEmpty()) return;
        ingestion.ingest("AQI", batch);
        syncState.saveWatermark("AQI", batch.stream().map(VendorReading::observedAt)
                                        .max(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElse(since));
    }
}

// 3) Ingestion: raw store → validate → map → idempotent upsert → publish
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class IngestionService {
    private final RawPayloadRepository rawRepo;
    private final SensorReadingRepository readingRepo;
    private final DeadLetterRepository dlq;
    private final ReadingMapper mapper;
    private final Validator validator;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, SensorReadingEvent> kafka;
    private final MeterRegistry metrics;

    @Transactional
    public void ingest(String source, List<VendorReading> batch) {
        for (VendorReading r : batch) {
            rawRepo.save(RawPayload.of(source, r.externalId(), toJson(r)));          // keep raw for audit/replay

            SensorReading reading = mapper.toCanonical(r);                           // units → SI, time → UTC
            Set<ConstraintViolation<SensorReading>> errors = validator.validate(reading);
            if (!errors.isEmpty()) {
                dlq.save(DeadLetter.of(source, r.externalId(), errors.toString()));
                metrics.counter("ingest.rejected", "source", source).increment();
                continue;
            }
            // Idempotent: unique (source, external_id) → INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING / upsert
            boolean inserted = readingRepo.insertIfAbsent(reading) == 1;
            if (inserted) {
                metrics.counter("ingest.accepted", "source", source).increment();
                // For strict consistency use the transactional outbox pattern instead of a direct send
                kafka.send("sensor.readings.normalized", reading.sensorId(), SensorReadingEvent.from(reading));
            }
        }
    }
}
// Webhook variant: verify, store, acknowledge fast, process async
@PostMapping("/webhooks/parking")
public ResponseEntity<Void> parkingWebhook(@RequestHeader("X-Signature") String sig,
                                           @RequestBody String body) {
    if (!hmacVerifier.isValid(body, sig)) return ResponseEntity.status(401).build();
    inboundQueue.publish(body);                 // e.g. to Kafka; processed by an idempotent consumer
    return ResponseEntity.accepted().build();   // 202 quickly, so the vendor does not time out and retry
}
resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      aqiVendor: { maxAttempts: 3, waitDuration: 2s, enableExponentialBackoff: true, exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2 }
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      aqiVendor: { slidingWindowSize: 20, failureRateThreshold: 50, waitDurationInOpenState: 60s }
  ratelimiter:
    instances:
      aqiVendor: { limitForPeriod: 50, limitRefreshPeriod: 1m, timeoutDuration: 5s }

Template answer for "Have you integrated third-party data?"

"Yes. In [project] we integrated [vendor/system: e.g. traffic signal controllers, GPS trackers, weather API, CCTV VMS, SMS gateway] using [pattern]. I built [adapter/poller/consumer] with [retries/circuit breaker/rate limiting]. We stored raw and normalised data, made processing idempotent with [key], and monitored [metrics]. The main challenge was [inconsistent data/rate limits/downtime], and I solved it by [approach]."

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you handle vendor downtime? A circuit breaker plus fallback, do not advance the watermark, catch up on recovery, and alert when data goes stale.
  • Polling vs webhooks? Polling is simple and under our control, but adds latency and wastes calls. Webhooks are real time but need a public endpoint, signature verification, idempotency, and reconciliation polling as a safety net.
  • How do you reprocess data after a mapping bug? Replay from the stored raw payloads (or the Kafka raw topic) through the fixed mapper, using idempotent upserts.
  • What about large files? Spring Batch chunk processing (read, process, write), with skip/retry policies, restartable jobs, and streaming parsers rather than loading everything into memory.
E24 Microservices in your project / how you handle microservices architecture (TEMPLATE) Co. 2G2

See Section D for the detailed concepts (gateway, discovery, config, resilience, Saga, tracing).

"Our platform is split into [N] services by business capability, for example [device, incident, alert, notification, user, report]. Each service owns its database and is deployed independently on [Docker/K8s]. Clients come in through [Spring Cloud Gateway], which handles [JWT] auth and routing. Services talk to each other synchronously over REST/[Feign], with timeouts and [Resilience4j] circuit breakers. They also talk asynchronously over [Kafka] for events such as IncidentCreated and SensorThresholdBreached. We use [Config Server/ConfigMaps] for configuration and [Eureka/K8s DNS] for discovery. For observability we use [ELK + Zipkin/Prometheus-Grafana] and propagate correlation IDs. Cross-service consistency is handled with [eventual consistency / Saga / outbox]. I personally [built/maintained X service, its APIs and its Kafka integration]."

Cross-reference: the microservices patterns themselves (service discovery, API gateway, config server, circuit breaker, Saga, outbox, distributed tracing, inter-service communication) are covered in depth in Section D. This answer is the project-story template that ties them to your experience.

Template answer

"Our platform is split into about [N] microservices, organised by business capability: for example [auth/user-service, device-service, event/alert-service, incident-service, notification-service, gis-service, report-service, integration adapters]. Each is a Spring Boot application with its own database/schema, packaged as a Docker image and deployed on [Kubernetes/OpenShift/VMs] through [Jenkins/GitLab CI]."

"Client entry: The Angular app calls an API gateway ([Spring Cloud Gateway/Nginx/Kong]), which handles routing, JWT validation, CORS and rate limiting."

"Service-to-service communication: For synchronous queries we use [OpenFeign/WebClient] with timeouts, retries and Resilience4j circuit breakers. For events such as SensorThresholdBreached or IncidentCreated we use Kafka, so producers and consumers are decoupled and can scale independently."

"Discovery and configuration: [Eureka / Kubernetes DNS] for discovery, and [Spring Cloud Config / ConfigMaps + Secrets] for externalised config per environment."

"Data consistency: There are no distributed transactions. We use [Saga choreography with events / the transactional outbox] and idempotent consumers. For example, when an incident is created, the notification and assignment services react to events; if something fails, we [retry / use the DLQ / compensate]."

"Observability: a correlation/trace ID through [Micrometer Tracing + Zipkin/Jaeger/OpenTelemetry], centralised logs in [ELK], metrics in [Prometheus/Grafana], Actuator health probes for Kubernetes liveness and readiness, and alerts on error rate, latency and Kafka consumer lag."

"Security: [Keycloak/OAuth2] issues tokens. The gateway validates them, and services also act as resource servers with role checks (@PreAuthorize). Service-to-service calls use [client credentials / mTLS]."

"My part: I own / owned [service(s)]. I [designed its APIs and events, wrote the Kafka consumers, added circuit breakers, wrote contract tests, handled deployment configuration]. One concrete example is [story from E21]."

How you "handle" microservices day to day (talking points)

  • Service boundaries: DDD bounded contexts, with one team or service owning one capability and its data. Avoid a "distributed monolith" with chatty synchronous chains.
  • API contracts and versioning: OpenAPI specs, /v1 and /v2 versions, backward-compatible changes, and consumer-driven contract tests ([Spring Cloud Contract/Pact]).
  • Resilience: timeouts everywhere, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks, and graceful degradation (the dashboard still loads if analytics is down).
  • Deployment: independent pipelines, rolling or blue-green deployments, feature flags, and backward-compatible DB migrations.
  • Local development: docker-compose for dependencies (Kafka, Postgres, Redis), and Testcontainers in tests.
  • Debugging across services: start from the trace ID in the UI error or log, then look at the Zipkin trace to find the slow or failing service, then at that service's logs.
  • Scaling: horizontal scaling of stateless services (Kubernetes HPA), Kafka partitions for consumer parallelism, and caching hot reads in Redis.

Honest variants

  • If your project is mostly a monolith: "Our core is a modular monolith, with [N] separate services for [integration/notification]. I understand the trade-offs: we split out [X] because it needed independent scaling. Here is how I would decompose further…"
  • If someone else set up the infrastructure: "The platform team owns Kubernetes and the gateway. I consume them: I write the Helm values, health checks and configuration for my service."

Delivery tips

  • Draw the services and arrows. Mark sync and async calls differently.
  • Mention at least one real problem (cascading failure, duplicate events, a debugging difficulty) and how you solved it. That proves hands-on experience.
  • Don't claim patterns you didn't use. "We didn't need Sagas because…" is a fine answer.

What interviewers look for: a real understanding of why microservices (and their costs), communication and consistency strategies, resilience and observability practice, and clear personal ownership.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you handle a transaction spanning services? A Saga (choreography or orchestration) with compensating actions, plus the outbox pattern for reliable event publishing. See Section D.
  • What happens if a downstream service is down? The circuit breaker opens, a fallback is used (cached or default data, or queue for later), the user gets a degraded but working UI, and alerts fire.
  • How do you keep services from becoming too chatty? Coarser APIs, event-carried state transfer (local read models), and BFF/aggregation at the gateway.
  • When would you NOT use microservices? With a small team, an unclear domain, or an early-stage product. A modular monolith is cheaper to build and operate.
E25 "Given a list of strings, write…" (question incomplete)

Note: the source cut this question off (G2Healthcare Q26). Fill in the full question if you remember it. Below are 3 likely completions with one-line Java Stream answers.

List<String> list = List.of("apple", "bat", "avocado", "cat", "apple", "banana");

// 1) Group strings by length
Map<Integer, List<String>> byLen = list.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length));

// 2) Find strings starting with a given letter (e.g. "a")
List<String> startsA = list.stream().filter(s -> s.startsWith("a")).toList();   // Java 16+; else collect(Collectors.toList())

// 3) Count the frequency of each string
Map<String, Long> freq = list.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));

Other common variants: remove duplicates (distinct()), sort by length (sorted(Comparator.comparing(String::length))), find the first non-repeated string (LinkedHashMap counting, then filter count == 1), join with commas (Collectors.joining(",")), and uppercase all (map(String::toUpperCase)).

Note: the source question (G2Healthcare Q26) was cut off after "Given a list of strings, write…". Candidate: please supply the complete question text so it can be answered exactly. Meanwhile, here are full solutions to the three most likely completions, using Java Streams.

Sample input used throughout:

List<String> words = List.of("apple", "bat", "cat", "banana", "kiwi", "apple", "avocado");

Completion 1: group the strings by length

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

Map<Integer, List<String>> byLength = words.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length));
// HashMap: order is not guaranteed by contract

// Sorted by length, with duplicates removed and each group sorted
Map<Integer, Set<String>> byLengthSorted = words.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                String::length,
                TreeMap::new,                                         // sorted keys
                Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new)));              // distinct and sorted values

System.out.println(byLengthSorted);

Output:

{3=[bat, cat], 4=[kiwi], 5=[apple], 6=[banana], 7=[avocado]}

Variations:

// Count per length
Map<Integer, Long> countByLength = words.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
// {3=2, 4=1, 5=2, 6=1, 7=1}

// Partition into short (<5) and long (>=5)
Map<Boolean, List<String>> parts = words.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(s -> s.length() >= 5));
// {false=[bat, cat, kiwi], true=[apple, banana, apple, avocado]}

Completion 2: filter strings starting with a given letter, then sort

// Starting with 'a', distinct, sorted alphabetically
List<String> aWords = words.stream()
        .filter(Objects::nonNull)                 // defensive: skip nulls
        .filter(s -> s.startsWith("a"))
        .distinct()
        .sorted()
        .collect(Collectors.toList());            // Java 16+: .toList() (unmodifiable)
System.out.println(aWords);                       // [apple, avocado]

// Case-insensitive, sorted by length then alphabetically, uppercase output
List<String> bWords = words.stream()
        .filter(s -> s != null && !s.isEmpty() && Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(0)) == 'b')
        .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()))
        .map(String::toUpperCase)
        .toList();
System.out.println(bWords);                       // [BAT, BANANA]

// Reusable method
static List<String> startingWith(List<String> list, String prefix) {
    return list.stream()
            .filter(s -> s != null && s.regionMatches(true, 0, prefix, 0, prefix.length()))
            .sorted(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)
            .toList();
}

Plain sorted() uses natural order, which is lexicographic and case-sensitive: uppercase letters sort before lowercase, so "Zebra" < "apple". Use String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER when case should not matter.

Completion 3: frequency of each string

// Frequency map, preserving first-seen order
Map<String, Long> freq = words.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                Function.identity(),
                LinkedHashMap::new,
                Collectors.counting()));
System.out.println(freq);
// {apple=2, bat=1, cat=1, banana=1, kiwi=1, avocado=1}

// Only the duplicates
List<String> duplicates = freq.entrySet().stream()
        .filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1)
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
        .toList();                                // [apple]

// Most frequent string
String mostFrequent = freq.entrySet().stream()
        .max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue())
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
        .orElse(null);                            // "apple"

// First non-repeating string (relies on LinkedHashMap encounter order)
String firstUnique = freq.entrySet().stream()
        .filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1)
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
        .findFirst()
        .orElse(null);                            // "bat"

// Sorted by frequency descending, then alphabetically
List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> ranked = freq.entrySet().stream()
        .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()
                .thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))
        .toList();
// [apple=2, avocado=1, banana=1, bat=1, cat=1, kiwi=1]

// Alternative without streams
Map<String, Integer> freq2 = new HashMap<>();
for (String w : words) freq2.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);

Case-insensitive frequency: groupingBy(s -> s.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT), LinkedHashMap::new, counting()). Character frequency inside a single string is another common variant:

Map<Character, Long> charFreq = "banana".chars()
        .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
// {b=1, a=3, n=2}

Other possible completions (quick answers)

String longest = words.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)).orElse("");   // "avocado"
String joined  = words.stream().distinct().collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));     // [apple, bat, cat, banana, kiwi, avocado]
List<String> reversed = words.stream().map(s -> new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()).toList();
Map<Character, List<String>> byFirstLetter = words.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(s -> s.charAt(0), TreeMap::new, Collectors.toList()));
// {a=[apple, apple, avocado], b=[bat, banana], c=[cat], k=[kiwi]}
List<String> palindromes = Stream.of("level", "kiwi", "madam")
        .filter(s -> new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString().equals(s)).toList();        // [level, madam]

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why does groupingBy need TreeMap::new or LinkedHashMap::new? The default is a HashMap, which guarantees no order. Supply a map factory for sorted or insertion-ordered output.
  • toList() vs Collectors.toList()? Java 16's Stream.toList() returns an unmodifiable list. Collectors.toList() returns a mutable ArrayList in practice, though the spec does not guarantee that.
  • How do you handle nulls in the list? Add filter(Objects::nonNull) first. groupingBy throws an NPE if the classifier returns a null key.
  • Parallel stream here? Not worth it for small lists. For large lists, use groupingByConcurrent and avoid order-dependent operations.
E26 Puzzle: 12 balls, one odd (heavier or lighter), find it in 3 weighings. Other rounds (Question List)
  • Why 3 weighings are enough: each weighing has 3 outcomes, so 3 weighings give 3³ = 27 outcomes. There are 24 possibilities (12 balls × heavy or light), and 27 ≥ 24.
  • Label the balls 1–12. Weighing 1: 1,2,3,4 vs 5,6,7,8.
  • If balanced: the odd ball is in 9–12, and 1–8 are known good. Weighing 2: 9,10,11 vs 1,2,3.
    • Balanced: 12 is the odd ball. Weigh 12 vs 1 to find out whether it is heavy or light.
    • 9–11 side heavier: the odd ball is heavy and is one of 9–11. Weigh 9 vs 10. The heavier one is odd; if balanced, it is 11.
    • 9–11 side lighter: same as above, but the lighter one is odd; if balanced, it is 11.
  • If 1,2,3,4 > 5,6,7,8: the odd ball is one of 1–4 (heavy) or one of 5–8 (light). Weighing 2: 1,2,5 vs 3,6,9 (9 is known good).
    • Balanced: it is 4 (heavy), 7 (light) or 8 (light). Weigh 7 vs 8. The lighter one is odd; if balanced, it is 4 (heavy).
    • Left heavier: it is 1 (heavy), 2 (heavy) or 6 (light). Weigh 1 vs 2. The heavier one is odd; if balanced, it is 6 (light).
    • Right heavier: it is 3 (heavy) or 5 (light). Weigh 3 vs 9. If 3 is heavier, 3 is the heavy ball; if balanced, 5 is the light ball.
  • If 1,2,3,4 < 5,6,7,8: use the same steps with heavy and light swapped.

Why it's possible: there are 12 × 2 = 24 possible answers (which ball, heavy or light), and 3 weighings with 3 outcomes each give 3³ = 27 distinguishable results. Each weighing must split the remaining possibilities roughly into thirds.

Label the balls 1–12. Weighing 1: 1 2 3 4 vs 5 6 7 8.

Case A: balanced. The odd ball is among 9–12; balls 1–8 are known good.

  • Weighing 2: 9 10 11 vs 1 2 3 (three good balls).
    • Balanced → ball 12 is odd. Weighing 3: 12 vs 1 tells you whether it's heavy or light.
    • 9 10 11 heavier → the odd ball is 9, 10 or 11 and is heavy. Weighing 3: 9 vs 10: the heavier one is odd; if balanced, 11 is heavy.
    • 9 10 11 lighter → the same, but light: the lighter of 9 and 10, or 11.

Case B: left side (1 2 3 4) heavier. Either one of 1–4 is heavy or one of 5–8 is light; 9–12 are good.

  • Weighing 2: 1 2 5 vs 3 6 9.
    • Balanced → the odd ball is 4 (heavy), or 7 or 8 (light). Weighing 3: 7 vs 8: the lighter is odd; if balanced, 4 is heavy.
    • Left heavier → 1 or 2 is heavy, or 6 is light. Weighing 3: 1 vs 2: the heavier is odd; if balanced, 6 is light.
    • Right heavier → 3 is heavy or 5 is light. Weighing 3: 3 vs 9: if 3 is heavier it's the odd (heavy) ball; if balanced, 5 is light.

Case C: left side lighter. Mirror case B with "heavy" and "light" swapped (one of 1–4 is light or one of 5–8 is heavy; same weighings).

How to present it in an interview: state the 24 vs 27 bound first, then explain the trick in weighing 2 of case B. Moving balls between pans and bringing in a known-good ball makes each outcome point to a different group of suspects. Interviewers care more about this structured reasoning than about a memorised tree.

Likely follow-ups:

  • If you know the odd ball is heavier? Up to 3³ = 27 balls: split into thirds each time.
  • Max balls in w weighings when heavy/light is unknown? (3ʷ − 3) / 2, which gives 12 for w = 3.
  • With an extra ball known to be good? 13 balls can be solved in 3 weighings.
E27 Puzzle: remove exactly half the water from a full cylindrical glass. Other rounds (Question List)
  • Tilt the glass slowly and let water pour out. Stop when the water surface touches the rim on one side and the very edge of the base on the other side.
  • That diagonal water surface passes through the cylinder's centre. Because a cylinder is symmetric about its centre, the plane cuts it into two equal volumes, so exactly half the water remains.
  • This does not work for a tapered (conical) glass. It is not symmetric about its centre, so the two parts would not be equal.

Answer: tilt the glass and pour slowly until the water surface runs exactly from the rim on one side to the bottom edge of the base on the other side, with the base just about to show. Stop there: exactly half the water is left.

Why it works: the water surface is then a plane through the cylinder's centre point (it joins the top edge on one side to the bottom edge directly opposite). A cylinder is point-symmetric about its centre, so that plane cuts it into two congruent pieces of equal volume: the water that stays and the empty space that was poured out.

Step by step

  1. Hold the glass over a sink and tilt it slowly.
  2. Keep pouring until the water line touches the edge of the base on the far side while still touching the rim on the pouring side.
  3. Stop and set the glass upright. The remaining water reaches exactly half the height.

Limits

  • It only works for a true cylinder. In a tapered glass (wider at the top) the same position leaves less than half, because more of the volume sits near the rim.
  • A ruler is the alternative: volume ∝ height in a cylinder, so measure the height and pour until the water is at half of it.
