What interviewers look for: a solution without measuring tools, a justification (symmetry), and awareness of the assumption (straight sides). Saying "it fails for a tapered glass" shows you check assumptions, the same habit as checking edge cases in code.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How to leave one third? Not possible by tilting alone; you'd need a measurement.
  • Glass with a thick base? Use the bottom of the water column, not the outside of the glass.
  • Why not estimate by eye? It isn't precise, and the question asks for exactly half.
F

Production & Troubleshooting Scenarios

F1 Your application suddenly throws OutOfMemoryError in production. How will you identify the root cause and fix it?
  1. Read the exact message: Java heap space, Metaspace, GC overhead limit exceeded and unable to create native thread each have a different cause.
  2. Make sure the JVM writes a dump when it fails: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps. If the pod is still alive, take one yourself with jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dumps/heap.hprof.
  3. Open the dump in Eclipse MAT. Use the Leak Suspects report and the Dominator Tree to find what retains the most memory, for example a static Map cache, an unbounded List, or ThreadLocals that are never cleared.
  4. Compare the trend of Actuator jvm.memory.used in Grafana with the deployment timeline.
  5. Fix the code, for example with a bounded Caffeine cache, streaming or pagination instead of findAll(), or closing resources. Only then size the heap correctly (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 in Kubernetes).
  6. Add an alert on heap usage above 85% after GC.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Read the exact OOM message, because each one means something different: Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded, Metaspace, unable to create native thread, Direct buffer memory. A pod that is OOMKilled (exit code 137) with no Java OOM in the logs is a container memory problem, not a heap problem.
  • kubectl describe pod <pod> shows Last State, Reason and restart count. In Grafana, check jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"}. A sawtooth whose floor keeps rising means a leak. A sudden spike means one large request.
  • Look at what changed recently: a deployment, a traffic spike, or a new report or export feature.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Make sure the next OOM leaves evidence: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError. Mount /dumps on a PVC so the dump survives the restart.
  2. If the pod is still alive, take a live dump: kubectl exec <pod> -- jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /dumps/heap.hprof, then kubectl cp it out.
  3. For a quick look without a full dump, run jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram | head -30 twice, a few minutes apart. Classes whose instance counts keep growing are your suspects.
  4. Open the dump in Eclipse MAT and run the Leak Suspects report. Then use the Dominator Tree and Path to GC Roots (exclude weak refs) to find who holds the memory, for example a static HashMap, a Hibernate PersistenceContext, or a ThreadLocal.
  5. Check the GC logs (-Xlog:gc*) to see whether full GCs ran back-to-back before the crash.
  6. For a Metaspace or native OOM, use jcmd 1 VM.metaspace and jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary (this needs -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary).

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Unbounded static cache or map MAT dominator shows a HashMap held by a static field Caffeine with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite
Loading a huge result set (findAll()) Dominator is an ArrayList of entities inside a request thread Pagination, streaming, projections
Long transaction or batch growing the persistence context StatefulPersistenceContext holds millions of entities flush() and clear() every N rows
ThreadLocal not cleaned up in a pooled thread GC root is a Thread → threadLocals try/finally { tl.remove(); }
Heap larger than the container limit OOMKilled with no Java OOM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 and set limits correctly

Fix / prevention

@Bean
public Cache<String, DeviceDto> deviceCache() {
    return Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(50_000)
            .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
            .recordStats()
            .build();
}
# deployment.yaml
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
resources:
  limits: { memory: "2Gi" }

Add a Prometheus alert for heap usage above 85% after GC for 10 minutes, and run a soak test before each release.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why use ExitOnOutOfMemoryError? After an OOM the JVM is in an undefined state. Exiting lets Kubernetes restart the pod cleanly.
  • Heap dump on a 4 GB heap freezes the pod? Yes. The JVM pauses during the dump. Take it from a pod that is out of rotation, or remove the pod from the Service first.
  • How do you tell a leak from under-sizing? With a leak, the old-gen floor keeps rising after each full GC. With under-sizing, the floor stays flat but sits close to the maximum.
F2 Multiple users are updating the same data simultaneously and wrong data is getting stored. How will you handle this concurrency issue?
  1. Confirm it is a lost update: two transactions read the same version and the last write wins.
  2. Optimistic locking (the default choice): add a @Version column. Hibernate adds WHERE version=? to the update and throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. Return 409 to the user or retry.
  3. Pessimistic locking when contention is high, for example a wallet balance: @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE), which issues SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
  4. Prefer an atomic SQL update to read-modify-write: UPDATE account SET bal = bal - :amt WHERE id=:id AND bal >= :amt.
  5. Across several instances, use a distributed lock (Redis/Redisson) only when the database cannot enforce the rule.
@Entity class Incident { @Id Long id; @Version Long version; String status; }

Symptoms & first checks

  • This is the classic lost update: two requests read the same row, both modify it, and the last write silently overwrites the first. Typical examples are incorrect counters, overwritten status changes, and parking-slot double booking.
  • Check the code for a read-modify-write pattern (findById → set → save) with no versioning. Check the transaction isolation level (the PostgreSQL default is READ COMMITTED). Check for any synchronized block, which does nothing across multiple pods.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Reproduce with concurrency: a JMeter or Gatling test, or a JUnit test that fires 50 CompletableFuture calls against the same ID.
  2. Turn on SQL logging (logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG) and confirm the UPDATE has no version predicate.
  3. Check the audit columns or pg_stat_activity for overlapping transactions on the same row.
  4. Decide on a strategy based on how much contention there is.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No optimistic lock UPDATE ... WHERE id=? only @Version
Counter computed in Java x = get(); set(x+1) Atomic SQL SET x = x + 1
JVM lock in a multi-pod setup synchronized / ReentrantLock DB lock or Redis lock
Check-then-insert race Duplicate rows appear Unique constraint plus handling the conflict

Fix / prevention For low contention, use optimistic locking:

@Entity
public class ParkingSlot {
    @Id private Long id;
    private String status;
    @Version private Long version;   // Hibernate adds "AND version=?"
}

@ExceptionHandler(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
ProblemDetail conflict() {
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
            "Record was modified by another user, reload and retry");
}

For high contention or critical sections, use a pessimistic lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE):

public interface SlotRepository extends JpaRepository<ParkingSlot, Long> {
    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "3000"))
    @Query("select s from ParkingSlot s where s.id = :id")
    Optional<ParkingSlot> findForUpdate(@Param("id") Long id);

    @Modifying
    @Query("update Wallet w set w.balance = w.balance - :amt where w.id = :id and w.balance >= :amt")
    int debit(@Param("id") Long id, @Param("amt") BigDecimal amt);   // atomic, returns 0 if insufficient
}

Call findForUpdate inside a @Transactional service method. Send the version to the UI (or as an ETag / If-Match header) so a stale form gets a 409 instead of overwriting newer data. For cross-service locks, use Redisson RLock with a lease time.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Optimistic or pessimistic? Optimistic when conflicts are rare, because it takes no locks and scales well. Pessimistic when conflicts are frequent or a retry is expensive.
  • Would SERIALIZABLE help? Yes, but PostgreSQL then raises serialization failures that you must retry, and throughput drops.
  • Retry on an optimistic lock failure? Only for server-side merges that are safe to repeat, for example @Retryable(retryFor = ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class). For user edits, return 409 and let the user reload.
F3 One API is taking 20 seconds response time only in production, but locally it works fine. How will you debug it?
  1. Look at the trace (Zipkin/Jaeger, Micrometer Tracing) to see which span takes the time: database, a downstream HTTP call, or the service's own code.
  2. Check Actuator /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=uri:/api/x for p95/p99 latency. Also check hikaricp.connections.pending, because waiting for a connection is a common cause.
  3. Database: production has far more data than local. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query and look for a missing index or a sequential scan. Enable pg_stat_statements to find slow queries.
  4. Take 3–4 jstack <pid> dumps a few seconds apart while the request runs, to see where threads are blocked (socket read, lock, pool wait).
  5. Check what differs in production: DNS or network latency, missing timeouts on RestClient/WebClient, SSL handshakes, logging set to DEBUG.
  6. Fix it (index, timeout, caching, async), then confirm with a load test.

Symptoms & first checks

  • "Only in prod" almost always comes down to data volume, network hops, or resource limits, not the code itself.
  • In Grafana, look at http_server_requests_seconds for that URI: is it p50 or only p99, and is it every request or only some? A consistent ~20 s often points to a timeout plus retry (for example 2 × 10 s), DNS, or a waiting connection pool.
  • Open a slow trace in Zipkin, Jaeger or Tempo. The span breakdown shows immediately whether the time goes to the DB, a downstream HTTP call, or the service itself.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Trace: find the span that takes most of the 20 s.
  2. If it is the DB: run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the captured SQL against prod-sized data. Check pg_stat_statements for mean time and pg_stat_activity for locks (wait_event_type = 'Lock').
  3. Check the connection pool: hikaricp_connections_pending and hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds. If threads are waiting for a connection, the pool is too small or connections are being leaked.
  4. Check for N+1 queries: enable spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true briefly and look at the query count per request.
  5. While a slow call is in flight, take thread dumps: kubectl exec <pod> -- jcmd 1 Thread.print, three times, 5 s apart. Threads stuck in SocketInputStream.read mean a slow downstream. Threads stuck in HikariPool.getConnection mean pool starvation.
  6. Check CPU throttling: rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m]). A 500m limit with a busy JVM causes stalls.
  7. Profile on the pod: asprof -d 30 -e wall -f /tmp/wall.html 1. A wall-clock profile shows where the time goes, including time spent blocked.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Missing index (prod has 50M rows, local has 1k) Seq Scan in EXPLAIN Composite index, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
N+1 lazy loading Hundreds of SELECTs per call JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, DTO projection
Downstream timeout and retry Span shows 2 × 10 s Proper timeouts, circuit breaker
Hikari starvation pending > 0 Fix the leak or long transaction, size the pool
CPU throttling Throttled periods are high Raise the CPU limit or request

Fix / prevention

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"sensors", "zone"})
@Query("select d from Device d where d.city.id = :cityId")
List<Device> findWithSensors(@Param("cityId") Long cityId);
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20
      connection-timeout: 3000
      leak-detection-threshold: 20000

Keep a staging database with production-like volume, and alert on p95 latency per endpoint.

Likely follow-ups:

  • No tracing in place? Log per-step timings with a request ID, or temporarily use /actuator/httpexchanges together with SQL timing logs.
  • Can you profile prod safely? Yes. JFR (jcmd 1 JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/r.jfr) and async-profiler both have low overhead.
  • What if it is slow only for one tenant or city? That points to data skew. That tenant has far more rows, so its plan or index differs.
F4 CPU usage suddenly increased to 95% in production server. What steps will you take to investigate?
  1. Find the process: top, or kubectl top pod. Check whether the spike lines up with a deployment, a traffic peak or a batch job.
  2. Find the busy threads: top -H -p <pid>. Convert the thread ID to hex (printf '%x' <tid>) and match it to nid=0x... in the jstack <pid> output.
  3. Take several thread dumps. If the same stack keeps showing up, that is usually the culprit: an infinite loop, regex backtracking, heavy JSON serialization or a busy-wait.
  4. Check whether GC is the cause with jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000. Frequent full GCs burn CPU.
  5. Profile with JFR (jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=cpu.jfr) or async-profiler to get a flame graph.
  6. Mitigate first (scale out with HPA, roll back), then fix the code and add CPU alerts.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Confirm whether the CPU belongs to the Java process or something else: top, then kubectl top pod.
  • Check whether traffic also went up (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[1m])). If load is unchanged, it is a bug.
  • Check GC: high GC CPU means a memory problem, not a compute problem (see F7). Look at jvm_gc_pause_seconds and process_cpu_usage.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Find the hot threads: top -H -p <pid> and note the TIDs with the highest CPU.
  2. Convert each TID to hex: printf '%x\n' 12345 gives 3039.
  3. Take a thread dump with jstack <pid> or jcmd <pid> Thread.print > td.txt, then grep -A 20 'nid=0x3039' td.txt. This shows the exact stack that is burning CPU.
  4. Repeat 3–4 times. If the same frames keep appearing, that is the hotspot.
  5. For a statistical view, use asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/cpu.html <pid> (a flame graph) or JFR, analysed in JDK Mission Control under Method Profiling.
  6. In Kubernetes: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh, then run the same jcmd commands. If top is missing, use kubectl debug with an ephemeral container.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Infinite or tight loop (e.g. while retry with no sleep) Same frame in every dump Fix the loop, add backoff
Catastrophic regex backtracking Stack sits in java.util.regex.Pattern$... Rewrite the regex, validate input length
GC thrashing GC Thread# threads are hot, high GC time Fix the leak or size the heap
Heavy JSON or serialization of huge payloads Hot in Jackson Paginate, use projections
Busy-spin consumer (poll(0) in a loop) Kafka/consumer thread hot Proper poll timeout
HashMap corruption from concurrent access (legacy) Hot in HashMap.put/get ConcurrentHashMap
Traffic surge RPS grew proportionally HPA, rate limiting, caching

Fix / prevention

// Bad: a hot retry loop
while (!client.isReady()) { }               // spins a core at 100%

// Good: bounded retry with backoff
RetryTemplate retry = RetryTemplate.builder()
        .maxAttempts(5)
        .exponentialBackoff(200, 2, 5000)
        .build();
retry.execute(ctx -> client.connect());
# HPA on CPU
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 8
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 } }

Short-term mitigation: scale out or roll back the last deployment, and keep the dumps for the root-cause analysis.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not just restart? A restart buys time but destroys the evidence. Take the dumps first.
  • What is nid in a thread dump? The native OS thread ID in hex, which maps to the TIDs shown by top -H.
  • What if CPU is high but no app thread is hot? Check GC Thread, C2 CompilerThread (JIT warm-up just after deploy), and logging threads (synchronous logging at DEBUG level).
F5 Your application is creating too many threads and server becomes slow. How will you identify thread leak?
  1. Watch the Actuator metric jvm.threads.live and jvm.threads.states over time. Steady growth without a plateau means a leak.
  2. Run jcmd <pid> Thread.print (or jstack) and group the threads by name. A large count of pool-N-thread-M threads points to a new ExecutorService being created per request.
  3. Typical causes: Executors.newFixedThreadPool() inside a method and never shut down, new Thread() in a loop, an HTTP client created per call, @Async running on the default executor.
  4. Fix it with one shared, bounded ThreadPoolTaskExecutor bean with names that show where the threads come from. Use shutdown() in @PreDestroy.
  5. Java 21 virtual threads are an option, but Java 17 needs bounded pools.
@Bean ThreadPoolTaskExecutor reportExecutor() {
  var ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
  ex.setCorePoolSize(8); ex.setMaxPoolSize(16); ex.setQueueCapacity(500);
  ex.setThreadNamePrefix("report-"); return ex;
}

Symptoms & first checks

  • jvm_threads_live_threads keeps rising without levelling off. This eventually leads to OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread, high context switching, and memory pressure (each thread reserves stack memory, about 1 MB by default).
  • Correlate the growth with traffic. A leak grows per request or per job run and never falls back.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Count the threads: jcmd <pid> Thread.print | grep -c '^"', or ls /proc/<pid>/task | wc -l.
  2. Group them by name prefix to see which pool is leaking:
    jcmd 1 Thread.print | grep '^"' | sed -E 's/^"([^"]*[^0-9-])[-0-9]*".*/\1/' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
    Typical culprits: pool-123-thread-1 (an Executors.newXxx() created per call), OkHttp ..., kafka-producer-network-thread, HttpClient-...-SelectorManager, SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor-4567.
  3. Take two dumps 10 minutes apart and diff the counts.
  4. Look at the thread states. Many WAITING (parking) threads on LinkedBlockingQueue.take means idle pools that were never shut down. Many BLOCKED threads means contention.
  5. Search the code for Executors.new, new Thread(, HttpClient.newHttpClient(), new KafkaProducer, WebClient.create() inside methods, and custom Executor beans.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
ExecutorService created per request, never shut down Many pool-N-thread-1 A single shared Spring-managed executor bean
@Async falling back to SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor (a new thread per task) SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor-N with growing N Define a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor
HTTP/Kafka client instantiated per call OkHttp/kafka-producer threads multiply Singleton client beans
Unbounded CachedThreadPool under load Thousands of pool-1-thread-* Bounded pool with a bounded queue

Fix / prevention

@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncConfig {
    @Bean(name = "taskExecutor")
    public ThreadPoolTaskExecutor taskExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        ex.setCorePoolSize(8);
        ex.setMaxPoolSize(16);
        ex.setQueueCapacity(500);                       // bounded
        ex.setThreadNamePrefix("city-async-");          // name it so it can be found in a dump
        ex.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        ex.setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true);
        ex.setAwaitTerminationSeconds(30);
        ex.initialize();
        return ex;
    }
}

Sizing rule of thumb: CPU-bound work gets about cores + 1 threads. IO-bound work gets cores × (1 + wait/compute). Always bound the queue. Expose executor_active_threads and executor_queued_tasks through Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics, and alert on the live-thread trend.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why CallerRunsPolicy? It applies backpressure: the submitting thread slows down instead of the task being dropped or memory growing without limit.
  • Does Spring Boot auto-configure an executor? Yes, applicationTaskExecutor. It backs off if you define your own Executor bean, which is a common source of surprises.
  • Would virtual threads help? On Java 21, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true makes threads cheap. But you still need to bound concurrency to the DB and downstream services, for example with a semaphore or bulkhead.
F6 One scheduled job is processing duplicate records multiple times. How will you prevent duplicate processing?
  1. Find out why. Either several pods run the same job, the previous run is still going when the next one starts, or records are not marked as processed atomically.
  2. Use a status column and claim rows atomically: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then set status='PROCESSING' in the same transaction.
  3. Make the processing idempotent with a unique constraint on a business key or an idempotency key, so a duplicate insert fails safely.
  4. For clustered deployments, use ShedLock so only one instance runs the job.
  5. Use fixedDelay instead of fixedRate so runs do not overlap.
SELECT * FROM events WHERE status='NEW' ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Symptoms & first checks

  • Duplicate notifications, double billing, or repeated Kafka events from one source row.
  • First decide which kind of duplication this is: (a) the same job running on several pods (see F20), (b) runs overlapping on one pod, (c) a record picked again because its status update did not commit, or (d) a retry after a partial failure.
  • Check the logs for the same record ID handled by different pods or threads, and check the job's timing against its interval.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Add log fields jobRunId, podName, recordId, then grep for the duplicated IDs.
  2. Check the scheduler type. fixedRate can overlap with a slow previous run when a multi-threaded scheduler is used. fixedDelay waits for the previous run to finish.
  3. Check the transaction boundaries. Is status set to PROCESSED in the same transaction as the work, or after an external call that can fail?
  4. Check whether the selection query is WHERE status='NEW' with no row claiming, so two workers read the same rows.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Several replicas run the job Different pod names for the same record ShedLock or leader election (F20)
Concurrent workers select the same rows Same ID handled by two threads FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claim
Status update rolled back after a side effect Exception after the email or API call Outbox pattern and idempotency key
No idempotency at the consumer Downstream inserts duplicates Unique constraint on the business key

Fix / prevention Claim rows atomically, so each row is picked by exactly one worker:

public interface AlertRepository extends JpaRepository<Alert, Long> {
    @Query(value = """
        SELECT * FROM alert
        WHERE status = 'NEW'
        ORDER BY created_at
        LIMIT :batch
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
        """, nativeQuery = true)
    List<Alert> claimBatch(@Param("batch") int batch);
}

@Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${jobs.alert.delay:30000}")
@Transactional
public void processAlerts() {
    for (Alert a : repo.claimBatch(200)) {
        notifier.send(a);              // idempotent: uses a.getId() as the idempotency key
        a.setStatus(Status.PROCESSED);
    }
}

Add a consumer-side guard as well:

CREATE TABLE processed_event (event_id VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY, processed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now());
-- INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; skip the record if 0 rows were inserted

For Kafka, enable enable.idempotence=true on the producer and keep a dedup table keyed by event ID on the consumer, because delivery is at-least-once.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why SKIP LOCKED? Workers skip rows another transaction has already locked, so they share the work without blocking each other.
  • Can you get exactly-once? Only within one store or transaction. End to end, aim for at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
  • Long batch holding locks? Commit in small chunks, or use a claim column (status='IN_PROGRESS', claimed_by, claimed_at) with a reaper that resets stale claims.
F7 Garbage collection time suddenly increased and application became slow. How will you troubleshoot?
  1. Enable GC logs: -Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m. Analyse them with GCEasy or GCViewer, looking at pause times, frequency and full GCs.
  2. Run jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000. If old gen stays near 100% after each GC, there is a leak or the heap is too small.
  3. Take a heap dump (jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump) and use MAT to find the objects that fill old gen.
  4. Use JFR's allocation profiling to find code that allocates heavily, such as large temporary collections, string concatenation in loops or loading whole result sets.
  5. Tune only after fixing the code: G1 (the default in Java 17) with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 and the right -Xmx/MaxRAMPercentage. Consider ZGC for large heaps.
  6. Check that the container memory limit is not causing throttling or OOMKills.

Symptoms & first checks

  • In Grafana, look at rate(jvm_gc_pause_seconds_sum[5m]) and jvm_gc_pause_seconds_max, alongside latency spikes. Check jvm_gc_memory_allocated_bytes_total: a rising allocation rate means more garbage is being produced.
  • Check jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap",id="G1 Old Gen"} after GC. If old gen does not drop, that is a leak (see F1).

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Enable and read the GC logs: -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m.
  2. Quick live view: jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000. Watch whether O (old %) stays high and FGC increases.
  3. Upload the GC log to GCeasy or GCViewer. Look for frequent full GCs, to-space exhausted or Evacuation Failure, Humongous Allocation, and long Pause Remark.
  4. Profile allocations: asprof -e alloc -d 30 -f alloc.html <pid>, or JFR (Allocation by class and TLAB views in JMC), to find who allocates the most.
  5. Check jcmd <pid> VM.flags for the effective heap. Is -Xmx too small for current traffic? Is it a container whose limit changed?
  6. Grep for explicit System.gc() calls, which some libraries make, and RMI DGC.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Memory leak keeps old gen full Post-GC old gen keeps rising Heap dump plus MAT, fix the reference
Heap too small for the load Old gen OK, frequent young GCs Increase MaxRAMPercentage or memory limit
High allocation rate (big DTOs, string concatenation, loading full lists) Alloc profile dominated by a few sites Stream or paginate, reuse buffers
G1 humongous objects (objects ≥ half a region) Humongous entries in the log -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m, avoid huge arrays
Explicit System.gc() Pause Full (System.gc()) -XX:+DisableExplicitGC
CPU throttled GC threads Container CPU throttling Raise the CPU limit, check ParallelGCThreads

Fix / prevention

env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: >-
      -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200
      -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75
      -Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m

For large heaps that need low pause times, consider -XX:+UseZGC (production-ready since JDK 15; generational ZGC from JDK 21). In code, avoid findAll() into memory, use projections, stream large exports, and set bounds on caches.

Alert rule:

rate(jvm_gc_pause_seconds_sum[5m]) > 0.1   # more than 10% of wall time spent in GC

Likely follow-ups:

  • G1 or ZGC? G1 is the balanced default. ZGC keeps pauses under a millisecond on large heaps, at some cost in throughput and memory.
  • Does a bigger heap always help? No. If there is a leak, it only delays the OOM, and with a parallel collector a bigger heap can make pauses longer.
  • What is a safepoint pause? A pause in which all threads are stopped. Long time-to-safepoint can come from counted loops, and shows up with -Xlog:safepoint.
F8 Large Excel/file processing causes application crash due to memory issue. How will you optimize it?
  1. Find the cause: loading the whole file into memory (XSSFWorkbook, Files.readAllBytes, MultipartFile.getBytes()).
  2. Read in streaming mode: Apache POI event model / XSSFReader (SAX), the excel-streaming-reader library, or EasyExcel. For CSV, read line by line with BufferedReader/Files.lines.
  3. Write large Excel files with SXSSFWorkbook(100), which keeps only 100 rows in memory.
  4. Process in chunks (for example 1,000 rows) with JDBC batch inserts. Spring Batch with a chunk-oriented step gives restartability.
  5. Move it to async: upload to S3/MinIO, return 202 with a job ID, and process in a background worker.
  6. Limit the upload size with spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size.
try (var wb = new SXSSFWorkbook(100)) { var sh = wb.createSheet(); /* write rows */ wb.write(out); wb.dispose(); }

Symptoms & first checks

  • An OOM or OOMKilled pod during upload or export, typically with XSSFWorkbook / WorkbookFactory.create() in the heap dump. XSSF loads the whole DOM, so a 50 MB .xlsx can need several GB of heap.
  • Check the multipart configuration: is the file being buffered fully into memory (MultipartFile.getBytes())?

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Heap dump plus MAT. The dominator is usually XSSFSheet / CTRow / XSSFCell objects, or a giant byte[].
  2. Measure the file sizes in production versus test.
  3. Check whether all parsed rows are collected into a List before saving, and whether they are saved with saveAll() without batching. That piles up rows in memory and entities in the persistence context.
  4. Check the request thread time. A synchronous 5-minute upload also blocks a Tomcat thread.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
DOM-based read (XSSFWorkbook) XSSF objects dominate Streaming reader (SAX / excel-streaming-reader)
DOM-based write for exports XSSFWorkbook with 1M rows SXSSFWorkbook with a row window
Accumulating rows in a list Huge ArrayList Process in chunks
Persistence context growth Millions of managed entities flush()/clear(), JDBC batching
getBytes() on upload Large byte[] getInputStream(), spool to disk

Fix / prevention Streaming read using com.github.pjfanning:excel-streaming-reader:

@Transactional
public void importReadings(InputStream in) throws IOException {
    try (Workbook wb = StreamingReader.builder()
            .rowCacheSize(200).bufferSize(8192).open(in)) {
        List<Reading> chunk = new ArrayList<>(1000);
        for (Row row : wb.getSheetAt(0)) {
            if (row.getRowNum() == 0) continue;
            chunk.add(mapRow(row));
            if (chunk.size() == 1000) { flushChunk(chunk); }
        }
        flushChunk(chunk);
    }
}

private void flushChunk(List<Reading> chunk) {
    repo.saveAll(chunk);
    em.flush();
    em.clear();          // detach entities so the persistence context stays small
    chunk.clear();
}

Streaming write:

try (SXSSFWorkbook wb = new SXSSFWorkbook(100);           // keep only 100 rows in memory
     OutputStream out = response.getOutputStream()) {
    Sheet sheet = wb.createSheet("Readings");
    try (Stream<ReadingView> rows = repo.streamAllBy()) {  // needs a @Transactional(readOnly = true) context
        AtomicInteger i = new AtomicInteger();
        rows.forEach(r -> {
            Row row = sheet.createRow(i.getAndIncrement());
            row.createCell(0).setCellValue(r.getDeviceId());
            row.createCell(1).setCellValue(r.getValue());
        });
    }
    wb.write(out);
    wb.dispose();   // deletes temp files (on POI 5.3+, close() also does this)
}
spring:
  servlet:
    multipart: { max-file-size: 100MB, max-request-size: 100MB, file-size-threshold: 2MB }
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate.jdbc.batch_size: 500
      hibernate.order_inserts: true

For very large files, accept the upload, store it in object storage (MinIO/S3), return 202 Accepted with a job ID, and process asynchronously (Spring Batch chunk step) with progress tracking. Prefer CSV where possible.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why does IDENTITY break batching? Hibernate must run each insert immediately to get the generated key. Use a SEQUENCE with allocationSize instead.
  • What does SXSSF write to disk? Temp XML files for rows outside the window, so make sure /tmp has space (an emptyDir volume in Kubernetes).
  • Is there a POI zip-bomb guard? ZipSecureFile.setMinInflateRatio and IOUtils max byte limits. Leave them on and validate file size and type.
F9 A production issue occurs randomly and logs are not clear. How will you debug step by step?
  1. Collect the facts: timestamps, affected users or endpoints, frequency. Look for a pattern such as a specific pod, a time of day or particular input.
  2. Improve observability: add a correlation or trace ID to the MDC (Micrometer Tracing does this automatically), use structured JSON logs, and log the inputs and outcomes at the important decision points.
  3. Raise log levels at runtime without redeploying: POST /actuator/loggers/com.trinity.x {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}.
  4. Correlate the logs with metrics in Grafana and traces in Zipkin/Jaeger. Check GC pauses, connection pool waits, and pod restarts (kubectl describe pod, kubectl logs --previous).
  5. Look for intermittent causes: race conditions, timeouts, cache expiry, one bad node.
  6. Reproduce it in staging with production-like data and load (JMeter/Gatling). Write a regression test, fix it, and add an alert.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Intermittent 500s or wrong results with no reproducible pattern. Logs such as Error occurred with no context or stack trace.
  • First look for correlation: time of day, a specific pod or node, a tenant or city, payload size, a deployment, or a downstream incident. Grafana error-rate panels split by pod, uri and status usually narrow it down quickly.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Define the failure: error code, endpoint, frequency (e.g. 0.5% of requests). Find one concrete failing request ID or time.
  2. Add correlation IDs. In Boot 3, Micrometer Tracing puts traceId and spanId into the MDC automatically, so a request can be followed across services in Loki/ELK.
  3. Raise log levels at runtime without redeploying:
    curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}' http://pod:8080/actuator/loggers/com.trinity.traffic
  4. Check whether it is pod-specific: kubectl logs -l app=traffic --prefix | grep ERROR. If it is always one pod, compare that pod's config, node and memory (kubectl describe pod).
  5. Check infrastructure events: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp (OOMKills, probe failures, node pressure), DB failovers, Kafka rebalances.
  6. Capture state while it happens: thread dumps, a JFR recording kept continuously (-XX:StartFlightRecording=maxage=1h,disk=true) and dumped on demand.
  7. Form a hypothesis and test it: reproduce in staging with concurrency (race conditions), production-like data, or chaos testing (kill a downstream service).
  8. Fix, add a regression test, and add a metric or alert so it is caught next time.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Race condition / shared mutable state Fails only under concurrency Immutable objects, proper locking (F2)
One bad pod (stale config, sick node) Errors grouped by pod label Fix config, drain the node
Downstream flakiness Error matches downstream timeouts Timeouts, retry, circuit breaker (F17)
Swallowed exceptions catch (Exception e) { log.error("failed"); } Log e with context
Data-specific bug (null field, special characters, timezone) Failing payload has an edge case Validation plus a test case

Fix / prevention

logging:
  pattern:
    level: "%5p [${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus,loggers
} catch (DownstreamException e) {
    log.error("Signal update failed junctionId={} cityId={}", junctionId, cityId, e);  // context + stack trace
    throw e;
}

Use structured JSON logs (Boot 3.4+ logging.structured.format.console=ecs), never log and swallow an exception, and include business IDs in log lines.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you debug without access to prod? Use observability: traces, metrics and logs. Ask for the trace ID. Don't attach a remote debugger to prod.
  • The bug disappears when DEBUG logging is on? That points to timing or concurrency. Use JFR or lightweight counters instead of heavy logging.
  • How do you make sure the trace ID reaches async threads? Use ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator on the executor, and Kafka observation (observation-enabled: true).
F10 One API works for small data but fails for huge data. What performance improvements will you do?
  1. Add pagination: Pageable, or keyset pagination for deep pages. Never return unbounded lists.
  2. Fix the queries: use projections or DTOs instead of whole entities, remove N+1 queries (JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size), add indexes, and run EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
  3. Stream large exports with Stream<T> plus @Transactional(readOnly=true) and a fetch size, or StreamingResponseBody, so they do not build a list in memory.
  4. Move heavy work to async processing (202 plus job status, or Kafka).
  5. Compress responses: server.compression.enabled=true.
  6. Cache hot reads with Redis.
  7. Tune timeouts and pool sizes, then confirm with a load test (Gatling).

Symptoms & first checks

  • Timeouts (gateway 504), OOM, or very large response payloads when the data grows. Example: a "get all sensor readings for a city" endpoint that returns 2 million rows.
  • Check the response size (http_server_requests together with ingress logs), the SQL generated, and whether the endpoint has any limit at all.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Capture the SQL and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) against large data. Look for sequential scans, sorts that spill to disk, and nested loops.
  2. Count the queries per request to find N+1.
  3. Profile CPU and allocation. Often the time goes to Jackson serialising huge object graphs, or to mapping entities to DTOs.
  4. Check heap during the call. A full list held in memory means OOM risk.
  5. Check gateway, ingress and client timeouts (e.g. NGINX proxy-read-timeout, 60 s by default).

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No pagination Query has no LIMIT Page or keyset pagination
OFFSET pagination on deep pages Slow at page 10,000 Keyset (WHERE id > :lastId)
Fetching full entities with relationships Wide SELECTs, lazy loads DTO/interface projections
Missing index Seq Scan Index on filter + sort columns
Serialising a huge response in one go Alloc profile in Jackson Streaming, compression, async export
Processing row-by-row in Java Many round trips Set-based SQL, batching

Fix / prevention

public record ReadingDto(Long id, String deviceId, double value, Instant ts) {}

public interface ReadingRepository extends JpaRepository<Reading, Long> {
    // Keyset pagination: constant cost per page
    @Query("""
        select new com.trinity.dto.ReadingDto(r.id, r.deviceId, r.value, r.ts)
        from Reading r
        where r.cityId = :cityId and r.id > :afterId
        order by r.id
        """)
    List<ReadingDto> nextPage(@Param("cityId") Long cityId,
                              @Param("afterId") Long afterId, Pageable limit);

    @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "org.hibernate.fetchSize", value = "1000"))
    @Query("select r from Reading r where r.cityId = :cityId")
    Stream<Reading> streamByCity(@Param("cityId") Long cityId);
}

@GetMapping("/cities/{cityId}/readings")
public List<ReadingDto> readings(@PathVariable Long cityId,
                                 @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") Long afterId,
                                 @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") @Max(1000) int size) {
    return repo.nextPage(cityId, afterId, PageRequest.ofSize(size));
}
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_reading_city_id ON reading(city_id, id);
server:
  compression:
    enabled: true
    mime-types: application/json
    min-response-size: 2KB

Other levers:

  • Cache hot aggregates in Redis.
  • Pre-aggregate with materialised views or rollup tables (time-series data suits TimescaleDB).
  • For big exports, use an asynchronous job: return 202, then provide a download link.
  • Use Slice instead of Page to avoid the COUNT(*) query.
  • Enforce a maximum page size on the server.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why is OFFSET slow? The database still reads and discards all the skipped rows, so deep pages cost O(offset).
  • Why Slice rather than Page? Page runs an extra count query, which is expensive on large tables. Slice only checks whether a next page exists.
  • Why is a Stream from a repository risky? It must be consumed inside a transaction and closed (try-with-resources), and the PostgreSQL driver only streams with a fetch size set and autocommit off.
F11 Two microservices are communicating and one dependent service is down. How will your service handle the failure without impacting users?
  1. Set connect and read timeouts on every outbound call so threads do not hang.
  2. Add a Resilience4j circuit breaker so the service fails fast once the dependency's error rate crosses a threshold.
  3. Add a fallback: cached data (Redis), a default response or a degraded feature. For example, show the last known sensor status.
  4. Use a bulkhead (a separate thread pool or semaphore) so one slow dependency cannot use up all request threads.
  5. For writes, go asynchronous: publish to Kafka and let the consumer process when the dependency recovers.
  6. Have Kubernetes readiness probes remove unhealthy pods, and alert on circuit breaker state changes.
@CircuitBreaker(name = "vehicleSvc", fallbackMethod = "cached")
public Vehicle get(String id) { return client.get(id); }
Vehicle cached(String id, Throwable t) { return cache.get(id); }

Symptoms & first checks

  • Without protection, calls to the dead service hang until a timeout (or forever if no timeout is set). Tomcat threads pile up, and the calling service also stops responding. That is a cascading failure.
  • First checks:
    • Is the dependency really down? Use kubectl get pods -l app=<svc>, its /actuator/health, and kubectl get endpoints <svc>.
    • Are our threads blocked? A thread dump shows many http-nio-* threads in SocketInputStream.read.
    • What are the circuit breaker states? Check /actuator/circuitbreakers or resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Confirm that timeouts are configured on the HTTP client. A missing read timeout is the most common gap.
  2. Check whether the call is synchronous on the critical path, or whether it could be asynchronous through Kafka.
  3. Decide what the user should see when the dependency fails: cached or last-known data, a default value, a partial response, or "request accepted, will be processed".
  4. Apply resilience patterns in layers, then test with chaos (scale the dependency to 0 replicas).

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No timeout Threads blocked indefinitely Connect and read timeouts
No circuit breaker Every request still hits the dead service Resilience4j CircuitBreaker
Shared thread pool for all dependencies One slow dependency starves others Bulkhead per dependency
Synchronous coupling for non-urgent work Writes fail when the dependency is down Kafka plus the outbox pattern

Fix / prevention

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class SignalClient {
    private final RestClient restClient;
    private final RedisTemplate<String, SignalStatus> redis;

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "signalService", fallbackMethod = "cachedStatus")
    @Bulkhead(name = "signalService")
    public SignalStatus status(String junctionId) {
        SignalStatus s = restClient.get().uri("/signals/{id}", junctionId)
                .retrieve().body(SignalStatus.class);
        redis.opsForValue().set("signal:" + junctionId, s, Duration.ofMinutes(30));
        return s;
    }

    // same signature + Throwable
    private SignalStatus cachedStatus(String junctionId, Throwable t) {
        SignalStatus cached = redis.opsForValue().get("signal:" + junctionId);
        return cached != null ? cached.markStale() : SignalStatus.unknown(junctionId);
    }
}
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      signalService:
        sliding-window-size: 20
        minimum-number-of-calls: 10
        failure-rate-threshold: 50
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 3
        automatic-transition-from-open-to-half-open-enabled: true
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      signalService:
        max-concurrent-calls: 20
        max-wait-duration: 100ms
management:
  health:
    circuitbreakers:
      enabled: true

For writes, save locally and publish to Kafka through an outbox table. The consumer processes the message when the downstream service comes back. Return 202 Accepted to the user. Avoid making readiness depend on downstream health, otherwise every caller pod is removed from rotation too.

Likely follow-ups:

  • What are the circuit breaker states? CLOSED: calls pass through and failures are counted. OPEN: calls fail fast to the fallback. HALF_OPEN: a few trial calls decide whether to close or reopen.
  • Fallback for a payment call? No fake success. Queue the request, or return a clear "temporarily unavailable" error (503 with Retry-After).
  • Dependencies needed: resilience4j-spring-boot3 plus spring-boot-starter-aop. The annotations are AOP-based, so self-invocation within the same class bypasses them.
F12 Your API is returning 401 Unauthorized randomly for valid users. How will you debug?
  1. Find the pattern: specific pods, near token expiry, after a key rotation, or only when requests go through the gateway.
  2. Enable logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG to see which filter rejects the request.
  3. Decode the JWT (jwt.io) and check exp, iss, aud and kid. Check for clock skew between nodes, which needs NTP plus an allowed clock skew in the validator.
  4. Check JWKS key rotation. A pod with a stale cached key rejects tokens signed with the new kid.
  5. Check for a session-based setup behind a load balancer without sticky sessions or a shared session store (Spring Session Redis). Use SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS.
  6. Check that the token refresh logic on the frontend handles parallel requests, and that proxies are not stripping the Authorization header.
  7. Check CORS preflight (OPTIONS) requests that are blocked by security.

Symptoms & first checks

  • "Random" usually means some pods, some times, or some requests. Find out which:
    • Is it always the same pod? Use the pod label in metrics and logs.
    • Does it happen near token expiry?
    • Is it only for async endpoints or after a redirect?
    • Is it only for OPTIONS (CORS preflight) requests?
  • Get the WWW-Authenticate header from a failing response. Spring's resource server includes error="invalid_token", error_description="Jwt expired at ..." or similar.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Temporarily enable logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG on one pod via /actuator/loggers and capture a failing request.
  2. Decode the failing token (jwt.io offline, or cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d) and check exp, iat, nbf, iss, aud and kid.
  3. Compare pods: kubectl exec <pod> -- date -u for clock skew, and kubectl exec <pod> -- env | grep JWT for the signing secret and issuer.
  4. Check the gateway or ingress: is it stripping or rewriting the Authorization header? Check its logs.
  5. If tokens are sessions or opaque tokens, check whether sessions are pod-local (in-memory HttpSession) with no sticky sessions.
  6. Check Keycloak (or the identity provider) for key rotation. A new kid that the service's cached JWKS does not contain yet causes failures.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Pods use different HMAC secrets (one generated at startup) Failures follow certain pods Single secret from a K8s Secret, or RS256 with JWKS
In-memory sessions, no sticky routing Login on pod A, 401 on pod B Spring Session Redis, or stateless JWT
Clock skew exp/nbf failures just at the edges NTP; allowed skew of ~60 s
Access token expires, frontend refresh race 401s spike at TTL Refresh before expiry, single-flight refresh
SecurityContext lost in @Async threads 401 or anonymous in async code DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor
CORS preflight blocked by security OPTIONS → 401 .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())

Fix / prevention

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
        return http.build();
    }

    @Bean
    JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(@Value("${security.jwt.issuer}") String issuer,
                          @Value("${security.jwt.jwks-uri}") String jwksUri) {
        NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = NimbusJwtDecoder.withJwkSetUri(jwksUri).build();
        decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(
                new JwtTimestampValidator(Duration.ofSeconds(60)),
                new JwtIssuerValidator(issuer)));
        return decoder;
    }
}

Add a custom AuthenticationEntryPoint that logs the reason (without logging the token) and returns a ProblemDetail. Track the 401 rate per pod as a metric.

Likely follow-ups:

  • 401 or 403? 401 means not authenticated: the token is missing or invalid. 403 means the user is authenticated but not allowed.
  • How does Nimbus handle key rotation? It re-fetches the JWKS when it sees an unknown kid, so the identity provider should publish new keys before signing with them.
  • Why does SecurityContext get lost? It is stored in a ThreadLocal by default, so it does not cross to new threads unless they are wrapped with a delegating executor.
F13 After deployment application is starting very slowly. What things will you check?
  1. Read the startup logs with timestamps to see where the time goes. Use Actuator /actuator/startup with BufferingApplicationStartup for per-bean timings.
  2. Check database and network: slow connections, Flyway/Liquibase migrations on large tables, ddl-auto=update (should be validate/none in production), Hikari waiting for the database.
  3. Check @PostConstruct or CommandLineRunner code that loads caches or calls remote services.
  4. Check classpath scanning: an overly broad @ComponentScan or unused auto-configurations (exclude them).
  5. Check container resources: a low CPU limit throttles JIT and startup. Tune resources.requests.cpu.
  6. Check Kubernetes probes: add a startupProbe so the liveness probe does not kill a slow-starting pod.
  7. Options to speed it up: spring.main.lazy-initialization=true (with care), CDS/AppCDS, GraalVM native image.

Symptoms & first checks

  • The pod stays 0/1 Ready for minutes, or ends up in CrashLoopBackOff because the liveness probe kills it before it finishes starting.
  • kubectl describe pod <pod> shows events, probe failures and restarts. kubectl logs <pod> --previous shows the previous attempt.
  • The Spring log line Started XApplication in 182.4 seconds (process running for 190.1) gives the total. Compare it with the previous release.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Look at the gaps between timestamps in the startup log. They show which phase stalls: Hibernate init, Flyway, Kafka, or bean creation.
  2. Use the Actuator startup endpoint to find slow beans:
    SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(CityApp.class);
app.setApplicationStartup(new BufferingApplicationStartup(10_000));
app.run(args);
    Then curl -X POST http://pod:8080/actuator/startup | jq '.timeline.events | sort_by(.duration) | reverse | .[0:10]' (expose the startup endpoint).
  3. Take thread dumps of the main thread during startup (jcmd 1 Thread.print) to see what it is waiting on: a socket, a DB lock, or DNS.
  4. Check for CPU throttling during startup. A 500m CPU limit makes JIT and classloading very slow, so check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total.
  5. Check the database: is Flyway or Liquibase waiting on a lock (flyway_schema_history, DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK)? Is there a long migration, such as an index build on a big table?
  6. Check external connections at startup: config server retries, Kafka bootstrap, Redis, or a downstream service called from @PostConstruct.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Heavy work in @PostConstruct (cache warm-up, loading data) Long gap after a specific bean ApplicationReadyEvent with async loading, or lazy loading
ddl-auto=update or validate on a large schema Hibernate phase is long ddl-auto=none, use Flyway
Slow or locked migration Flyway logs pause Release the stale lock, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
Low CPU limit Throttling metrics Raise CPU request/limit, or use startup boost
Unreachable dependency with retries Connection retry logs optional: imports, fail-fast with a timeout
Large classpath scanning Many beans or auto-configurations Narrow @ComponentScan, exclude unused auto-configs

Fix / prevention

spring:
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: none
    open-in-view: false
  main:
    lazy-initialization: false   # true speeds startup but moves failures to the first request
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,startup,prometheus
---
# deployment.yaml probes
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 36          # allows up to 3 minutes before liveness starts
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }

Further options: Class Data Sharing (-XX:SharedArchiveFile, Boot 3.3 -Djarmode=tools extract plus CDS training run), Spring AOT, or GraalVM native image for a very fast start.

Likely follow-ups:

  • What is the startupProbe for? It holds off liveness checks until the app has started, so slow starts are not killed in a restart loop.
  • Is lazy initialization safe? It is faster, but configuration errors only surface at the first request, and the first-request latency is higher.
  • Why is it slow only in Kubernetes? Usually the CPU limit, DNS (ndots:5 search domains), or pulling a large image (check Pulling image in the events).
F14 One API is receiving too many requests and server becomes overloaded. How will you implement rate limiting?
  1. Decide the key (per user, API key, or IP) and the limit, for example 100 requests per minute.
  2. Prefer enforcing it at the edge: Spring Cloud Gateway RequestRateLimiter with Redis (token bucket, shared across instances), or NGINX/Ingress limit_req.
  3. Inside the service, use the Resilience4j @RateLimiter or Bucket4j with Redis for a distributed limit.
  4. Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.
  5. Also protect the service with a bulkhead and timeouts, scale with HPA, and cache hot responses.
spring.cloud.gateway.routes:
  - id: incidents
    uri: lb://incident-service
    predicates: [Path=/api/incidents/**]
    filters:
      - name: RequestRateLimiter
        args: { redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 50, redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 100, key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}" }

Symptoms & first checks

  • High CPU, thread pool exhaustion, and increasing latency on all endpoints because of one hot endpoint, a buggy client in a retry loop, a bot, or an IoT device storm.
  • In Grafana, look at rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{uri="/api/v1/events"}[1m]) broken down by client. In the ingress or gateway logs, find the top client IPs or API keys.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Identify whether the traffic is legitimate growth (scale out and cache) or abuse or a misbehaving client (limit and block).
  2. Choose the limit key: per user, per API key, per IP, or per tenant or city.
  3. Choose where to enforce it. The edge (API gateway or ingress) is best because rejected requests never reach the service. Use a distributed store (Redis) when there are several replicas.
  4. Choose the algorithm: a token bucket allows bursts, a sliding window gives smooth limits.
  5. Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Client retry storm (no backoff) Burst of identical requests from one client Rate limit, ask the client to use exponential backoff
Scraper or bot Unknown IPs, high volume IP limits, WAF
Legitimate peak All clients grow together HPA, caching, queue-based processing
Expensive endpoint Low RPS but high CPU per call Lower limit for that endpoint, async processing

Fix / prevention Spring Cloud Gateway with the Redis token bucket:

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: events
          uri: lb://event-service
          predicates: [ Path=/api/v1/events/** ]
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 50     # tokens per second
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 100
                redis-rate-limiter.requestedTokens: 1
                key-resolver: "#{@apiKeyResolver}"
@Bean
KeyResolver apiKeyResolver() {
    return exchange -> Mono.justOrEmpty(exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst("X-API-Key"))
            .switchIfEmpty(Mono.just(exchange.getRequest().getRemoteAddress().getAddress().getHostAddress()));
}

Inside the service (Bucket4j 8.x, a per-instance bucket; use bucket4j-redis for a distributed limit):

@Component
public class RateLimitFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    private final Map<String, Bucket> buckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();  // bound with Caffeine in prod

    private Bucket newBucket() {
        return Bucket.builder()
                .addLimit(Bandwidth.builder().capacity(100).refillGreedy(100, Duration.ofMinutes(1)).build())
                .build();
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String key = Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-API-Key")).orElse(req.getRemoteAddr());
        ConsumptionProbe probe = buckets.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> newBucket()).tryConsumeAndReturnRemaining(1);
        if (probe.isConsumed()) {
            res.setHeader("X-RateLimit-Remaining", String.valueOf(probe.getRemainingTokens()));
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } else {
            res.setStatus(HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS.value());
            res.setHeader("Retry-After", String.valueOf(probe.getNanosToWaitForRefill() / 1_000_000_000));
        }
    }
}

Also add a Resilience4j @Bulkhead on expensive operations, and for spiky IoT ingestion, buffer through Kafka instead of synchronous processing.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why is a local bucket not enough with several replicas? Each pod enforces its own limit, so the effective limit becomes N × the limit. Use Redis (the gateway or bucket4j-redis) for a global limit.
  • Token bucket vs fixed window? A fixed window allows a double burst at the window boundary. A token bucket allows a controlled burst with a steady refill rate.
  • Rate limiting vs throttling vs backpressure? Rate limiting rejects excess requests (429), throttling delays them, and backpressure slows the producer.
F15 Your Spring Boot application works locally but fails in QA/PROD environment. How will you troubleshoot?
  1. Read the actual stack trace: kubectl logs <pod>, kubectl logs --previous, kubectl describe pod (OOMKilled, CrashLoopBackOff, failing probes).
  2. Check the active profile and the resolved properties with /actuator/env and /actuator/configprops (secured). Look for a missing env var, ConfigMap or Secret.
  3. Check connectivity from inside the pod: database, Kafka, external APIs, DNS, firewall rules or NetworkPolicy, TLS certificates.
  4. Compare versions: JDK, base image, dependency versions (mvn dependency:tree), and the database version or schema (Flyway history).
  5. Check environment-specific behaviour: file paths, timezone or locale, case-sensitive table names in MySQL on Linux, memory limits.
  6. Reproduce locally with the same image and config (docker run with the QA env vars), then fix it.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Startup failure (APPLICATION FAILED TO START, a bean creation exception, Could not resolve placeholder), connection errors, or functional differences.
  • Read the first root-cause exception in the logs (kubectl logs <pod> --previous), not the last line.
  • List what differs between environments: active profile, environment variables, secrets, network, data, Java version, OS (file paths, case sensitivity), timezone and locale.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Check the active profile: the log line The following 1 profile is active: "qa". Is SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE set in the Deployment?
  2. Check the effective configuration: /actuator/env/spring.datasource.url and /actuator/configprops (values are masked by default; set management.endpoint.env.show-values: when-authorized for admins).
  3. Check what the pod actually received: kubectl exec <pod> -- env | sort, kubectl get configmap <cm> -o yaml, and kubectl get secret <s> -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d.
  4. Test the network from inside the pod: kubectl exec <pod> -- nc -zv postgres 5432, nslookup, and curl to downstream services. NetworkPolicies and firewalls often differ between environments.
  5. Check certificates: PKIX path building failed means an internal CA is missing from the truststore in the image.
  6. Check the image and runtime: compare the base image JDK with local (java -version), plus TZ and file paths (C:\ on Windows versus / in containers).
  7. Check the data: run the Flyway migration status for that environment, and look for missing reference data or real data that triggers edge cases.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Missing property or secret Could not resolve placeholder Add it to the ConfigMap/Secret, use @Validated properties to fail fast
Wrong profile active Startup log Set SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE in the manifest
Network/DNS/policy nc fails from the pod NetworkPolicy or firewall rule, correct service name
TLS truststore PKIX error Add the CA to the image or mount it with -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore
Local-only beans or config (application-local.yml committed as default) Works only with the local profile Proper profile separation
Case-sensitive paths or resources FileNotFoundException on Linux Use classpath resources with exact case
Schema drift Hibernate validate fails Run the Flyway migrations in the pipeline

Fix / prevention

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "integrations.traffic")
public record TrafficProperties(
        @NotBlank String baseUrl,
        @NotNull Duration timeout,
        @NotBlank String apiKey) {}
@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan
public class CityApp { public static void main(String[] a) { SpringApplication.run(CityApp.class, a); } }

With this setup, a missing value fails at startup with a clear message instead of an NPE at runtime. Make the environments as similar as possible: the same Docker image promoted through DEV, QA and PROD with config injected; Testcontainers for PostgreSQL, Kafka and Redis in integration tests; and a docker-compose setup that matches production versions.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you see the property source that won? /actuator/env/<property> lists each property source and the value it supplies, in precedence order.
  • Why build once and promote? Rebuilding per environment can change dependencies and code. Promoting one immutable image means only the config differs.
  • How do you debug a pod that crashes immediately? kubectl logs --previous, temporarily override the command with sleep infinity, or use kubectl debug to get a shell.
F16 A REST API is exposing sensitive data accidentally. What security improvements will you implement?
  1. Never return entities. Map to response DTOs (Java records) that contain only the fields the client needs. Use @JsonIgnore or @JsonProperty(access = WRITE_ONLY) for passwords as a backstop.
  2. Mask PII (phone, Aadhaar, email) in responses and logs. Use a Logback masking pattern and never log full request bodies or tokens.
  3. Enforce authorization: @PreAuthorize, plus ownership checks on the object to prevent IDOR.
  4. Use generic error messages. Set server.error.include-stacktrace=never and include-message=never.
  5. Lock down Actuator: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus and secure everything else.
  6. Use HTTPS only, encrypt sensitive columns at rest, and add security tests and a ZAP scan to CI.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Responses contain password hashes, Aadhaar or phone numbers, internal IDs, tokens, or entire related entities. Stack traces appear in error responses. /actuator/env or /actuator/heapdump is publicly reachable.
  • Act immediately: assess the scope (which endpoint, since when, who called it, from the access logs), hotfix or block the endpoint at the gateway, rotate any exposed secrets, and inform the security team or DPO if personal data was involved (DPDP/GDPR obligations).

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Find the controllers that return JPA entities directly. Jackson serialises every getter, including lazy relations.
  2. Check the global Jackson settings, @JsonIgnore usage, and whether toString() is logged with PII.
  3. Check the error configuration: server.error.include-stacktrace and include-message.
  4. Check Actuator exposure: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* is a red flag.
  5. Check authorization: can user A fetch /users/{id} for user B (IDOR / broken object-level authorization)?
  6. Scan with OWASP ZAP and review the OpenAPI spec for fields that should not be exposed.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Entity returned directly Controller returns @Entity Response DTOs/records
Password hash serialised Field visible in JSON DTO; @JsonProperty(access = WRITE_ONLY)
Stack traces in errors 500 body contains a trace include-stacktrace: never, ProblemDetail
Actuator exposed /actuator/env reachable Limit exposure, separate management port, secure it
Missing ownership check Changing an ID returns other users' data @PreAuthorize with an ownership check
PII in logs Grep the logs Masking, log DTOs not entities

Fix / prevention

public record CitizenResponse(Long id, String name, String maskedPhone) {
    public static CitizenResponse from(Citizen c) {
        return new CitizenResponse(c.getId(), c.getName(),
                "******" + c.getPhone().substring(c.getPhone().length() - 4));
    }
}

public class CitizenRequest {
    @NotBlank private String name;
    @JsonProperty(access = JsonProperty.Access.WRITE_ONLY)
    @NotBlank private String password;          // accepted in requests, never written to responses
}

@GetMapping("/citizens/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #id == authentication.principal.claims['citizenId']")
public CitizenResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return CitizenResponse.from(service.find(id));
}
server:
  error:
    include-stacktrace: never
    include-message: never
management:
  server:
    port: 8081                   # not exposed through the ingress
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus

Also:

  • Enable @EnableMethodSecurity.
  • Use HTTPS only, with HSTS.
  • Encrypt sensitive columns (pgcrypto, or a JPA AttributeConverter) and keep secrets in Vault or K8s Secrets.
  • Mask PII in logs with a Logback converter.
  • Add contract tests that assert sensitive fields are absent from responses.

Likely follow-ups:

  • @JsonIgnore or DTOs? DTOs. They make the API contract explicit and decouple it from the schema, whereas @JsonIgnore is easy to forget on new fields.
  • How do you prevent IDOR? Derive the owner from the token, never trust IDs from the client alone, and check ownership in the service or a @PreAuthorize expression.
  • What is the risk with /actuator/heapdump? A heap dump contains secrets, tokens and PII from memory. Never expose it publicly.
F17 One external API dependency is timing out frequently. How will you implement retry and fallback mechanism?
  1. Set explicit timeouts first: a connect timeout of about 2s and a read timeout based on the API's SLA.
  2. Retry only idempotent calls and only transient errors (timeouts, 5xx), using exponential backoff with jitter and at most about 3 attempts.
  3. Put a circuit breaker around the retry so the service stops calling once the dependency is clearly down.
  4. Provide a fallback: a cached response, a default value, or queue the request for later.
  5. Monitor the Resilience4j metrics in Prometheus.
resilience4j:
  retry.instances.weatherApi: { maxAttempts: 3, waitDuration: 500ms, enableExponentialBackoff: true, exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2, retryExceptions: [java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException] }
  circuitbreaker.instances.weatherApi: { slidingWindowSize: 20, failureRateThreshold: 50, waitDurationInOpenState: 30s }
  timelimiter.instances.weatherApi: { timeoutDuration: 3s }

Use it as @Retry(name="weatherApi") @CircuitBreaker(name="weatherApi", fallbackMethod="fallback").

Symptoms & first checks

  • SocketTimeoutException / ResourceAccessException in the logs, and higher p99 latency on our endpoints.
  • Check the latency distribution of the external API (http_client_requests_seconds from the instrumented RestClient or WebClient). Is it slow every time, or only some of the time?
  • Check the provider's status page and our timeout settings. Retries without a timeout make the problem worse.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Measure the provider's p95/p99 latency and set a timeout slightly above p99.
  2. Classify the errors. Retryable: timeouts, connection resets, 502/503/504, and 429 (respect Retry-After). Not retryable: 400, 401, 404, and validation errors.
  3. Confirm the operation is idempotent (GET, or a POST with an idempotency key) before retrying it.
  4. Make sure the total time budget (attempts × timeout + backoff) fits inside our own SLA and the gateway timeout.
  5. Define the fallback: cached data, default data, queue for later, or a clear error.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No or very long timeouts Threads hang Connect 2 s, read 3–5 s
Retry storm amplifying load Calls multiplied 3× during an outage Exponential backoff plus a circuit breaker
Provider rate limiting us 429 responses Client-side rate limiter, honour Retry-After
Connection pool exhaustion Waiting for a connection Pool sizing per route

Fix / prevention

resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      weatherApi:
        max-attempts: 3
        wait-duration: 500ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
        retry-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException
        ignore-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpClientErrorException
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      weatherApi:
        sliding-window-size: 20
        failure-rate-threshold: 50
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 3s
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 60
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      weatherApi:
        timeout-duration: 4s
        cancel-running-future: true
@Configuration
public class HttpConfig {
    @Bean
    RestClient weatherRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
        SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory rf = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
        rf.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
        rf.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3));
        return builder.baseUrl("https://api.weather.example").requestFactory(rf).build();
    }
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class WeatherClient {
    private final RestClient weatherRestClient;
    private final Cache<String, Forecast> lastGood;   // Caffeine

    @Retry(name = "weatherApi")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "weatherApi", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
    public Forecast forecast(String city) {
        Forecast f = weatherRestClient.get().uri("/forecast?city={c}", city)
                .retrieve().body(Forecast.class);
        lastGood.put(city, f);
        return f;
    }

    private Forecast fallback(String city, Throwable t) {
        Forecast cached = lastGood.getIfPresent(city);
        if (cached != null) return cached.asStale();
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException("Weather provider unavailable", t);
    }
}

The default aspect order is Retry( CircuitBreaker( RateLimiter( TimeLimiter( Bulkhead(call) ) ) ) ), so every retry attempt is counted by the circuit breaker, and once it opens the retries stop quickly. @TimeLimiter only works with CompletableFuture or reactive return types. For synchronous RestClient calls, rely on the HTTP read timeout.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why add jitter? It spreads retries from many clients so they don't arrive in synchronised waves. Use enable-randomized-wait or a custom IntervalBiFunction.
  • Is it safe to retry a POST? Only with an idempotency key that the provider de-duplicates on. Otherwise you risk duplicate side effects.
  • How do you monitor this? Use resilience4j_retry_calls_total{kind="failed_with_retry"}, the circuit breaker state, and fallback counters, and alert on an OPEN breaker.
F18 Application configuration differs between DEV, QA, and PROD causing issues. How will you manage environment-specific configs?
  1. Put common settings in application.yml and only the differences in application-{dev,qa,prod}.yml. Activate the profile with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE.
  2. Externalize configuration: Kubernetes ConfigMaps for settings and Secrets (or Vault) for credentials. Never commit secrets.
  3. Centralize with Spring Cloud Config Server backed by Git so changes are versioned and reviewed, or use Helm values per environment.
  4. Bind configuration to typed @ConfigurationProperties records with @Validated, so a missing or wrong value fails at startup.
  5. Use the same image in every environment and change only the configuration.
  6. Check the effective configuration with /actuator/env and compare environments as part of the release checklist.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Typical incidents: a feature works in QA but breaks in PROD, a wrong URL points at a QA database, or a timeout value was changed in one environment only. Configuration is scattered across application.yml, hardcoded values, manually edited ConfigMaps, and the CI pipeline.
  • Compare the effective configuration (/actuator/env, kubectl get cm -o yaml) across environments, and diff the config files in Git.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Inventory every property and classify it as: same everywhere (defaults), varies per environment (URLs, pool sizes, feature flags), or secret.
  2. Find hardcoded values in code with grep (http://, localhost, IP addresses).
  3. Find manual drift: are ConfigMaps edited with kubectl edit instead of being taken from Git?
  4. Decide on a single source of truth: Git with Helm values per environment (GitOps with ArgoCD), or Spring Cloud Config, plus Vault or Sealed Secrets for secrets.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Hardcoded values Grep the code @ConfigurationProperties
Manual edits in the cluster Live ConfigMap differs from Git GitOps (ArgoCD drift detection)
Profile file missing a key Default used unexpectedly Defaults in application.yml, overrides only per environment
Secrets in Git or in images Repository scan K8s Secrets / Vault / External Secrets
Untyped @Value everywhere Typos fail silently or at runtime Typed, validated properties

Fix / prevention

# application.yml: shared defaults
spring:
  application:
    name: traffic-service
  config:
    import: "optional:configserver:"      # or rely only on K8s ConfigMaps
  profiles:
    group:
      prod: [ "prod", "observability" ]
integrations:
  traffic:
    base-url: ${TRAFFIC_BASE_URL:http://localhost:8085}
    timeout: 3s
    api-key: ${TRAFFIC_API_KEY}
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 30
logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
# Kubernetes: same image everywhere, environment injected
envFrom:
  - configMapRef: { name: traffic-config }       # per-namespace values from Helm
  - secretRef:    { name: traffic-secrets }      # synced from Vault via External Secrets
env:
  - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
    value: prod

Bind the configuration to a validated @ConfigurationProperties record (see F15) so a missing value stops startup with a clear error. Spring Boot's precedence order means environment variables (INTEGRATIONS_TRAFFIC_TIMEOUT) override files, which makes per-environment overrides predictable. Use feature flags (Unleash or Togglz) instead of profile-specific code paths, and add a CI check that every key in the defaults has a value in each environment's Helm values.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Can you refresh config without a restart? Use Spring Cloud Config with @RefreshScope and /actuator/refresh (or Spring Cloud Bus), or roll the pods after a ConfigMap change, which is simpler and more predictable.
  • Profile-specific beans? Use @Profile("!prod") sparingly. Prefer config values and @ConditionalOnProperty.
  • Where do secrets go? Vault, or the cloud secret manager synced to K8s Secrets. Never in Git, the image, or plain ConfigMaps.
F19 Your API is throwing exceptions but frontend only sees generic error. How will you implement global exception handling?
  1. Create a @RestControllerAdvice with an @ExceptionHandler for each exception type: validation, not found, conflict, and a generic fallback.
  2. Return a consistent body. Spring Boot 3's ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) gives the right status code, an error code, a message and the trace ID.
  3. Map business exceptions to 4xx and unexpected ones to 500 with a safe message. Log the full stack trace on the server side only.
  4. Set spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true for the built-in exceptions.
  5. The frontend displays detail and reads the error code.
@RestControllerAdvice
class GlobalHandler {
  @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
  ProblemDetail notFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
    var pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
    pd.setProperty("code", "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND"); return pd;
  }
}

Symptoms & first checks
