  • The frontend gets 500 Internal Server Error with the default Whitelabel or {"error":"Internal Server Error"} body for everything, including validation errors and "not found". Each controller has its own try/catch with inconsistent formats.
  • Check: is there any @RestControllerAdvice? Is spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled set? Are exceptions swallowed and rethrown as RuntimeException("Error")?

Step-by-step investigation

  1. List the exception types thrown across the code base: business, validation, not-found, conflict, downstream, and security.
  2. Define an error contract with the frontend: RFC 9457 Problem Details (type, title, status, detail, instance) plus custom fields (errorCode, traceId, errors[]).
  3. Map each exception to a status code: 400 validation, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 business rule, 503 downstream unavailable, 500 unknown (generic message, full details only in the logs).
  4. Make sure security exceptions (401/403) also return the same format. They are thrown in filters, before @ControllerAdvice runs.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No global handler Default error body @RestControllerAdvice
Everything wrapped as RuntimeException Logs show a generic wrapper Typed domain exceptions
Filter-level exceptions bypass the advice 401 bodies differ AuthenticationEntryPoint / AccessDeniedHandler
Message hidden by config include-message: never with no advice Explicit ProblemDetail details

Fix / prevention

public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public ResourceNotFoundException(String resource, Object id) {
        super(resource + " not found: " + id);
    }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
@Slf4j
public class GlobalExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setTitle("Resource not found");
        pd.setType(URI.create("https://api.trinity.city/errors/not-found"));
        pd.setInstance(URI.create(req.getRequestURI()));
        pd.setProperty("errorCode", "RES_404");
        return pd;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleConflict(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException ex) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Record modified by another user");
    }

    @Override
    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,
            HttpHeaders headers, HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Validation failed");
        pd.setProperty("errors", ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
                .map(fe -> Map.of("field", fe.getField(), "message", String.valueOf(fe.getDefaultMessage())))
                .toList());
        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(pd);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleUnknown(Exception ex) {
        log.error("Unhandled error", ex);                       // full stack trace only in the logs
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
                "Something went wrong. Please contact support with the traceId.");
        pd.setProperty("traceId", MDC.get("traceId"));
        return pd;
    }
}

Extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler makes Spring MVC's built-in exceptions (bad JSON, unsupported method, missing parameter) return ProblemDetail as well. ProblemDetail responses use the content type application/problem+json.

Likely follow-ups:

  • @ControllerAdvice vs @RestControllerAdvice? The Rest variant adds @ResponseBody, so return values are serialised as the response body.
  • Should internal messages go to the client? No. Send a safe message, an error code and the trace ID. Keep details in the logs.
  • How do you handle exceptions in filters? Use a custom AuthenticationEntryPoint or AccessDeniedHandler, or delegate to HandlerExceptionResolver from the filter.
F20 A scheduled task is running multiple times in clustered deployment. How will you prevent duplicate execution?
  1. Cause: every pod runs its own @Scheduled methods.
  2. Use ShedLock: a lock row in the database (or Redis) means only one instance runs each scheduled execution.
  3. Set lockAtMostFor above the worst-case runtime, and lockAtLeastFor to absorb clock differences between nodes.
  4. Alternatives: Quartz in clustered JDBC mode, a Kubernetes CronJob, or leader election (Spring Integration / Kubernetes leader).
  5. Still make the job idempotent as a safety net.
@EnableSchedulerLock(defaultLockAtMostFor = "10m")
// ...
@Scheduled(cron = "0 */5 * * * *")
@SchedulerLock(name = "syncSensors", lockAtMostFor = "4m", lockAtLeastFor = "30s")
public void syncSensors() { ... }

You also need a LockProvider bean, for example JdbcTemplateLockProvider, and a shedlock table.

Symptoms & first checks

  • With 3 replicas, @Scheduled runs on every pod, so reports are emailed 3 times and the same records are processed in parallel. @Scheduled has no awareness of the cluster.
  • Grep the logs for the job start line grouped by pod: kubectl logs -l app=report --prefix | grep "Daily report started". You will see one line per pod per trigger.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Confirm the replica count (kubectl get deploy) and HPA behaviour. The duplicates scale with the number of pods.
  2. Decide on the requirement: run once per trigger on any one node (a distributed lock), always on one leader (leader election), or parallel but partitioned (each node takes different rows, see F6 SKIP LOCKED).
  3. Choose the tool: ShedLock (simple, DB or Redis based), Quartz clustered (needs persistent scheduling and misfire handling), a Kubernetes CronJob (a separate one-off process), or leader election (Spring Cloud Kubernetes or Spring Integration LockRegistryLeaderInitiator).

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Plain @Scheduled on N replicas One run per pod ShedLock
Lock released too early (job shorter than clock drift) Two pods run seconds apart lockAtLeastFor, usingDbTime()
Lock held after a crash Job skipped for a long time Sensible lockAtMostFor
Job longer than lockAtMostFor Overlap during long runs Increase it, or keep extending the lock

Fix / prevention

<dependency><groupId>net.javacrumbs.shedlock</groupId><artifactId>shedlock-spring</artifactId><version>5.16.0</version></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>net.javacrumbs.shedlock</groupId><artifactId>shedlock-provider-jdbc-template</artifactId><version>5.16.0</version></dependency>
CREATE TABLE shedlock (
  name       VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  lock_until TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
  locked_at  TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
  locked_by  VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);
@Configuration
@EnableScheduling
@EnableSchedulerLock(defaultLockAtMostFor = "PT10M")
public class SchedulerConfig {
    @Bean
    public LockProvider lockProvider(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new JdbcTemplateLockProvider(
                JdbcTemplateLockProvider.Configuration.builder()
                        .withJdbcTemplate(new JdbcTemplate(dataSource))
                        .usingDbTime()                // use DB clock, avoids pod clock skew
                        .build());
    }
}

@Component
@Slf4j
public class DailyReportJob {
    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 6 * * *", zone = "Asia/Kolkata")
    @SchedulerLock(name = "dailyReportJob", lockAtMostFor = "PT30M", lockAtLeastFor = "PT1M")
    public void run() {
        LockAssert.assertLocked();
        log.info("Daily report started");
        // ... make the work itself idempotent too (F6)
    }
}

With this in place, only the pod that acquires the row lock runs the job, and the others skip that trigger silently. lockAtLeastFor stops a fast job from running again on another pod whose clock is slightly behind. lockAtMostFor makes sure a crashed pod does not hold the lock forever. Alternatively, use a Kubernetes CronJob with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid for heavy batch jobs, which also isolates their resource usage from the API pods.

Likely follow-ups:

  • ShedLock or Quartz? ShedLock only prevents concurrent runs and has no persistent schedule or misfire recovery. Quartz clustered (org.quartz.jobStore.isClustered=true, JDBC job store) gives you both, at the cost of more complexity.
  • What if the job takes longer than lockAtMostFor? Another pod could start it. Set it well above the worst-case runtime, or use ShedLock's KeepAliveLockProvider to extend the lock.
  • Can you use Redis instead of the DB? Yes, with shedlock-provider-redis-spring. Use the DB if it is already a dependency, since it adds no new infrastructure.
F21 Your application suddenly becomes slow because of database queries. How will you identify the problematic query?
  1. Find the slow requests in APM or traces (Micrometer Tracing / Zipkin), then the slow database spans inside them.
  2. On the database: PostgreSQL pg_stat_statements (order by total_exec_time or mean_exec_time), pg_stat_activity for running queries and locks. MySQL: the slow query log with long_query_time=1, then SHOW PROCESSLIST.
  3. In the application, log slow statements: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.session.events.log.LOG_QUERIES_SLOWER_THAN_MS=500, or use datasource-proxy / p6spy. Enable Hibernate statistics to count queries per request and catch N+1.
  4. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the query and look for sequential scans, bad join order or row estimates that are far off.
  5. Fix it: an index, a rewritten query, JOIN FETCH, a projection. Then ANALYZE the table and confirm the improvement.

Symptoms & first checks

  • p95/p99 latency jumps on many endpoints at once, HikariCP hikaricp_connections_pending rises, DB CPU or IOPS is pinned.
  • First question: what changed? A deploy, a data spike (for example a sensor backfill in the Smart City platform), a migration, or autovacuum/statistics drift.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Find the slow endpoint in traces. In Zipkin/Tempo, sort by duration and open a slow trace. JDBC spans (via datasource-micrometer or p6spy) show which SQL takes the time.
  2. See what is running now.
    SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS runtime, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, query
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY runtime DESC;
  3. Rank queries by total cost, not just by the slowest single run:
    SELECT queryid, calls, round(total_exec_time) total_ms, round(mean_exec_time,1) mean_ms, rows, query
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;
    A query that takes 5 ms but runs 2 million times (an N+1 pattern) often costs more than one 3 s report. On MySQL, use slow_query_log=ON, long_query_time=0.5, pt-query-digest, or performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest.
  4. Explain the culprit with real parameters: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) .... Look for Seq Scan on big tables, estimated rows that differ a lot from actual rows, Sort Method: external merge, and high shared read counts.
  5. Check the application side. Set spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true (only briefly in prod) and logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug. One HTTP request firing 300 statements means N+1.
  6. Check for lock waits. If wait_event_type = 'Lock', the query is blocked, not slow. pg_blocking_pids(pid) shows the blocker.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Missing or unused index Seq Scan in the EXPLAIN plan Composite index matching the WHERE and ORDER BY
N+1 from lazy associations Hibernate statistics show a high statement count JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or @BatchSize
Stale statistics or bloat Row estimates far off; n_dead_tup high in pg_stat_user_tables ANALYZE, autovacuum tuning
Blocking lock pg_blocking_pids returns a PID Shorten transactions, kill the blocker
Plan flip with prepared statements Generic plan is slow, custom plan is fast plan_cache_mode=force_custom_plan for that role/query

Fix / prevention

spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate.session.events.log.LOG_QUERIES_SLOWER_THAN_MS: 200   # Hibernate 6 slow-query log
  • Enable auto_explain.log_min_duration = '500ms' on PostgreSQL.
  • Alert on mean_exec_time regressions.
  • Review query plans in pull requests that touch repositories.

Likely follow-ups:

  • pg_stat_statements vs slow log? pg_stat_statements gives normalized, aggregated cost across all calls. The slow log shows individual outliers.
  • How do you reset the stats for a clean baseline? SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset(); before a load test.
  • EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE? ANALYZE actually executes the query, so wrap DML in BEGIN … ROLLBACK.
F22 Hibernate lazy loading exception occurs only in production. How will you fix it?
  1. Cause: a lazy association is accessed after the session has closed, for example during Jackson serialization or in async code. It shows up only in production because spring.jpa.open-in-view behaves differently there, or a code path is not covered locally.
  2. Fetch what the use case needs inside the transaction: JOIN FETCH in JPQL or @EntityGraph(attributePaths="sensors").
  3. Map to DTOs inside the @Transactional service method and never return entities to the controller.
  4. Keep spring.jpa.open-in-view=false in all environments so the problem shows up early.
  5. Do not use FetchType.EAGER everywhere or enable_lazy_load_no_trans, because they hide N+1 problems.
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"sensors"})
Optional<Junction> findWithSensorsById(Long id);

Symptoms & first checks

  • LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy … no Session, often thrown during Jackson serialization or in a background thread.
  • "Only in prod" usually means a config or code path differs between environments. Compare profiles: spring.jpa.open-in-view (defaults to true; dev often relies on it, prod sets it to false). Also check whether prod-only code paths run, such as @Async, Kafka listeners, the Redis cache, or schedulers.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Read the full stack trace. Is the access in a controller or serializer (outside the transaction), in an @Async or CompletableFuture thread, or in a @Cacheable result that was deserialized from Redis (a detached entity)?
  2. Diff application-prod.yml against dev for open-in-view and hibernate.enable_lazy_load_no_trans.
  3. Enable org.hibernate.SQL=debug in a staging environment with the prod profile to reproduce the failure.
  4. Check whether the entity is returned straight from a controller. That is a design smell.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
OSIV off in prod, on in dev Profile diff Fetch what you need inside the service transaction
Entity passed to @Async or another thread Thread name in the trace Pass IDs or DTOs, then reload in the new transaction
Cached entity (Redis, Caffeine) is detached Exception happens only on a cache hit Cache DTOs, not entities
Self-invocation skips @Transactional Calling method is in the same class Move the method to another bean

Fix / prevention Load exactly the graph you need inside the transaction and return a DTO:

public interface IncidentRepository extends JpaRepository<Incident, Long> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"assignee", "attachments"})
    Optional<Incident> findWithDetailsById(Long id);

    @Query("""
           select new com.trinity.incident.IncidentSummary(i.id, i.status, a.name)
           from Incident i join i.assignee a where i.zone = :zone""")
    List<IncidentSummary> findSummaries(@Param("zone") String zone);
}

public record IncidentSummary(Long id, Status status, String assigneeName) {}

@Service
class IncidentService {
    private final IncidentRepository repo;
    IncidentService(IncidentRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public IncidentDto get(Long id) {
        return repo.findWithDetailsById(id).map(IncidentDto::from)
                   .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id));
    }
}

Set spring.jpa.open-in-view: false in every environment so dev fails the same way prod does. Never enable enable_lazy_load_no_trans: it opens a new session and connection for each lazy access, which hides N+1 problems.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not just turn OSIV on? It holds a DB connection for the whole HTTP request, including view rendering, and hides N+1 queries.
  • JOIN FETCH a collection with pagination? Hibernate paginates in memory (HHH90003004). Page the IDs first, then fetch by IDs, or use @BatchSize.
  • What about Hibernate.initialize()? It works inside the transaction, but explicit fetch plans are clearer.
F23 Database connections are exhausted and new users cannot access application. How will you debug connection leak?
  1. Confirm it from the metrics: hikaricp.connections.active is pinned at max, pending is above 0, and the logs show Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms.
  2. Enable leak detection: spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=20000. Hikari logs the stack trace of the code that borrowed a connection and did not return it.
  3. Check pg_stat_activity for connections that are idle in transaction and long-running queries.
  4. Typical causes: manual JDBC without try-with-resources, long @Transactional methods that make remote calls, Stream results that are never closed, slow queries holding connections.
  5. Fix it: try-with-resources, short transactions, set maximum-pool-size and connection-timeout correctly. Make sure the total across all pods stays under the database's max_connections, or use PgBouncer.

Symptoms & first checks

  • SQLTransientConnectionException: HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms.
  • Metrics: hikaricp_connections_active sits at the maximum, hikaricp_connections_pending grows, and hikaricp_connections_timeout_total increases.
  • Decide first whether this is a leak (active connections never return, even at low traffic) or saturation (slow queries or long transactions under high traffic).

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Enable leak detection without a redeploy if config refresh is available:
    spring.datasource.hikari:
  maximum-pool-size: 20
  leak-detection-threshold: 20000   # ms; logs a stack trace of who borrowed the connection
  connection-timeout: 5000
    The log line Connection leak detection triggered for … on thread … includes the stack trace of the code that borrowed the connection.
  2. Look at the DB side:
    SELECT application_name, client_addr, state, count(*), max(now() - state_change) AS oldest
FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 4 DESC;
    Many idle in transaction sessions mean code opened a transaction and is doing something else, such as an HTTP call or a sleep. On MySQL, use SHOW PROCESSLIST with information_schema.innodb_trx.
  3. Take a thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.print or kubectl exec … jstack). Threads blocked in HikariPool.getConnection are waiters. Find what the connection holders are doing.
  4. Do the math: pods × maximum-pool-size must stay below max_connections minus the reserved connections. HPA scale-out can break this.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Manual DataSource.getConnection() without close Leak-detection stack trace try-with-resources, or JdbcTemplate
Remote call or Kafka send inside @Transactional idle in transaction sessions plus trace Move I/O outside the transaction boundary
OSIV holding the connection for the whole request open-in-view=true Set it to false
Slow queries (saturation, not a leak) pg_stat_statements Index or optimize the query
Too many pods for the DB count(*) in pg_stat_activity near max_connections PgBouncer, smaller pools

Fix / prevention

try (Connection c = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("select 1")) {
    ps.execute();
}
ALTER ROLE app_user SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
ALTER ROLE app_user SET statement_timeout = '15s';

Alert when pending > 0 for more than one minute. Keep the pool small: roughly cores × 2 per DB node, shared across all pods.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is a bigger pool the fix? Rarely. It moves the queue into the DB and makes contention worse.
  • What does leakDetectionThreshold cost? Very little. It is a timer per borrow, so it is safe in prod at 10–60 s.
  • How do you handle many pods? Put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of the DB.
F24 One query works fast initially but becomes slow after data grows to millions of records. What optimizations will you do?
  1. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and look for sequential scans, sorts that spill to disk and stale statistics. Run ANALYZE, and check autovacuum.
  2. Add the right indexes. Composite indexes follow the column order of the WHERE clause and then ORDER BY. Use covering indexes (INCLUDE) and partial indexes (WHERE status='OPEN').
  3. Make the conditions sargable: no functions on indexed columns, no leading %LIKE, no implicit type casts.
  4. Select only the columns you need and use keyset pagination instead of a large OFFSET.
  5. Partition large time-series tables by month (sensor or event data), and archive old data.
  6. Cache results or use read replicas and materialized views for reporting queries.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_incident_city_status_created ON incident (city_id, status, created_at DESC);

Symptoms & first checks

  • Latency grows roughly in line with table size, so it was "fine in UAT".
  • Typical example: SELECT * FROM sensor_reading WHERE device_id=? AND recorded_at > ? ORDER BY recorded_at DESC LIMIT 50 on a table with hundreds of millions of rows.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with production-like parameters. Look for a Seq Scan, a Bitmap Heap Scan with many Rows Removed by Filter, a Sort, and high buffer reads.
  2. Check statistics and bloat: SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='sensor_reading';
  3. Check selectivity: how many rows does each predicate match? A low-cardinality column alone (such as status) is a poor index.
  4. Look for non-sargable predicates that prevent index use: lower(email)=?, date(recorded_at)=?, col::text, leading-wildcard LIKE '%x', and implicit type casts.
  5. Look for OFFSET deep pages and COUNT(*) on every request.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No index or wrong column order Seq Scan or Sort node Composite index: equality columns first, then range/sort columns
Index used, then heap lookups Many heap fetches Covering index with INCLUDE
Function on the column Filter shown instead of Index Cond Expression index, or rewrite as a range
Stale statistics or bloat Estimates far off; dead tuples high ANALYZE; per-table autovacuum settings
Table simply too big Index itself is GBs in size Partitioning plus archival

Fix / prevention

-- equality first, then the range/sort column; covering to enable Index Only Scan
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_reading_device_time
  ON sensor_reading (device_id, recorded_at DESC) INCLUDE (value);

-- partial index for the hot subset
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_incident_open ON incident (zone_id, created_at)
  WHERE status = 'OPEN';

-- non-sargable -> sargable
-- BAD:  WHERE date(recorded_at) = '2026-10-01'
-- GOOD: WHERE recorded_at >= '2026-10-01' AND recorded_at < '2026-10-02'

-- time-range partitioning for append-heavy telemetry
CREATE TABLE sensor_reading (
  id bigint, device_id bigint, recorded_at timestamptz, value numeric
) PARTITION BY RANGE (recorded_at);
CREATE TABLE sensor_reading_2026_10 PARTITION OF sensor_reading
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-01') TO ('2026-11-01');

Other steps:

  • Select only the columns you need (a DTO projection, not the full entity).
  • Use keyset pagination (see F28).
  • Use estimated counts or no total count.
  • Use materialized views or rollup tables for dashboards.
  • Move read-only analytics to a replica.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why CONCURRENTLY? It avoids an exclusive write lock, but it cannot run inside a transaction block. Flyway needs a non-transactional migration for it.
  • Is there a downside to more indexes? Slower writes, WAL growth, and bloat. Drop indexes that pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 shows are unused.
  • When do you partition? When maintenance or retention on a single table becomes painful (roughly 100M+ rows with a natural time key).
F25 Duplicate records are inserted during concurrent transactions. How will you avoid it?
  1. Cause: a check-then-insert race. Both transactions see "not exists" and both insert.
  2. The database is the real guard. Add a unique constraint on the business key, for example (vehicle_no, event_time) or an idempotency key.
  3. Use an upsert: PostgreSQL INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING/UPDATE, MySQL INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
  4. Catch DataIntegrityViolationException and treat it as "already exists".
  5. For API retries, have the client send an Idempotency-Key header and store the processed keys.
  6. For Kafka consumers, use idempotent processing with a processed-message table.
ALTER TABLE challan ADD CONSTRAINT uk_challan UNIQUE (vehicle_no, violation_time);
INSERT INTO challan(...) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT (vehicle_no, violation_time) DO NOTHING;

Symptoms & first checks

  • Two identical rows (for example two complaints with the same external_ref, or two payments) created milliseconds apart.
  • The code does "check then insert": if (!repo.existsByRef(ref)) repo.save(...). Under READ COMMITTED, both transactions see "not exists" and both insert.
  • Triggers include double-clicks, client or gateway retries, and Kafka redelivery.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Compare created_at and request or trace IDs of the duplicates. Same trace ID means a retry. Different trace IDs means concurrent users or a double submit.
  2. Check whether a unique constraint exists: \d complaint or SHOW INDEX FROM complaint.
  3. Check the Kafka consumer: was it rebalanced, or did it process the message before committing the offset?

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Check-then-act race Code review, concurrent load test DB unique constraint plus upsert
Client or gateway retries without idempotency Same payload, same client, different requests Idempotency-Key header table
At-least-once Kafka delivery Same message offset or key processed twice Idempotent consumer (processed-message table)
SELECT … FOR UPDATE on a missing row Nothing to lock in PostgreSQL Constraint, or pg_advisory_xact_lock

Fix / prevention Let the database enforce uniqueness, because only it sees every transaction:

ALTER TABLE complaint ADD CONSTRAINT uq_complaint_ref UNIQUE (source_system, external_ref);

-- PostgreSQL
INSERT INTO complaint (source_system, external_ref, status, created_at)
VALUES (:src, :ref, 'NEW', now())
ON CONFLICT (source_system, external_ref) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;
-- MySQL: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = id;
@Transactional
public Complaint create(CreateComplaint cmd) {
    try {
        return repo.saveAndFlush(Complaint.from(cmd));     // flush so the violation surfaces here
    } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
        return repo.findBySourceSystemAndExternalRef(cmd.source(), cmd.ref())
                   .orElseThrow(() -> e);
    }
}

Note: on PostgreSQL, a constraint violation aborts the current transaction. Do the lookup in a new transaction, or prefer ON CONFLICT through a native query. For APIs, store (idempotency_key, response_hash) with a unique key and return the stored response on replay. On the UI, disable the submit button after the first click, but treat that only as a convenience, not a safeguard.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not SERIALIZABLE isolation? It works, but it causes serialization failures that you must retry, and it is costlier than a single constraint.
  • Is synchronized in Java enough? No. It fails with multiple pods.
  • What about uniqueness with soft deletes? Use a partial unique index WHERE deleted = false.
F26 A transaction partially updates data and application crashes in middle. How will you maintain consistency?
  1. Within one database, put all related writes in one @Transactional service method. The database rolls back everything if the process crashes before commit.
  2. Watch for the common pitfalls. By default only unchecked exceptions trigger rollback, so use rollbackFor = Exception.class for checked ones. Self-invocation bypasses the proxy. Do not catch and swallow exceptions inside the method.
  3. Keep remote calls and Kafka publishes out of the database transaction. Use the transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, then publish it with a relay (Debezium CDC or a poller).
  4. Across services, use a Saga with compensating actions.
  5. For batch jobs, use Spring Batch chunk commits plus restartable job metadata, so a restart resumes from the last committed chunk.
  6. Make operations idempotent so retries are safe.

Symptoms & first checks

  • An order exists without its line items, or a stock decrement happened without the order. A crash or OOMKill happened during the operation.
  • Key insight: if all writes were inside one local DB transaction, a crash cannot leave partial data, because uncommitted work is rolled back by the DB. Partial state therefore means the writes were not atomic.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Map every write in the flow and the transaction it ran in. Use logging.level.org.springframework.transaction=DEBUG (or org.springframework.orm.jpa.JpaTransactionManager=DEBUG) to see begin and commit boundaries.
  2. Look for these patterns:
    • Methods called via this. (self-invocation, so no proxy and no transaction).
    • @Transactional on private methods.
    • REQUIRES_NEW that commits early.
    • A caught exception that is swallowed.
    • A checked exception that does not trigger rollback.
  3. Look for non-DB side effects: Kafka publish, REST call, file or S3 write, Redis update.
  4. Check batch jobs: was each chunk committed independently with no restart state?

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No or ineffective @Transactional (self-call, private method) TX debug log shows several commits Single service method transaction on a public proxied bean
Checked exception, so no rollback Exception type in logs rollbackFor = Exception.class
DB write plus Kafka/HTTP side effect (dual write) Event sent, DB rolled back, or the reverse Transactional outbox
Multi-step batch without checkpoints Half the file was processed Spring Batch chunks plus idempotent writes

Fix / prevention

@Service
public class WorkOrderService {
    private final WorkOrderRepository orders;
    private final InventoryRepository inventory;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;

    public WorkOrderService(WorkOrderRepository o, InventoryRepository i, OutboxRepository ob) {
        this.orders = o; this.inventory = i; this.outbox = ob;
    }

    @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
    public Long create(CreateWorkOrder cmd) throws Exception {
        WorkOrder wo = orders.save(WorkOrder.from(cmd));
        int updated = inventory.decrement(cmd.partId(), cmd.qty());   // UPDATE ... WHERE qty >= :q
        if (updated == 0) throw new InsufficientStockException(cmd.partId());
        outbox.save(OutboxEvent.of("WorkOrderCreated", wo.getId(), wo)); // same TX, no Kafka call here
        return wo.getId();
    }
}

A relay (a poller, or Debezium CDC) publishes outbox rows to Kafka after commit, which gives at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent. Make operations retry-safe with idempotency keys and run a reconciliation job that detects orphaned or stuck states (for example PENDING older than 15 minutes) and repairs or alerts.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Default rollback rules? Rollback happens on RuntimeException and Error, not on checked exceptions.
  • Why not XA/2PC? Kafka has no XA support, plus it brings blocking coordinators and poor availability.
  • What if the crash happens after commit but before the response? The client retries with the same idempotency key and gets the stored result.
F27 Deadlock occurs frequently in database during peak traffic. How will you analyze and fix it?
  1. Get the deadlock details. PostgreSQL writes both statements to the server log (deadlock detected). Set log_lock_waits=on. MySQL: SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS (LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK), or innodb_print_all_deadlocks=ON.
  2. Find the pattern. It is usually two transactions locking the same rows in opposite order, or missing indexes that cause wide range or gap locks.
  3. Fix it by locking in a consistent order (for example sort the IDs before updating), keeping transactions short, and doing no remote calls inside them.
  4. Add indexes on the WHERE and FK columns so fewer rows get locked.
  5. Use optimistic locking (@Version) where it fits, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for queue-like tables.
  6. Retry deadlock victims (CannotAcquireLockException / DeadlockLoserDataAccessException) with Spring Retry and backoff.

Symptoms & first checks

  • PostgreSQL: ERROR: deadlock detected … Process 123 waits for ShareLock on transaction 456; blocked by process 789.
  • MySQL: Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction.
  • Spring surfaces these as CannotAcquireLockException or PessimisticLockingFailureException.
  • Correlate with peak traffic, batch jobs running at the same time, or a new code path.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Get both statements. In PostgreSQL, the server log shows both queries when log_lock_waits = on (logs waits longer than deadlock_timeout, default 1 s). In MySQL:
    SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G         -- section: LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
SET GLOBAL innodb_print_all_deadlocks = ON;  -- log every one, not just the latest
    This shows each transaction's held locks, waited-for locks, index, and lock mode (including gap and next-key locks).
  2. See live blocking:
    SELECT a.pid, pg_blocking_pids(a.pid) AS blocked_by, a.query
FROM pg_stat_activity a WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)) > 0;
  3. Map statements to code using the trace ID or application name. Usually two code paths update the same rows in opposite order, for example a transfer A→B and B→A, or a batch updating ascending while the API updates a parent then its child.
  4. Check foreign keys without indexes. In PostgreSQL, FK checks take row locks on the parent. In MySQL, a missing index makes InnoDB lock far more rows (range or table scans).

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Inconsistent lock order Deadlock graph shows A→B vs B→A Always lock in deterministic order (sorted IDs)
Long transactions holding locks xact_start age in pg_stat_activity Shorter transactions, no I/O inside them
Unindexed WHERE or FK (InnoDB locks the scanned range) Lock on PRIMARY index, many rows Add the index
Gap/next-key locks under REPEATABLE READ (MySQL) lock_mode X locks gap in status READ COMMITTED, or a narrower predicate
Batch updates in random order Batch job in the deadlock graph Sort the batch by primary key, use smaller chunks

Fix / prevention

@Repository
public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {
    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @Query("select a from Account a where a.id in :ids order by a.id")   // deterministic order
    List<Account> lockAll(@Param("ids") Collection<Long> ids);
}

@Service
public class TransferService {
    private final TransferTx tx;
    public TransferService(TransferTx tx) { this.tx = tx; }

    // retry OUTSIDE the transaction: each attempt is a fresh TX (spring-retry + @EnableRetry)
    @Retryable(retryFor = PessimisticLockingFailureException.class,
               maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 50, multiplier = 2, random = true))
    public void transfer(long from, long to, BigDecimal amt) { tx.transfer(from, to, amt); }
}

TransferTx.transfer is @Transactional and calls lockAll(List.of(from, to)) first. Monitor pg_stat_database.deadlocks.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Deadlock vs lock timeout? A deadlock is a cycle, so the DB kills one victim immediately. A timeout is just a long wait (lock_timeout, innodb_lock_wait_timeout).
  • Would optimistic locking help? Yes, for low-contention updates: @Version avoids holding locks and retries on OptimisticLockException.
  • Why retry outside the transaction? The failed transaction is already rolled back. Retrying inside it reuses an aborted session.
F28 Pagination API becomes slow for huge tables. How will you optimize database performance?
  1. Cause: OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 20 still scans and discards 500k rows, and Spring Data Page also runs a COUNT(*) on every request.
  2. Use keyset (seek) pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:lastTs, :lastId) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, backed by a matching composite index.
  3. Return Slice instead of Page to avoid the count query, or cache or estimate the total (PostgreSQL reltuples).
  4. Select only the needed columns through a DTO projection, and do not fetch collections with paging (Hibernate HHH90003004 warns about in-memory pagination).
  5. Use cursor-based API responses (nextCursor) for infinite scroll.
  6. For filtered searches, add suitable indexes or move the search to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Page 1 is fast, but page 5000 takes seconds. GET /incidents?page=N&size=50 uses LIMIT 50 OFFSET 250000, so the DB reads and throws away 250,000 rows.
  • Spring Data Page<T> also runs a COUNT(*) on every request, which is a full scan in PostgreSQL.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on deep pages. Look at the Limit node's input rows and at a Sort node if no index matches the ORDER BY.
  2. pg_stat_statements usually shows the count(*) query as one of the top total-cost queries.
  3. Check whether the sort is deterministic: ORDER BY created_at alone gives duplicates or skipped rows across pages when timestamps tie.
  4. Check whether users actually jump to page 5000, or whether it is a scroller or crawler. That decides between "infinite scroll" and "page numbers".

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Deep OFFSET Time grows with page number Keyset (seek) pagination
Count query on every page Second query in the SQL log Slice<T> / Window<T>, or a cached or estimated count
No index on sort plus filter columns Sort node in the plan Composite index (filter, sort_key, id)
Fetching full entities or collections Wide rows, N+1 DTO projection

Fix / prevention Keyset pagination: the client sends the last seen sort key and the DB seeks via the index.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_incident_zone_created_id
  ON incident (zone_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);

SELECT id, title, status, created_at
FROM incident
WHERE zone_id = :zone
  AND (created_at, id) < (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId)     -- row-value comparison
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;

Spring Data 3.1+ supports this natively:

public interface IncidentRepository extends JpaRepository<Incident, Long> {
    Window<IncidentView> findFirst50ByZoneIdOrderByCreatedAtDescIdDesc(Long zoneId, ScrollPosition pos);
}

// first call
Window<IncidentView> w = repo.findFirst50ByZoneIdOrderByCreatedAtDescIdDesc(zone, ScrollPosition.keyset());
// next page: encode w.positionAt(w.size() - 1) into an opaque cursor for the client

API response: { "items": [...], "nextCursor": "eyJjcmVhdGVkQXQiOi4uLn0=" }.

If page numbers are mandatory:

  • Cap the depth (for example 100 pages).
  • Use the "deferred join" SELECT … FROM incident JOIN (SELECT id FROM incident … LIMIT 50 OFFSET n) t USING (id) so the offset scans only the index.
  • Show an approximate total from pg_class.reltuples.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Downside of keyset? No random page jumps, and the cursor must contain every sort column.
  • Slice vs Page? Slice fetches size+1 rows to know if there is a next page, with no count query.
  • Does MySQL support row-value comparison? Yes, but older versions use the index poorly. Expand it to created_at < ? OR (created_at = ? AND id < ?).
F29 Users report inconsistent data between UI and database. How will you debug end-to-end?
  1. Reproduce with a specific record and request. Compare the actual network response in browser DevTools with the database row.
  2. Follow the request through each layer using the trace ID: UI state or cache, then CDN or browser cache (Cache-Control), then the API gateway, then the service, then Redis, then the database.
  3. Check caching. A stale Redis or Caffeine entry means a missing @CacheEvict/@CachePut on update, or a TTL that is too long.
  4. Check read replicas for replication lag, which shows up as read-after-write inconsistency.
  5. Check the transaction and mapping layer: uncommitted reads, DTO mapping bugs, timezone conversion (store UTC, use OffsetDateTime), Kafka consumer lag for event-driven updates.
  6. Fix the root cause and add a cache-invalidation or contract test.

Symptoms & first checks

  • The UI shows status OPEN but the DB row says CLOSED. Or one user's edit "disappears". Or values differ (time off by 5.5 hours, rounded amounts).
  • Get one concrete example: user, record ID, timestamp, screenshot, and ideally the trace ID from the response header.

Step-by-step investigation Walk the layers from the browser down to the DB, comparing the value at each hop:

  1. Browser: in DevTools Network, check whether the API response already has the stale value (a backend issue) or the UI state is stale (frontend store, missed WebSocket update, browser or service-worker cache, Cache-Control headers).
  2. CDN / gateway: look for Age or X-Cache: HIT headers. Call the service directly with curl -v and compare.
  3. Service cache: compare the Redis key (redis-cli GET incident::42, TTL incident::42) with the DB value. Check the Hibernate second-level cache if it is enabled.
  4. Read replica: check whether the read path hits a replica. Measure lag with SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(); on the replica.
  5. Mapping layer: DTO mapping bugs, LocalDateTime vs OffsetDateTime and the JVM timezone, BigDecimal scale, enum name changes.
  6. Write path: concurrent edits without @Version cause lost updates (last write wins silently). The audit table or trace history shows two updates.
  7. Events: is the UI fed by a projection or read model built from Kafka? Check consumer lag with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group ui-projection.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Stale cache (Redis, HTTP, CDN) Cache value ≠ DB value Evict on write after commit; short TTL; ETag
Replica lag Lag query, read routing Read-your-writes from primary for N seconds after a write
Lost update Two writers, no version column @Version optimistic locking, return 409
Projection consumer lag or failure Lag metric, DLT messages Fix the consumer, replay, alert on lag
Timezone or serialization Consistent offset in values Store timestamptz/UTC; serialize ISO-8601 with offset

Fix / prevention

@Entity
public class Incident {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
    @Version private long version;          // UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=?
    private String status;
}

Return the version as an ETag and require If-Match on PUT; map ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException to 409 Conflict. Propagate the traceId to the UI (response header) so support tickets carry it.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why evict instead of update the cache? Concurrent updates can write the cache out of order. Delete-on-write plus re-read from the DB is safer.
  • Why evict after commit? Evicting before commit lets a reader re-cache the old value.
  • How do you detect lost updates historically? Audit tables or Hibernate Envers revisions.
F30 Batch insert operation is taking too much time. How will you improve performance?
  1. Enable JDBC batching: hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=500, order_inserts=true, order_updates=true.
  2. Do not use GenerationType.IDENTITY, because it disables insert batching. Use SEQUENCE with allocationSize=50, and a pooled optimizer.
  3. Call flush() and clear() on the EntityManager every batch so the persistence context does not grow without limit.
  4. For pure bulk loads, use JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate. Add reWriteBatchedInserts=true (PostgreSQL) or rewriteBatchedStatements=true (MySQL) to the JDBC URL. Use PostgreSQL COPY for millions of rows.
  5. Use one transaction per chunk, not per row, and not one huge transaction. Process chunks in parallel if ordering does not matter.
  6. Drop or defer non-essential indexes and triggers during very large loads.
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate:
  jdbc.batch_size: 500
  order_inserts: true
  order_updates: true

Symptoms & first checks

  • Importing 1M rows (for example a nightly streetlight asset import) takes hours. The SQL log shows one INSERT per round trip.
  • Check the ID strategy first: GenerationType.IDENTITY silently disables JDBC insert batching in Hibernate, because it needs the generated key after each insert.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Enable hibernate.generate_statistics=true. The summary shows "executing N JDBC batches". Zero batches means batching is off.
  2. Check the driver logs or pg_stat_statements.calls for the insert. Calls equal to the row count means no multi-row rewrite.
  3. Profile the JVM: is the time in the DB, in the Hibernate persistence context (dirty checking a 1M-entity first-level cache causes GC pressure), or in parsing?
  4. Check the DB side: many indexes, triggers, FK checks, synchronous replication, or one giant transaction producing huge WAL.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
IDENTITY ids Entity mapping SEQUENCE with pooled allocationSize
batch_size not set Statistics show 0 batches hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
Persistence context grows without limit Heap/GC, slowing over time flush() + clear() every N rows
Driver sends rows individually One call per row in DB stats reWriteBatchedInserts / rewriteBatchedStatements
One huge transaction or many indexes WAL size, lock duration Chunked commits; drop and recreate indexes for bulk loads

Fix / prevention

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/city?reWriteBatchedInserts=true   # MySQL: rewriteBatchedStatements=true
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate.jdbc.batch_size: 50
      hibernate.order_inserts: true
      hibernate.order_updates: true
@Entity
public class Asset {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "asset_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "asset_seq", sequenceName = "asset_seq", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long id;
    private String code;
}
// DB: CREATE SEQUENCE asset_seq INCREMENT BY 50;  -- must match allocationSize

@Service
public class AssetImporter {
    @PersistenceContext private EntityManager em;

    @Transactional
    public void importChunk(List<AssetRow> rows) {
        for (int i = 0; i < rows.size(); i++) {
            em.persist(rows.get(i).toEntity());
            if ((i + 1) % 50 == 0) { em.flush(); em.clear(); }
        }
    }
}

For pure bulk loads, skip the ORM:

jdbcTemplate.batchUpdate("insert into asset(id, code) values (nextval('asset_seq'), ?)",
        rows, 1000, (ps, r) -> ps.setString(1, r.code()));

For the fastest option, use PostgreSQL COPY via CopyManager, or MySQL LOAD DATA, into a staging table, then INSERT … SELECT … ON CONFLICT. Commit in chunks of 1k–10k rows, use Spring Batch for restartability, and run parallel partitions when ordering does not matter.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why does IDENTITY break batching? Hibernate must execute each insert immediately to learn the ID for the persistence context.
  • saveAll vs persist? saveAll calls save() per entity, which issues a merge() (an extra SELECT) when the entity has an assigned ID. Prefer persist, or implement Persistable#isNew.
  • What about StatelessSession? It has no first-level cache or dirty checking, which makes it good for ETL.
F31 One microservice is down and another service continuously retries causing system overload. How will you handle it?
  1. This is a retry storm. Limit retries to about 3 attempts with exponential backoff and jitter instead of immediate retries.
  2. Put a circuit breaker in front of the retry so calls stop entirely while the dependency is down, then probe again in HALF_OPEN state.
  3. Make sure retries are not stacked at several layers (client, gateway, service mesh). Retry at one layer only.
  4. Use a bulkhead and timeouts so waiting threads cannot exhaust the pool.
  5. For asynchronous work, use Kafka retry topics or a DLT (@RetryableTopic with backoff) instead of synchronous loops.
  6. Return fallbacks or 503 quickly, and alert on circuit breaker state.
@RetryableTopic(attempts = "4", backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2.0))
@KafkaListener(topics = "incident-events")
public void consume(IncidentEvent e) { ... }

Symptoms & first checks

  • notification-service is down. incident-service threads are all stuck in retries, its CPU and thread pools are saturated, and its own callers start timing out. When the downstream recovers, it is hit by a thundering herd and falls over again.
  • Count the retry layers: client library, Resilience4j, Feign/RestClient, service mesh (Istio retries), API gateway, frontend. Three layers of 3 attempts each means 27 times the load.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Metrics: request rate to the failing service (http_client_requests_seconds_count{uri=..., outcome="SERVER_ERROR"}) vs the inbound rate. A ratio above 1 shows retry amplification.
  2. Zipkin trace: several child spans to the same downstream for a single request.
  3. Thread dump: Tomcat threads waiting on socket reads mean timeouts are missing or too long.
  4. Check the retry config: is there backoff and jitter? Are non-idempotent POSTs retried? Are 4xx responses retried?
  5. Check Kafka consumers: is a listener retrying in a tight loop and blocking its partition?

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No circuit breaker Calls continue at full rate to a dead service Resilience4j CircuitBreaker
Retry without backoff or jitter Evenly spaced burst of calls Exponential backoff plus randomization
Retries at several layers Mesh + client + gateway config Retry at one layer only; set a retry budget
Missing or long timeouts Threads blocked in socket read Connect/read timeouts and a TimeLimiter
Infinite consumer retry Same offset reprocessed repeatedly DefaultErrorHandler with backoff plus DLT

Fix / prevention

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      notification:
        sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED
        sliding-window-size: 50
        failure-rate-threshold: 50
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 60
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 5
  retry:
    instances:
      notification:
        max-attempts: 3
        wait-duration: 200ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
        enable-randomized-wait: true
        retry-exceptions: [java.io.IOException, org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException]
        ignore-exceptions: [org.springframework.web.client.HttpClientErrorException]
@CircuitBreaker(name = "notification", fallbackMethod = "queueForLater")
@Retry(name = "notification")
public void notifyCitizen(Alert a) { notificationClient.send(a); }

private void queueForLater(Alert a, Throwable t) { outbox.save(OutboxEvent.of("AlertPending", a.id(), a)); }

By default Retry wraps CircuitBreaker, so once the breaker is open, retries fail fast with CallNotPermittedException. Add CallNotPermittedException to ignore-exceptions so that open-breaker failures are not retried at all.

Better still, make non-critical calls asynchronous (Kafka) so an outage only builds a backlog. For consumers, use DefaultErrorHandler(new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template), new ExponentialBackOff(500, 2)).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Which requests are safe to retry? Idempotent ones (GET, PUT, or anything with an idempotency key) and transient errors (IOException, 503, 429 honoring Retry-After).
  • What does half-open mean? After the wait duration, a few trial calls decide whether to close the breaker or re-open it.
  • What is a retry budget? Cap retries to a percentage of requests (for example 10%) so they can never multiply the load.
F32 Service-to-service communication is failing intermittently in production. How will you debug network or application issue?
  1. Classify the errors from logs and traces: connection refused or reset, timeout, 5xx, UnknownHostException. Network errors point to infrastructure, while 5xx or slow responses point to the application.
  2. Check Kubernetes: kubectl get endpoints <svc>, pod restarts, readiness probe failures, OOMKills. Pods being removed during rolling deploys need graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful) plus a preStop sleep.
  3. Test from inside a pod with curl / nslookup. Check DNS, NetworkPolicies, Istio sidecar logs.
  4. Check connection pool problems: stale keep-alive connections closed by a load balancer, which needs an idle timeout shorter than the LB's. Check pool exhaustion in the HTTP client.
  5. Check the callee: thread pool saturation, GC pauses, database waits.
  6. Fix with tuned timeouts, safe retries, circuit breakers and graceful shutdown.

Symptoms & first checks

  • A small percentage of calls fail with Connection reset, ConnectTimeoutException, 503 UH/UF (Envoy), UnknownHostException, or SocketTimeoutException. Errors are often clustered around deployments or after idle periods.
  • First, classify by error type and timing: during rollouts, after idle periods, under load, or from specific nodes or pods.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Tracing: in Zipkin, filter error spans. Does the server span exist? If not, the request never reached the app, which points to the network, LB, or mesh. If it exists, the error came from the app.
  2. Pod health: kubectl get pods -o wide (restarts? concentrated on one node?), kubectl describe pod (OOMKilled, probe failures), kubectl logs --previous, kubectl top pod.
  3. Endpoints: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=order-svc. Check whether terminating pods still receive traffic.
  4. Reproduce from inside the cluster:
    kubectl debug -it deploy/incident-svc --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
curl -v --max-time 5 http://order-svc.city.svc.cluster.local:8080/actuator/health
dig order-svc.city.svc.cluster.local
tcpdump -i any -nn port 8080 -w /tmp/cap.pcap     # look for RST, retransmits
  5. Mesh logs: in kubectl logs pod -c istio-proxy, response flags like UC (upstream connection termination) or UF (connect fail) are useful.
  6. JVM: GC pauses (jvm_gc_pause_seconds_max), CPU throttling (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total), and exhaustion of the HTTP client connection pool.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Stale keep-alive (client idle timeout > server/LB idle timeout) RST on reused connection after idle Client idle eviction shorter than the server's keepAliveTimeout; retry idempotent calls once
Traffic to terminating pods Errors only during rollout server.shutdown=graceful plus preStop sleep
DNS issues (ndots, conntrack) UnknownHostException, slow lookups Use FQDN, NodeLocal DNSCache
CPU throttling or GC pauses Throttle and GC metrics spike Right-size limits, tune heap
Client pool exhausted Pending-connection metric Size the pool, set timeouts

Fix / prevention

server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
---
# Deployment snippet
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"] }   # let endpoints/LB deregister first
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45

Always set connect and read timeouts on RestClient/WebClient, propagate trace context, and include the downstream host and status in error logs.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you tell network from application? If there is no server span or server access log entry, it is network, LB, or mesh. If the server logged a 5xx, it is the app.
  • Why the preStop sleep? Endpoint removal is asynchronous. Without it, kube-proxy or the LB can still route requests to a pod that has stopped accepting them.
  • Which tool shows connection resets? tcpdump or Wireshark (RST flags), or the Envoy response flags.
F33 One microservice deployment breaks communication with another service because of API contract change. How will you avoid such issues?
  1. Make only backward-compatible changes: add optional fields, do not rename or remove fields, set FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false on consumers (Spring Boot's default).
  2. Version breaking changes (/api/v2/... or a header) and run both versions until consumers have migrated, then deprecate the old one.
  3. Add contract testing: Spring Cloud Contract or Pact (consumer-driven) in CI, so a provider build fails if it breaks a consumer.
  4. Keep an OpenAPI spec as the source of truth and diff it in CI (openapi-diff).
  5. For Kafka events, use a Schema Registry (Avro/JSON Schema) with BACKWARD compatibility.
  6. Use canary or blue-green deployments with quick rollback.

Symptoms & first checks

  • After a deploy, consumers get 400/500 errors or null fields. Typical causes: a renamed JSON field, a changed type (id int→string), a new required request field, a removed endpoint, or changed enum values.
  • Immediate action: roll back the provider, or route traffic to the previous version. Then identify the breaking diff.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Compare the old and new specs: openapi-diff old.yaml new.yaml --fail-on-incompatible (or oasdiff breaking old.yaml new.yaml).
  2. Check the consumer logs for HttpMessageNotReadableException, UnrecognizedPropertyException, or enum deserialization errors.
  3. Find out which consumers call the changed endpoint: gateway access logs, Zipkin service dependency graph.
  4. For Kafka, check whether the Avro/JSON schema changed and the registry compatibility mode.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Breaking field rename or removal OpenAPI diff Expand–contract: add new, deprecate old, remove later
New required request field 400 errors from old clients Make it optional with a default
Strict deserialization on the consumer UnrecognizedPropertyException Tolerant reader (ignore unknown fields)
Enum value added Consumer fails on unknown constant READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_USING_DEFAULT_VALUE plus @JsonEnumDefaultValue
No contract tests in CI Breakage found only in prod Pact or Spring Cloud Contract gates

Fix / prevention

  1. Consumer-driven contracts (Pact). The consumer publishes its expectations to a Pact Broker. Provider CI verifies them, and the pipeline runs pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant order-service --version $GIT_SHA --to-environment production before deploying.
    @Provider("order-service")
@PactBroker
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class OrderProviderPactTest {
    @LocalServerPort int port;
    @BeforeEach void target(PactVerificationContext ctx) { ctx.setTarget(new HttpTestTarget("localhost", port)); }
    @TestTemplate @ExtendWith(PactVerificationInvocationContextProvider.class)
    void verify(PactVerificationContext ctx) { ctx.verifyInteraction(); }
    @State("order 42 exists") void order42() { /* seed data */ }
}
  2. OpenAPI diff in CI to fail the build on incompatible changes.
  3. Versioning for real breaking changes: /api/v2/orders or a media-type version. Run v1 and v2 side by side, emit a Deprecation/Sunset header, and remove v1 once its metrics show zero traffic.
  4. Tolerant reader: Spring Boot already disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES. Keep it that way and never make new fields required.
  5. Kafka: Schema Registry with BACKWARD (or FULL) compatibility.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Pact vs Spring Cloud Contract? Pact is consumer-driven and language-agnostic, with a broker. SCC is provider-driven and generates stubs, so it fits a JVM-only setup.
  • What is a backward-compatible change? Adding optional fields or endpoints. Never rename, remove, or retype.
  • Deployment order with expand–contract? Provider adds the field, then consumers migrate, then the provider removes the old field.
F34 Distributed transaction failed between payment service and order service. How will you maintain consistency?
  1. Avoid 2PC/XA across microservices. Use the Saga pattern with eventual consistency.
  2. Choreography: Order creates PENDING and emits OrderCreated. Payment charges and emits PaymentCompleted or PaymentFailed. Order then moves to CONFIRMED, or CANCELLED as the compensating action. Orchestration (a central orchestrator, Temporal/Camunda) suits more complex flows.
  3. Use a transactional outbox in each service so a database update and its event are never lost or sent half-way.
  4. Make consumers idempotent (a processed-event table, unique payment reference) because Kafka delivers at least once.
  5. Handle timeouts: a scheduler finds orders stuck in PENDING and queries Payment or compensates.
  6. Send failed messages to a DLT, and reconcile with the payment gateway.

Symptoms & first checks

  • The customer was charged but the order shows PENDING or FAILED, or the order was confirmed without payment. The cause can be a timeout between services, a crash after the gateway charge, or a lost event.
  • Identify which step's outcome is unknown. A timeout does not mean failure: the payment may have succeeded.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Find the trace by order ID or idempotency key, and see which span failed or timed out.
  2. Compare states across orders.status, payments.status, and the payment provider dashboard or API (the source of truth for money).
  3. Check the outbox table for unpublished rows, Kafka consumer lag, and the DLT for failed events.
  4. Check idempotency: did a retry create a second charge?

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Dual write (DB commit + publish not atomic) Event missing for a committed row Transactional outbox
Timeout treated as failure Provider shows the charge as success Idempotent query or retry with the same key; UNKNOWN state
No compensation path Order cancelled, money kept Saga with refund compensation
Non-idempotent consumers Duplicate charges or rows Idempotency key plus processed-events table

Fix / prevention 2PC/XA is not practical across services, Kafka, and external gateways. Use a saga: a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event, with compensating actions.

Orchestrated flow:

  1. order-service: create the order as PENDING_PAYMENT and write the outbox event OrderCreated, in one local transaction.
  2. payment-service consumes it and charges with Idempotency-Key = orderId, then records the result and its outbox event (PaymentSucceeded or PaymentFailed) in one local transaction.
  3. order-service consumes the result: CONFIRMED, or CANCELLED (compensation). If a later step fails, for example inventory, it emits RefundRequested.
@Transactional
public void onPaymentResult(PaymentEvent e) {
    if (!processed.markIfFirst(e.eventId())) return;          // idempotent consumer (unique PK insert)
    Order o = orders.findById(e.orderId()).orElseThrow();
    switch (e.type()) {
        case SUCCEEDED -> o.confirm();
        case FAILED    -> o.cancel("payment failed");
    }
    outbox.save(OutboxEvent.of("Order" + o.getStatus(), o.getId(), o));
}

Also:

  • Timeouts: the saga state machine moves the order to PAYMENT_UNKNOWN, and a reconciler polls the provider's API by idempotency key.
  • Reconciliation job: nightly settlement file vs orders, to catch anything that slipped through.
  • Use semantic locks (the PENDING status) so the user cannot act on half-finished orders.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Orchestration vs choreography? An orchestrator (a state machine or Temporal/Camunda) is clearer for more than 3 steps. Choreography couples fewer services but is harder to trace.
  • Can you get exactly-once delivery? Not end to end. Combine at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers.
  • Outbox relay options? A polling publisher (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) or Debezium CDC reading the WAL.
F35 Users are seeing old data because services are not synchronized properly. How will you solve it?
  1. Find where the staleness comes from: a cache TTL, Kafka consumer lag (kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe), read replica lag, or a missed event.
  2. Cache: evict or update on write (@CacheEvict/@CachePut), shorten TTLs, publish invalidation events (Redis pub/sub or Kafka) so all instances evict their local Caffeine caches.
  3. Events: use the outbox pattern so no update is missed. Use partition keys (entity ID) to keep per-entity ordering. Use idempotent, version-checked consumers that ignore events older than the stored version.
  4. Reduce consumer lag by scaling consumers up to the partition count and tuning batch size.
  5. For read-your-writes, read from the primary after a write, or return the updated resource in the response.
  6. Run a periodic reconciliation job, and tell users when data is eventually consistent (a "last updated" timestamp).

Symptoms & first checks

  • dashboard-service shows a sensor as offline long after device-service marked it online. Or a citizen updates their profile and other screens still show the old value.
  • Determine where the copy lives: a Redis cache, a local Caffeine cache in each pod, a read model or projection built from events, a read replica, or a CDN/browser cache.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Compare the source-of-truth row with the copy, using timestamps or versions on both sides.
  2. Kafka lag: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server … --describe --group dashboard-projection. A growing LAG means the consumer is slow or stuck (a poison message, or a rebalance loop).
  3. Check whether the event is published at all: outbox rows unsent, or a publish that happened before the transaction committed (or got lost on rollback).
  4. Cache: TTL key in Redis; check whether eviction runs on every write path, including admin and batch jobs that bypass the service.
  5. Ordering: check whether events for the same entity go to different partitions (wrong key), so an older update overwrites a newer one.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Cache never invalidated, or invalidated before commit Cache value differs from the DB well past the write Evict via @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) or CDC event
Local in-pod caches Values differ between pods Broadcast invalidation (Redis pub/sub, Kafka) or a short TTL
Consumer lag or stuck partition Lag metric Scale consumers up to the partition count; DLT for poison messages
Out-of-order events Same key on different partitions Partition key = entity ID; apply only if event.version > stored.version
Lost events from dual write DB changed, no event Outbox or Debezium

Fix / prevention

@Service
public class DeviceService {
    private final DeviceRepository repo;
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
    public DeviceService(DeviceRepository r, ApplicationEventPublisher e) { repo = r; events = e; }

    @Transactional
    public void updateStatus(long id, Status s) {
        Device d = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
        d.setStatus(s);
        events.publishEvent(new DeviceChanged(id, d.getVersion() + 1));
    }
}

@Component
class DeviceCacheInvalidator {
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, DeviceChanged> kafka;
    DeviceCacheInvalidator(StringRedisTemplate r, KafkaTemplate<String, DeviceChanged> k) { redis = r; kafka = k; }

    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    void on(DeviceChanged e) {
        redis.delete("device::" + e.id());
        kafka.send("device-changed", String.valueOf(e.id()), e);   // keyed => per-device ordering
    }
}

(For guaranteed delivery, replace the Kafka send with an outbox write before commit.)

Consumers upsert the projection with a version check:

UPDATE device_view SET status = :s, version = :v WHERE id = :id AND version < :v;

Set a TTL on every cache as a safety net. Alert on consumer lag and on projection staleness, measured as now() - last_event_ts. Tell the product team plainly which views are eventually consistent, and use read-your-writes for the user's own data.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Write-through vs cache-aside? Cache-aside with delete-on-write is simpler and safer under concurrent writes.
  • Delayed double delete? Delete, commit, then delete again after a short delay, to cover a reader that re-cached stale data in between.
  • Ordering in Kafka? It is guaranteed only within a partition, so key by entity ID.
F36 API gateway is routing traffic incorrectly after deployment. How will you troubleshoot?
  1. Confirm the symptom: which paths go to the wrong place, and whether it's all traffic or only some. Check gateway access logs for the matched route ID and the upstream URI.
  2. Diff the route config between the previous and current release (Spring Cloud Gateway predicates/filters, order). A broader Path=/api/** placed before a specific route wins first.
  3. Hit /actuator/gateway/routes to see the routes actually loaded at runtime, not just what's in Git.
  4. Check service discovery. lb://traffic-service resolves through Eureka or a K8s Service, so confirm with kubectl get endpoints that the new pods are registered and old ones are gone.
  5. Check StripPrefix/RewritePath filters. Wrong prefix handling often shows up as 404s from the upstream.
  6. Fix the order or predicate, roll it out with a canary, and add a contract test for each route.
- id: incidents
  uri: lb://incident-service
  order: 0
  predicates: [ "Path=/api/incidents/**" ]
  filters: [ "StripPrefix=1" ]

Symptoms & first checks

  • /api/incidents/** lands on asset-service (404), or traffic goes to old pods, or only some users hit the new version, or paths arrive at the service with the wrong prefix.
  • First question: what was deployed? The gateway config, a service, an Ingress, or a canary weight change. Roll back that change if the impact is wide.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Inspect the effective routes in Spring Cloud Gateway. Set management.endpoint.gateway.enabled=true and expose gateway, then:
    curl -s http://gateway:8080/actuator/gateway/routes | jq '.[] | {route_id, predicate, uri, order}'
    Check route order: the first matching predicate wins, so a broad /api/** above /api/incidents/** swallows its traffic.
  2. Trace one request: set logging.level.org.springframework.cloud.gateway=DEBUG to see the matched route ID and target URI. Check headers such as X-Forwarded-Prefix and Host with curl -v.
  3. Filters: StripPrefix=1 vs RewritePath. An off-by-one prefix sends /incidents/42 to the service as /42.
  4. Discovery: for lb://incident-service, check Eureka or the Kubernetes discovery cache. Stale registry entries point to dead or old instances.
  5. Kubernetes layer:
    kubectl get ingress -A; kubectl describe ingress city-gw    # pathType Prefix vs Exact, rule order, host
kubectl get svc incident-svc -o yaml | grep -A3 selector
kubectl get endpoints incident-svc                          # do the selector labels match the new pods?
    A Service selector like app: incident that also matches the canary pods (or the old ReplicaSet) splits traffic unexpectedly.
  6. Config source: check whether the gateway picked up the new config (Config Server refresh, a mounted ConfigMap version), and whether different gateway replicas have different configs.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Route order or overlapping predicates /actuator/gateway/routes output Explicit order, most specific route first
Wrong StripPrefix or RewritePath Service access log shows the wrong path Correct the filter; add a test
Stale discovery cache Registry shows old IPs Lower cache TTL; deregister on shutdown
Service selector or label mismatch kubectl get endpoints Fix labels; version-specific selectors
Config drift across replicas Routes differ by pod Immutable config per release, rolling restart

Fix / prevention

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: incidents
          uri: lb://incident-service
          order: 1
          predicates: [ "Path=/api/incidents/**" ]
          filters: [ "StripPrefix=1" ]
        - id: api-fallback
          uri: lb://legacy-service
          order: 100
          predicates: [ "Path=/api/**" ]

Keep the route config in Git and add integration tests (WebTestClient against the gateway with WireMock backends asserting the target path). Run smoke tests per route after deploy, and use canary releases with automated rollback on 4xx/5xx spikes.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Default route ordering? Lower order wins. With equal order, definition order applies.
  • How do you verify canary traffic weights? Gateway metrics per route ID (spring.cloud.gateway.requests tagged routeId), or Istio VirtualService weights.
  • Can you refresh routes without a restart? Yes, with POST /actuator/gateway/refresh (or a config bus), but changes must still be reviewed.
F37 One microservice scales properly but another becomes bottleneck under high traffic. How will you identify issue?
  1. Compare RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) per service in Grafana. The bottleneck shows rising p99 latency while its upstream services wait on it.
  2. Use the distributed trace waterfall (Micrometer Tracing to Tempo/Zipkin) to find the span where most of the time is spent.
  3. Check resource saturation: CPU throttling (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total), HPA status (kubectl get hpa), and whether the pods have hit maxReplicas.
  4. Check the pools inside the service: Hikari hikaricp_connections_pending, Tomcat busy threads, HTTP client pool size. Adding pods doesn't help if they all share one saturated DB.
  5. Take a thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) to look for BLOCKED threads, locks, or synchronous calls.
  6. Fix the actual constraint: caching, async work, a read replica, bigger pools, or HPA on a custom metric.

Symptoms & first checks

  • During a city event (for example a traffic surge), gateway and incident-service scale fine but geo-service latency climbs. Adding replicas does not help, or HPA does not add any.
  • Apply the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) to resources and RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) to each service, and find where the queue builds up.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Traces: in Zipkin, the critical path of slow requests shows whether time is spent inside geo-service or in its dependencies (DB, Redis, an external maps API).
  2. Kubernetes: kubectl top pods -l app=geo, kubectl get hpa geo -o wide (current vs target metrics, max replicas reached?), kubectl describe hpa (FailedGetResourceMetric?), and pending pods caused by insufficient node capacity.
  3. CPU throttling: a high container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total means the CPU limit is too low, even though utilization looks moderate.
  4. JVM internals:
    • Tomcat tomcat_threads_busy_threads at its maximum (default 200).
    • hikaricp_connections_pending > 0.
    • GC pause time.
    • Thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.print): many threads BLOCKED on one monitor means lock contention, such as a synchronized cache or logging.
    • JFR (jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/geo.jfr) or async-profiler for CPU hotspots.
  5. Shared bottlenecks: if all replicas share one DB or Redis, scaling pods only adds contention. Check DB CPU, locks, and max_connections.
  6. Kafka: consumer parallelism is capped at the partition count. Extra pods beyond that sit idle, so lag grows despite scaling.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Downstream DB or external API limit Trace shows the time in the DB span Indexes, caching, read replicas, bulk APIs
HPA scaling on the wrong metric or capped kubectl describe hpa Scale on RPS, latency, or lag (KEDA); raise max
CPU limit throttling Throttle metric Raise or remove CPU limits; set correct requests
Thread or connection pool saturation Busy threads / pending connections Tune pools, virtual threads, async I/O
Lock contention or a hotspot Thread dump, JFR Remove the global lock, use concurrent structures
Too few Kafka partitions Partitions < consumers Increase partitions (with key-ordering caveats)

Fix / prevention

spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true          # Boot 3.2+, Java 21: blocking I/O no longer pins platform threads
server:
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 400

Note that spring.threads.virtual.enabled needs Java 21. On Java 17, tune the pools instead. Cache hot reads in Redis with a TTL, apply bulkheads per dependency, and load-test each service in isolation with Gatling or k6 to know its saturation point before a city-scale event.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why doesn't adding pods help? The bottleneck is a shared resource (DB, partitions, an external quota), so more pods means more contention.
  • How do you scale Kafka consumers? KEDA with a lag-based scaler, up to the partition count.
  • What does Little's law say here? Concurrency = throughput × latency. If latency doubles, the threads needed double too.
F38 Logs are distributed across multiple services and difficult to trace. How will you implement centralized logging and tracing?
  1. Log structured JSON to stdout (logstash-logback-encoder or Spring Boot 3.4 logging.structured.format.console=ecs).
  2. Ship the logs with Fluent Bit (DaemonSet) to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch or Loki, and view them in Kibana or Grafana.
  3. Add Micrometer Tracing with the OpenTelemetry bridge. It propagates W3C traceparent across RestClient/WebClient/Kafka and puts traceId/spanId into the MDC.
  4. Export spans over OTLP to Tempo or Jaeger, and link logs to traces using the traceId.
  5. Follow a standard: same field names, no PII, and a correlation ID returned in a response header.
management:
  tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1
  otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
logging.pattern.level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId},%X{spanId}]"

Symptoms & first checks

  • Debugging one citizen complaint means running kubectl logs on 8 services and matching timestamps by hand. Logs are lost when pods restart, and there is no common request ID.

Step-by-step investigation (design and rollout)

  1. Structured JSON logs to stdout. Spring Boot 3.4+ supports this natively (logging.structured.format.console: ecs or logstash). Earlier versions can use logstash-logback-encoder. Never write to files inside the pod.
  2. Collect at the node: Fluent Bit or Promtail DaemonSet, shipping to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (EFK) or Grafana Loki. Add Kubernetes metadata (namespace, pod, container, app labels).
  3. Distributed tracing with Micrometer Tracing (which replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth in Boot 3). Add micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel with opentelemetry-exporter-otlp, or micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave with zipkin-reporter-brave. W3C traceparent headers propagate automatically through RestClient.Builder, WebClient.Builder, and RestTemplateBuilder beans (only if you use the auto-configured builders).
  4. Correlate: traceId and spanId go into the MDC automatically, so every log line carries them. Grafana links Loki to Tempo/Zipkin, and Kibana links to the APM trace.
  5. Propagate through Kafka: enable observation on the producer and listener.
