  6. Verify: call the gateway, take the traceId from the response, and search all logs by it.

Likely root causes of "untraceable" logs

Cause How to confirm Fix
Hand-built new RestTemplate() or RestClient.create() No traceparent header downstream Inject the auto-configured builder
@Async or custom executors lose the MDC traceId empty in the async thread ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator on the executor
Kafka not instrumented New trace starts at the consumer observation-enabled: true
Sampling at 10% Trace missing for the incident Tail-based sampling in the OTel Collector; always keep errors
Plain-text multiline stack traces Broken events in Kibana JSON encoder

Fix / prevention

management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1          # head sampling; use OTel Collector tail sampling to keep all errors
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://otel-collector.observability:4318/v1/traces
spring:
  application:
    name: incident-service
  kafka:
    template:
      observation-enabled: true
    listener:
      observation-enabled: true
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs              # Boot 3.4+; includes traceId/spanId from MDC
  # pre-3.4 plain pattern alternative:
  # pattern.level: "%5p [${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"
@Bean
RestClient geoClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {          // builder is instrumented
    return builder.baseUrl("http://geo-service:8080").build();
}

@Bean
ThreadPoolTaskExecutor appExecutor() {
    var ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    ex.setTaskDecorator(new ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator());   // carries trace + MDC
    ex.initialize();
    return ex;
}

Return traceId in a response header so the UI and support tickets can quote it. Mask PII (citizen phone numbers, Aadhaar) in logs, and set retention per environment.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Trace vs span? A trace is the whole request tree. A span is one operation within it, with timing and tags.
  • Loki vs ELK? Loki indexes only labels, so it is cheap and needs grep-style queries. Elasticsearch indexes everything, so it searches faster but costs more.
  • Head vs tail sampling? Head sampling decides at the start, which is cheap. Tail sampling decides after seeing the whole trace, so it can keep every error.
F39 A dependent service becomes slow and entire system response time increases. What resiliency patterns will you implement?
  1. Timeouts on every outbound call (connect plus read). Never rely on the default infinite wait.
  2. Circuit breaker (Resilience4j). It opens on slow-call or failure rate and fails fast.
  3. Bulkhead: a separate thread pool or semaphore per dependency, so one slow service can't use up all Tomcat threads.
  4. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, only for idempotent calls and limited to 2–3 attempts.
  5. Fallback: cached or default data, or a degraded response.
  6. Move work that doesn't need to be synchronous to Kafka.
@CircuitBreaker(name = "gis", fallbackMethod = "cachedLocation")
@Bulkhead(name = "gis")
@TimeLimiter(name = "gis")
public CompletableFuture<Location> locate(String id) {
    return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> gisClient.get(id));
}

Config: slowCallDurationThreshold: 2s, failureRateThreshold: 50, waitDurationInOpenState: 10s.

Symptoms & first checks

  • maps-provider latency rises from 100 ms to 8 s. All incident-service endpoints slow down, including ones that never call maps, because Tomcat threads are stuck waiting. The failure cascades up to the gateway.
  • Slowness is worse than an outage: an outage fails fast, while slow calls hold resources.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Zipkin: confirm the long spans are on the dependency.
  2. Thread dump: many threads in SocketInputStream.read for that host shows a missing or too-long read timeout.
  3. Metrics: http_client_requests_seconds per host, Tomcat busy threads, and Hikari pending connections (if a transaction is held during the call, which is even worse).

Patterns to implement (layered)

Pattern Purpose Implementation
Timeouts Bound how long any call can wait Connect 1–2 s, read sized to the SLO; Resilience4j TimeLimiter for async
Circuit breaker Fail fast while the dependency is sick; includes the slow-call threshold slow-call-duration-threshold, slow-call-rate-threshold
Bulkhead Isolate the dependency so it cannot consume all threads Semaphore or thread-pool bulkhead per downstream
Fallback / graceful degradation Serve something useful Cached last-known value, default, or "map unavailable"
Retry (limited) Absorb transient blips only Max 2–3 attempts, backoff plus jitter, idempotent calls only
Rate limiting / load shedding Protect self and downstream Resilience4j RateLimiter, gateway RequestRateLimiter (Redis)
Caching Avoid calling at all Redis/Caffeine with TTL; stale-while-revalidate
Async decoupling Remove from the request path Kafka plus eventual update

Fix / prevention

@Configuration
class HttpClients {
    @Bean
    RestClient mapsClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
        var rf = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
        rf.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
        rf.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
        return builder.baseUrl("https://maps.internal").requestFactory(rf).build();
    }
}

@Service
class GeoLookup {
    private final RestClient maps;
    private final Cache<String, Address> lastKnown = Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(50_000).expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofHours(6)).build();
    GeoLookup(RestClient mapsClient) { this.maps = mapsClient; }

    @Bulkhead(name = "maps")                                  // semaphore: max-concurrent-calls
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "maps", fallbackMethod = "cached")
    public Address reverseGeocode(String latLng) {
        Address a = maps.get().uri("/reverse?ll={p}", latLng).retrieve().body(Address.class);
        lastKnown.put(latLng, a);
        return a;
    }

    private Address cached(String latLng, Throwable t) {
        Address a = lastKnown.getIfPresent(latLng);
        return a != null ? a : Address.unknown(latLng);
    }
}
resilience4j.bulkhead.instances.maps:
  max-concurrent-calls: 20
  max-wait-duration: 0
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.maps:
  slow-call-duration-threshold: 1500ms
  slow-call-rate-threshold: 50
  failure-rate-threshold: 50
  wait-duration-in-open-state: 20s

Set timeout budgets top-down: the gateway timeout must be larger than the sum of downstream timeouts × retries. Test with chaos tools (Toxiproxy latency, Chaos Mesh).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Semaphore vs thread-pool bulkhead? A semaphore limits concurrency on the caller's thread. A thread pool isolates fully and allows a timeout, but adds context-switching.
  • Why does the circuit breaker need a slow-call threshold? Without it, slow-but-successful calls never open the breaker.
  • Never do what inside a transaction? Call a remote service. It holds a DB connection for the whole wait.
F40 Your microservice is healthy but Kubernetes/load balancer marks it unhealthy. What will you check?
  1. Run kubectl describe pod and read the Events for "Readiness probe failed", including the HTTP status or timeout.
  2. Probe path and port: is it /actuator/health/readiness on the management port (if management.server.port is separate)? Is a context path missing?
  3. Timing: initialDelaySeconds or a startupProbe that is too short for a slow Spring boot, or a timeoutSeconds: 1 probe on a busy JVM.
  4. Health groups: a downstream indicator (Redis, mail, DB) included in readiness makes the pod show DOWN while the app itself works. Keep liveness limited to livenessState.
  5. Security: Spring Security returning 401 on actuator endpoints.
  6. For the LB: the target group health-check path, port, and expected codes, plus NetworkPolicy and security groups.
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include: readinessState,db

Symptoms & first checks

  • The app works when called directly (kubectl port-forward plus curl returns 200), but pods restart in CrashLoopBackOff, show 0/1 READY, or the cloud LB marks targets unhealthy and returns 502/503.
  • kubectl describe pod events tell you which probe failed and how: Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.1.2.3:8080/actuator/health/liveness": context deadline exceeded, or Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Probe definition vs reality: compare path, port, and scheme (HTTP vs HTTPS) with what the app serves. Common mismatches: server.servlet.context-path=/incident (so the path is /incident/actuator/health), or management.server.port: 8081 while the probe targets 8080.
  2. Call it from inside the pod network, exactly as the kubelet does:
    kubectl exec -it pod/incident-7d9 -- curl -sv http://localhost:8081/actuator/health/readiness
kubectl get pod incident-7d9 -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].readinessProbe}'
  3. Status code and auth: Spring Security returning 401/302 for /actuator/health counts as a failure (the kubelet accepts only 200–399, and a 302 to a login page leads to a failure).
  4. Composite health: the readiness group may include db, redis, kafka, or diskSpace. One dependency being DOWN gives a 503 even though the app itself is fine. Run curl …/actuator/health with show-details to see which component is down.
  5. Timing:
    • timeoutSeconds defaults to 1 s, so a GC pause or CPU throttling during startup makes the probe fail.
    • A slow JVM start with no startupProbe lets liveness kill the pod before it is ready.
    • Check initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold.
  6. Cloud LB / Ingress health checks are configured separately: ALB target group path and port, GCP BackendConfig, or NGINX. NetworkPolicies or security groups may block the LB's source ranges from the health port.
  7. Resources: kubectl top pod, throttling, OOMKilled in lastState.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Wrong path, port, or context path Probe spec vs curl from the pod Align with management.server.port and base path
Actuator secured 401/302 in curl permitAll for health endpoints
External dependency in liveness Pods restart when the DB blips Liveness checks only the app state; DB only in readiness, if at all
Probe timeout too short, or slow start context deadline exceeded during startup startupProbe, timeoutSeconds: 3
LB health check misconfigured Target group status Same path and port as readiness

Fix / prevention

management:
  server:
    port: 8081
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true                       # auto-enabled on Kubernetes; exposes /liveness and /readiness
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState, db       # keep liveness = livenessState only
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, prometheus
---
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8081 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 30                      # up to 150 s to start
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8081 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8081 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  failureThreshold: 3
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain actuator(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())
               .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to("health")).permitAll()
                                            .anyRequest().hasRole("OPS"))
               .build();
}

Likely follow-ups:

  • Liveness vs readiness? A failed liveness check restarts the container. A failed readiness check only removes the pod from Service endpoints.
  • Why keep the DB out of liveness? A DB outage would restart every pod (a restart storm) without fixing anything.
  • Why a separate management port? It isolates health and metrics from public traffic, but every probe, LB check, and NetworkPolicy must use that port.
F41 Kafka consumers are processing same message multiple times. How will you make processing idempotent?

Kafka gives at-least-once delivery by default, so duplicates will happen. Make the consumer idempotent:

  1. Give every event a unique eventId (UUID) in a header or the payload.
  2. Keep a processed_events(event_id PK) table and insert into it in the same DB transaction as the business update. A duplicate key means skip.
  3. Or use natural idempotency: an upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE), a status transition guard (WHERE status='PENDING'), or a version check.
  4. Reduce how often duplicates happen: commit offsets after processing (AckMode.RECORD/MANUAL), and tune max.poll.interval.ms so rebalances don't replay batches.
  5. For Kafka-to-Kafka flows, use transactions (transactional.id, isolation.level=read_committed).
@Transactional
public void handle(Event e) {
    if (processedRepo.insertIfAbsent(e.id()) == 0) return; // ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    service.apply(e);
}

Symptoms & first checks

  • Duplicate rows (two challans for one violation, an SMS sent twice), or counters/aggregates higher than expected.
  • Look at the consumer logs around the time of the duplicates for Revoking previously assigned partitions, CommitFailedException, or max.poll.interval.ms exceeded.
  • Remember that Kafka gives at-least-once delivery by default. Duplicates are normal; the consumer has to tolerate them.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Take one duplicated business ID and find its record or records with kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic challan-events --property print.offset=true --property print.key=true --from-beginning | grep <id>. One offset processed twice points to a consumer-side redelivery. Two offsets means the producer published it twice.
  2. Run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --describe --group billing and check whether the consumer IDs change often (rebalances).
  3. Compare the listener's processing time with max.poll.interval.ms. A slow batch gets the consumer kicked from the group, and its uncommitted offsets are redelivered to another consumer.
  4. Check the producer config for enable.idempotence and acks, and check for app-level retries that call send() again.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Crash or rebalance after processing but before the commit Same offset in logs on two pods Idempotent consumer (dedupe table)
Processing slower than max.poll.interval.ms "Member ... leaving group" in logs Lower max.poll.records, speed up processing
Producer resends (app-level retry, no idempotence) Same payload at two offsets enable.idempotence=true, a stable eventId
Upstream replays or reprocessing jobs Offsets reset in the audit trail Dedupe by eventId, not by offset

Fix / prevention. Every event carries a stable eventId (a UUID set by the producer). The consumer records the ID in a processed_event table that has a unique key, inside the same DB transaction as the business change.

CREATE TABLE processed_event (
  consumer_group VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  event_id       UUID         NOT NULL,
  processed_at   TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (consumer_group, event_id)
);
@Service
public class ChallanProcessor {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final ChallanRepository challans;

    public ChallanProcessor(JdbcTemplate jdbc, ChallanRepository challans) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc; this.challans = challans;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void process(ViolationEvent e) {
        int inserted = jdbc.update("""
            INSERT INTO processed_event(consumer_group, event_id) VALUES (?, ?)
            ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING""", "billing", e.eventId());
        if (inserted == 0) return;                // duplicate -> skip silently
        challans.save(Challan.from(e));           // same TX as dedupe row
    }
}

@Component
public class ViolationListener {
    private final ChallanProcessor processor;
    public ViolationListener(ChallanProcessor p) { this.processor = p; }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "violation-events", groupId = "billing")
    public void onEvent(ViolationEvent event, Acknowledgment ack) {
        processor.process(event);   // DB TX commits first
        ack.acknowledge();          // then the offset (ack-mode: manual)
    }
}

There are other ways to get idempotency. You can use natural idempotency (UPSERT or UPDATE ... SET status='PAID' instead of incrementing), version checks, or Redis SET key NX EX 86400 when the side effect is not in the DB. Purge the dedupe table with a TTL job, keeping a window larger than the maximum replay window.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not exactly-once (EOS)? Kafka transactions only cover Kafka-to-Kafka. A DB write or an SMS still needs idempotency.
  • Why dedupe by eventId and not offset? Offsets change if the event is republished or the data is mirrored to another cluster.
  • Redis or DB for dedupe? Use the DB when the side effect is in the same DB, because that gives you atomicity. Redis is faster but not atomic with the DB write.
F42 Consumer lag is increasing continuously in production. How will you investigate?
  1. Run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server ... --describe --group alerts-cg. Check whether lag is on all partitions (throughput) or one partition (hot key or stuck consumer).
  2. Compare the producer rate with the consumer rate in Grafana (kafka_consumer_fetch_manager_records_lag_max, or Burrow).
  3. Look for rebalance storms in the logs ("Revoking partitions"). These are usually caused by processing that exceeds max.poll.interval.ms.
  4. Profile per-record processing time: slow DB calls, external API calls, retries blocking the thread.
  5. Check the consumer count against the partition count. Consumers beyond the number of partitions sit idle.
  6. Fix it: add partitions and consumers, raise concurrency, batch DB writes, tune max.poll.records, or move slow work out of the listener.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Dashboards show records-lag-max growing, and Kafka UI or Burrow reports the group as WARN or STOP. Downstream data is stale (for example, the traffic dashboard is minutes behind).
  • First question: is the lag on all partitions, which means a throughput problem, or on one partition, which means a stuck consumer or a hot key?

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --describe --group analytics. Compare CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG per partition, and check that every partition has a CONSUMER-ID. If CURRENT-OFFSET is not moving at all, the consumer is stuck.
  2. Compare the produce rate with the consume rate. Use the broker metric BytesInPerSec and the topic's MessagesInPerSec against the consumer's records-consumed-rate. A traffic spike (an event day, or a camera fleet coming back online) explains steady growth.
  3. Check for rebalance storms. Grep the logs for Revoking/Assigned, and track the rebalance-rate-per-hour metric.
  4. Look at processing time per record: Micrometer timers on the listener, plus jstack <pid> or a thread dump through Actuator. Are threads blocked on a downstream REST call, JDBC (Hikari pending connections > 0), or a lock?
  5. Check whether the consumer is retrying one record forever: the same offset repeating in error logs.
  6. Check partition skew with kafka-run-class.sh kafka.tools.GetOffsetShell --topic t (or kafka-get-offsets.sh) to see per-partition end offsets.
  7. Check pod CPU throttling, GC pauses, and whether the HPA scaled replicas beyond the partition count, which leaves idle consumers.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Slow downstream (DB/API) Thread dump, Hikari pending, p99 latency Batch writes, caching, bulkheads, async IO
Too few consumers or partitions Lag on all partitions, CPU busy Raise concurrency (≤ partitions), add partitions
Hot key / partition skew Lag on one partition only Better key (composite), split hot entity
Poison message retried forever Same offset in logs DefaultErrorHandler + DLT
Rebalance storm Frequent Revoking logs Tune max.poll.*, static membership, cooperative assignor

Fix / prevention

spring:
  kafka:
    listener:
      concurrency: 6            # <= partition count
      ack-mode: batch
    consumer:
      max-poll-records: 200
      properties:
        max.poll.interval.ms: 300000
        partition.assignment.strategy: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
        group.instance.id: ${HOSTNAME}   # static membership: no rebalance on quick restarts

Alert on lag trend and on time-lag rather than on the absolute count. Burrow evaluates sliding windows, which works well for this. You can also autoscale on lag with KEDA (see F48).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Lag is high but consumers are idle? There are more consumers than partitions, or the consumers are subscribed to the wrong topic or group.
  • Is lag in messages enough? No. Also track time lag (consumer records-lag converted into seconds), because message size and rate vary.
  • Quick mitigation? Scale up to the partition count and shed non-critical work. Pause non-critical listeners through KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry.
F43 Messages are not reaching consumer even though producer sends successfully. What all things will you verify?
  1. Confirm the producer write really succeeded: check the send() future/callback for RecordMetadata (partition and offset). Fire-and-forget hides errors.
  2. Confirm the topic name matches exactly, including environment prefixes, and that auto.create.topics didn't create a typo topic.
  3. Run kafka-console-consumer --topic t --from-beginning to check the data is actually on the broker.
  4. Consumer group: run kafka-consumer-groups --describe. Are partitions assigned? Is a different group.id already ahead? auto.offset.reset=latest skips older messages.
  5. Deserialization: a schema or type mismatch can make the error handler skip records silently. Check logs and the DLT.
  6. Transactions: a read_committed consumer won't see aborted or uncommitted producer transactions.
  7. ACLs, SSL/SASL config, and a listener filter or RecordFilterStrategy dropping records.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Producer logs show send() success (or no error), but the consumer receives nothing.
  • First, define "success." Did the code check the CompletableFuture<SendResult>? With acks=0, or if you fire-and-forget without a callback, "success" means nothing.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Is the data actually in the topic? Run kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --topic incident-events (or GetOffsetShell) twice and check that the end offsets increase. Then run kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic incident-events --from-beginning --max-messages 5.
  2. Same cluster and topic? Check bootstrap-servers per environment and look for typos such as incident-event vs incident-events. With auto.create.topics.enable=true, a typo silently creates a new topic. Run kafka-topics.sh --list.
  3. Consumer group state. Run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group notifier. Does the group exist, is it subscribed to this topic, does each partition have an owner, and is the offset moving?
  4. Another app sharing the groupId. If a different service uses the same group.id, it "steals" partitions. Check the CLIENT-ID/HOST columns.
  5. auto.offset.reset=latest on a new group. Messages sent before the group's first join are skipped.
  6. Transactions. If the producer is transactional but never commits (or aborts), consumers with isolation.level=read_committed see nothing. The console consumer shows the records with the default read_uncommitted.
  7. Deserialization or filtering. ErrorHandlingDeserializer plus a recoverer that just logs, a RecordFilterStrategy, or a @KafkaListener condition can silently drop records. Check the DLT and the error logs.
  8. ACLs/auth. TopicAuthorizationException or GroupAuthorizationException in the consumer logs.
  9. Retention. If the consumer was down longer than retention.ms, the data is gone. Run kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name X.
  10. Container not started. Check autoStartup=false, a listener paused by ops, or a missing @EnableKafka / wrong factory bean.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Wrong topic or cluster Topic list, offsets in each env Externalised config, topic constants, disable auto-create
latest reset on new group Group created after the messages auto-offset-reset: earliest for new groups
Uncommitted transactions read_committed sees none, console sees them Fix the transaction boundary, check abortTransaction logs
Groupid collision Unknown hosts in describe Unique group.id per service
Silent deserialization failure DLT has records, WARN logs Alert on DLT, fix the schema

Fix / prevention. Always verify the send result.

kafkaTemplate.send("incident-events", incident.id(), incident)
    .whenComplete((res, ex) -> {
        if (ex != null) log.error("Publish failed id={}", incident.id(), ex);
        else log.debug("Published p={} o={}", res.getRecordMetadata().partition(),
                       res.getRecordMetadata().offset());
    });

Use acks=all, disable auto topic creation in prod, and alert on DLT depth and on per-topic lag.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Console consumer sees data but the app doesn't? Suspect the group/offset, isolation.level, a filter, or deserialization.
  • How to replay for a new group? kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --to-earliest --group g --topic t --execute (the group must be inactive).
  • Why is fire-and-forget dangerous? Errors such as buffer full or a timeout are lost unless you inspect the future.
F44 Kafka broker goes down during high traffic. How will your system handle it?

The goal is that this is a non-event if we designed for it:

  1. Topics use replication.factor=3 and min.insync.replicas=2. When a broker dies, the controller elects new partition leaders from the ISR.
  2. Producers use acks=all and enable.idempotence=true (the default in Kafka 3.x). They retry until delivery.timeout.ms without creating duplicates or reordering.
  3. Clients get a bootstrap list of several brokers and refresh metadata automatically.
  4. If the producer still fails, write to an outbox table or local buffer and alert. Don't drop data.
  5. Consumers rebalance, reconnect to the new leaders, and resume from committed offsets.
  6. Monitor UnderReplicatedPartitions and OfflinePartitionsCount, and keep unclean.leader.election.enable=false.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Producers log NotLeaderOrFollowerException or NETWORK_EXCEPTION and retry. Latency spikes briefly, and the UnderReplicatedPartitions and OfflinePartitionsCount metrics rise.
  • If the cluster is configured correctly, this is a non-event: the controller elects new leaders from the ISR within seconds, and the clients refresh metadata and retry.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Run kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --describe --under-replicated-partitions and --unavailable-partitions to see which partitions lost a replica or have no leader.
  2. Run kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic payment-events and read Leader, Replicas and Isr. If the ISR is smaller than min.insync.replicas, acks=all producers get NotEnoughReplicasException.
  3. Check the broker logs (server.log) for OOM, disk full (log.dirs), long GC, or the ZooKeeper session / KRaft fencing. Use kubectl describe pod kafka-1 for eviction or node failure.
  4. On the client side, check the producer metrics record-error-rate, record-retry-rate, buffer-available-bytes, and bufferpool-wait-time. If the buffer is full, send() blocks up to max.block.ms.
  5. Consumers: if the broker hosting the group coordinator dies, the group fails over to a new coordinator and rebalances. Watch for a lag bump.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
RF=1 or ISR=1 topics --describe shows one replica RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2
Disk full / OOM Broker logs, node metrics Retention tuning, disk alerts, JVM heap sizing
Node drained in K8s with no PDB K8s events PodDisruptionBudget maxUnavailable: 1, rack awareness
Producer buffer exhausted bufferpool-wait-time high Increase buffer.memory, back-pressure, outbox

Fix / prevention. On the broker/topic side: replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean.leader.election.enable=false (no data loss), and broker.rack spread across zones. The producer:

spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      acks: all
      retries: 2147483647
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true            # no dupes/reordering on retry
        max.in.flight.requests.per.connection: 5
        delivery.timeout.ms: 120000         # total time budget incl. retries
        request.timeout.ms: 30000
        linger.ms: 10
        buffer.memory: 67108864
        max.block.ms: 10000

For critical events (payments, incident creation), use the outbox pattern (F51). Even if Kafka is unavailable for minutes, the event is safely in PostgreSQL and is relayed later. On the consumer side, use idempotent processing, because a rebalance can cause redelivery. With 3 brokers, RF=3 and minISR=2, you tolerate one broker down for both reads and writes. Two brokers down blocks acks=all writes, which is the C-over-A choice.

Likely follow-ups:

  • What does unclean leader election do? It lets an out-of-sync replica become leader, which restores availability but loses data. Keep it off for business data.
  • acks=1 risk? The leader acks, then dies before replication, and the message is lost.
  • How long is failover? Usually seconds with KRaft. Clients retry within delivery.timeout.ms.
F45 Events are processed out of order causing wrong business logic. How will you maintain ordering?
  1. Kafka only guarantees order within a partition, so use the entity ID (e.g. incidentId) as the message key. All events for that entity go to the same partition.
  2. On the producer, enable.idempotence=true keeps order during retries (allowed with max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5).
  3. On the consumer, don't hand records to an unordered thread pool. Use container concurrency (one thread per partition) or key-ordered parallelism (Confluent Parallel Consumer).
  4. Be careful with retry topics and DLTs: non-blocking retries break ordering. For strictly ordered flows, use blocking retries.
  5. Defend against stale events anyway: store a version or event timestamp and ignore anything older than the current state.
kafkaTemplate.send("incident-events", incident.id(), event);

Symptoms & first checks

  • Example: an incident shows OPEN after it was CLOSED, because IncidentClosed was applied before IncidentUpdated.
  • Kafka guarantees order only within a partition. First check whether related events go to the same partition, and whether the consumer processes them sequentially.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Consume with keys and partitions shown: kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic incident-events --property print.key=true --property print.partition=true --property print.offset=true. Do events for one incidentId land on different partitions? Is the key null?
  2. Check whether the partition count was increased recently (kafka-topics.sh --describe). hash(key) % partitions changes, so old and new events for a key split across partitions.
  3. Producer: is enable.idempotence=false combined with max.in.flight > 1 and retries? A retried batch can then land after a later batch.
  4. Are there multiple producers for the same entity (two services emitting status changes)? There is no global order across producers.
  5. Consumer: does the listener hand records to an @Async executor or CompletableFuture? That breaks order. Does it use @RetryableTopic (non-blocking retry)? A failed event moves to a retry topic while later events proceed.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No or incorrect key print.key shows null/random Key = aggregate ID (incidentId)
Partition count changed Topic history Plan partitions up front, or migrate to a new topic
Non-idempotent producer retries Config check enable.idempotence=true
Async processing in consumer Code review Process sequentially per partition, or key-ordered parallelism
Non-blocking retry topics Record in -retry-0 topic Blocking retries for order-critical topics

Fix / prevention

// Producer: key by aggregate id -> same partition -> ordered
kafkaTemplate.send("incident-events", event.incidentId().toString(), event);

Also add a defensive version check in the consumer, because ordering can still break across replays or multiple producers:

@Transactional
public void apply(IncidentEvent e) {
    int updated = jdbc.update("""
        UPDATE incident SET status = ?, version = ?
        WHERE id = ? AND version < ?""",
        e.status().name(), e.version(), e.incidentId(), e.version());
    if (updated == 0) log.info("Stale/duplicate event ignored id={} v={}", e.incidentId(), e.version());
}

version is a monotonic sequence assigned by the owning service, for example a JPA @Version or a per-aggregate sequence. For throughput with ordering, scale by partitions, or use Confluent Parallel Consumer with ProcessingOrder.KEY. Order-critical topics should use DefaultErrorHandler blocking retries and a DLT, not @RetryableTopic.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Global ordering? Only with one partition, which removes parallelism. Usually per-entity ordering is all you need.
  • Does idempotence preserve order with in-flight=5? Yes. The broker uses sequence numbers per producer/partition.
  • Hot key problem? One busy entity limits that partition. Accept it, or split the work into sub-entities.
F46 One failed message blocks entire consumer processing. How will you handle poison messages?
  1. Classify the error as transient (DB down) or permanent (bad JSON, validation failure).
  2. Wrap deserialization in ErrorHandlingDeserializer so a bad payload doesn't loop forever.
  3. Configure DefaultErrorHandler with a bounded backoff, then DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer to send the record to <topic>.DLT and move on.
  4. Mark permanent exceptions as not retryable so they go straight to the DLT.
  5. Alert on DLT volume, and give ops a tool to inspect and replay messages after the fix.
@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> t) {
    var h = new DefaultErrorHandler(new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(t),
                                    new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3));
    h.addNotRetryableExceptions(ValidationException.class, DeserializationException.class);
    return h;
}

Symptoms & first checks

  • Lag grows on one partition while the others are fine. The logs show the same exception at the same offset in a loop, for example a DeserializationException, an NPE on a missing field, or a validation failure.
  • A poison message is one that will never succeed, no matter how often it is retried.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group g. One partition's CURRENT-OFFSET is frozen.
  2. Read that exact record: kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic t --partition 3 --offset 18234 --max-messages 1 --property print.headers=true.
  3. Classify the error. Deserialization means a bad schema or producer bug. A business validation error is non-retryable. A transient error (DB down, timeout) should be retried with backoff.
  4. Check the error-handler config. Old setups used SeekToCurrentErrorHandler with infinite retries, or no recoverer.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Bad JSON / schema mismatch DeserializationException ErrorHandlingDeserializer + DLT
Infinite retry of non-retryable error Same offset in a loop addNotRetryableExceptions
No recoverer configured No DLT topic exists DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer
Downstream outage treated as poison Many offsets failing Back off, pause the container, circuit breaker

Fix / prevention. Spring Boot 3 auto-wires a CommonErrorHandler bean into the default listener container factory.

@Configuration
public class KafkaErrorConfig {
    @Bean
    public DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaOperations<Object, Object> template) {
        var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
            (rec, ex) -> new TopicPartition(rec.topic() + ".DLT", rec.partition()));
        var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(3);
        backOff.setInitialInterval(1_000L);
        backOff.setMultiplier(2.0);
        backOff.setMaxInterval(10_000L);
        var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backOff);
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(InvalidEventException.class,
                                          DeserializationException.class);
        return handler;
    }
}
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
        spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.trinity.events"

After the retries are exhausted, the record goes to <topic>.DLT with headers carrying the exception, the original topic, partition and offset, and the offset is committed, so the partition moves on. The DLT must have at least as many partitions as the source, because the resolver above reuses the partition number. Run a DLT consumer or dashboard to alert, inspect, fix, and replay (republish to the main topic). For transient outages, don't send everything to the DLT: let backoff ride through the outage, or pause the container.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why ErrorHandlingDeserializer? A deserialization failure happens before the listener runs. Without this, the consumer loops inside poll().
  • Blocking vs non-blocking retry? Blocking retry keeps order but stalls the partition. @RetryableTopic doesn't block but breaks order.
  • How to replay DLT? Use a small admin tool or listener that republishes, after the fix is deployed and idempotency is in place.
F47 Retry mechanism causes duplicate event processing. How will you avoid duplicates?
  1. Producer side: enable.idempotence=true and acks=all. Broker-side sequence numbers remove duplicates caused by network retries.
  2. Consumer side: an idempotent handler. Store eventId in a processed table in the same transaction as the update, or use upserts and state guards.
  3. Make side effects idempotent too. Pass an idempotency key to the payment, SMS, or notification provider.
  4. Retry only the failing step, not the whole flow. Don't re-publish events from a retry loop.
  5. For consume-transform-produce, use Kafka transactions (@Transactional with a KafkaTransactionManager, consumers on read_committed) for exactly-once within Kafka.
  6. Make sure the retry happens before the offset commit and stays under max.poll.interval.ms, or a rebalance will replay the batch.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Two notifications, a double ledger entry, or the same event visible in both orders and orders-retry-0.
  • Retries happen at three layers: producer retries, consumer/listener retries, and app-level retries such as Resilience4j or a manual send() in a catch block. Find out which layer created the duplicate.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Duplicate at two offsets in the topic: producer side. Check enable.idempotence, and whether code calls send() again after a timeout (the first send may have succeeded).
  2. Duplicate at one offset, processed twice: the listener partially succeeded. For example, the SMS was sent, then the DB update threw, so the whole listener ran again on retry.
  3. Check the @RetryableTopic / DefaultErrorHandler attempt headers (kafka_retry_topic-attempts, kafka_delivery-attempt when enabled) in the logs.
  4. Check whether an HTTP client retry (Feign/WebClient) wraps a non-idempotent POST.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Producer retry without idempotence Same payload at two offsets enable.idempotence=true, acks=all
App resends after a timeout Logs show manual re-send Rely on producer retries; use an outbox for durability
Listener has a side effect before the failure point Side effect logs ×N Idempotency key + status check; side effect last
HTTP retries on POST Gateway logs Idempotency-Key header at the provider

Fix / prevention. Make every retried unit idempotent:

@Component
public class NotificationListener {
    private final IdempotencyStore store;   // DB table or Redis with status
    private final SmsGateway sms;

    public NotificationListener(IdempotencyStore store, SmsGateway sms) {
        this.store = store; this.sms = sms;
    }

    @RetryableTopic(attempts = "4",
        backoff = @Backoff(delay = 2000, multiplier = 2.0),
        exclude = InvalidEventException.class,
        topicSuffixingStrategy = TopicSuffixingStrategy.SUFFIX_WITH_INDEX_VALUE)
    @KafkaListener(topics = "notification-requests", groupId = "notifier")
    public void handle(NotificationRequest req) {
        if (store.isCompleted(req.requestId())) return;           // already done
        sms.send(req.phone(), req.text(), req.requestId());        // provider dedupes on this key
        store.markCompleted(req.requestId());
    }

    @DltHandler
    public void dlt(NotificationRequest req,
                    @Header(name = KafkaHeaders.DLT_EXCEPTION_MESSAGE, required = false) String err) {
        store.markFailed(req.requestId(), err);
    }
}

There is a gap between send and markCompleted, and the provider-side idempotency key closes it. For Kafka-in to Kafka-out flows, use EOS: transactional.id, a KafkaTransactionManager-backed container, and isolation.level=read_committed. The consumed offset and the produced record then commit atomically. EOS does not cover DB writes or HTTP calls, so those still need dedupe tables (F41).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is idempotence on by default? Yes, since Kafka clients 3.0 (acks=all, enable.idempotence=true), unless conflicting configs disable it.
  • Why "side effect last"? Fewer steps re-run on retry, and the external call is the hardest to undo.
  • Retry storms? Use exponential backoff with jitter, a max-attempts limit, and a circuit breaker on the downstream.
F48 High volume event traffic slows down consumers. How will you scale Kafka consumers?
  1. The partition count limits parallelism. Increase partitions (this changes the key-to-partition mapping, so plan for that) and run replicas up to the partition count.
  2. Raise ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory.setConcurrency(n) per pod.
  3. Autoscale pods on lag with KEDA's Kafka scaler instead of CPU.
  4. Make each record cheaper: batch listener with saveAll and JDBC batching, cache lookups, move slow I/O off the listener.
  5. Tune fetching: max.poll.records, fetch.min.bytes, fetch.max.wait.ms.
  6. Split topics by priority (critical alerts vs telemetry) so bulk traffic doesn't starve important events.
spring.kafka.listener: { type: batch, concurrency: 6 }
spring.kafka.consumer.max-poll-records: 500

Symptoms & first checks

  • Lag grows during peaks (rush-hour ANPR/camera events, sensor bursts), and CPU on the consumer pods is high, or the pods are waiting on IO.
  • Parallelism limit: in one group, at most one consumer thread per partition. If pods × concurrency > partitions, the extra threads sit idle.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic anpr-events gives the partition count. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group g gives the consumers per partition and the lag per partition.
  2. Find out where the time goes: deserialization, business logic, or IO. Use Micrometer timers, async-profiler, and Hikari metrics.
  3. Check the fetch efficiency metrics fetch-rate, records-per-request-avg, and fetch-latency-avg.
  4. Check skew, meaning one partition far behind (hot key).

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Partitions < needed parallelism Lag on all partitions, all busy Add partitions (plan the key remap)
Per-record DB/HTTP calls Profiler, many small queries Batch listener + JDBC batch / COPY
Under-sized pods or CPU throttling container_cpu_cfs_throttled Resource requests/limits, more replicas
Hot partition One partition lagging Better key distribution

Fix / prevention

  1. Vertical within a pod: concurrency (threads) ≤ partitions/pods.
  2. Batching: a batch listener with bulk inserts cuts per-record overhead dramatically.
spring:
  kafka:
    listener:
      type: batch
      concurrency: 4
      ack-mode: batch
    consumer:
      max-poll-records: 500
      fetch-min-size: 64KB
      fetch-max-wait: 200ms
      properties:
        max.poll.interval.ms: 300000   # must exceed worst-case batch time
@KafkaListener(topics = "anpr-events", groupId = "anpr-ingest")
public void onBatch(List<AnprEvent> events) {
    jdbc.batchUpdate("""
        INSERT INTO anpr_read(event_id, plate, camera_id, read_at) VALUES (?,?,?,?)
        ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING""",
        events, 500, (ps, e) -> {
            ps.setObject(1, e.eventId()); ps.setString(2, e.plate());
            ps.setString(3, e.cameraId()); ps.setObject(4, e.readAt());
        });
}
  1. Horizontal: autoscale pods on lag with KEDA.
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: anpr-ingest }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: anpr-ingest }
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 12        # <= partitions / concurrency
  triggers:
    - type: kafka
      metadata:
        bootstrapServers: kafka:9092
        consumerGroup: anpr-ingest
        topic: anpr-events
        lagThreshold: "1000"
  1. Separate the paths: send slow enrichment to another topic or consumer group, so the hot path only does fast work.
  2. If more parallelism than partitions is needed, use Confluent Parallel Consumer with key ordering.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Downside of adding partitions? Key to partition mapping changes, so ordering for existing keys breaks briefly. You also get more open files and longer rebalances.
  • Why not unlimited max.poll.records? The batch may exceed max.poll.interval.ms, which triggers a rebalance and redelivery.
  • Scaling causes rebalances? Use the CooperativeStickyAssignor and static membership to minimise pauses.
F49 Offsets are committed incorrectly and messages are lost. How will you troubleshoot?
  1. Check the config. enable.auto.commit=true commits on a timer even if processing failed. Spring Kafka sets it to false and uses container AckMode by default, but confirm nobody overrode it.
  2. Look for async handoff. If the listener submits to an executor and returns, the offset gets committed before the work is done.
  3. Look for swallowed exceptions. A try/catch that logs and continues means the record counts as processed.
  4. Check auto.offset.reset=latest on a new or expired group, and offsets.retention.minutes.
  5. Compare kafka-consumer-groups --describe offsets with DB records to find the gap. Replay with --reset-offsets --to-datetime ... --execute (group stopped), relying on idempotent consumers.
  6. Fix with AckMode.RECORD or MANUAL plus ack.acknowledge() after processing, and a DLT for failures.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Some events are never processed (missing challans or alerts), yet there is zero lag. The offsets moved past records that were never handled successfully.
  • First, find out how offsets are committed: enable.auto.commit, the container ack-mode, manual Acknowledgment, or async hand-off.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Take a missing event ID and locate it with kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic t --property print.offset=true --property print.partition=true | grep <id>. This confirms that it was in Kafka, and shows its partition and offset.
  2. Run kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group g. The committed offset is past that offset, so it was "consumed."
  3. Search the consumer logs for that partition/offset: an exception that got swallowed, or a "Backoff exhausted ... skipping" message from DefaultErrorHandler. With no recoverer, the default recoverer logs and commits.
  4. Code review:
    • Does @Async, an executor, or CompletableFuture process records while the container commits on return?
    • Is ack.acknowledge() called before the work is done?
    • Is a catch (Exception e) { log... } hiding failures?
  5. In a batch listener, check whether one record failed and the whole batch was acknowledged anyway. Use BatchListenerFailedException(index).
  6. Check offset expiry. If the group was inactive longer than offsets.retention.minutes (default 7 days), the committed offset is deleted. On restart, auto.offset.reset=latest jumps to the end and skips the backlog.
  7. Check topic retention (retention.ms/retention.bytes). Data may have been deleted before it was consumed. The consumer logs Fetch position ... is out of range and resets.
  8. Producer side: acks=1 with a leader failure, or unclean.leader.election.enable=true. The message was "sent" but truncated. Check the broker logs for Truncating.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Async processing + container auto-commit Code uses executor in listener Process synchronously, or manual ack after the future completes
Swallowed exceptions try/catch + log only Rethrow so the error handler retries or sends to DLT
Error handler without DLT "skipping" logs DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer
Offset expiry + latest Group gap > 7 days earliest, longer offset retention
Retention deleted data Out-of-range reset log Retention > max outage, lag alerts

Fix / prevention

spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      enable-auto-commit: false        # container manages commits
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
    listener:
      ack-mode: manual                 # commit only what we acknowledge
@KafkaListener(topics = "violation-events", groupId = "billing")
public void onEvent(ViolationEvent e, Acknowledgment ack) {
    processor.process(e);   // throws on failure -> DefaultErrorHandler retries -> DLT
    ack.acknowledge();      // only after successful processing
}

To recover, stop the group, then run a dry run followed by the reset: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --group billing --topic violation-events --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-10-04T09:00:00.000 --dry-run, then --execute. Replay is safe only because the consumer is idempotent (F41). For prevention, run a reconciliation job that compares source counts with processed counts, and alert on DLT depth.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Spring Kafka auto-commit default? The container sets enable.auto.commit=false and commits per ack-mode (BATCH by default) after the listener returns.
  • At-most-once vs at-least-once? Commit before processing gives at-most-once (loss). Commit after gives at-least-once (duplicates). Choose at-least-once and make the consumer idempotent.
  • Inspect committed offsets history? Read __consumer_offsets with the offsets message formatter, or use Kafka UI.
F50 Different services consume same event differently causing inconsistency. How will you design event contracts?
  1. Treat events as public APIs. Put the schema (Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema) in a Schema Registry with BACKWARD or FULL compatibility enforced.
  2. Use a standard envelope: eventId, eventType, version, occurredAt, source, correlationId, and payload (CloudEvents style).
  3. Document field meaning precisely: units, time zone (UTC ISO-8601), enums, nullability, and what "status=CLOSED" means.
  4. Evolve by adding only optional fields. Breaking changes get a new version or topic, with both running in parallel during migration.
  5. Add consumer-driven contract tests (Spring Cloud Contract or Pact) in CI.
  6. Give each event type one owning producer, and have consumers treat the event as fact. Don't re-derive state differently.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Billing treats amount as rupees while analytics treats it as paise. One service reads status=CLOSED as final while another expects RESOLVED. After a producer deploy, one consumer breaks or silently defaults a renamed field to null.
  • The root issue is that there is no single, versioned, enforced schema with documented semantics.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Collect the consumer DTOs for the event across repos and diff the field names, types, units, enums, and nullability.
  2. Inspect real payloads: kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic payment-events --property print.headers=true. Are there multiple shapes in the same topic?
  3. Check whether a schema registry is used. Run curl $SR/subjects/payment-events-value/versions and curl $SR/config/payment-events-value to see the compatibility level.
  4. Review the producer's git history for field renames or semantic changes released without a version bump.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Hand-copied DTOs in each service Diverging classes Generated classes from one schema (Avro/JSON Schema)
No compatibility enforcement No registry or NONE Registry with BACKWARD/FULL compatibility
Undocumented semantics (units, enum meaning) Wiki silence Field docs, AsyncAPI spec, explicit unit field names
Breaking change in place Rename in history Additive changes only; new version/topic for breaks

Fix / prevention

  1. Envelope + schema owned by the producing team:
{
  "type": "record", "name": "PaymentCompleted", "namespace": "com.trinity.payment.v1",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "eventId",      "type": {"type": "string", "logicalType": "uuid"}},
    {"name": "occurredAt",   "type": {"type": "long", "logicalType": "timestamp-millis"}},
    {"name": "paymentId",    "type": "string"},
    {"name": "amountPaise",  "type": "long", "doc": "Amount in paise (INR x 100)"},
    {"name": "status",       "type": {"type": "enum", "name": "PaymentStatus",
                                       "symbols": ["SUCCESS", "FAILED", "UNKNOWN"], "default": "UNKNOWN"}},
    {"name": "channel",      "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}
  ]
}
  1. Schema registry with BACKWARD compatibility: new consumers can read old data. You may add optional fields with defaults or delete fields that have defaults, but never rename or change a type. Producers in prod use auto.register.schemas=false, and CI registers or tests the schemas.
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      value-serializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroSerializer
      properties:
        schema.registry.url: http://schema-registry:8081
        auto.register.schemas: false
        use.latest.version: true
    consumer:
      value-deserializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroDeserializer
      properties:
        schema.registry.url: http://schema-registry:8081
        specific.avro.reader: true
  1. Rules:
    • Publish one event type per business fact, named in the past tense.
    • Include units in field names.
    • Give enums a default.
    • Consumers must tolerate unknown fields.
    • A breaking change gets a new version (payment-events.v2) and the old one is dual-published during migration.
  2. Contract tests: run a schema compatibility check in CI with the registry Maven plugin, plus consumer-driven contracts (Pact / Spring Cloud Contract messaging).
  3. Document the contract in AsyncAPI, and give the topic and schema a named owner.

Likely follow-ups:

  • BACKWARD vs FORWARD? With BACKWARD, consumers are upgraded first (new reader, old data). With FORWARD, producers are upgraded first. FULL means both.
  • Fat vs thin events? Fat events carry state, so consumers don't call back. Thin events carry only an ID and need a lookup, which risks reading stale data.
  • JSON without registry? It's possible with JSON Schema validation in CI, but nothing is enforced at runtime.
F51 Payment updated successfully but notification service failed. How will you ensure eventual consistency?
  1. Never dual-write ("save to DB, then call Kafka/HTTP"). Use the transactional outbox: in the same DB transaction as the payment, insert a PaymentCompleted row into an outbox table.
  2. A relay (Debezium CDC, or a @Scheduled poller with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) publishes outbox rows to Kafka and marks them sent.
  3. The notification service consumes with retries and backoff, uses a DLT, and dedupes on eventId.
  4. Notification failure must not roll back the payment. It's a separate step that gets retried.
  5. Add a reconciliation job and alerts for outbox rows stuck older than N minutes.
@Transactional
public void complete(Payment p) {
    paymentRepo.save(p.markPaid());
    outboxRepo.save(Outbox.of("PaymentCompleted", p.id(), toJson(p)));
}

Symptoms & first checks

  • A citizen paid the e-challan (the DB shows SUCCESS) but got no SMS or email, or the challan service never marked it paid.
  • Typical bug: the code commits to the DB and then calls kafkaTemplate.send() or a REST call to notification. If that call fails, or the pod dies in between, the event is lost. This is the dual-write problem.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Trace the paymentId across services using the correlation ID in logs (ELK/Loki) and the tracing (Zipkin/Tempo).
  2. Check whether the event exists in payment-events (console consumer + grep). If not, the publish failed. If yes, check the notification consumer group lag and the DLT.
  3. Check the notification service logs and the provider (SMS gateway) responses: rate limit, timeout, 5xx.
  4. Find how many payments are affected with SQL: payments SUCCESS with no notification_log entry.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Dual write (DB commit, then publish) Event missing from topic Transactional outbox
Synchronous REST to notification 5xx/timeouts in logs Async via Kafka, retries
Consumer failed, no DLT Error logs, offset moved DefaultErrorHandler + DLT + replay
Provider outage Gateway errors Retry w/ backoff, fallback channel

Fix / prevention. Use the transactional outbox: the business row and the event row are written in one local ACID transaction, and a relay publishes the events.

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    private final PaymentRepository payments;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public PaymentService(PaymentRepository p, OutboxRepository o, ObjectMapper m) {
        this.payments = p; this.outbox = o; this.mapper = m;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void completePayment(UUID paymentId) throws JsonProcessingException {
        Payment p = payments.findById(paymentId).orElseThrow();
        p.markSuccess();
        outbox.save(new OutboxEvent(UUID.randomUUID(), "Payment", p.getId().toString(),
                "PaymentCompleted", mapper.writeValueAsString(PaymentCompleted.from(p))));
    }
}

@Component
public class OutboxRelay {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;

    public OutboxRelay(JdbcTemplate jdbc, KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc; this.kafka = kafka;
    }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
    @Transactional
    public void relay() throws Exception {
        List<Map<String, Object>> rows = jdbc.queryForList("""
            SELECT id, aggregate_id, payload FROM outbox
            WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at
            LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED""");
        for (Map<String, Object> r : rows) {
            kafka.send("payment-events", (String) r.get("aggregate_id"), (String) r.get("payload"))
                 .get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);                       // wait for broker ack
            jdbc.update("UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = ?", r.get("id"));
        }
    }
}

SKIP LOCKED lets several relay pods run safely. For lower latency and less polling, use Debezium CDC (the outbox event router) on the WAL instead of a poller. The relay is at-least-once, so the notification consumer must be idempotent (dedupe on eventId), with retries, a DLT, and replay. Add a reconciliation job as the safety net: find payments that are SUCCESS with no notification older than N minutes, and republish. Avoid 2PC/XA, because Kafka doesn't support it and it couples availability. For multi-step flows with compensation (for example, refund if the challan update fails), use a saga.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not @TransactionalEventListener AFTER_COMMIT + send? If the pod crashes after the commit, the event is lost. The outbox survives crashes.
  • Outbox table growth? Purge or partition published rows on a schedule.
  • Ordering in outbox? Order by created_at/sequence per aggregate, and key the record by aggregate_id.
F52 Distributed cache contains stale data and users see outdated information. How will you handle cache invalidation?
  1. Use cache-aside: on write, update the DB first, then evict the key (@CacheEvict). Don't update the cache in place, because concurrent writes cause races.
  2. Always set a TTL (spring.cache.redis.time-to-live) as a safety net.
  3. For multi-instance local caches (Caffeine L1), broadcast invalidation through Redis Pub/Sub or a Kafka event, or drop L1 for volatile data.
  4. To close the read-after-write race, use a delayed second delete or versioned keys (user:42:v7).
  5. For cross-service data, invalidate from a CDC or Kafka event when the source changes.
  6. Monitor hit ratio and staleness, and use short TTLs for frequently changing data like live traffic status.
@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "sensor", key = "#s.id")
@Transactional
public Sensor update(Sensor s) { return repo.save(s); }

Symptoms & first checks

  • A user updates a vehicle or complaint status, but the API keeps returning the old value until a TTL expires, or forever. Different pods return different values when there is a local (Caffeine) L1 cache.
  • First, identify the pattern: cache-aside? Is the cache updated or deleted on write? What is the TTL? Is there any L1 cache?

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Run redis-cli GET complaint:123 and redis-cli TTL complaint:123. A TTL of -1 means the key never expires. Compare the value with SELECT ... FROM complaint WHERE id=123.
  2. Run redis-cli MONITOR | grep complaint:123 briefly in non-prod, or for a few seconds in prod, because it is expensive. Do you see a DEL after the update, and a later SET with old data (a race)?
  3. Run redis-cli INFO stats and look at keyspace_hits/misses, plus INFO keyspace.
  4. Code review: is the eviction in the same method before the commit (@CacheEvict inside @Transactional), only on one code path, or missing for bulk SQL updates and batch jobs?
  5. Are there multiple pods with Caffeine and nobody broadcasting the invalidation?

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Write path doesn't evict (batch job, direct SQL) DB changed, no DEL in MONITOR Event-driven invalidation from all writers/CDC
Evict before commit, then a reader repopulates old data DEL then SET old value Evict AFTER_COMMIT, delayed double delete
No TTL TTL = -1 TTL with jitter as a safety net
Local L1 not invalidated on other pods Pods disagree Redis pub/sub or Kafka broadcast eviction
Update-cache-on-write race Concurrent writers Delete instead of set, or versioned values

Fix / prevention. Use cache-aside: delete on write, after commit, and broadcast the invalidation.

@Service
public class ComplaintService {
    private final ComplaintRepository repo;
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;

    public ComplaintService(ComplaintRepository repo, ApplicationEventPublisher events) {
        this.repo = repo; this.events = events;
    }

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "complaint", key = "#id")
    public ComplaintDto get(long id) { return ComplaintDto.from(repo.findById(id).orElseThrow()); }

    @Transactional
    public void updateStatus(long id, Status s) {
        repo.findById(id).orElseThrow().setStatus(s);
        events.publishEvent(new ComplaintChanged(id));
    }
}

@Component
public class CacheInvalidator {
    private final CacheManager cacheManager;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;

    public CacheInvalidator(CacheManager cm, KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka) {
        this.cacheManager = cm; this.kafka = kafka;
    }

    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    public void onChange(ComplaintChanged e) {
        cacheManager.getCache("complaint").evict(e.id());            // Redis
        kafka.send("cache-invalidation", "complaint", String.valueOf(e.id())); // L1 on all pods
    }
}

Each pod listens to cache-invalidation with a unique group id (for example cache-${HOSTNAME}), so every pod gets every message, and it evicts its Caffeine entry. Always set a TTL with ±10% jitter to avoid a stampede. For hot keys, use @Cacheable(sync = true) or a lock to prevent a thundering herd. For writers you don't control, drive invalidation from Debezium CDC.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why delete rather than update cache? Two concurrent writers can set the cache in the wrong order. A delete is idempotent and order-safe.
  • Delayed double delete? Delete, commit, then delete again after about 500 ms to kill a racing stale repopulate.
  • Which data shouldn't be cached? Balances or payment status that need strong consistency. Read those from the primary.
F53 One server has updated data but another server still shows old data. How will you solve replication delay issue?
  1. Measure the lag: Postgres SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(); on the replica, or pg_stat_replication. MySQL: SHOW REPLICA STATUS → Seconds_Behind_Source.
  2. Read-your-writes: send reads that follow a write (same user or session) to the primary for N seconds, or use @Transactional(readOnly=false) routing through AbstractRoutingDataSource.
  3. Keep critical reads (payment status, balances) on the primary. Use replicas for reports and dashboards.
  4. If needed, use synchronous replication (synchronous_commit=remote_apply) for strict cases. Writes get slower.
  5. Fix the cause of the lag: long-running queries on the replica, heavy write bursts, network or IO. Alert when lag exceeds a threshold.
  6. If the issue is app-level caches, invalidate them through events (see F52).

Symptoms & first checks

  • A user saves, the next GET (load-balanced to a different pod) shows the old value, and a refresh a second later is fine. Classic read-your-writes violation.
  • Two possible layers: DB read replicas (writes go to the primary, reads to a lagging replica) or per-pod local caches (see F52). Rule out caching first.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Confirm the routing. Does @Transactional(readOnly = true) route to the replica? Log the datasource used, or check inet_server_addr().
  2. On the PostgreSQL primary:
SELECT client_addr, state, sent_lsn, replay_lsn,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;
  1. On the replica:
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_delay,
       pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();
  1. Correlate the lag spikes with write bursts (bulk imports), long queries on the replica (replay paused by max_standby_streaming_delay), network, or replica disk IO.
  2. Check how cloud-managed replicas are monitored, for example the RDS ReplicaLag metric.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Async replication (normal lag) replay_lag ms to s Read-your-writes routing
Long replica queries blocking replay pg_stat_activity on replica, conflicts Tune max_standby_streaming_delay, separate analytics replica
Heavy write burst / IO-bound replica WAL rate vs replay rate Batch throttling, bigger replica
Local cache per pod DB fine, pods differ Broadcast invalidation

Fix / prevention

  1. Route reads that must be fresh to the primary. Use primary-for-N-seconds after a write (session or header flag), or route by transaction type:
public class ReadWriteRoutingDataSource extends AbstractRoutingDataSource {
    @Override
    protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() {
        boolean readOnly = TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly();
        return (readOnly && !ReadYourWritesContext.isPinnedToPrimary()) ? "replica" : "primary";
    }
}

@Configuration
public class DataSourceConfig {
    @Bean
    @Primary
    public DataSource dataSource(@Qualifier("primaryDs") DataSource primary,
                                 @Qualifier("replicaDs") DataSource replica) {
        var routing = new ReadWriteRoutingDataSource();
        routing.setTargetDataSources(Map.<Object, Object>of("primary", primary, "replica", replica));
        routing.setDefaultTargetDataSource(primary);
        routing.afterPropertiesSet();
        return new LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy(routing);   // resolve after readOnly flag is set
    }
}

ReadYourWritesContext is a request-scoped flag, set when the user's last write happened less than X seconds ago (for example, a timestamp in a cookie or in Redis keyed by user). 2. LSN-based: after a write, return pg_current_wal_lsn() to the client. Use the replica only if pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= thatLsn, otherwise fall back to the primary. 3. Critical writes: SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = remote_apply with synchronous_standby_names. The commit waits for the replica to apply. This costs latency, and if the sync standby is down, writes block. 4. The UI can also use the write response directly (return the updated entity) instead of re-reading. 5. Alert on replay_lag above a threshold, and take a replica out of the read pool when it lags.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy? Without it, the connection is fetched before the transaction's readOnly flag is set, so routing always picks the default.
  • Sync replication everywhere? It costs latency and availability. Use it only for data that must never be stale.
  • Monotonic reads? Make the user sticky to one replica, or use an LSN token, so time never appears to go backwards.
F54 Network partition occurs between services in distributed system. How will system behave?

By CAP, during a partition we choose consistency or availability for each use case:

  1. Callers fail fast. Timeouts and circuit breakers open, and fallbacks serve cached or degraded data (availability).
  2. For strongly consistent operations (payments, unique allocation), reject or queue the request instead of guessing.
  3. Async flows keep working: producers buffer or write to the outbox, Kafka holds events, and consumers catch up after the partition heals.
  4. Clustered stores: Kafka keeps acks=all writes only on the side with ISR quorum. min.insync.replicas stops writes on the minority side. Redis Sentinel/Cluster or etcd use quorum to avoid split-brain.
  5. After healing: idempotent replay, reconciliation jobs, and conflict resolution (version or last-write-wins where acceptable).
  6. Test it with chaos tools (Chaos Mesh, Toxiproxy).

Symptoms & first checks

  • Timeouts or connection resets between a subset of pods, AZs, or a DC and the cloud. Some instances can reach the DB or Kafka and others cannot. Circuit breakers open, and you may see split-brain (two leaders).
  • CAP: during a partition, each component either refuses requests (stays Consistent) or serves possibly stale or divergent data (stays Available). The answer is to design that choice per component, not to leave it to chance.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Map the partition boundaries. From a pod: kubectl exec -it pod -- curl -m 2 http://svc:8080/actuator/health, nc -zv kafka-0 9092, and nslookup svc. Check NetworkPolicies, Istio/mesh config, and cloud security groups.
  2. Kafka: run kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions, and check whether the controller quorum (KRaft) still has a majority. Producers on the minority side get NotEnoughReplicas/timeouts with acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2.
  3. PostgreSQL HA (Patroni): run patronictl list. A primary that loses the DCS (etcd) leader key demotes itself, which prevents two primaries.
  4. Redis Sentinel/Cluster: is a minority-side master still accepting writes? Check with INFO replication.
  5. Look at the Resilience4j metrics: circuit breaker state, retry counts, and bulkhead saturation.

Likely root causes / behaviours

Component Behaviour in partition Design choice
Kafka (RF=3, minISR=2, acks=all) Minority side can't write CP. Clients buffer and retry; outbox holds the events
Postgres + Patroni Only the side with the DCS quorum keeps a primary CP with fencing (no split-brain)
Redis Sentinel Old master may accept writes, which are lost on heal min-replicas-to-write 1 limits the loss window
REST between services Timeouts, cascading failures Timeouts, circuit breaker, fallback (AP read paths)
Caches / dashboards Serve stale data AP. Show "last updated"

Fix / prevention

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      challanService:
        slidingWindowSize: 20
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        waitDurationInOpenState: 10s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 3
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      challanService:
        timeoutDuration: 2s
  retry:
    instances:
      challanService:
        maxAttempts: 3
        waitDuration: 300ms
        enableExponentialBackoff: true
        retryExceptions: [java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException]
@CircuitBreaker(name = "challanService", fallbackMethod = "cachedSummary")
@Retry(name = "challanService")
public ChallanSummary summary(String vehicleNo) { return client.summary(vehicleNo); }

private ChallanSummary cachedSummary(String vehicleNo, Throwable t) {
    return cache.getStale(vehicleNo).orElse(ChallanSummary.unavailable(vehicleNo));
}
  • Always set timeouts, because an infinite wait means thread exhaustion.
  • Retry only idempotent operations, and use idempotency keys.
  • Use bulkheads per downstream service.
  • Communicate asynchronously through Kafka, so producers aren't blocked by a consumer outage. Kafka absorbs the partition and the consumers catch up afterwards.
  • Use quorum-based leader election and fencing tokens (F55) so the minority side can't keep acting as leader.
  • After the partition heals, run reconciliation jobs, replay the DLT, and drain the outbox.
  • Test with chaos experiments (Chaos Mesh / Litmus network-partition).

Likely follow-ups:

  • PACELC? Even without a partition, you trade latency against consistency. Async replication picks L, sync picks C.
  • Which smart-city paths are AP vs CP? Payments and challan issuance are CP. Live dashboards and sensor views are AP with staleness indicators.
  • How do you avoid split-brain? Majority quorum (odd number of nodes), lease/leader keys with TTL, and fencing the old leader.
F55 Multiple services update same resource causing inconsistency. How will distributed locking help?
  1. A distributed lock ensures only one instance performs the critical section at a time across pods, e.g. assigning one ambulance to one incident.
  2. Use Redisson RLock with a wait time and lease time (or its watchdog), always released in finally.
  3. Locks can expire during GC pauses, so also protect the DB with optimistic locking (@Version) or a fencing token. Treat the lock as an optimization and the DB constraint as the guarantee.
  4. Simpler options when everything is in one DB: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, Postgres advisory locks, or a conditional update (UPDATE ... WHERE status='FREE').
  5. ShedLock for scheduled jobs.
RLock lock = redisson.getLock("vehicle:" + id);
if (lock.tryLock(2, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    try { assignVehicle(id); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}

Symptoms & first checks

  • Lost updates. Example: two operators or services change the same traffic junction signal plan, or two schedulers on different pods both run "generate monthly challans," producing a double run. The final state depends on who wrote last.
  • First, ask whether you actually need a distributed lock. Often a cheaper mechanism prevents the conflict: optimistic locking (@Version), a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE, a unique constraint, or single-writer by Kafka key.

Step-by-step investigation

  1. Check the audit or DB history for interleaved updates on the same row within milliseconds from different pods or services.
  2. Review the code for the read-modify-write pattern (find, modify in Java, save) without @Version or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
  3. For jobs, check whether @Scheduled runs on every replica, which it does by default.
  4. If a Redis lock already exists: is the lease shorter than the operation? Look for GC pauses (GC logs) longer than the lease. With redis-cli TTL lock:junction:42, check whether unlock() is skipped on exceptions.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Read-modify-write without concurrency control No @Version, interleaved writes Optimistic lock + retry, or atomic SQL
Scheduler runs on all pods Duplicate job logs per pod ShedLock / Redisson lock / leader election
Cross-service updates to a shared resource Multiple writers Single owner service, or a distributed lock
Lock expired mid-operation (GC, slow IO) Lease < op time, GC logs Watchdog renewal + fencing token

Fix / prevention

1. Redisson RLock, for cross-service, short critical sections:

@Service
public class SignalPlanService {
    private final RedissonClient redisson;
    private final SignalPlanRepository repo;

    public SignalPlanService(RedissonClient redisson, SignalPlanRepository repo) {
        this.redisson = redisson; this.repo = repo;
    }

    public void updatePlan(long junctionId, PlanChange change) throws InterruptedException {
        RLock lock = redisson.getLock("lock:junction:" + junctionId);
        // wait max 2s; leaseTime -1 => watchdog auto-renews while this JVM holds it
        if (!lock.tryLock(2, -1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Junction " + junctionId + " is being updated");
        }
        try {
            long fence = redisson.getAtomicLong("fence:junction:" + junctionId).incrementAndGet();
            repo.applyWithFence(junctionId, change, fence);
        } finally {
            if (lock.isHeldByCurrentThread()) lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

2. Fencing token. The lock alone is not safe: a paused holder can wake up after its lease expired. The storage layer must reject stale tokens:

UPDATE signal_plan SET plan = ?, fence_token = ?
WHERE junction_id = ? AND fence_token < ?;   -- 0 rows => stale holder, abort

3. PostgreSQL advisory lock. Use this when all writers share the DB. It is released automatically at commit or rollback, and needs no extra infra:

@Transactional
public void generateMonthlyChallans(String month) {
    Boolean got = jdbc.queryForObject(
        "SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(?, 0))", Boolean.class, "challan-gen:" + month);
    if (!Boolean.TRUE.equals(got)) return;     // another pod is running it
    // ... work ...
}

4. Prefer optimistic locking for user edits: a JPA @Version field throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException, and you retry or return 409 to the client.

Trade-offs:

  • A Redis single-master lock can be lost on failover, so it is not safe for correctness alone. Pair it with fencing.
  • Redlock is debated.
  • etcd/ZooKeeper locks are stronger (CP) but heavier.
  • Keep locked sections short and never hold a lock across remote calls without timeouts.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why fencing tokens? A lock lease can expire during a GC pause. A monotonically increasing token lets storage reject the late writer.
  • Optimistic vs pessimistic? Optimistic for low contention (user edits). A lock or FOR UPDATE for high contention or expensive conflicts.
  • Schedulers on many pods? ShedLock (backed by a DB/Redis table) or K8s leader election, so the job runs once.
F56 One region/server goes down completely. How will high availability architecture handle it?
  1. No single points of failure: at least 2 replicas per service, spread across zones (topologySpreadConstraints/pod anti-affinity), and a PodDisruptionBudget.
