  2. The load balancer or ingress health checks remove dead nodes, and K8s reschedules pods onto healthy nodes.
  3. Data tier: Postgres primary plus standby with automatic failover (Patroni, RDS Multi-AZ), Redis Sentinel/Cluster, and Kafka RF=3 across racks/AZs.
  4. Multi-region: active-passive with DNS failover (Route 53 health checks) and async replication, or active-active for stateless tiers. MirrorMaker 2 for Kafka.
  5. Define RPO and RTO, keep backups in another region, and run DR drills regularly.
  6. Keep services stateless (sessions in Redis or JWT) so any instance can serve any request.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Alerts fire: ALB/Route 53 health checks fail, node NotReady, pods Pending/Terminating, DB primary unreachable, Kafka under-replicated partitions.
  • First question: is it one node, one AZ, or a whole region? Each one fails over in a different way.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. kubectl get nodes -o wide and kubectl get pods -A -o wide --field-selector=status.phase!=Running show which nodes or AZs are gone.
  2. kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -50 shows evictions, FailedScheduling and volume attach errors.
  3. Check that the ALB target groups list only healthy targets in the AZs that are still up (AWS console or aws elbv2 describe-target-health).
  4. Database: confirm the Multi-AZ RDS or Patroni failover finished (patronictl list) and that apps reconnected. HikariCP reconnects on its own if maxLifetime is shorter than the DB/NLB idle timeout.
  5. Kafka: kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions. With RF=3 and min.insync.replicas=2, producers using acks=all keep working when one broker or AZ is lost.
  6. Region loss: Route 53 failover or latency records move traffic to the DR region. Promote the cross-region read replica and scale the warm-standby cluster up.
  7. Tell stakeholders what is degraded, what still works and the ETA.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
All replicas on one node/AZ kubectl get pods -o wide topologySpreadConstraints / anti-affinity
Single-AZ DB RDS config Multi-AZ / Patroni with sync replica
Stateful data on node-local disk PV type EBS/replicated storage; externalize state
DR never tested No runbook Quarterly game days

Fix / prevention

spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: ticket-service }
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: ticket-service-pdb }
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: ticket-service }
  • Keep services stateless: sessions go in Redis (Sentinel or Cluster, replicas in other AZs) or in JWTs.
  • Agree RPO and RTO with the business. Example: same-region multi-AZ gives RPO ≈ 0 and RTO of minutes. Cross-region async replication gives RPO of seconds to minutes and RTO of 15–30 minutes.
  • Use readiness probes so traffic only reaches pods that are actually ready.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Active-active vs active-passive? Active-active is more expensive and needs conflict handling for writes. Active-passive (warm standby) is simpler and enough for most city platforms.
  • What about split-brain? Use a consensus or quorum system (etcd for Patroni, KRaft for Kafka) and fence the old primary.
  • How do you prove HA works? Chaos tests: drain a node, block an AZ, and measure the actual RTO.
F57 Traffic suddenly increases 10x during sale/event. How will distributed system scale?
  1. Before the event: load test (JMeter/Gatling/k6) at 10x, pre-scale pods and nodes, warm caches, and raise DB and connection limits.
  2. HPA on CPU or RPS with a reasonable maxReplicas, and Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter for nodes.
  3. Offload reads: CDN for static content, Redis for hot data, read replicas.
  4. Absorb writes asynchronously: accept the request, push it to Kafka, process at a steady rate (queue-based load leveling).
  5. Protect the core: rate limiting at the gateway (RequestRateLimiter with Redis), bulkheads, and circuit breakers.
  6. Degrade gracefully by turning off non-critical features with feature flags. Watch dashboards live with an on-call bridge.
filters:
  - name: RequestRateLimiter
    args: { redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 500, redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 1000 }

Symptoms & first checks

  • p99 latency rises, 5xx/502/504 errors at the ALB or Nginx, CPU above 80%, HikariCP pending > 0, Kafka consumer lag grows.
  • Find out whether the bottleneck is compute (pods), DB connections, or a downstream service.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. kubectl get hpa and check whether TARGETS is above target and REPLICAS is already at MAX.
  2. kubectl top pods and kubectl describe hpa <name> (look for "unable to fetch metrics" or a maxReplicas limit).
  3. kubectl get pods | grep Pending means the cluster has no room. Check Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter logs.
  4. Grafana: hikaricp_connections_pending, pg_stat_activity count against max_connections. Adding pods multiplies pool connections: 30 pods × 20 = 600 connections, which can exhaust Postgres.
  5. Short-term relief: raise maxReplicas, scale nodes, turn on rate limiting at the gateway, and use feature flags to switch off non-critical features such as recommendations or heavy reports.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
HPA max too low / slow scale-up kubectl describe hpa Raise max, tune behavior
Node capacity Pending pods Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter, pre-scale
DB connections exhausted Hikari pending, PG too many clients PgBouncer, read replicas, cache
Synchronous heavy writes Thread dumps blocked on DB Queue via Kafka, process async
Cold caches Redis hit ratio Pre-warm cache before the event

Fix / prevention

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: booking-service }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: booking-service }
  minReplicas: 4
  maxReplicas: 40
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
  • Pre-scale for events you know about (raise minReplicas the day before) instead of relying only on reactive HPA.
  • Serve static and cacheable GET content from CDN and Redis. Accept writes as 202 Accepted, put them on a Kafka topic, and let consumers scale with KEDA based on lag.
  • Load-test at 10–15x with k6 or Gatling before the event. Protect the core with rate limits (Nginx limit_req, gateway RequestRateLimiter).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not just scale the DB? Vertical scaling has a ceiling and takes time. Cache, use read replicas, and queue writes first.
  • Scale on CPU or custom metrics? For I/O-bound services, request rate or Kafka lag (KEDA/Prometheus adapter) tracks load better than CPU.
  • JVM warm-up? New pods start slow because of JIT. Use readiness delays, CDS/AppCDS, or keep a higher baseline.
F58 Data synchronization failed between microservices and database. How will you recover safely?
  1. Stop the bleeding: pause the failing consumer or sync job so it doesn't make the divergence worse.
  2. Find the scope: compare source and target by ID and updated_at/version, with counts and checksums per time window.
  3. Recover from a reliable source: the outbox table, Kafka retention (reset consumer offsets to before the failure), or a CDC replay.
  4. Make sure replay is idempotent (upserts, eventId dedupe, version checks), so reprocessing a window twice is harmless.
  5. Replay into staging first or in small batches, then verify counts and business totals.
  6. Add prevention: an outbox for dual writes, a DLT, a periodic reconciliation job, and alerts on drift.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Service A's DB shows the order as PAID but service B never received the event, or B processed it twice.
  • Check how big the gap is (time window, entity count) and whether writes are still diverging. Stop the bleeding first.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Find the failure point: producer logs (TimeoutException, NotEnoughReplicas), consumer logs, DLT topic.
  2. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server ... --describe --group billing-consumer shows lag and whether the group is stuck on a poison message.
  3. Pause the faulty consumer or feature if it is writing bad data (scale it to 0, or call KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry.getListenerContainer(id).pause()).
  4. Measure the divergence with reconciliation SQL between the source of truth and the downstream store.
  5. Recover with idempotent replay: reset offsets to before the incident, or republish from the outbox table. Never do manual one-off inserts without an audit trail. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --group billing-consumer --topic payments --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-10-05T10:00:00.000 --execute (the group must be inactive).
  6. Run reconciliation again until the difference is 0, then resume consumers.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Dual write (DB commit + Kafka send, one failed) DB row with no event Transactional outbox / Debezium CDC
Non-idempotent consumer Duplicate rows after rebalance Dedupe table / unique key / upsert
Poison message blocking partition Lag stuck on one partition DefaultErrorHandler + DLT
Offset committed before processing Missing records Commit after processing (ack mode)

Fix / prevention (outbox in the same transaction as the business write)

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentService {
    private final PaymentRepository payments;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    @Transactional
    public void markPaid(UUID paymentId) throws JsonProcessingException {
        Payment p = payments.findById(paymentId).orElseThrow();
        p.setStatus(Status.PAID);
        outbox.save(new OutboxEvent(UUID.randomUUID(), "Payment", paymentId.toString(),
                "PaymentPaid", mapper.writeValueAsString(p), Instant.now()));
    }
}

Consumer side, made idempotent:

INSERT INTO processed_event(event_id, processed_at) VALUES (:eventId, now())
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING;  -- 0 rows affected => already processed, skip

Debezium (or a poller with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) publishes outbox rows. Schedule a nightly reconciliation job so drift is caught early.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not a distributed transaction (2PC/XA)? Kafka and most microservice stacks don't support it well, and it couples availability. Use outbox plus Saga.
  • Kafka transactions solve it? Only for Kafka-to-Kafka exactly-once. They don't make a DB commit and a Kafka send atomic.
  • How do you replay safely? Idempotent consumers keyed by event ID, so a replay can't create duplicates.
F59 A service continuously retries failed requests and creates cascading failure. How will you stop it?

This is a retry storm. Retries multiply load on a service that's already struggling.

  1. Immediate fix: open the circuit or disable retries with a config or feature flag, and scale or rate limit the victim service.
  2. Limit retries to 2–3 with exponential backoff and jitter, and only for idempotent requests on transient errors (503, timeouts). Never retry 4xx.
  3. Retry at one layer only, not in the gateway, client, and Kafka all at once (3×3×3 = 27x).
  4. Put a circuit breaker in front of retries (Resilience4j order: Retry wraps CircuitBreaker), so an open circuit stops calls.
  5. Respect Retry-After and set a timeout budget per request.
resilience4j.retry.instances.gis:
  maxAttempts: 3
  waitDuration: 200ms
  enableExponentialBackoff: true
  enableRandomizedWait: true

Symptoms & first checks

  • Downstream service is slow or down, and upstream request rate to it is multiplied: 3 layers × 3 retries = 27x load. Thread pools are exhausted and timeouts spread across services.
  • Grafana shows the downstream RPS far above user RPS and http_client_requests_seconds_count{outcome="SERVER_ERROR"} spiking.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Stop the bleeding: switch off the caller feature with a flag, set retry max-attempts to 1 through config (Spring Cloud Config refresh or a ConfigMap plus rollout), or rate-limit at the gateway or mesh.
  2. Give the failing service room to recover: scale it, shed load, and clear any backed-up queue.
  3. Thread dump the callers (jcmd <pid> Thread.print). Threads stuck in SocketInputStream.read mean there are no read timeouts.
  4. Map every layer that retries (client lib, Feign, Istio VirtualService retries, Nginx proxy_next_upstream, Kafka consumer) and keep retries at one layer only.
  5. Check whether non-idempotent POSTs are being retried, which creates duplicate side effects.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No timeouts Threads blocked on socket read Connect/read timeouts on every client
Retries at many layers Config audit (app + mesh + Nginx) Retry at one layer only
Immediate retries, no backoff Retry timestamps in logs Exponential backoff + jitter
No circuit breaker Calls continue to dead service Resilience4j CB + fallback
One slow dependency consumes all threads Tomcat busy threads = max Bulkhead per dependency

Fix / prevention

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      parkingClient:
        sliding-window-size: 50
        failure-rate-threshold: 50
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 60
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 5
  retry:
    instances:
      parkingClient:
        max-attempts: 3
        wait-duration: 200ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
        enable-randomized-wait: true
        randomized-wait-factor: 0.5
        retry-exceptions: [java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException]
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      parkingClient: { max-concurrent-calls: 20, max-wait-duration: 50ms }
@Retry(name = "parkingClient")
@CircuitBreaker(name = "parkingClient", fallbackMethod = "cachedAvailability")
@Bulkhead(name = "parkingClient")
public Availability availability(String zoneId) {
    return restClient.get().uri("/zones/{id}/availability", zoneId)
            .retrieve().body(Availability.class);
}

private Availability cachedAvailability(String zoneId, Throwable t) {
    return cache.getOrDefault(zoneId, Availability.unknown(zoneId));
}

With the default aspect order, Retry wraps the CircuitBreaker, so an open circuit fails fast and a retry does not hit the dead service. Set timeouts on the client too, e.g. SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory#setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) and setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)). Add a retry budget: retries should be at most about 10% of requests, so a system-wide failure never multiplies load.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why jitter? Without it, all clients retry at the same moments (thundering herd) and knock the recovering service down again.
  • Which errors should not be retried? 4xx errors, validation failures, and non-idempotent calls unless they carry an idempotency key.
  • Circuit breaker vs bulkhead? The breaker stops calls to a failing dependency. The bulkhead stops one dependency from taking every thread.
F60 Distributed tracing is missing for some requests. How will you debug cross-service issues?
  1. Check sampling first: management.tracing.sampling.probability below 1.0 drops traces by design. Use tail sampling in the OTel Collector to keep errors and slow requests.
  2. Find where propagation breaks. Use the Spring-managed RestClient.Builder/WebClient.Builder/RestTemplateBuilder (a new RestTemplate() isn't instrumented).
  3. Async code: @Async, CompletableFuture, and custom executors lose context unless you wrap them with ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator or context-propagation.
  4. Kafka: enable spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled=true and spring.kafka.listener.observation-enabled=true.
  5. Proxies or gateways stripping the traceparent header. Legacy services using B3: align management.tracing.propagation.type.
  6. In the meantime, correlate by a correlation ID in logs, timestamps, and gateway access logs.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Tempo, Jaeger or Zipkin shows broken traces: the gateway span exists but downstream spans start a new traceId, or some requests have no trace at all.
  • Check whether this is sampling (by design) or propagation loss (a bug). Compare the traceId in the MDC log fields across services.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Check management.tracing.sampling.probability. The default 0.1 drops 90% of traces. For debugging, raise it temporarily or use tail-based sampling in the OTel Collector.
  2. Check the propagation format: W3C traceparent vs B3. A gateway sending B3 to a service that expects W3C breaks the chain.
  3. Log the incoming headers at Nginx/ingress ($http_traceparent) and at the service with a debug filter to see where the header disappears.
  4. Look for uninstrumented clients: new RestTemplate() instead of RestTemplateBuilder, a manually built WebClient, or a raw HttpClient. These skip the Micrometer Observation instrumentation.
  5. Async hops: @Async, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, and custom executors lose ThreadLocal context.
  6. Kafka: observation is off by default in Spring Kafka.
  7. Until tracing is fixed, correlate with an X-Correlation-Id in the MDC and query logs: Loki {namespace="smartcity"} | json | correlationId="c-123".

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Low sampling Config value Raise / tail sampling
Propagation mismatch (B3 vs W3C) Header dump management.tracing.propagation.type aligned
Client built with new Code search Inject RestClient.Builder/RestTemplateBuilder
Async thread hop Span missing after executor ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator
Kafka not observed No producer/consumer spans Enable observation
Proxy strips headers Nginx/ingress logs Allow/forward trace headers

Fix / prevention

management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0        # temporarily; 0.1-0.2 in steady state
    propagation:
      type: w3c
spring:
  kafka:
    template:
      observation-enabled: true
    listener:
      observation-enabled: true
logging:
  pattern:
    level: "%5p [${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"
@Configuration
class AsyncConfig {
    @Bean
    ThreadPoolTaskExecutor appExecutor() {
        var ex = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        ex.setCorePoolSize(8);
        ex.setTaskDecorator(new ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator()); // Spring 6.1+
        ex.initialize();
        return ex;
    }
}

@Service
class NotificationClient {
    private final RestClient client;
    NotificationClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {          // auto-instrumented builder
        this.client = builder.baseUrl("http://notification-service").build();
    }
}

Likely follow-ups:

  • Sleuth in Boot 3? It was replaced by Micrometer Tracing with a Brave or OpenTelemetry bridge.
  • Head vs tail sampling? Head sampling decides at the start of the request, which is cheap. Tail sampling decides after the request finishes, so it can keep every error or slow trace, at the cost of collector memory.
  • Does tracing help with Kafka lag? Yes. Producer and consumer spans show how long a message waited in the topic.
F61 Production is down and users cannot login. What will be your immediate action plan?
  1. Declare an incident, start a war room, set the severity, and post a status update to stakeholders. Then post updates every 15–30 minutes.
  2. Find the scope: all users or some, which app, since when, and whether it matches a recent deploy or config or cert change.
  3. Check the login path from end to end: gateway or ingress → auth service (Keycloak or our auth) → DB or LDAP → Redis sessions. Use kubectl get pods, kubectl logs, and the dashboards.
  4. Common causes: expired cert or JWKS key rotation, DB connection pool exhausted, Redis down, a bad secret or config, or a clock skew breaking JWT exp/nbf.
  5. Mitigate first: roll back (kubectl rollout undo), restart, scale, or fail over. Find the root cause after service is restored.
  6. Verify recovery with a synthetic login, then write a blameless postmortem with action items.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Login returns 5xx, 401 for valid users, a redirect loop, or a timeout. Check whether this affects all users or some, and web, mobile or both.
  • First 5 minutes: declare a SEV-1, name an incident commander, open a war-room channel, and post a status page note saying "We're investigating login failures".

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. What changed? Recent deploys (kubectl rollout history deploy/auth-service), config or secret changes, IdP (Keycloak/Cognito) changes, cert renewals, DB migrations. A recent change is the most likely cause, so roll it back first (kubectl rollout undo deploy/auth-service).
  2. Path check: DNS → ALB/Nginx → gateway → auth-service → Redis (sessions/tokens) → PostgreSQL (users) → IdP. Run curl -v https://portal/api/auth/login from outside and inside the cluster.
  3. kubectl get pods -l app=auth-service, kubectl describe pod (CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled), kubectl logs --previous.
  4. Dependencies: redis-cli -h ... ping, psql -c 'select 1', a pg_stat_activity connection count. IdP: is the JWKS endpoint reachable? Did the signing key rotate (kid mismatch, which gives 401 for everyone)?
  5. TLS: openssl s_client -connect idp.example:443 | openssl x509 -noout -dates.
  6. Clock skew: a node clock drift of a few minutes makes JWTs fail nbf/exp checks. Run timedatectl and check the chrony status.
  7. Keep the status page updated every 15–30 minutes, even when there is no news.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Bad deploy/config Timeline matches rollout rollout undo
Redis/session store down Connection errors in logs Failover / restart; fallback to stateless JWT
DB connection exhaustion Hikari timeout, PG too many clients Kill idle sessions, scale pool sensibly
IdP key rotation / JWKS cache 401 invalid signature, kid unknown Refresh JWKS cache, restart pods
Expired cert openssl dates Renew (see F67)
Clock skew timedatectl Fix NTP; allow small clock skew

Fix / prevention

  • Synthetic login probe every minute (blackbox exporter or a k6 cron) that pages on failure.
  • Canary deploys for auth-service, and alerts on login success rate (rate(login_success_total[5m]) / rate(login_attempt_total[5m]) < 0.9).
  • After the incident, hold a blameless postmortem: timeline, impact (users and minutes), root cause, what went well and badly, and action items with owners and dates.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Fix first or find the root cause first? Restore service first (rollback, failover). Find the root cause afterwards from logs and metrics you kept.
  • Who communicates? The incident commander or comms lead. Engineers keep working on the problem.
  • How do you avoid a single point of failure in auth? Run multiple replicas across AZs, use HA Redis, cache JWKS, and validate JWTs locally.
F62 After deployment users report major issue. How will you decide rollback or hotfix?
  1. Assess impact quickly: severity, number of users, data corruption risk, and whether it's getting worse.
  2. Default to rollback if the impact is high and rollback is safe. It's the fastest known-good state (kubectl rollout undo deployment/x, Helm rollback, or flipping the feature flag off).
  3. Check what blocks rollback: irreversible DB migrations (Flyway changes without backward compatibility), events already published in a new schema, or external contracts. This is why we use expand/contract migrations.
  4. Choose a hotfix when the fix is small, well understood, quick to test, and rollback would cause more harm.
  5. Either way: communicate, verify with metrics and a smoke test, then do an RCA and add a test or canary gate so it doesn't happen again.

Symptoms & first checks

  • Error rate or latency jumps right after the release, or there is a functional bug (wrong fare calculation, missing data).
  • Confirm the link to the release: does the metric change line up with the rollout time? Is the issue only on new-version pods (filter by the version label)?

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Measure the impact: users affected, revenue or safety impact, and whether data is being corrupted.
  2. Ask the key question: can we roll back safely? Check DB migrations (was a column dropped or renamed?), message formats published to Kafka, and external side effects.
  3. Decision rule:
    • Rollback is safe and the impact is high: roll back now, then investigate. kubectl rollout undo deployment/fare-service (or --to-revision=N), or switch blue/green traffic back, or abort the canary (kubectl argo rollouts abort fare-service).
    • Rollback is unsafe (irreversible migration, new data written in the new format): roll forward with a minimal hotfix through the fast-track pipeline. Tests still run.
    • Issue sits behind a feature flag: turn the flag off. This is the fastest and lowest-risk fix.
  4. Verify recovery with metrics, not opinion: error rate back to baseline, synthetic checks green.
  5. If bad data was written, fix it with a data-repair script after the code is fixed.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Code bug Errors only on new pods Rollback / flag off
Config/env mismatch Diff ConfigMap/secrets Revert config
Breaking DB migration Flyway history, errors on old pods Expand-contract migrations
API contract break Consumer 4xx Versioned APIs, contract tests

Fix / prevention

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: { name: fare-service }
spec:
  replicas: 6
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: fare-service }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: fare-service }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: registry/fare-service:1.8.0
  • Use expand-contract migrations: add the column (nullable) → deploy code that writes to both → backfill → switch reads → drop the old column in a later release. Every step can then be rolled back.
  • Put new behaviour behind flags (Unleash/FF4J), and attach automated analysis (Prometheus error rate) to canary steps so a bad release aborts automatically.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Default bias? Roll back. It's a known-good state. A hotfix under pressure risks a second incident.
  • Rollback with Flyway? Flyway Community has no automatic undo. Make migrations backward-compatible rather than relying on down scripts.
  • Who decides? The incident commander, using impact data together with the service owner. Pre-agree rollback criteria in the release checklist.
F63 Logs are huge and issue is not reproducible locally. How will you debug production issue?
  1. Narrow it down: get the exact time window, user, and request ID, then filter in Kibana or Loki by traceId, service, and level instead of using grep.
  2. Open the trace for a failing request to see which service or span errored.
  3. Compare failing and successful requests: payload, tenant, data volume, headers, pod or node.
  4. Change log levels at runtime without a redeploy: POST /actuator/loggers/com.trinity.incident {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"} for a short window.
  5. Inspect the JVM live: thread dump, heap histogram (jcmd GC.class_histogram), or Arthas watch/trace on a method.
  6. Reproduce in staging with production-like data (masked) and similar load. Add targeted logs or metrics if needed.

Symptoms & first checks

  • A user or ticket reports an error (e.g. "challan payment failed at 10:42"), but the logs hold GBs per hour across 20+ pods, so grepping them is no use.
  • First get the facts: the exact time window, the user/tenant ID, the request ID or traceId from the error response or UI, the endpoint, and the build version deployed then.
  • Check whether it is one user, one pod, one zone or everyone. That tells you if the cause is data-specific or infra-specific.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Correlate, don't grep. Every request carries a traceId (Micrometer Tracing / OpenTelemetry puts it into the MDC). In Kibana use traceId:"6f1c..." AND level:ERROR. In Loki use {app="payment-svc"} |= "6f1c..." | json | level="ERROR". This follows one request across gateway → service → Kafka consumer.
  2. Narrow the window: filter by @timestamp ±2 min, kubernetes.pod_name, and userId (put into the MDC by a filter).
  3. Look at the trace in Jaeger/Tempo. The slow or failed span shows which hop broke (DB, Redis, downstream HTTP).
  4. Compare to a good request from the same endpoint. What differs: payload, tenant, feature flag, pod version?
  5. Check the pod: kubectl logs <pod> --previous (if it restarted), kubectl describe pod (OOMKilled, probe failures), kubectl top pod.
  6. Pull the failing data with a read-only replica query (the exact record, nulls, encoding, size) and replay it locally or in staging with the same config profile.
  7. If you still lack data, raise the log level for one logger at runtime, with no redeploy: POST /actuator/loggers/com.trinity.payment {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}. Revert it afterwards.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Data-specific edge case (null, unicode, huge payload) Fetch the record; replay it in staging Validation + unit test for the case
Environment/config drift Diff ConfigMap/Secret vs staging; /actuator/env GitOps-managed config
Concurrency/race seen only at prod load Several traceIds hit the same entity in the same ms Optimistic locking, idempotency key
One bad pod/node Errors cluster on one pod_name Cordon/drain the node, restart the pod

Fix / prevention: use structured JSON logs that carry the traceId, and log one line per request at INFO, not dumps of every payload.

logging:
  pattern:
    level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"
management:
  tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,loggers,prometheus

Return the traceId in the error response body (ProblemDetail) so support can quote it.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How does the traceId reach the Kafka consumer? Micrometer Observation propagates it through record headers (traceparent) when you enable observation-enabled on the KafkaTemplate/listener container.
  • Logs cost too much? Keep ERROR/WARN in full, sample INFO, put retention tiers in place (hot 7d, cold 30d), and stop logging payloads.
  • Can you debug a live JVM? Yes, with care. Use JFR or async-profiler, or Arthas watch/trace on one pod pulled out of the Service. Never use a blocking remote debugger in prod.
F64 One API fails only during peak traffic hours. How will you identify bottleneck?
  1. Correlate the error spike with load: RPS, p95/p99, 5xx vs timeouts in Grafana for that endpoint only.
  2. Check pool saturation: Hikari connections.pending/timeout, Tomcat threads.busy vs max, HTTP client pool, Redis connections.
  3. Database: pg_stat_activity for waiting or locked queries, slow query log, EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the endpoint's query under real data volume, and lock contention.
  4. JVM: GC pauses (jvm_gc_pause), heap, CPU throttling. Take thread dumps at peak.
  5. Downstream dependencies: trace spans show whether an external call slows down or hits rate limits.
  6. Reproduce with a k6/Gatling test at peak RPS, fix the constraint (index, pool size, cache, async), and retest.

Symptoms & first checks

  • /api/v1/violations/search returns 503/504 or times out between 9–11 AM. It works fine off-peak.
  • Check whether errors come from the ALB/Nginx (504 = upstream timeout, 502 = connection reset) or from the app (500 with a stack trace). Check whether p99 latency rises before the errors start. That points to saturation, not a bug.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Grafana RED metrics for that endpoint: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le)(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{uri="/api/v1/violations/search"}[5m]))) plotted against request rate.
  2. USE metrics per resource for the same window:
    • Tomcat threads: tomcat_threads_busy_threads vs max (200 default)
    • Hikari: hikaricp_connections_pending, hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds; pending > 0 means pool starvation
    • JVM: GC pause jvm_gc_pause_seconds, CPU process_cpu_usage, plus CPU throttling container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total
    • Downstream: Redis latency, the client timeout of the external API
  3. DB side: SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, now()-query_start, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY 5 DESC; Use pg_stat_statements to find the top queries by total_exec_time, and look for lock waits.
  4. Thread dump during the peak: kubectl exec <pod> -- jcmd 1 Thread.print. If many threads are stuck in HikariPool.getConnection or a socket read, you have found the blocking hop.
  5. HPA/K8s: kubectl get hpa, kubectl top pods. Did it scale? Were pods throttled or restarted by a liveness probe under load?
  6. Reproduce with k6/Gatling in staging at peak RPS, then change one variable at a time.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Hikari pool exhausted pending > 0, threads waiting in getConnection Fix slow query; size pool vs PG max_connections
Slow query / missing index at volume EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows Seq Scan Add index, paginate (keyset)
Slow downstream with no timeout Threads blocked on socket read Timeouts + Resilience4j circuit breaker/bulkhead
CPU throttling / no autoscale cfs_throttled high, HPA at max Raise CPU limit, tune HPA, add replicas
Cache stampede on expiry Redis misses spike, DB QPS spikes TTL jitter, request coalescing

Fix / prevention

spring:
  datasource.hikari:
    maximum-pool-size: 20
    connection-timeout: 3000
  mvc.async.request-timeout: 5s
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker.instances.rtoApi:
    sliding-window-size: 50
    failure-rate-threshold: 50
    slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
  bulkhead.instances.rtoApi.max-concurrent-calls: 30

Add rate limiting at the gateway, load-test before festival/peak seasons, and alert on p99 and pool saturation, not only on 5xx.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not just increase the pool size? PG pays a process per connection. Pods × pool must stay below max_connections, so fix the slow query first and use PgBouncer if you need more.
  • 504 vs 502? 504: the proxy waited past its timeout. 502: the upstream closed or reset the connection (pod killed, keep-alive mismatch).
  • Do virtual threads help? For I/O-bound waits, yes (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true on Java 21). They don't fix a DB pool bottleneck.
F65 Application works fine from Postman but frontend users face errors. What will you check?
  1. Browser DevTools first: the Console and Network tabs show the actual status and error.
  2. CORS: Postman ignores CORS but browsers enforce it. Check the preflight OPTIONS response, Access-Control-Allow-Origin/-Headers, and credentials settings. Configure CorsConfigurationSource in Spring Security.
  3. Auth differences: the token is missing or expired in the browser, cookies are blocked (SameSite, Secure), or there's a CSRF token for cookie-based sessions.
  4. Request differences: Content-Type, payload shape, encoding, and header size.
  5. Environment: the frontend points at a different base URL, a proxy or CDN caches old responses, or there's mixed content on HTTP vs HTTPS.
  6. Client-side: a JS parsing error, timeout settings, or behavior specific to one browser.

Symptoms & first checks

  • The same endpoint returns 200 in Postman, but the browser shows "Network Error", a status of (failed), 401, 403 or a blank page.
  • Postman is not a browser. It skips CORS, preflight, cookie SameSite rules, mixed content and CSP. So suspect the browser's rules first.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. DevTools → Network tab: find the failing request. Is there an OPTIONS preflight before it? What status does it return, and which response headers? Read the Console for a "blocked by CORS policy" message.
  2. Reproduce the preflight with curl:
    curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.city.gov.in/api/v1/incidents \
  -H "Origin: https://portal.city.gov.in" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type"
    Look for Access-Control-Allow-Origin (it must equal the exact origin when credentials are sent, never *), plus Allow-Methods, Allow-Headers and Allow-Credentials: true.
  3. Compare the requests. Right-click → "Copy as cURL" and diff it with the Postman request: headers, Content-Type, the token, cookies, and the base URL (staging vs prod).
  4. Auth: was the JWT expired or refreshed, or is it missing because the cookie has SameSite=Lax on a cross-site call? Is Spring Security blocking OPTIONS (401 on the preflight)? Is CSRF enabled for cookie auth?
  5. Proxy layer: Nginx/ALB may strip headers (Authorization, underscores in header names), add duplicate CORS headers (app + Nginx), or set a body-size limit (413).
  6. Other browser-only issues: mixed content (HTTPS page calling HTTP), CSP connect-src, a stale cached JS bundle pointing at an old API, a corporate proxy or ad blocker.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
CORS not configured / wrong origin Console CORS error; preflight lacks ACAO CorsConfigurationSource in Spring Security
Preflight blocked by security (401/403) OPTIONS returns 401 http.cors(withDefaults()) so preflight is allowed
Duplicate ACAO header (Nginx + app) Response shows two values Configure CORS in one place only
Cookie not sent (SameSite/Secure) No Cookie header in request SameSite=None; Secure, or same-site domain
Frontend env points to wrong API Request URL in Network tab Fix build-time env, cache-bust bundle

Fix / prevention

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
               .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) // stateless JWT API
               .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
               .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
               .build();
}

@Bean
CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
    var cfg = new CorsConfiguration();
    cfg.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://portal.city.gov.in"));
    cfg.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
    cfg.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type"));
    cfg.setAllowCredentials(true);
    cfg.setMaxAge(3600L);
    var src = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
    src.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", cfg);
    return src;
}

Add an end-to-end test (Playwright/Cypress) against staging that runs in a real browser.

Likely follow-ups:

  • When does a preflight happen? For non-simple requests: methods other than GET/HEAD/POST, custom headers such as Authorization, or a Content-Type of application/json.
  • Is CORS a security control for the server? No. The browser enforces it to protect users. Server-side auth still applies.
  • Is allowedOrigins("*") with credentials allowed? No. The spec rejects it. Use explicit origins or allowedOriginPatterns.
F66 Monitoring alerts show high memory usage but application still runs. How will you analyze future risk?
  1. Separate JVM heap from container memory. Look at jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} after GC compared with pod RSS. Off-heap (metaspace, threads, direct buffers) can get the pod OOMKilled even when heap looks fine.
  2. Watch the trend: if post-GC heap stays flat, it's normal caching. If it keeps rising, it's a leak.
  3. Check GC behavior: rising GC time or frequency and longer pauses show the risk is getting worse.
  4. Take evidence: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram twice to compare, a heap dump (GC.heap_dump) analyzed in Eclipse MAT, and Native Memory Tracking for off-heap.
  5. Check config: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75, container limits, and unbounded caches or collections.
  6. Set alerts on post-GC heap > 80% and on growth rate, and plan the fix before it turns into an OOM.

Symptoms & first checks

  • An alert reads "pod memory 88% of limit". There are no errors and latency looks normal.
  • First work out which memory is high. Container RSS/working set (what the OOM killer acts on), JVM heap used, or non-heap (metaspace, direct buffers, thread stacks)? High heap use on its own is normal for the JVM. The real question is whether the post-GC baseline is trending up.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Grafana over 7–14 days, not 1 hour:
    • jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"} after each GC (the "floor" of the saw-tooth). A rising floor means a leak. A flat floor means a healthy, fully used heap.
    • container_memory_working_set_bytes vs kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"}.
    • jvm_gc_pause_seconds_sum rate and GC frequency. Rising GC time is the early warning before OOM.
    • Also jvm_buffer_memory_used_bytes{id="direct"} (Netty/Kafka/NIO), jvm_threads_live_threads and metaspace.
  2. Heap histogram trend: jcmd 1 GC.class_histogram | head -30, taken now and again 6 hours later. If one class keeps growing (HashMap$Node, a cache entry type, byte[]), that is your suspect.
  3. Native memory: start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then jcmd 1 VM.native_memory summary.diff against a baseline.
  4. JFR: jcmd 1 JFR.start duration=30m filename=/tmp/app.jfr settings=profile. In JMC, look at allocation hot spots and Old Object Sample.
  5. If you see a leak, take a heap dump from a pod drained out of the Service: jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /tmp/h.hprof. Analyse it with Eclipse MAT (Leak Suspects, dominator tree).
  6. Project the trend: at the current growth slope, when does the working set reach the limit? Use Prometheus predict_linear(container_memory_working_set_bytes[6h], 3600*24) > limit.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Unbounded cache/static map Histogram growth of entry class; MAT dominator Caffeine with maximumSize + TTL; Redis
Heap sized too close to container limit -Xmx ≈ limit; RSS > limit risk MaxRAMPercentage=70–75
Direct/native memory leak NMT diff; direct buffer metric rises Close streams; cap MaxDirectMemorySize
ThreadLocal / listener not removed MAT GC roots → thread remove() in finally
Normal: heap fills before GC Post-GC floor flat Tune the alert to post-GC usage

Fix / prevention

env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: >-
      -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
      -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
resources:
  requests: { memory: "1Gi" }
  limits:   { memory: "1Gi" }
Cache<String, Junction> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(10_000).expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
        .recordStats().build();

Alert on the predict_linear trend and on GC time above 10%, not on raw heap %. Run a soak test (8–24h) before release.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Pod OOMKilled but no Java OutOfMemoryError? The container limit was hit by heap plus non-heap (native, threads, metaspace). That is a kernel kill (exit 137), so check kubectl describe pod.
  • Why requests = limits for memory? It gives a Guaranteed QoS class and avoids eviction under node pressure.
  • G1 vs ZGC? G1 is the default and fine for most apps. Generational ZGC (Java 21) suits large heaps that need sub-ms pauses.
F67 SSL certificate expired in production. What impact can happen and how will you resolve urgently?

Impact: browsers block users, mobile apps and API clients fail with PKIX path/SSLHandshakeException, service-to-service mTLS breaks, and webhooks and partner integrations stop.

  1. Confirm: openssl s_client -connect api.city.gov:443 -servername api.city.gov | openssl x509 -noout -dates.
  2. Find where TLS terminates: LB, ingress, gateway, or the app keystore.
  3. Renew or reissue (cert-manager or Let's Encrypt, or the CA), then update the K8s TLS secret: kubectl create secret tls api-tls --cert=... --key=... --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -.
  4. Reload or restart the components that don't hot-reload certificates, and verify the full chain including intermediates.
  5. Prevent recurrence: cert-manager auto-renewal, and an expiry alert at 30 and 7 days (blackbox exporter probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry).

Symptoms & first checks

  • Browsers show NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID. The mobile app fails every call, worst of all with cert pinning. Partner webhooks (payment gateway, SMS) start failing. Java service-to-service calls throw SSLHandshakeException: PKIX path building failed / CertificateExpiredException.
  • Impact: full outage for users, lost transactions, failed IoT/device uploads (cameras, sensors), broken trust and SLA penalties, and security teams flagging it.
  • First check which endpoint and which cert: public domain, wildcard, internal mTLS, Kafka broker or DB TLS?

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Confirm expiry and the chain:
    echo | openssl s_client -connect api.city.gov.in:443 -servername api.city.gov.in 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
    notAfter in the past confirms it. Also check the intermediate chain (-showcerts).
  2. Find where TLS terminates: ALB (ACM), Nginx (ssl_certificate path), K8s Ingress (TLS Secret) or the app itself (keystore).
  3. If cert-manager is in use: kubectl get certificate -A, then kubectl describe certificate api-tls -n prod and kubectl get certificaterequest,order,challenge -n prod. Typical reasons it failed: an HTTP-01 challenge blocked by an Ingress rule or WAF, DNS-01 credentials expired, or a Let's Encrypt rate limit. Force renewal with cmctl renew api-tls -n prod.
  4. Manual urgent renewal if there is no automation: reissue from the CA (or ACME certbot certonly) and deploy it:
    • Nginx: replace the fullchain + key, then nginx -t && nginx -s reload (zero downtime).
    • ALB: import or request in ACM and update the listener certificate.
    • K8s: kubectl create secret tls api-tls --cert=fullchain.pem --key=key.pem -n prod --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -.
    • Java keystore/truststore: update it and roll out a restart, or use Spring Boot SSL bundle hot reload.
  5. Verify again with openssl s_client, an SSL Labs scan, and the mobile app plus partner callbacks. Ask partners to retry failed webhooks.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
No auto-renewal / manual cert No cert-manager/ACM managed cert Automate (ACM, cert-manager)
cert-manager challenge failing kubectl describe challenge errors Fix ingress path/DNS creds
Renewed but not deployed/reloaded File new, served cert old Reload Nginx / restart pods
Expired intermediate / wrong chain -showcerts shows broken chain Serve full chain
Pinned cert in mobile app Only app fails after rotation Pin the public key/CA, keep backup pins

Fix / prevention

spring:
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        server:
          reload-on-update: true
          keystore:
            certificate: file:/etc/tls/tls.crt
            private-key: file:/etc/tls/tls.key
server:
  ssl:
    bundle: server

Set an alert with blackbox_exporter: probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry - time() < 86400 * 21. Keep a cert inventory with owners, and renew at 30 days (Let's Encrypt certs last 90 days).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Can you bypass it temporarily in Java clients? Never disable verification in prod. Fix the cert, or import the right CA into the truststore.
  • Why -servername? SNI. Without it the server may return its default cert, not the one for your domain.
  • Who is impacted after the fix? Clients that cached a failed state, and partners whose retry windows have expired. Run a reconciliation for missed webhooks.
F68 A batch job failed in middle after processing lakhs of records. How will you restart safely without duplicates?
  1. Use Spring Batch's restartability. JobRepository stores the ExecutionContext and commit count per chunk, so restarting the same JobInstance (same identifying parameters) resumes from the last committed chunk.
  2. Use chunk-oriented processing (e.g. 500 per chunk). Each chunk's writes and checkpoint commit in one transaction.
  3. Use readers that save their position (JdbcPagingItemReader with a sort key, saveState=true), or a processed flag or status column.
  4. Make writers idempotent (upsert or ON CONFLICT), so a partially written chunk is safe to redo.
  5. Use faultTolerant().skip(...).skipLimit(...) and retry for bad records, and log skipped items.
  6. Fix the root cause, restart with JobOperator.restart(executionId), then reconcile counts.

Symptoms & first checks

  • The nightly challanSettlementJob failed at about 6.2 lakh of 10 lakh records (DB failover, pod OOMKilled, or a bad record).
  • Check BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION / BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION: status, EXIT_MESSAGE, READ_COUNT, WRITE_COUNT, COMMIT_COUNT, ROLLBACK_COUNT. If the pod was killed, the status may still be STARTED. Spring Batch then refuses to restart (JobExecutionAlreadyRunningException).

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Find the failure point:
    SELECT step_name, status, read_count, write_count, commit_count, exit_message
FROM batch_step_execution WHERE job_execution_id = :id;
SELECT short_context FROM batch_step_execution_context WHERE step_execution_id = :sid;
    The step ExecutionContext holds the reader checkpoint (e.g. reader.start.after / read.count).
  2. Fix the root cause first: a bad data row (add a skip policy), a DB outage, or memory.
  3. If the execution is stuck in STARTED (the process died), mark it failed. Only do this after confirming no instance is running:
    UPDATE batch_step_execution SET status='FAILED', exit_code='FAILED', end_time=now()
 WHERE job_execution_id=:id AND status='STARTED';
UPDATE batch_job_execution SET status='FAILED', exit_code='FAILED', end_time=now()
 WHERE job_execution_id=:id;
  4. Restart the same JobInstance: either use the same identifying JobParameters (e.g. runDate=2026-10-04) or call jobOperator.restart(executionId). The JobRepository resumes the failed step from the last committed chunk. Completed steps are skipped.
  5. Verify with counts and a duplicate check: SELECT challan_id, count(*) FROM settlement GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1;.

Why there are no duplicates: in a chunk-oriented step, reading, processing and writing N items plus updating the ExecutionContext all commit in one transaction. A chunk that was in flight when the job crashed rolls back completely. Chunks that committed are recorded in the checkpoint, so they are never re-read. Side effects outside the transaction (Kafka sends, REST calls, files) can still repeat. That is why the writer must also be idempotent.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Poison record Exception in exit_message with item data faultTolerant().skip(...).skipLimit(n) + skip listener
Pod killed / OOM Status STARTED, kubectl describe OOMKilled Smaller chunk, paging reader, more memory
Non-restartable reader (saveState=false) Context has no reader keys Use paging reader with unique sort key
Non-idempotent writer Duplicates after restart Upsert / unique constraint

Fix / prevention (Spring Batch 5)

@Bean
Step settleStep(JobRepository repo, PlatformTransactionManager tx, DataSource ds) {
    return new StepBuilder("settleStep", repo)
            .<Challan, Settlement>chunk(1000, tx)
            .reader(reader(ds)).processor(this::toSettlement).writer(writer(ds))
            .faultTolerant().skip(DataIntegrityViolationException.class).skipLimit(50)
            .build();
}

@Bean
JdbcPagingItemReader<Challan> reader(DataSource ds) {
    return new JdbcPagingItemReaderBuilder<Challan>()
            .name("challanReader")                 // key prefix in ExecutionContext
            .dataSource(ds).pageSize(1000)
            .selectClause("SELECT id, amount, paid_at")
            .fromClause("FROM challan")
            .whereClause("WHERE paid_at::date = :runDate")
            .parameterValues(Map.of("runDate", LocalDate.parse("2026-10-04")))
            .sortKeys(Map.of("id", Order.ASCENDING))  // unique key -> exact resume
            .rowMapper(new DataClassRowMapper<>(Challan.class))
            .build();
}

@Bean
JdbcBatchItemWriter<Settlement> writer(DataSource ds) {
    return new JdbcBatchItemWriterBuilder<Settlement>()
            .dataSource(ds).beanMapped()
            .sql("""
                 INSERT INTO settlement (challan_id, amount, settled_on)
                 VALUES (:challanId, :amount, :settledOn)
                 ON CONFLICT (challan_id) DO UPDATE
                   SET amount = EXCLUDED.amount, settled_on = EXCLUDED.settled_on
                 """)
            .build();
}

Use a UNIQUE (challan_id) constraint as the last line of defence. In a real job, inject runDate with @StepScope and @Value("#{jobParameters['runDate']}"). Processed-flag alternative: the reader selects WHERE processed = false and the writer sets processed = true in the same transaction. In that case set saveState(false), because the result set shrinks and an offset checkpoint would skip rows.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Restart vs a new run? Same identifying params give a restart of the same JobInstance. New params give a fresh instance that starts from zero, so don't do that for a half-done day.
  • How do you handle a COMPLETED job that must re-run? It cannot be restarted. Use a new identifying param (e.g. rerun=2) and rely on idempotent upserts.
  • Is chunk size a trade-off? Larger chunks give better throughput but bigger rollbacks and more memory. 500–2000 is typical. Tune it with metrics.
F69 Server restarted automatically at midnight. How will you investigate root cause?
  1. Find out what restarted: the pod, the container, or the node. kubectl describe pod → Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled / Error, Exit Code (137 = SIGKILL/OOM, 143 = SIGTERM).
  2. kubectl logs <pod> --previous for the last lines before the crash, and kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp.
  3. Check whether it's scheduled: cron jobs, a midnight batch or report causing a memory spike, log rotation, backups, a CronJob doing rollout restart, or cluster autoscaler/node upgrade windows.
  4. Liveness probe failures during heavy midnight load can make kubelet kill the container.
  5. VM or bare metal: journalctl -b -1, last reboot, dmesg | grep -i oom, and cloud maintenance events.
  6. Correlate metrics (memory, CPU, GC) around midnight, and enable -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError.

Symptoms & first checks

  • At 00:00–00:05 the app went down and came back by itself. Users of the night-shift control room saw errors.
  • First decide what restarted: the whole VM/node, the JVM process (systemd service), or the K8s pod/container? Each leaves different evidence. Midnight strongly suggests something scheduled.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. VM/OS-level reboot:
    last -x reboot shutdown | head        # reboot timestamps
uptime -s
journalctl --list-boots
journalctl -b -1 -e                   # tail of the PREVIOUS boot: who/what triggered shutdown
journalctl -k -b -1 | grep -iE "oom|killed process|panic|watchdog"
    A clean systemd: Stopping... sequence means an orderly reboot (a command or a patch). An abrupt end with no shutdown logs means a crash, power loss, a hypervisor event or a kernel panic.
  2. Scheduled jobs: crontab -l, sudo crontab -l -u root, ls /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.daily, systemctl list-timers --all. Look in /var/log/unattended-upgrades/ or /var/log/dnf.rpm.log for auto-patching with Automatic-Reboot, and at needrestart.
  3. Process-level restart (VM still up): systemctl status app.service (restart count), journalctl -u app.service --since "23:50" --until "00:15". Check dmesg -T | grep -i oom for the OOM killer (exit 137), and whether Restart=always brought it back.
  4. Kubernetes: kubectl get pods -o wide (RESTARTS), kubectl describe pod <p> → Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled / Error, Exit Code. Then kubectl logs <p> --previous, kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp. Check CronJobs: kubectl get cronjob -A (e.g. a kubectl rollout restart), node maintenance windows (EKS/GKE auto-upgrade), cluster-autoscaler or spot interruption.
  5. Correlate in Grafana for 23:30–00:10: memory, CPU, GC, disk, the liveness probe. A midnight batch, report or log rotation can spike load so the liveness probe fails and the kubelet restarts the container.
  6. Cloud console: AWS EC2 scheduled events, the ASG activity history (instance refresh, health-check replacement), CloudTrail for RebootInstances/StopInstances.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Auto OS patching with reboot unattended-upgrades log, orderly shutdown Controlled maintenance window, rolling
Cron/systemd timer or K8s CronJob restart Timer/cron entry at 00:00 Remove, or make rolling and approved
OOM from midnight batch dmesg/describe OOMKilled Move batch to separate pod, set limits
Liveness probe fails under load Events: "Liveness probe failed" Separate liveness/readiness, longer timeouts
Disk full by logrotate/backup df -h, journal "No space left" Retention, separate volume

Fix / prevention

livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  failureThreshold: 6
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }

Liveness must not depend on the DB or downstream services. Run batches as separate K8s Jobs with their own limits. Add a PodDisruptionBudget, alert on restarts (increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[15m]) > 0), and write an RCA with a change-calendar entry.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Exit code 137 vs 143? 137 = SIGKILL (OOM killer, or a kill after the grace period). 143 = SIGTERM (a graceful stop requested).
  • dmesg is empty after a reboot? The kernel ring buffer resets on boot. Use journalctl -k -b -1 (needs a persistent journal, Storage=persistent).
  • How do you make restarts harmless? At least 2 replicas, graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful), a PDB, and idempotent consumers.
F70 Business team says reports show wrong data in production. How will you validate and fix issue?
  1. Get specifics: which report, filters, expected vs actual values, and since when. Get a sample record.
  2. Recompute the number directly from the source tables with SQL and compare it to the report output at each layer: source DB → ETL/view → API → UI.
  3. Usual causes: time zone or date boundaries (UTC vs IST), duplicate rows from joins, NULL handling, soft-deleted records counted, replica lag, stale cache or materialized view, or a failed or partial ETL run.
  4. Check recent changes: deploys, query changes, or upstream data issues.
  5. Fix the logic, add a test with known data, then backfill or recompute the affected period (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, rerun the job idempotently).
  6. Tell the business which reports were affected and for what dates, and add data quality checks (row counts, totals reconciliation).

Symptoms & first checks

  • An example complaint: "Yesterday's violation count shows 12,430 on the dashboard, but the field team counted about 13,100." Or revenue doesn't match the payment gateway settlement.
  • Get specifics first: which report, filters, date range and timezone, expected vs actual figures, the source of truth they compare against, and when it started. Ask whether all reports are wrong or one, and all wards/tenants or one.

Step-by-step investigation / action plan

  1. Reproduce the number by running the report's exact query (from the logs, the repository code or the BI tool) against prod or a read replica. Is the report displaying wrongly, or is the data itself wrong?
  2. Reconcile against the source layer by layer: raw events (Kafka topic / source table) → staging → aggregate table/materialized view → API → UI. Find the layer where the count first diverges.
    SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS d, count(*), count(DISTINCT violation_id)
FROM violation WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-03' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
    If count ≠ count(DISTINCT), you have duplicates.
  3. Check freshness: when did the ETL/Spring Batch job last succeed (batch_job_execution)? When was the materialized view last refreshed? Is there a Redis cache TTL, read replica lag (now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()), or Kafka consumer lag?
  4. Check recent changes: deployments, query or mapping changes, schema migrations (Flyway history), new master data (ward boundaries, fine slabs).
  5. Use the sample-record approach: pick 5 records the business says are missing or wrong, then trace each one end to end by ID.
  6. Fix, backfill and communicate: correct the logic, recompute the affected period (idempotent re-run), state which reports or dates were affected, and get the business to sign off on the corrected numbers.

Likely root causes

Cause How to confirm Fix
Timezone (UTC vs IST day boundary) Counts shift for 00:00–05:30 IST Store timestamptz, group in Asia/Kolkata
Duplicates (Kafka at-least-once, retries) count ≠ count(DISTINCT) Idempotent consumer, unique key, upsert
Join fan-out Row count rises after JOIN Aggregate before join / EXISTS
Stale data (failed ETL, MV not refreshed, cache) Last success timestamp Alert on job failure; refresh; evict cache
Soft-deleted/cancelled rows included Filter on status/deleted missing Fix WHERE clause, shared view
NULL/rounding issues COUNT(col) vs COUNT(*), double money COALESCE, BigDecimal/numeric

Fix / prevention

// Money and time handled correctly in the report DTO
public record RevenueRow(LocalDate day, BigDecimal amount, long challans) {}

@Query(value = """
        SELECT (paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS day,
               SUM(amount) AS amount, COUNT(DISTINCT challan_id) AS challans
        FROM payment
        WHERE status = 'SUCCESS' AND deleted = false
          AND paid_at >= :from AND paid_at < :to
        GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
        """, nativeQuery = true)
List<RevenueRowView> dailyRevenue(@Param("from") OffsetDateTime from, @Param("to") OffsetDateTime to);

Add automated data-quality checks after each ETL run: row counts vs source, duplicate checks, null checks and a reconciliation total vs the payment gateway. Alert on any mismatch. Keep report SQL in version control with tests on known fixtures, and show a "data as of" timestamp on dashboards.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you fix already-shared wrong reports? Correct the data, regenerate the affected period, then publish a correction note with the impact window and root cause.
  • Report queries slow down the OLTP database? Run them on a read replica or pre-aggregated tables/MVs (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY with a unique index).
  • How do you prevent a recurrence? Reconciliation jobs, contract tests on report queries, and owner sign-off on business definitions ("what counts as a violation").
G

Java Practice Programs

G1 Declare and initialize variables of different data types (int, double, char, boolean).

Declare each primitive with a literal of the matching type and print it.

public class G1 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 25;
        double price = 99.5;
        char grade = 'A';
        boolean active = true;
        System.out.println(age + " " + price + " " + grade + " " + active);
    }
}
// Output: 25 99.5 A true

Approach. Java has exactly 8 primitive types. Each has a fixed size that does not depend on the platform, and each has a matching wrapper class that the compiler boxes and unboxes for you automatically. The program below declares every primitive with the right literal syntax. It then shows the details interviewers like to ask about: char arithmetic, silent integer overflow, the Integer cache, and var type inference.

Type Size Range / precision Default (fields only) Wrapper
byte 8 bit -128 .. 127 0 Byte
short 16 bit -32,768 .. 32,767 0 Short
int 32 bit -2^31 .. 2^31-1 (about ±2.1 billion) 0 Integer
long 64 bit -2^63 .. 2^63-1 (about ±9.2e18) 0L Long
float 32 bit about ±3.4e38, ~7 significant digits 0.0f Float
double 64 bit about ±1.8e308, ~15-16 significant digits 0.0d Double
char 16 bit unsigned '\u0000' .. '￿' (0..65535) '\u0000' Character
boolean JVM-defined true / false false Boolean

Fields and array elements get these defaults. Local variables get no default: if you read one before assigning it, the code does not compile.

public class DataTypesDemo {

    // Fields get default values; local variables do not.
    static int defaultInt;
    static double defaultDouble;
    static char defaultChar;
    static boolean defaultBoolean;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        byte    b    = 100;
        short   s    = 30_000;               // underscores improve readability (Java 7+)
        int     i    = 2_000_000_000;
        long    l    = 9_000_000_000L;       // L suffix required: literal exceeds int range
        float   f    = 3.14f;                // f suffix required: 3.14 alone is a double
        double  d    = 3.141592653589793;
        char    c    = 'A';                  // single quotes, 16-bit UTF-16 code unit
        boolean flag = true;

        System.out.println("byte=" + b + ", short=" + s + ", int=" + i + ", long=" + l);
        System.out.println("float=" + f + ", double=" + d);
        System.out.println("char=" + c + ", boolean=" + flag);
        System.out.println("hex=" + 0x1F + ", binary=" + 0b1010 + ", octal=" + 017);

        System.out.println("defaults: " + defaultInt + " " + defaultDouble + " "
                + (int) defaultChar + " " + defaultBoolean);

        // --- char arithmetic ---
        System.out.println(c + 1);            // int promotion -> 66
        System.out.println((char) (c + 1));   // cast back -> B
        char cc = 'A';
        cc++;                                 // ++ and += include an implicit cast
        System.out.println(cc);               // B
        System.out.println('A' + 'B');        // 65 + 66 = 131 (numeric addition!)
        System.out.println("" + 'A' + 'B');   // AB (string concatenation)

        // --- integer overflow is silent ---
        int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        System.out.println(max + 1);          // -2147483648 (wraps around)
        long wrong = 1_000_000 * 1_000_000;   // int * int overflows BEFORE widening
        long right = 1_000_000L * 1_000_000;  // make one operand long
        System.out.println(wrong + " vs " + right);
        try {
            Math.addExact(max, 1);
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("addExact -> " + e.getMessage());
        }

        // --- floating point is binary, not decimal ---
        System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);

        // --- wrappers, autoboxing, Integer cache ---
        Integer boxed = i;                    // autoboxing  (Integer.valueOf(i))
        int unboxed = boxed;                  // unboxing    (boxed.intValue())
        Integer a1 = 127, a2 = 127, b1 = 128, b2 = 128;
        System.out.println((a1 == a2) + " " + (b1 == b2) + " " + b1.equals(b2));

        // --- var (Java 10+): type inferred from the initializer, still static typing ---
        var inferred = 10L;                   // long
        var text = "hello";                   // String
        System.out.println(((Object) inferred).getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + text.length());
        System.out.println(unboxed + Integer.MIN_VALUE);
    }
}
/* Output:
byte=100, short=30000, int=2000000000, long=9000000000
float=3.14, double=3.141592653589793
char=A, boolean=true
hex=31, binary=10, octal=15
defaults: 0 0.0 0 false
66
B
B
131
AB
-2147483648
-727379968 vs 1000000000000
addExact -> integer overflow
0.30000000000000004
true false true
Long 5
-147483648
*/

Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space. Every statement is a constant-time operation.

Edge cases and pitfalls:

  • long x = 1_000_000 * 1_000_000; is still wrong. The multiplication runs in int and overflows before the result is widened to long.
  • byte b = 10; b = b + 1; does not compile, because b + 1 is an int. b += 1 does compile, because compound assignment includes an implicit cast.
  • == on wrapper objects compares references. Integer caches -128..127, so 127 == 127 is true but 128 == 128 is usually false. Always compare wrappers with equals.
  • Unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException.
  • var needs an initializer. It is not allowed on fields, and var x = null; is illegal.
  • Use BigDecimal for money, because double cannot represent 0.1 exactly.

Alternative: if you need to detect overflow, use Math.addExact, Math.multiplyExact or Math.toIntExact. If values may exceed long, use BigInteger or BigDecimal.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is Java pass-by-reference for objects? No. Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value that gets copied is the reference.
  • Why is char 16 bits? It stores UTF-16 code units. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (such as emoji) need two chars (a surrogate pair), so use codePointAt for them.
  • Primitive vs wrapper: when to use which? Use primitives for performance and when null is not meaningful. Use wrappers for collections and generics, and when a value can be "absent".
G2 Swap two numbers without using a temporary variable.

Use arithmetic: a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b; (XOR works too and cannot overflow).

public class G2 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 5, b = 10;
        a = a + b;   // 15
        b = a - b;   // 5
        a = a - b;   // 10
        System.out.println("a=" + a + " b=" + b);
    }
}
// Output: a=10 b=5

Time O(1), space O(1).

Approach. There are two classic tricks. The arithmetic trick is a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b;. The XOR trick is a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;. Both rely on being able to recover one value from a combination of the two. Because Java int/long arithmetic wraps around in two's complement, the arithmetic swap still gives the right answer even when a + b overflows. It does not work for floating-point types, because rounding loses information. The XOR swap has a different trap: it zeroes the value when both operands are the same storage location.

import java.util.Arrays;

public class SwapNoTemp {

    // Does NOT work: Java passes copies of primitive values.
    static void swapAttempt(int x, int y) {
        int t = x; x = y; y = t;          // only the local copies change
    }

    // Works: swap inside a shared array (the array reference is copied, its contents are shared).
    static void swapInArray(int[] arr, int i, int j) {
        if (i == j) return;               // guard required for the XOR trick
        arr[i] ^= arr[j];
        arr[j] ^= arr[i];
        arr[i] ^= arr[j];
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 5, b = 9;

        // 1) Arithmetic swap
        a = a + b;   // a = 14
        b = a - b;   // b = 5
        a = a - b;   // a = 9
        System.out.println("arithmetic: a=" + a + ", b=" + b);

        // 2) XOR swap (swaps back)
        a ^= b;
        b ^= a;
        a ^= b;
        System.out.println("xor:        a=" + a + ", b=" + b);

        // 3) One-liner (relies on left-to-right evaluation; clever, but hard to read)
        b = a + b - (a = b);
        System.out.println("one-liner:  a=" + a + ", b=" + b);

        // Overflow: int arithmetic wraps, so the swap still works
        int x = Integer.MAX_VALUE, y = 1;
        x = x + y;   // overflows to MIN_VALUE
        y = x - y;   // wraps back to MAX_VALUE
        x = x - y;   // 1
        System.out.println("overflow:   x=" + x + ", y=" + y);

        // Floating point: precision loss breaks the arithmetic swap
        double p = 1e20, q = 1.0;
        p = p + q; q = p - q; p = p - q;
        System.out.println("double:     p=" + p + ", q=" + q + "  (q=1.0 was lost)");

        // Method parameter swap fails
        int m = 1, n = 2;
        swapAttempt(m, n);
        System.out.println("method:     m=" + m + ", n=" + n);

        // Array swap works; i == j guard prevents XOR zeroing
        int[] arr = {10, 20, 30};
        swapInArray(arr, 0, 2);
        swapInArray(arr, 1, 1);
        System.out.println("array:      " + Arrays.toString(arr));
    }
}
/* Output:
arithmetic: a=9, b=5
xor:        a=5, b=9
one-liner:  a=9, b=5
overflow:   x=1, y=2147483647
double:     p=0.0, q=1.0E20  (q=1.0 was lost)
method:     m=1, n=2
array:      [30, 20, 10]
*/

Complexity: O(1) time, O(1) space.

Edge cases:

  • Overflow: in Java the arithmetic swap on int/long is correct even when a + b overflows, because wraparound is well defined. (In C, signed overflow is undefined behaviour.) Still mention the caveat in an interview.
  • Floating point: never use the arithmetic swap on double/float (see the 1e20 example above).
  • Same location: arr[i] ^= arr[i] sets the value to 0. Always guard with i != j. Two different variables that happen to hold equal values are fine.
  • Negative numbers and zero: both techniques handle them correctly.

Why a swap(int a, int b) method can't work: Java is strictly pass-by-value. The method receives copies of a and b, so swapping the copies has no effect on the caller. The same applies to swap(Integer a, Integer b): reassigning a parameter only changes the local reference, and wrappers are immutable. Workarounds: swap elements of an array or a mutable holder, or return the swapped pair (for example record Pair(int a, int b)).

Alternative: in real code, just use a temporary variable. It is clearer, works for every type, and the JIT optimises it just as well. These tricks exist only to answer the interview question.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Which trick is faster? Neither, in practice. Modern CPUs and the JIT make the temp-variable version at least as fast, and the XOR version has data dependencies that prevent parallel execution.
  • How do you swap two Strings without a temp? a = a + b; b = a.substring(0, a.length() - b.length()); a = a.substring(b.length());
  • How does Collections.swap work? It uses list.set(i, list.set(j, list.get(i))), relying on set returning the old value.
G3 Calculate the area and perimeter (circumference) of a circle.

Area = πr², circumference = 2πr, using Math.PI.

public class G3 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double r = 5;
        double area = Math.PI * r * r;
        double circumference = 2 * Math.PI * r;
        System.out.printf("Area=%.2f Circumference=%.2f%n", area, circumference);
    }
}
// Output: Area=78.54 Circumference=31.42

Approach. Area = π·r² and circumference = 2·π·r. Use Math.PI (a double accurate to about 15 digits) instead of typing 3.14. Validate the input first: a negative, NaN or infinite radius is not a valid circle. Format the output with printf/String.format, and pass an explicit Locale so the decimal separator does not change from machine to machine.

import java.util.Locale;

public class CircleCalc {

    record Circle(double radius) {
        Circle {
            if (!Double.isFinite(radius) || radius < 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Radius must be a finite, non-negative number: " + radius);
            }
        }
        double area()          { return Math.PI * radius * radius; } // r*r is faster/more exact than Math.pow(r, 2)
        double circumference() { return 2 * Math.PI * radius; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double[] inputs = {7, 2.5, 0, -3, Double.NaN};

        for (double r : inputs) {
            try {
                Circle c = new Circle(r);
                System.out.printf(Locale.US, "r=%-5.2f area=%10.2f circumference=%8.2f%n",
                        r, c.area(), c.circumference());
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
                System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }

        // String.format returns the string instead of printing it
        String s = String.format(Locale.US, "Area of r=7 to 4 dp: %.4f", new Circle(7).area());
        System.out.println(s);
        System.out.println("Raw double: " + new Circle(7).area());
    }
}
/* Output:
r=7.00  area=    153.94 circumference=   43.98
r=2.50  area=     19.63 circumference=   15.71
r=0.00  area=      0.00 circumference=    0.00
Error: Radius must be a finite, non-negative number: -3.0
Error: Radius must be a finite, non-negative number: NaN
Area of r=7 to 4 dp: 153.9380
Raw double: 153.93804002589985
*/

Complexity: O(1) time, O(1) space.

Edge cases:

  • Negative radius: reject it with IllegalArgumentException. Don't silently take Math.abs, since that hides bad input.
  • Zero radius: this is a valid degenerate circle; area and circumference are both 0.
  • NaN/Infinity: NaN < 0 is false, so a plain r < 0 check lets NaN through. Use Double.isFinite.
  • Very large r: r * r overflows to Infinity once r exceeds about 1.34e154.
  • Locale: with a German locale, %.2f prints 153,94. Pass Locale.US (or Locale.ROOT) for consistent output.
  • Scanner input: scanner.nextDouble() throws InputMismatchException for non-numeric input. Catch it, or check hasNextDouble() first.

Alternative: if you need exact decimal rounding (for billing, for example), use BigDecimal.valueOf(area).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP). printf rounds with HALF_UP on the binary value, which can surprise you on values like 2.675.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not Math.pow(r, 2)? r * r is simpler, faster and exactly rounded. pow is a general function intended for non-integer exponents.
  • How would you model several shapes? Use a sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle with area()/perimeter(), and records as the implementations.
  • %n vs \n? %n emits the platform line separator; \n is always LF.
G4 Check whether a number is prime.

Reject n < 2, then test divisors only up to √n.

public class G4 {
    static boolean isPrime(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        for (int i = 2; (long) i * i <= n; i++)
            if (n % i == 0) return false;
        return true;
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(isPrime(29) + " " + isPrime(15));
    }
}
// Output: true false

Time O(√n), space O(1).

Approach. A number n > 1 is prime if no integer from 2 to √n divides it. If n = a·b, one factor must be at most √n, so you never need to test past that. Handle 2 and 3 specially, reject multiples of 2 and 3, and then test only divisors of the form 6k ± 1 (5, 7, 11, 13, ...). Every prime above 3 has that form, so this cuts the work to about one third. To find many primes up to a limit N, use the Sieve of Eratosthenes instead.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class PrimeCheck {

    // Basic trial division, skipping even numbers.
    static boolean isPrimeBasic(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        if (n == 2) return true;
        if (n % 2 == 0) return false;
        for (int i = 3; i <= n / i; i += 2) {   // i <= n / i avoids i*i overflow
            if (n % i == 0) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    // 6k +/- 1 optimisation.
    static boolean isPrime(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;               // negatives, 0, 1
        if (n < 4) return true;                // 2, 3
        if (n % 2 == 0 || n % 3 == 0) return false;
        for (long i = 5; i * i <= n; i += 6) { // long so i*i can't overflow near Integer.MAX_VALUE
            if (n % i == 0 || n % (i + 2) == 0) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
