    // ASCII-only variant: treats accented / non-Latin letters as "other" instead of consonants.
    static Counts countAscii(String s) {
        int vowels = 0, consonants = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char c = Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(i));
            if (c < 'a' || c > 'z') {
                continue;
            }
            switch (c) {
                case 'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u' -> vowels++;
                default -> consonants++;
            }
        }
        return new Counts(vowels, consonants);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(count("Hello World 123!"));   // Counts[vowels=3, consonants=7]
        System.out.println(count("AEIOU aeiou"));        // Counts[vowels=10, consonants=0]
        System.out.println(count("rhythm"));             // Counts[vowels=0, consonants=6]
        System.out.println(count("   42 !? "));          // Counts[vowels=0, consonants=0]
        System.out.println(count(""));                   // Counts[vowels=0, consonants=0]

        System.out.println(count("Café"));               // Counts[vowels=1, consonants=3]  ('é' counted as consonant!)
        System.out.println(countAscii("Café"));          // Counts[vowels=1, consonants=2]  ('é' ignored)

        // Stream one-liner for vowels only:
        long v = "Programming".toLowerCase().chars().filter(ch -> VOWELS.indexOf(ch) >= 0).count();
        System.out.println(v);                           // 3
    }
}

Complexity. Time is O(n). VOWELS.indexOf scans a 5-character constant, so it costs O(1). Space is O(1).

Edge cases.

  • An empty string or null gives (0, 0).
  • A string with only digits or symbols gives (0, 0).
  • Upper-case vowels are handled by the lowercasing.
  • 'y' counts as a consonant here. Some definitions treat it as a vowel, so ask the interviewer.
  • Accented letters such as 'é' pass Character.isLetter, so the general version counts them as consonants. That is why there is also an ASCII-only variant with an explicit a–z range check.

Design notes.

  • Returning a record is cleaner than printing inside the method or using an int[]. It is immutable, and equals/toString come for free, which makes it easy to test.
  • The Java 14+ arrow switch with several labels per case (case 'a', 'e', ...) is a readable alternative to indexOf.
  • A boolean[128] lookup table or a Set<Character> also works. With only five vowels, the difference is negligible.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Count each vowel separately? Use int[5], or Map<Character, Long> via Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()).
  • Count digits, spaces and special characters too? Add branches for Character.isDigit and Character.isWhitespace, and put everything else under "special".
  • Make it Unicode-aware? Iterate s.codePoints() and use Normalizer to strip diacritics, so é becomes e and counts as a vowel.
G21 Person class with encapsulated fields (name, age/birth date, address), getters/setters and a method to calculate age.

Private fields with validated setters; age is derived from the birth date with Period.between, so it is never stale.

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.Period;

public class Person {
    private String name;
    private LocalDate birthDate;
    private String address;

    public Person(String name, LocalDate birthDate, String address) {
        setName(name); setBirthDate(birthDate); this.address = address;
    }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public void setName(String name) {
        if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name required");
        this.name = name;
    }
    public LocalDate getBirthDate() { return birthDate; }
    public void setBirthDate(LocalDate d) {
        if (d == null || d.isAfter(LocalDate.now())) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid date");
        this.birthDate = d;
    }
    public String getAddress() { return address; }
    public void setAddress(String address) { this.address = address; }

    public int ageOn(LocalDate date) { return Period.between(birthDate, date).getYears(); }
    public int getAge() { return ageOn(LocalDate.now()); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Person p = new Person("Asha", LocalDate.of(1995, 8, 20), "Bengaluru");
        System.out.println(p.getName() + " is " + p.ageOn(LocalDate.of(2025, 1, 1)));
    }
}
// Output: Asha is 29

Approach. Store the birth date, not the age. An age goes out of date every birthday; a birth date never changes, and the age can always be worked out from it. All fields are private. Every setter validates its input, and the constructor goes through the setters, so an invalid Person can't exist. The age comes from Period.between(birthDate, today).getYears(). There is also an overload that takes the "as of" date, which makes it testable.

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.Period;
import java.util.Objects;

public class PersonDemo {

    record Address(String street, String city, String zip) {
        Address {
            Objects.requireNonNull(street, "street");
            Objects.requireNonNull(city, "city");
            Objects.requireNonNull(zip, "zip");
        }
    }

    static class Person {
        private String name;
        private LocalDate birthDate;
        private Address address;

        Person(String name, LocalDate birthDate, Address address) {
            setName(name);
            setBirthDate(birthDate);
            setAddress(address);
        }

        public String getName() { return name; }
        public LocalDate getBirthDate() { return birthDate; }
        public Address getAddress() { return address; }

        public void setName(String name) {
            if (name == null || name.isBlank()) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name must not be blank");
            }
            this.name = name.strip();
        }

        public void setBirthDate(LocalDate birthDate) {
            Objects.requireNonNull(birthDate, "birthDate");
            if (birthDate.isAfter(LocalDate.now())) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Birth date cannot be in the future: " + birthDate);
            }
            this.birthDate = birthDate;
        }

        public void setAddress(Address address) {
            this.address = Objects.requireNonNull(address, "address");
        }

        /** Age in whole years as of today. */
        public int getAge() {
            return getAge(LocalDate.now());
        }

        /** Testable overload: age as of a given date. */
        public int getAge(LocalDate asOf) {
            return Period.between(birthDate, asOf).getYears();
        }

        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return "Person[name=" + name + ", birthDate=" + birthDate + ", address=" + address + "]";
        }
    }

    // Immutable alternative: a record with validation in the compact constructor.
    record PersonRecord(String name, LocalDate birthDate, Address address) {
        PersonRecord {
            if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name must not be blank");
            Objects.requireNonNull(birthDate, "birthDate");
            Objects.requireNonNull(address, "address");
        }
        int ageOn(LocalDate date) { return Period.between(birthDate, date).getYears(); }
        PersonRecord withAddress(Address a) { return new PersonRecord(name, birthDate, a); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Address home = new Address("12 MG Road", "Bengaluru", "560001");
        Person p = new Person("  Asha  ", LocalDate.of(1990, 5, 15), home);
        System.out.println(p);
        // Person[name=Asha, birthDate=1990-05-15, address=Address[street=12 MG Road, city=Bengaluru, zip=560001]]

        System.out.println(p.getAge(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 5)));  // 36
        System.out.println(p.getAge(LocalDate.of(2026, 5, 14)));  // 35 (day before birthday)

        try {
            p.setBirthDate(LocalDate.now().plusDays(1));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());     // Rejected: Birth date cannot be in the future: ...
        }
        try {
            p.setName("   ");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());     // Rejected: Name must not be blank
        }

        PersonRecord r = new PersonRecord("Ravi", LocalDate.of(2000, 2, 29), home);
        System.out.println(r.ageOn(LocalDate.of(2026, 2, 28)));   // 25 (leap-day birthday not reached yet)
        System.out.println(r.withAddress(new Address("1 Park St", "Kolkata", "700016")).address().city()); // Kolkata
    }
}

Edge cases.

  • A birth date in the future is rejected.
  • null values are rejected.
  • A blank name is rejected, and a valid name is stripped of surrounding spaces.
  • Someone born on 29 February has their birthday counted on 1 March in non-leap years. Period handles this calendar arithmetic correctly.
  • The day before a birthday still gives the lower age.

Design notes.

  • Encapsulation here means more than "private fields with getters". The class enforces its own rules (its invariants) in one place, and callers can't get around them.
  • Calling the setters from the constructor reuses the validation. Mark those setters final, or keep the class final, so a subclass can't override a setter and observe a half-built object.
  • LocalDate is immutable, so the getter can return it directly with no defensive copy. If the field were a mutable java.util.Date, you'd have to copy it on the way in and on the way out.
  • LocalDate.now() inside getAge() makes the method hard to test. Inject a java.time.Clock, or use the overload that takes a date.
  • The record alternative: If people don't change after creation, a record gives you immutability plus equals, hashCode and toString. "Setters" become withX methods that return a new copy.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not store age as an int? It goes stale every year and duplicates information you already have. Derived data should be computed, not stored.
  • How do you implement equals/hashCode for the class version? Base them on the identifying fields (name and birthDate, or an id), keep them consistent with each other, and use Objects.hash.
  • Shallow vs deep copy of address? Address is an immutable record, so sharing it is safe. A mutable address would need copying.
G22 BankAccount class with deposit, withdraw and check balance.

Private balance changed only through methods that validate the amount and reject overdrafts.

public class BankAccount {
    private final String accountNo;
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(String accountNo, double opening) { this.accountNo = accountNo; this.balance = opening; }

    public void deposit(double amt) {
        if (amt <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        balance += amt;
    }
    public void withdraw(double amt) {
        if (amt <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        if (amt > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
        balance -= amt;
    }
    public double getBalance() { return balance; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BankAccount acc = new BankAccount("ACC-1", 1000);
        acc.deposit(500);
        acc.withdraw(200);
        System.out.println("Balance: " + acc.getBalance());
        try { acc.withdraw(5000); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
// Output:
// Balance: 1300.0
// Insufficient funds

In production use BigDecimal for money and synchronized (or locks) for concurrent access.

Approach. The balance is a private BigDecimal with a fixed scale of 2. Using double for money gives rounding errors, for example 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. Every operation validates the amount: it must be non-null and greater than zero. withdraw throws a checked InsufficientFundsException when the balance is too low, so the caller has to handle that case. The methods are synchronized, so concurrent deposits and withdrawals can't corrupt the balance through lost updates.

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.util.Objects;

public class BankDemo {

    static class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        private final BigDecimal shortfall;

        InsufficientFundsException(String message, BigDecimal shortfall) {
            super(message);
            this.shortfall = shortfall;
        }

        BigDecimal getShortfall() { return shortfall; }
    }

    static class BankAccount {
        private final String accountNumber;
        private final String owner;
        private BigDecimal balance = BigDecimal.ZERO.setScale(2);

        BankAccount(String accountNumber, String owner) {
            this.accountNumber = Objects.requireNonNull(accountNumber);
            this.owner = Objects.requireNonNull(owner);
        }

        private static BigDecimal validate(BigDecimal amount) {
            Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount");
            if (amount.signum() <= 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive: " + amount);
            }
            if (amount.stripTrailingZeros().scale() > 2) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("At most 2 decimal places: " + amount);
            }
            return amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY);
        }

        public synchronized void deposit(BigDecimal amount) {
            balance = balance.add(validate(amount));
        }

        public synchronized void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) throws InsufficientFundsException {
            BigDecimal amt = validate(amount);
            if (balance.compareTo(amt) < 0) {
                throw new InsufficientFundsException(
                        "Insufficient funds: balance " + balance + ", requested " + amt,
                        amt.subtract(balance));
            }
            balance = balance.subtract(amt);
        }

        public synchronized BigDecimal getBalance() {
            return balance;            // BigDecimal is immutable: safe to return
        }

        @Override
        public synchronized String toString() {
            return "BankAccount[" + accountNumber + ", " + owner + ", balance=" + balance + "]";
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        BankAccount acc = new BankAccount("ACC-001", "Asha");
        acc.deposit(new BigDecimal("1000"));
        System.out.println(acc.getBalance());                      // 1000.00

        try {
            acc.withdraw(new BigDecimal("250.50"));
            System.out.println(acc.getBalance());                  // 749.50
            acc.withdraw(new BigDecimal("1000"));
        } catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());                    // Insufficient funds: balance 749.50, requested 1000.00
            System.out.println("Short by " + e.getShortfall());    // Short by 250.50
        }

        try {
            acc.deposit(new BigDecimal("-5"));
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());                    // Amount must be positive: -5
        }

        // Thread-safety check: 2 threads x 1000 deposits of 1.00
        Runnable task = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) acc.deposit(BigDecimal.ONE); };
        Thread t1 = new Thread(task), t2 = new Thread(task);
        t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join();
        System.out.println(acc);                                   // BankAccount[ACC-001, Asha, balance=2749.50]

        System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);                                              // 0.30000000000000004
        System.out.println(new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2")));       // 0.3
    }
}

Edge cases.

  • Zero, negative and null amounts are rejected with IllegalArgumentException. That is a programming or input error, not a business rule.
  • An amount with more than two decimal places, such as 10.005, is rejected rather than silently rounded.
  • Withdrawing exactly the balance is allowed and leaves 0.00.
  • Always create BigDecimal with new BigDecimal("0.1") or BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1). Never use new BigDecimal(0.1), which captures the binary error of the double.

Design notes.

  • balance += x is a read-modify-write sequence. Without synchronization, two threads can both read 100 and both write 150, and one deposit is lost. synchronized on the instance makes each operation atomic and visible to other threads.
  • A transfer between two accounts needs a fixed order for taking locks (for example, by account number) to avoid deadlock. Alternatively, use ReentrantLock.tryLock.
  • Compare amounts with compareTo, not equals. equals also compares scale, so 2.0 is not equal to 2.00.
  • In real systems, money is often stored as a long count of minor units (paise or cents), with a currency attached (javax.money). Balances are also usually derived from an append-only ledger of transactions.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Checked or unchecked for insufficient funds? Checked. It is an expected business outcome the caller should handle. Invalid arguments are unchecked.
  • Alternative to synchronized? AtomicReference<BigDecimal> with updateAndGet, or a ReentrantReadWriteLock if balance reads far outnumber writes.
  • How do you add an overdraft limit or a transaction history? Add an overdraftLimit field to the check. Append an immutable Transaction record to a list inside the same synchronized block.
G23 Animal with eat() and sleep(); Dog and Cat override them; polymorphism with an Animal array.

Subclasses override the methods; calls through Animal references dispatch at runtime to the actual object type.

class Animal {
    void eat()   { System.out.println("Animal eats"); }
    void sleep() { System.out.println("Animal sleeps"); }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override void eat()   { System.out.println("Dog eats bones"); }
    @Override void sleep() { System.out.println("Dog sleeps in kennel"); }
}
class Cat extends Animal {
    @Override void eat()   { System.out.println("Cat eats fish"); }
    @Override void sleep() { System.out.println("Cat sleeps on sofa"); }
}
public class G23 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal[] animals = {new Dog(), new Cat()};
        for (Animal a : animals) { a.eat(); a.sleep(); }
    }
}
// Output:
// Dog eats bones
// Dog sleeps in kennel
// Cat eats fish
// Cat sleeps on sofa

Approach. Write a base class Animal that gives default eat() and sleep() behaviour. Dog and Cat extend it and override those methods with @Override. When you loop over an Animal[] and call a.eat(), the JVM runs the version for the object's actual (runtime) class, not the declared type. This is called dynamic dispatch, or runtime polymorphism. A subclass can also add to the parent's behaviour instead of replacing it, by calling super.sleep().

public class AnimalDemo {

    static class Animal {
        protected final String name;

        Animal(String name) {
            this.name = name;
        }

        void eat()   { System.out.println(name + " is eating."); }
        void sleep() { System.out.println(name + " is sleeping."); }
        String sound() { return "..."; }

        // Template method: fixed algorithm, overridable step.
        final void describe() { System.out.println(name + " says " + sound()); }
    }

    static class Dog extends Animal {
        Dog(String name) { super(name); }

        @Override void eat() { System.out.println(name + " the dog is eating kibble."); }

        @Override void sleep() {
            super.sleep();                                     // reuse parent behaviour
            System.out.println(name + " curls up in its kennel.");
        }

        @Override String sound() { return "Woof"; }

        void fetch() { System.out.println(name + " fetches the ball."); }  // Dog-only
    }

    static class Cat extends Animal {
        Cat(String name) { super(name); }

        @Override void eat()   { System.out.println(name + " the cat is eating fish."); }
        @Override void sleep() { System.out.println(name + " naps in the sun for 16 hours."); }
        @Override String sound() { return "Meow"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal[] animals = { new Dog("Rex"), new Cat("Tom"), new Animal("Generic") };

        for (Animal a : animals) {          // declared type: Animal
            a.eat();                        // runtime type decides which eat() runs
            a.sleep();
            a.describe();
            System.out.println("---");
        }

        // Subclass-specific behaviour needs a type check (Java 16+ pattern matching):
        for (Animal a : animals) {
            if (a instanceof Dog d) {
                d.fetch();
            }
        }
    }
}
/* Output:
Rex the dog is eating kibble.
Rex is sleeping.
Rex curls up in its kennel.
Rex says Woof
---
Tom the cat is eating fish.
Tom naps in the sun for 16 hours.
Tom says Meow
---
Generic is eating.
Generic is sleeping.
Generic says ...
---
Rex fetches the ball.
*/

How dispatch works.

  • The compiler checks that eat() exists on the declared type, Animal. That is why a.fetch() doesn't compile.
  • At runtime, the JVM looks the method up in the object's class through its virtual method table and calls the most specific override.
  • describe() is final, but it calls the overridable sound(). So even a fixed algorithm can produce polymorphic output.

Edge cases and pitfalls.

  • Static methods aren't overridden, they're hidden. Animal.info() versus Dog.info() is resolved by the declared type.
  • Fields aren't polymorphic either. If you redeclare name in Dog, it hides the parent's field.
  • private and final methods can't be overridden.
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor runs the subclass version before the subclass fields have been initialized.
  • @Override turns a typo into a compile error. Without it, void eats() would quietly add a new method.

Abstract vs concrete base.

  • A concrete Animal allows new Animal("Generic"), which may be meaningless in the domain.
  • Declaring abstract class Animal { abstract String sound(); } blocks direct instantiation and forces every subclass to supply sound(). Shared code such as eat() can still live in the base class.
  • If there is no shared state at all, use an interface Animal with default methods. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.

Override rules. An override must keep the same signature. It may return a narrower (covariant) type, it can't reduce visibility, and it can't throw broader checked exceptions.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Overloading vs overriding? Overloading means the same name with different parameters, resolved at compile time. Overriding means the same signature in a subclass, resolved at runtime.
  • Can you override a static or private method? No. A static method is hidden. A private method isn't inherited, so a method with the same name in the subclass is a new method.
  • Why prefer List<Animal> over Animal[]? Arrays are covariant: Animal[] a = new Dog[2]; a[0] = new Cat("x"); compiles but throws ArrayStoreException. Generics catch that at compile time.
G24 Vehicle hierarchy (Car, Bike, Truck) with speed, color, start(), stop(), accelerate(); call start() polymorphically.

Abstract base holds shared state and behaviour; each subclass supplies its own start().

abstract class Vehicle {
    protected int speed;
    protected final String color;
    Vehicle(String color) { this.color = color; }
    abstract void start();
    void stop() { speed = 0; System.out.println(getClass().getSimpleName() + " stopped"); }
    void accelerate(int by) { speed += by; System.out.println(getClass().getSimpleName() + " speed " + speed); }
}
class Car extends Vehicle {
    Car(String c) { super(c); }
    @Override void start() { System.out.println(color + " Car starts with key"); }
}
class Bike extends Vehicle {
    Bike(String c) { super(c); }
    @Override void start() { System.out.println(color + " Bike starts with kick"); }
}
class Truck extends Vehicle {
    Truck(String c) { super(c); }
    @Override void start() { System.out.println(color + " Truck starts with diesel engine"); }
}
public class G24 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Vehicle[] vs = {new Car("Red"), new Bike("Black"), new Truck("White")};
        for (Vehicle v : vs) v.start();
        vs[0].accelerate(40);
        vs[0].stop();
    }
}
// Output:
// Red Car starts with key
// Black Bike starts with kick
// White Truck starts with diesel engine
// Car speed 40
// Car stopped

Approach. An abstract class Vehicle holds everything the vehicles share: color, the current speed, a running flag and a per-type maxSpeed. It also implements start(), stop() and accelerate() once, including the rules: you can't accelerate before starting, and speed is capped at the maximum. Each subclass passes its own top speed up to the base constructor and supplies one abstract piece, startSound(). Truck also overrides start() itself to add a safety check before calling super.start(). The client code only ever sees Vehicle.

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

public class VehicleDemo {

    static abstract class Vehicle {
        private final String color;
        private final int maxSpeed;
        private int speed;          // private + getter: subclasses cannot break the invariant 0 <= speed <= max
        private boolean running;

        protected Vehicle(String color, int maxSpeed) {
            if (maxSpeed <= 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxSpeed must be positive");
            }
            this.color = Objects.requireNonNull(color, "color");
            this.maxSpeed = maxSpeed;
        }

        public void start() {
            if (running) {
                System.out.println(label() + " is already running");
                return;
            }
            running = true;
            System.out.println(label() + " started: " + startSound());
        }

        public void stop() {
            speed = 0;
            running = false;
            System.out.println(label() + " stopped");
        }

        public void accelerate(int delta) {
            if (!running) {
                throw new IllegalStateException(label() + " must be started first");
            }
            if (delta <= 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("delta must be positive: " + delta);
            }
            speed = Math.min(maxSpeed, speed + delta);
            System.out.println(label() + " accelerating to " + speed + " km/h"
                    + (speed == maxSpeed ? " (max)" : ""));
        }

        protected abstract String startSound();      // hook each subtype must supply

        protected String label() { return color + " " + getClass().getSimpleName(); }

        public String getColor()  { return color; }
        public int getSpeed()     { return speed; }
        public int getMaxSpeed()  { return maxSpeed; }
        public boolean isRunning() { return running; }
    }

    static final class Car extends Vehicle {
        Car(String color) { super(color, 180); }
        @Override protected String startSound() { return "Vroom"; }
    }

    static final class Bike extends Vehicle {
        Bike(String color) { super(color, 120); }
        @Override protected String startSound() { return "Brrm"; }
    }

    static final class Truck extends Vehicle {
        private final int loadTons;

        Truck(String color, int loadTons) {
            super(color, loadTons > 10 ? 80 : 100);   // heavier load -> lower top speed
            if (loadTons < 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("load cannot be negative");
            }
            this.loadTons = loadTons;
        }

        @Override
        public void start() {
            System.out.println(label() + ": checking air brakes (load " + loadTons + " t)");
            super.start();
        }

        @Override protected String startSound() { return "Rumble"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Vehicle> fleet = List.of(new Car("Red"), new Bike("Black"), new Truck("White", 12));

        for (Vehicle v : fleet) v.start();          // polymorphic start()
        for (Vehicle v : fleet) v.accelerate(150);
        for (Vehicle v : fleet) v.stop();

        try {
            new Car("Blue").accelerate(10);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
/* Output:
Red Car started: Vroom
Black Bike started: Brrm
White Truck: checking air brakes (load 12 t)
White Truck started: Rumble
Red Car accelerating to 150 km/h
Black Bike accelerating to 120 km/h (max)
White Truck accelerating to 80 km/h (max)
Red Car stopped
Black Bike stopped
White Truck stopped
Blue Car must be started first
*/

Edge cases.

  • Accelerating before start() throws IllegalStateException.
  • A zero or negative delta throws IllegalArgumentException.
  • Calling start() twice does nothing the second time.
  • stop() resets the speed to 0.
  • Speed is clamped to the maximum, so it never overflows past it.

Design notes.

  • protected fields vs private fields plus getters. With protected int speed, any subclass (or any class in the same package) could set speed = 999 and break the invariant. Private state and protected or public methods keep the rules in one place.
  • The maxSpeed choice. It is passed through the constructor and stored as final, so it's set once. The alternative is an abstract getMaxSpeed(), but calling it from the base constructor is unsafe, because subclass fields aren't initialized yet.
  • Template-method style. The base class controls the order of operations, and subclasses fill in hooks (startSound). Truck shows the other style: override, then delegate to super.start().
  • The subclasses are final, because nothing should extend them further. Mark the class abstract, because "a vehicle" with no type has no sensible top speed.
  • getClass().getSimpleName() is convenient for labels. A real system would use an explicit type() method or an enum.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you add an electric car that charges instead of refuelling? Add an interface Chargeable { void charge(); } and implement it only where it applies. Don't put charge() in Vehicle, because that would break the Liskov substitution principle.
  • Why is Vehicle abstract rather than an interface? It has shared mutable state (speed, running) and a constructor. Interfaces can't hold instance state.
  • How do you make accelerate thread-safe? Mark the methods synchronized, or store the speed in an AtomicInteger and update it with updateAndGet(s -> Math.min(max, s + d)).
G25 Abstract class Shape with area() and perimeter(); Circle, Rectangle and Triangle implementations.

Abstract methods force each subclass to implement both; triangle area uses Heron's formula.

abstract class Shape {
    abstract double area();
    abstract double perimeter();
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    private final double r;
    Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
    double perimeter() { return 2 * Math.PI * r; }
}
class Rectangle extends Shape {
    private final double w, h;
    Rectangle(double w, double h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    double area() { return w * h; }
    double perimeter() { return 2 * (w + h); }
}
class Triangle extends Shape {
    private final double a, b, c;
    Triangle(double a, double b, double c) { this.a = a; this.b = b; this.c = c; }
    double perimeter() { return a + b + c; }
    double area() { double s = perimeter() / 2; return Math.sqrt(s * (s - a) * (s - b) * (s - c)); }
}
public class G25 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Shape[] shapes = {new Circle(1), new Rectangle(4, 5), new Triangle(3, 4, 5)};
        for (Shape s : shapes)
            System.out.printf("%s area=%.2f perimeter=%.2f%n", s.getClass().getSimpleName(), s.area(), s.perimeter());
    }
}
// Output:
// Circle area=3.14 perimeter=6.28
// Rectangle area=20.00 perimeter=18.00
// Triangle area=6.00 perimeter=12.00

Approach. Shape declares area() and perimeter() as abstract and implements a shared toString() on top of them. Each subclass validates its dimensions in the constructor, so an invalid shape can't exist: every side must be positive and finite, and a triangle must also satisfy the triangle inequality. The triangle's area uses Heron's formula. In Java 17 the hierarchy can be sealed, which means the compiler knows the complete list of subclasses.

import java.util.List;

abstract sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {
    abstract double area();
    abstract double perimeter();

    static double requirePositive(double v, String name) {
        if (!(v > 0) || Double.isInfinite(v)) {        // !(v > 0) also rejects NaN
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(name + " must be a positive finite number: " + v);
        }
        return v;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return String.format("%s area=%.2f perimeter=%.2f",
                getClass().getSimpleName(), area(), perimeter());
    }
}

final class Circle extends Shape {
    private final double radius;
    Circle(double radius) { this.radius = requirePositive(radius, "radius"); }
    @Override double area()      { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
    @Override double perimeter() { return 2 * Math.PI * radius; }
}

final class Rectangle extends Shape {
    private final double width, height;
    Rectangle(double width, double height) {
        this.width = requirePositive(width, "width");
        this.height = requirePositive(height, "height");
    }
    @Override double area()      { return width * height; }
    @Override double perimeter() { return 2 * (width + height); }
}

final class Triangle extends Shape {
    private final double a, b, c;
    Triangle(double a, double b, double c) {
        requirePositive(a, "a");
        requirePositive(b, "b");
        requirePositive(c, "c");
        if (a + b <= c || a + c <= b || b + c <= a) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                    "Sides " + a + ", " + b + ", " + c + " violate the triangle inequality");
        }
        this.a = a; this.b = b; this.c = c;
    }
    @Override double perimeter() { return a + b + c; }
    @Override double area() {                          // Heron's formula
        double s = perimeter() / 2;
        return Math.sqrt(s * (s - a) * (s - b) * (s - c));
    }
}

public class ShapesDemo {

    // Exhaustive handling over a sealed hierarchy (Java 17: instanceof patterns;
    // pattern-matching switch is a preview in 17 and final in Java 21).
    static String kind(Shape s) {
        if (s instanceof Circle) return "round";
        if (s instanceof Rectangle) return "four-sided";
        if (s instanceof Triangle) return "three-sided";
        throw new AssertionError("unreachable: sealed hierarchy");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Shape> shapes = List.of(new Circle(1), new Rectangle(3, 4), new Triangle(3, 4, 5));

        for (Shape s : shapes) {
            System.out.println(s + " (" + kind(s) + ")");
        }
        System.out.printf("Total area: %.2f%n", shapes.stream().mapToDouble(Shape::area).sum());

        try {
            new Triangle(1, 2, 3);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            new Circle(-2);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
/* Output:
Circle area=3.14 perimeter=6.28 (round)
Rectangle area=12.00 perimeter=14.00 (four-sided)
Triangle area=6.00 perimeter=12.00 (three-sided)
Total area: 21.14
Sides 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 violate the triangle inequality
radius must be a positive finite number: -2.0
*/

Complexity. Every operation is O(1).

Edge cases.

  • Zero, negative, NaN and infinite dimensions are rejected.
  • Degenerate triangles, where a + b == c, are rejected because their area is 0. That is why the check uses <=.
  • Rounding can make the product inside Heron's square root slightly negative for nearly-degenerate triangles. A defensive version uses Math.max(0, ...).
  • For very thin triangles, the numerically stable form of Heron's formula sorts the sides so that a ≥ b ≥ c and uses ¼·√((a+(b+c))(c−(a−b))(c+(a−b))(a+(b−c))).

Design notes.

  • Abstract class vs interface. Shape could just as well be an interface. An abstract class makes sense when there is shared behaviour (toString, requirePositive) or shared state.
  • sealed ... permits (Java 17) limits who can extend Shape. Permitted subclasses must be final, sealed or non-sealed. The benefit is exhaustiveness: with Java 21's pattern switch, the compiler checks that every case is covered, so no default branch is needed.
  • The fields are final, which makes the shapes immutable and thread-safe. A record Circle(double radius) would also work, but records can't extend an abstract class, only implement a sealed interface.
  • Use Math.PI rather than 3.14. Format with %.2f only for display, and keep full precision in the calculations.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you sort shapes by area? shapes.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble(Shape::area)).
  • How do you add a Square? Either final class Square extends Shape added to permits, or make Rectangle non-sealed and extend it. The second option invites the classic Square/Rectangle LSP problem if the shapes are mutable.
  • What does the Java 21 version look like? sealed interface Shape permits Circle, ... with record implementations, and switch (s) { case Circle c -> ...; case Rectangle r -> ...; case Triangle t -> ...; }, with no default.
G26 Handle ArithmeticException and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Wrap each risky operation in its own try and catch the specific unchecked exception. finally always runs.

public class G26 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            int x = 10 / 0;
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("Arithmetic: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        try {
            int[] a = new int[3];
            a[5] = 1;
        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
            System.out.println("Index: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            System.out.println("done");
        }
    }
}
// Output:
// Arithmetic: / by zero
// Index: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3
// done

Note: both exceptions are unchecked (they extend RuntimeException). Integer division by zero throws, but 10.0 / 0 gives Infinity.

Approach. Show each exception caught in its own try/catch, then both handled by a single multi-catch, with finally blocks proving that cleanup always runs. Both are unchecked exceptions (subclasses of RuntimeException) that signal programming errors. So the program also shows the better approach: a guard check that stops the exception from happening at all.

import java.util.OptionalInt;

public class ExceptionBasics {

    static int divide(int a, int b) {
        return a / b;                       // throws ArithmeticException when b == 0
    }

    static int elementAt(int[] arr, int index) {
        return arr[index];                  // throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when out of range
    }

    static int risky(int mode, int[] data) {
        return mode == 0 ? divide(data[0], 0) : elementAt(data, data.length);
    }

    // Prevention: validate instead of catching
    static OptionalInt safeDivide(int a, int b) {
        return b == 0 ? OptionalInt.empty() : OptionalInt.of(a / b);
    }

    static boolean inBounds(int[] arr, int i) {
        return i >= 0 && i < arr.length;
    }

    static int tricky() {
        try {
            return 1;
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally runs before the return completes");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] data = {10, 20, 30};

        // 1. ArithmeticException
        try {
            System.out.println("Result: " + divide(10, 0));
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.out.println("ArithmeticException caught: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally #1");
        }

        // 2. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
        try {
            System.out.println(elementAt(data, 5));
        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
            System.out.println("AIOOBE caught: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally #2");
        }

        // 3. Multi-catch (Java 7+): one handler for unrelated exception types
        for (int mode = 0; mode < 2; mode++) {
            try {
                risky(mode, data);
            } catch (ArithmeticException | ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
                System.out.println("Multi-catch: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }

        // 4. finally runs even when try returns
        System.out.println("tricky() returned " + tricky());

        // 5. Prevention beats catching
        System.out.println(safeDivide(10, 0).isPresent());        // false
        System.out.println(inBounds(data, 5) ? data[5] : -1);     // -1

        // 6. Floating-point division does NOT throw
        System.out.println(10.0 / 0);                             // Infinity
        System.out.println(0.0 / 0);                              // NaN
    }
}
/* Output:
ArithmeticException caught: / by zero
finally #1
AIOOBE caught: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3
finally #2
Multi-catch: ArithmeticException - / by zero
Multi-catch: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException - Index 3 out of bounds for length 3
finally runs before the return completes
tricky() returned 1
false
-1
Infinity
NaN
*/

Why these are unchecked. They point to bugs (a missing zero check, an off-by-one index), not to conditions the caller can be expected to recover from. If they were checked, every division and every array access would need try/catch or a throws clause. The JLS therefore makes them RuntimeException subclasses, which the compiler doesn't force you to handle. The right fix is to prevent them: check the divisor, check 0 <= i < length, or use an enhanced for loop so there's no index at all.

Edge cases and rules.

  • Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1 doesn't throw. It overflows silently to MIN_VALUE. Use Math.floorDiv or Math.divideExact if you need detection.
  • % by zero on integers also throws ArithmeticException.
  • Order catch blocks from most specific to most general. Putting catch (RuntimeException) before catch (ArithmeticException) is a compile error, because the second block is unreachable.
  • The alternatives in a multi-catch can't be subclasses of each other (compile error), and the variable e is implicitly final.
  • finally always runs, except after System.exit or a JVM crash.
  • A return inside finally swallows any exception and overrides the try's return value. Never do that.

Design notes.

  • Catching Exception or Throwable "just in case" hides bugs. Catch only what you can handle.
  • Log with the exception object (log.error("msg", e)) so the stack trace is kept.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Checked vs unchecked? Checked exceptions (IOException) must be caught or declared, and are for recoverable external conditions. Unchecked ones (RuntimeException and Error) are for programming errors.
  • What happens if an exception is thrown inside finally? It replaces the original exception, which is lost unless you add it with addSuppressed. Try-with-resources does that automatically.
  • Does try need a catch? No. try/finally and try-with-resources without a catch are both valid.
G27 Custom exception InvalidAgeException: throw and catch it for invalid input.

Extend Exception to make it checked, so callers have to handle it. Throw it from the validator and catch it in main.

class InvalidAgeException extends Exception {
    InvalidAgeException(String msg) { super(msg); }
}

public class G27 {
    static void validate(int age) throws InvalidAgeException {
        if (age < 0 || age > 150) throw new InvalidAgeException("Invalid age: " + age);
        System.out.println("Valid age: " + age);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int age : new int[]{25, -5}) {
            try {
                validate(age);
            } catch (InvalidAgeException e) {
                System.out.println("Caught: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}
// Output:
// Valid age: 25
// Caught: Invalid age: -5

Note: extend RuntimeException instead if you want it unchecked (no throws needed).

Approach. Define InvalidAgeException extends Exception, making it checked. Invalid user input is an expected, recoverable condition, and the caller should be forced to deal with it, for example by asking again. Give it the standard constructors: message only, and message plus cause. Validation methods declare throws InvalidAgeException and use throw new ... when a rule is broken. A Scanner loop catches the exception, shows the message, and asks again until it gets a valid age or the input ends.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class InvalidAgeDemo {

    static class InvalidAgeException extends Exception {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

        InvalidAgeException(String message) {
            super(message);
        }

        InvalidAgeException(String message, Throwable cause) {
            super(message, cause);
        }
    }

    static final int MIN_AGE = 0;
    static final int MAX_AGE = 150;

    static void validateAge(int age) throws InvalidAgeException {
        if (age < MIN_AGE || age > MAX_AGE) {
            throw new InvalidAgeException("Age must be between " + MIN_AGE + " and " + MAX_AGE + ", got " + age);
        }
    }

    static int parseAge(String input) throws InvalidAgeException {
        int age;
        try {
            age = Integer.parseInt(input.trim());
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            throw new InvalidAgeException("Not a number: '" + input + "'", e);   // wrap, keep cause
        }
        validateAge(age);
        return age;
    }

    static void register(String name, int age) throws InvalidAgeException {
        validateAge(age);
        if (age < 18) {
            throw new InvalidAgeException(name + " must be at least 18 to register, got " + age);
        }
        System.out.println("Registered " + name + " (age " + age + ")");
    }

    static int readAge(Scanner sc) {
        while (true) {
            System.out.print("Enter age: ");
            if (!sc.hasNextLine()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Input ended before a valid age was entered");
            }
            String line = sc.nextLine();
            try {
                return parseAge(line);
            } catch (InvalidAgeException e) {
                String cause = e.getCause() == null ? "" : " (cause: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName() + ")";
                System.out.println("Invalid age: " + e.getMessage() + cause);
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            register("Asha", 25);
            register("Kid", 12);
            register("Never", 30);                 // skipped: exception above jumps to catch
        } catch (InvalidAgeException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        try (Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in)) {
            int age = readAge(sc);
            System.out.println("Valid age entered: " + age);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
/* Sample session (user input after "Enter age: "):
Registered Asha (age 25)
Caught: Kid must be at least 18 to register, got 12
Enter age: abc
Invalid age: Not a number: 'abc' (cause: NumberFormatException)
Enter age: -4
Invalid age: Age must be between 0 and 150, got -4
Enter age: 200
Invalid age: Age must be between 0 and 150, got 200
Enter age: 30
Valid age entered: 30
*/

Edge cases.

  • Non-numeric text, empty lines, values beyond int range (NumberFormatException), negative numbers and absurd values are all reported, and the loop asks again.
  • End of input (Ctrl+D or Ctrl+Z, or a piped file running out) ends the loop cleanly. Without the hasNextLine check, it would loop forever or throw NoSuchElementException.
  • nextLine() plus parseInt avoids the classic bug where nextInt() leaves the newline in the buffer.

Design notes.

  • Checked vs unchecked. Choose checked when the caller can reasonably recover, as in "ask the user again". If the age comes from trusted internal code and a bad value means a bug, make it extends RuntimeException, or simply use IllegalArgumentException. Many modern APIs (Spring, for example) prefer unchecked exceptions to avoid throws clutter. Be ready to argue either side.
  • throw vs throws. throw raises one exception object at a specific point. throws in a method signature declares which checked exceptions can escape the method.
  • Keep the cause. When converting one exception into another, always pass the original as the cause, so the stack trace shows the root problem ("Caused by: NumberFormatException").
  • Add serialVersionUID, because exceptions are Serializable. Optionally store the rejected value in a field, for example getInvalidAge(), for programmatic handling.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why extend Exception and not Throwable or Error? Error is for JVM-level failures such as OutOfMemoryError. Extending Throwable directly breaks the conventions callers rely on.
  • Can an overriding method throw a new checked exception? No, only the same exceptions, subtypes of them, or none. Unchecked exceptions are always allowed.
  • How do you validate in a constructor? Throw from the constructor. No object is created, so a half-initialized instance never escapes.
G28 Exception propagation: a method throws when a file is not found; handle it in the caller.

The method declares throws IOException and does not catch anything. The exception goes up the call stack to main, which handles it.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class G28 {
    static String read(String path) throws IOException {   // propagates, doesn't handle
        return Files.readString(Path.of(path));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            System.out.println(read("missing.txt"));
        } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {                  // more specific first
            System.out.println("File not found: " + e.getMessage());
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("I/O error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
// Output: File not found: missing.txt

Note: NIO throws NoSuchFileException. The legacy FileReader throws FileNotFoundException instead. Both are IOException subclasses.

Approach. The lowest-level method calls Files.readString, which throws NoSuchFileException (a subclass of IOException) when the file is missing. That method doesn't catch anything; it declares throws IOException. The middle layer doesn't catch either; it declares the same thing, so the exception propagates up the call stack. Each frame is unwound until a caller with a matching catch is found. The program then shows the other common pattern: catching at a boundary and wrapping the error in a domain exception, keeping the original as the cause.

import java.io.FileInputStream;
import java.io.FileNotFoundException;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStream;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class PropagationDemo {

    static class ConfigLoadException extends Exception {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        ConfigLoadException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }
    }

    // Level 3 (lowest): throws, does not handle.
    static String readFile(Path path) throws IOException {
        return Files.readString(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);   // NoSuchFileException if missing
    }

    // Level 2: simply lets it propagate.
    static int countConfigLines(Path path) throws IOException {
        String content = readFile(path);
        return content.isEmpty() ? 0 : content.split("\\R").length;
    }

    // Level 2b: translate at a layer boundary, preserving the cause.
    static int loadConfig(Path path) throws ConfigLoadException {
        try {
            return countConfigLines(path);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new ConfigLoadException("Could not load config " + path.getFileName(), e);
        }
    }

    // Legacy java.io equivalent: FileNotFoundException
    static int firstByte(String fileName) throws IOException {
        try (InputStream in = new FileInputStream(fileName)) {
            return in.read();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Path missing = Path.of("missing-config.properties");

        // 1. Caller handles the propagated exception, most specific first.
        try {
            countConfigLines(missing);
        } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
            System.out.println("File not found: " + e.getFile());
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Other I/O problem: " + e);
        }

        // 2. Wrapped exception: domain message + root cause.
        try {
            loadConfig(missing);
        } catch (ConfigLoadException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
            System.out.println("  caused by: " + e.getCause());
        }

        // 3. Legacy API throws FileNotFoundException instead.
        try {
            firstByte("missing.dat");
        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
            System.out.println("Legacy: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        // 4. Happy path with a real temp file.
        Path tmp = Files.createTempFile("config", ".properties");
        try {
            Files.writeString(tmp, "a=1\nb=2\nc=3\n");
            System.out.println("Lines: " + loadConfig(tmp));
        } finally {
            Files.deleteIfExists(tmp);
        }
    }
}
/* Output:
File not found: missing-config.properties
Could not load config missing-config.properties
  caused by: java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException: missing-config.properties
Legacy: missing.dat (The system cannot find the file specified)     <- Windows; Linux: (No such file or directory)
Lines: 3
*/

How propagation works.

  • The call stack is main → countConfigLines → readFile → Files.readString.
  • When readString throws, readFile has no handler, so its frame is popped. The same happens to countConfigLines, and main's catch (NoSuchFileException) matches.
  • If no frame catches it, the thread's uncaught-exception handler prints the stack trace and the thread ends.
  • With checked exceptions, every method along the way must either catch the exception or declare it in throws, and the compiler enforces this. Unchecked exceptions propagate without any declaration.

Edge cases.

  • An existing file without read permission throws AccessDeniedException.
  • A directory instead of a file throws an IOException.
  • Invalid UTF-8 in the file throws MalformedInputException.
  • All of these are IOException subclasses, so the general catch covers them.
  • Don't check Files.exists(path) before reading. That is a time-of-check/time-of-use race, because the file can disappear in between. Attempt the operation and handle the exception.

Design notes.

  • Where to catch. Catch where you can do something meaningful: retry, fall back to defaults, or show a message to the user. Low-level code should usually let the exception propagate.
  • Wrapping. Translate exceptions at layer boundaries so callers aren't tied to implementation details. For example, a service throws ConfigLoadException, not IOException. Always pass e as the cause.
  • UncheckedIOException is the standard unchecked wrapper, for use inside lambdas and streams.
  • NoSuchFileException (NIO) and FileNotFoundException (legacy java.io) mean the same thing. New code should use Files/Path.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why does catch order matter? The first matching block wins. Putting IOException before NoSuchFileException makes the specific block unreachable, and the compiler rejects it.
  • How do you rethrow while keeping the original stack trace? Use throw e; to rethrow as-is, or throw new X("msg", e) to wrap. Never use throw new X(e.getMessage()), which loses the stack trace.
  • What does the "precise rethrow" feature (Java 7) do? In catch (Exception e) { throw e; }, if e is effectively final, the compiler knows it can only be the checked exceptions the try block actually throws. So the method can declare just those.
G29 Read a text file and count its words and lines.

Read the file line by line with a BufferedReader. Each line adds one to the line count, and splitting the trimmed line on \s+ gives its words.

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class G29 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path p = Path.of("sample.txt");
        Files.writeString(p, "Hello world\nJava is fun\n\nBye");
        long lines = 0, words = 0;
        try (BufferedReader br = Files.newBufferedReader(p)) {
            String line;
            while ((line = br.readLine()) != null) {
                lines++;
                String t = line.trim();
                if (!t.isEmpty()) words += t.split("\\s+").length;
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Lines: " + lines + ", Words: " + words);
    }
}
// Output: Lines: 4, Words: 6

Note: O(n) in file size. Check for blank lines, because "".split("\\s+") returns 1 element.

Approach. Stream the file with Files.lines(path, UTF_8) inside try-with-resources. It reads lazily, one line at a time, so memory use is bounded by the longest line, not the file size. Each line adds one to the line count. To count words, strip the line and split it on the regex \s+. Stripping first matters: leading whitespace would otherwise produce an empty first token. Blank lines add zero words. The results come back as a record.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class WordLineCounter {

    record Stats(long lines, long words, long chars, long blankLines) { }

    private static final Pattern WHITESPACE = Pattern.compile("\\s+");   // compile once, reuse

    static Stats count(Path file) throws IOException {
        long lines = 0, words = 0, chars = 0, blank = 0;
        try (Stream<String> stream = Files.lines(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            Iterator<String> it = stream.iterator();
            while (it.hasNext()) {
                String line = it.next();
                lines++;
                chars += line.length();                  // excludes line terminators
                String trimmed = line.strip();
                if (trimmed.isEmpty()) {
                    blank++;
                    continue;
                }
                words += WHITESPACE.split(trimmed).length;
            }
        } catch (UncheckedIOException e) {
            throw e.getCause();                          // e.g. MalformedInputException mid-stream
        }
        return new Stats(lines, words, chars, blank);
    }

    // Pure-stream version when you only need the word count.
    static long countWords(Path file) throws IOException {
        try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            return lines.map(String::strip)
                        .filter(l -> !l.isEmpty())
                        .mapToLong(l -> WHITESPACE.split(l).length)
                        .sum();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path file = args.length > 0 ? Path.of(args[0]) : Files.createTempFile("words", ".txt");
        boolean demo = args.length == 0;
        try {
            if (demo) {
                Files.writeString(file, "Hello world\n\n  Java   streams are   lazy  \nlast line");
            }
            System.out.println(count(file));        // Stats[lines=4, words=8, chars=49, blankLines=1]
            System.out.println(countWords(file));   // 8
        } finally {
            if (demo) {
                Files.deleteIfExists(file);
            }
        }

        try {
            count(Path.of("does-not-exist.txt"));
        } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
            System.out.println("No such file: " + e.getFile());   // No such file: does-not-exist.txt
        }
    }
}

Complexity. Time is O(total characters). Memory is O(longest line). By contrast, Files.readAllLines or readString load the whole file into memory, which is fine for small files and an OutOfMemoryError risk for multi-GB logs.

Edge cases.

  • An empty file gives 0 lines and 0 words.
  • A missing trailing newline: the last line is still counted. Unix wc -l counts newline characters instead, so its answer differs by one for such files.
  • Blank and whitespace-only lines count as lines but contribute zero words.
  • Several spaces or tabs between words are absorbed by \s+.
  • Encoding: Files.lines decodes UTF-8 strictly. Bad bytes surface as UncheckedIOException (wrapping MalformedInputException) during iteration, which is why the code unwraps it. If the file uses another encoding, pass the correct Charset.
  • Unicode whitespace: by default \s matches only ASCII whitespace, while strip() is Unicode-aware. Use Pattern.compile("\\s+", Pattern.UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS) if non-breaking spaces matter.

Design notes.

  • Always close the stream. Files.lines holds an open file handle until the stream is closed, so it must be in try-with-resources. Forgetting this leaks file descriptors.
  • One pass. An iterator over the stream keeps several counters in a single pass. Doing it with two streams would read the file twice.
  • Defining a "word". What counts as a word is a business rule. Tokens like don't and e-mail count as one each here. Ask the interviewer whether punctuation should split words; if so, use [^\p{L}\p{N}']+.
  • Large files. Files.lines(...).parallel() splits work poorly for line-oriented input before Java 9. Usually the job is I/O-bound anyway.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Find the most frequent words? flatMap(l -> WHITESPACE.splitAsStream(l.toLowerCase())), then groupingBy(identity(), counting()), then sort the entries by value and take the top k. A min-heap gives O(n log k).
  • BufferedReader instead of streams? try (BufferedReader r = Files.newBufferedReader(p)) { String line; while ((line = r.readLine()) != null) {...} }. It is equivalent and also lazy.
  • How do you count characters including newlines, or bytes? Files.size(p) gives bytes. For exact characters, read with a Reader into a char[] buffer.
G30 Append text to an existing file, and write a list of numbers to a file.

Use StandardOpenOption.APPEND (with CREATE) to append. To write the numbers, use a BufferedWriter from Files.newBufferedWriter.

import java.io.BufferedWriter;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption;
import java.util.List;

public class G30 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path log = Path.of("log.txt");
        Files.writeString(log, "first\n");                       // overwrite / create
        Files.writeString(log, "appended\n",
                StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.APPEND);
        System.out.print(Files.readString(log));

        Path nums = Path.of("numbers.txt");
        try (BufferedWriter w = Files.newBufferedWriter(nums)) {
            for (int n : List.of(10, 20, 30)) { w.write(String.valueOf(n)); w.newLine(); }
        }
        System.out.println(Files.readAllLines(nums));
    }
}
// Output:
// first
// appended
// [10, 20, 30]

Note: if you leave out APPEND, the default options are CREATE, TRUNCATE_EXISTING and WRITE, so the file is overwritten. w.write(int) writes a char, not the number, so convert with String.valueOf first.

Approach. Use Files.writeString with StandardOpenOption.CREATE, APPEND to append text, creating the file if it doesn't exist. Use Files.write(path, lines) to write a list of numbers, after converting them to strings. Its default options are CREATE, TRUNCATE_EXISTING, WRITE, so it overwrites. When writing many small pieces, use a BufferedWriter from Files.newBufferedWriter inside try-with-resources. Always pass an explicit charset.

import java.io.BufferedWriter;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.FileAlreadyExistsException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

import static java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption.APPEND;
import static java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption.CREATE;
import static java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption.CREATE_NEW;

public class FileWriteDemo {

    static final String NL = System.lineSeparator();

    static void appendLine(Path file, String text) throws IOException {
        Files.writeString(file, text + NL, StandardCharsets.UTF_8, CREATE, APPEND);
    }

    static void writeNumbers(Path file, List<Integer> numbers) throws IOException {
        List<String> lines = numbers.stream().map(String::valueOf).toList();
        Files.write(file, lines, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);          // CREATE + TRUNCATE_EXISTING + WRITE
    }

    static void appendSquares(Path file, int from, int to) throws IOException {
        try (BufferedWriter w = Files.newBufferedWriter(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8, CREATE, APPEND)) {
            for (int i = from; i <= to; i++) {
                w.write(i + "^2 = " + (i * i));
                w.newLine();
            }
        }   // close() flushes the buffer
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path dir = Files.createTempDirectory("g30");
        try {
            // 1. Append to an existing file
            Path log = dir.resolve("log.txt");
            Files.writeString(log, "first line" + NL, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);   // create / overwrite
            appendLine(log, "appended line 1");
            appendLine(log, "appended line 2");
            System.out.println("log.txt -> " + Files.readAllLines(log));
            // log.txt -> [first line, appended line 1, appended line 2]

            // 2. Write a list of numbers (overwrites each time)
            Path numbers = dir.resolve("numbers.txt");
            writeNumbers(numbers, List.of(10, 20, 30, 40, 50));
            System.out.println("numbers.txt -> " + Files.readAllLines(numbers));
            // numbers.txt -> [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
            writeNumbers(numbers, List.of(1, 2, 3));
            System.out.println("numbers.txt -> " + Files.readAllLines(numbers));
            // numbers.txt -> [1, 2, 3]          (old content truncated)

            // 3. BufferedWriter in append mode, called twice
            Path squares = dir.resolve("squares.txt");
            appendSquares(squares, 1, 3);
            appendSquares(squares, 4, 5);
            System.out.println("squares.txt -> " + Files.readAllLines(squares));
            // squares.txt -> [1^2 = 1, 2^2 = 4, 3^2 = 9, 4^2 = 16, 5^2 = 25]

            // 4. Option semantics
            try {
                Files.writeString(log, "x", CREATE_NEW);
            } catch (FileAlreadyExistsException e) {
                System.out.println("CREATE_NEW failed: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
                // CREATE_NEW failed: FileAlreadyExistsException
            }
            try {
                Files.writeString(dir.resolve("absent.txt"), "x", APPEND);       // APPEND without CREATE
            } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
                System.out.println("APPEND without CREATE failed: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
                // APPEND without CREATE failed: NoSuchFileException
            }
        } finally {
            try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(dir)) {
                for (Path p : (Iterable<Path>) files::iterator) {
                    Files.delete(p);
                }
            }
            Files.delete(dir);
        }
    }
}

Edge cases.

  • APPEND without CREATE fails on a missing file (NoSuchFileException).
  • CREATE_NEW fails if the file exists. That makes it useful as an atomic "create only once" or lock-file check.
  • A missing parent directory throws NoSuchFileException. Call Files.createDirectories(file.getParent()) first.
  • Line separators: System.lineSeparator() and newLine() write \r\n on Windows. If the file is consumed on other platforms, write "\n" explicitly.
  • The trailing newline: Files.write(path, lines) adds a line separator after every line, including the last.

Design notes.

  • writeString vs write vs BufferedWriter.
    • writeString and write(lines) open, write and close in a single call, which suits small payloads.
    • Calling appendLine in a loop of 10,000 iterations would open and close the file 10,000 times. Use one BufferedWriter, or collect the lines and write them once.
  • Charset. Before Java 18 the default charset was platform-dependent: windows-1252 on many Windows machines. Files.* methods default to UTF-8, but FileWriter used the platform default. Being explicit avoids mojibake (garbled characters from decoding with the wrong charset).
  • Durability. close() flushes to the operating system, not necessarily to disk. Use StandardOpenOption.SYNC/DSYNC or FileChannel.force(true) when the data must survive a crash.
  • Safe overwrites. For atomic replacement, write to a temp file in the same directory, then call Files.move(tmp, target, ATOMIC_MOVE, REPLACE_EXISTING).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is appending thread-safe across processes? On POSIX, small O_APPEND writes are atomic per write() call, but interleaving across writers is still possible. Use FileChannel.lock() or a single writer thread.
  • How do you write numbers as binary instead of text? Use DataOutputStream(new BufferedOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(p))) with writeInt. It is more compact, but not human-readable.
  • PrintWriter vs BufferedWriter? PrintWriter adds printf/println, but it swallows IOExceptions. You must check checkError().
G31 Read a number from the user and print its square root.

Use Scanner to read the input, check it with hasNextDouble(), reject negative numbers, then call Math.sqrt.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class G31 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in)) {
            System.out.print("Enter a number: ");
            if (!sc.hasNextDouble()) { System.out.println("Not a number"); return; }
            double n = sc.nextDouble();
            if (n < 0) System.out.println("Negative input: no real root");
            else System.out.printf("sqrt(%.2f) = %.4f%n", n, Math.sqrt(n));
        }
    }
}
// Input: 20
// Output: Enter a number: sqrt(20.00) = 4.4721

Note: Math.sqrt(-1) returns NaN and does not throw, so check for negatives yourself.

Approach. Wrap System.in in a Scanner set to Locale.ROOT, so the decimal separator is always .. In a loop, check hasNextDouble() before reading. If the token isn't a number, consume it with next() and report it, otherwise the same bad token would be read again forever. Reject negative input explicitly rather than printing whatever Math.sqrt returns: for negatives it returns NaN, not an exception. The program also reports the imaginary root as a bonus.

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.Scanner;

public class SquareRoot {

    static String fmt(double x) {
        return BigDecimal.valueOf(x).stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString();   // 9.0 -> "9", 2.5 -> "2.5"
    }

    static String describeSqrt(double x) {
        if (Double.isNaN(x) || Double.isInfinite(x)) {
            return "Please enter a finite number";
        }
        x = x + 0.0;                              // normalises -0.0 to 0.0 (Math.sqrt(-0.0) == -0.0)
        if (x < 0) {
            return String.format("%s is negative: no real square root (it is %.4fi)", fmt(x), Math.sqrt(-x));
        }
        double root = Math.sqrt(x);
        String exact = (root == Math.rint(root)) ? " (perfect square)" : "";
        return String.format("sqrt(%s) = %.4f%s", fmt(x), root, exact);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Math.sqrt(-9) = " + Math.sqrt(-9));   // Math.sqrt(-9) = NaN

        try (Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in).useLocale(Locale.ROOT)) {
            while (true) {
                System.out.print("Enter a number: ");
                if (!sc.hasNext()) {                               // EOF (Ctrl+D / Ctrl+Z)
                    System.out.println();
                    System.out.println("No input received.");
                    return;
                }
                if (!sc.hasNextDouble()) {
                    System.out.println("Not a number: " + sc.next());   // consume the bad token
                    continue;
                }
                double x = sc.nextDouble();
                System.out.println(describeSqrt(x));
                if (Double.isFinite(x) && x >= 0) {
                    break;                                         // done after one valid answer
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
/* Sample session:
Math.sqrt(-9) = NaN
Enter a number: abc
Not a number: abc
Enter a number: -9
-9 is negative: no real square root (it is 3.0000i)
Enter a number: NaN
Please enter a finite number
Enter a number: 2
sqrt(2) = 1.4142
   (another run)  Enter a number: 49   ->  sqrt(49) = 7.0000 (perfect square)
*/

Edge cases.

  • Non-numeric tokens are reported and skipped.
  • Negative numbers: Math.sqrt returns NaN, so the program handles them explicitly.
  • NaN and Infinity: Scanner accepts these strings as doubles, so check Double.isFinite.
  • -0.0: Math.sqrt(-0.0) returns -0.0, which would print as -0.0000, so the program normalizes it.
  • Locale: in a German locale, hasNextDouble expects 2,5, which is why the Scanner is pinned to Locale.ROOT.
  • End of input exits cleanly instead of throwing NoSuchElementException.

Design notes.

  • Validate before reading. hasNextDouble() followed by nextDouble() avoids catching InputMismatchException. If you do catch it, you must still call sc.next() to discard the token.
  • Closing the Scanner. Closing it also closes System.in. That is acceptable in main, but a helper method shouldn't close a Scanner it didn't create.
  • Precision. Math.sqrt is correctly rounded to the nearest double. For integers above 2^53, the double can't represent the input exactly. Use BigDecimal.sqrt(MathContext) (Java 9+) or BigInteger.sqrt() for exact integer square roots.
  • Keep logic separate from I/O. describeSqrt is pure, so you can unit-test it without simulating console input.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Square root without Math.sqrt? Newton's method: x_{n+1} = (x_n + a/x_n) / 2 until the change is below an epsilon. It converges quadratically. Binary search also works for integer roots.
  • Integer square root of a large long? (long) Math.sqrt(n), then adjust by ±1 for rounding, or BigInteger.valueOf(n).sqrt().
  • How do you read the whole line and parse it instead? Double.parseDouble(sc.nextLine().trim()) inside a try/catch (NumberFormatException). It rejects inputs like "2 3" that token-based reading would split.
G32 Calculate simple interest using input from the user.

SI = P x R x T / 100. Read the three values with Scanner and format the result to 2 decimal places.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class G32 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in)) {
            System.out.print("Principal, rate (% per year), time (years): ");
            double p = sc.nextDouble(), r = sc.nextDouble(), t = sc.nextDouble();
            double si = p * r * t / 100;
            System.out.printf("Simple Interest = %.2f, Total = %.2f%n", si, p + si);
        }
    }
}
// Input: 10000 5 2
// Output: Principal, rate (% per year), time (years): Simple Interest = 1000.00, Total = 11000.00

Note: non-numeric input throws InputMismatchException. Use BigDecimal for real money calculations.

Approach. Read the principal P, the annual rate R (as a percentage) and the time T (in years) as BigDecimal using Scanner.hasNextBigDecimal(). Re-prompt on non-numeric or out-of-range input: P and T must be positive, and R may be zero. Compute SI = P × R × T / 100 and do the division with an explicit scale and RoundingMode.HALF_UP, giving 2 decimal places for money. For comparison, also compute compound interest compounded annually, A = P(1 + R/100)^T, which is exact with BigDecimal.pow when T is a whole number.

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.MathContext;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.Scanner;

public class SimpleInterest {

    private static final BigDecimal HUNDRED = BigDecimal.valueOf(100);

    static BigDecimal simpleInterest(BigDecimal p, BigDecimal r, BigDecimal t) {
        return p.multiply(r).multiply(t).divide(HUNDRED, 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }

    static BigDecimal compoundAmount(BigDecimal p, BigDecimal r, int years) {
        BigDecimal factor = BigDecimal.ONE.add(r.divide(HUNDRED, MathContext.DECIMAL128));
        return p.multiply(factor.pow(years)).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }

    static BigDecimal readAmount(Scanner sc, String prompt, boolean allowZero) {
        while (true) {
            System.out.print(prompt);
            if (!sc.hasNext()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Input ended");
            }
            if (!sc.hasNextBigDecimal()) {
                System.out.println("  Not a number: " + sc.next());
                continue;
            }
            BigDecimal v = sc.nextBigDecimal();
            if (v.signum() < 0 || (v.signum() == 0 && !allowZero)) {
                System.out.println("  Must be " + (allowZero ? "zero or positive" : "positive") + ": " + v.toPlainString());
                continue;
            }
            return v;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in).useLocale(Locale.ROOT)) {
            BigDecimal p = readAmount(sc, "Principal: ", false);
            BigDecimal r = readAmount(sc, "Rate (% per year): ", true);
            BigDecimal t = readAmount(sc, "Time (years): ", false);

            BigDecimal si = simpleInterest(p, r, t);
            BigDecimal total = p.add(si).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
            System.out.println("Simple interest  : " + si.toPlainString());
