            System.out.println("Total amount     : " + total.toPlainString());

            if (t.stripTrailingZeros().scale() <= 0 && t.compareTo(BigDecimal.valueOf(1000)) <= 0) {
                BigDecimal amount = compoundAmount(p, r, t.intValueExact());
                BigDecimal ci = amount.subtract(p).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
                System.out.println("Compound amount  : " + amount.toPlainString());
                System.out.println("Compound interest: " + ci.toPlainString());
                System.out.println("Extra vs simple  : " + ci.subtract(si).toPlainString());
            } else {
                System.out.println("(Compound comparison shown only for whole years up to 1000)");
            }
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
/* Sample session:
Principal: -500
  Must be positive: -500
Principal: 10000
Rate (% per year): 8
Time (years): 3
Simple interest  : 2400.00
Total amount     : 12400.00
Compound amount  : 12597.12
Compound interest: 2597.12
Extra vs simple  : 197.12

   (another run: P=10000, R=8, T=2.5 -> Simple interest: 2000.00, compound comparison skipped)
*/

Formula check. 10000 × 8 × 3 / 100 = 2400. For compound interest, 1.08³ = 1.259712, so A = 12597.12 and the compound interest is 2597.12. Compound earns 197.12 more because each year's interest itself earns interest.

Edge cases.

  • Negative principal or time is rejected.
  • A zero rate is allowed and gives an SI of 0.00.
  • Non-numeric input is re-prompted.
  • Fractional years work for SI. For compound interest they need Math.pow on doubles, or a monthly or daily compounding convention.
  • Huge T values are capped before calling pow.
  • End of input is reported cleanly.

Design notes.

  • Why BigDecimal. It represents decimal amounts exactly, so 0.1 is really 0.1. divide(HUNDRED, 2, HALF_UP) states the rounding policy explicitly.
  • Unbounded division. A plain divide(x) throws ArithmeticException when the decimal expansion doesn't terminate, as with 1/3. Always pass a scale or a MathContext.
  • Round once. Round only at the end. Rounding intermediate values accumulates error.
  • Banking rounding. Banks often use HALF_EVEN (banker's rounding) to avoid systematic upward bias. Ask the interviewer which policy to use.
  • Input format. Scanner.hasNextBigDecimal respects the locale, so pin it to Locale.ROOT, or parse with new BigDecimal(token). The calculation methods are pure and can be unit-tested without the console.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Compound interest with n compounding periods per year? A = P(1 + R/(100n))^(nT). Monthly compounding means n = 12. Continuous compounding is P·e^(RT/100).
  • Why not double? 1000 * 0.07 * 3 / 100 may print 2.1000000000000005. Errors also compound across many transactions.
  • How do you print with currency formatting? NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.of("en", "IN")).format(total) in Java 19+. In Java 17, use new Locale("en", "IN"). Indian grouping looks like ₹12,400.00.
G33 Implement a custom ArrayList class.

Store elements in an Object[]. When it is full, double its size with Arrays.copyOf. To remove, shift the later elements left with System.arraycopy.

import java.util.Arrays;

public class MyArrayList<T> {
    private Object[] data = new Object[4];
    private int size;

    public void add(T e) {
        if (size == data.length) data = Arrays.copyOf(data, size * 2);
        data[size++] = e;
    }
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public T get(int i) { check(i); return (T) data[i]; }
    public T remove(int i) {
        T old = get(i);
        System.arraycopy(data, i + 1, data, i, size - i - 1);
        data[--size] = null;                          // help GC
        return old;
    }
    public int size() { return size; }
    private void check(int i) { if (i < 0 || i >= size) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException("Index: " + i); }
    @Override public String toString() { return Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOf(data, size)); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyArrayList<String> list = new MyArrayList<>();
        for (String s : new String[]{"a", "b", "c", "d", "e"}) list.add(s);   // triggers resize
        list.remove(1);
        System.out.println(list + " size=" + list.size() + " get(0)=" + list.get(0));
    }
}
// Output: [a, c, d, e] size=4 get(0)=a

Note: add is amortized O(1). get is O(1). remove(i) is O(n) because it shifts elements.

Approach. Back the list with an Object[] plus a size counter. You can't create a new E[] because of type erasure, so the array is Object[] and get casts with @SuppressWarnings("unchecked"). add puts the element at elements[size++]. When the array is full, it grows to 1.5× (old + (old >> 1)) via Arrays.copyOf. remove(index) shifts the tail left with System.arraycopy and nulls out the freed slot so it can be garbage-collected. Every index-based method checks bounds. The class implements Iterable<E> with a fail-fast iterator, so it works in for-each loops.

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.ConcurrentModificationException;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;
import java.util.Objects;

public class MyArrayListDemo {

    static class MyArrayList<E> implements Iterable<E> {
        private static final int DEFAULT_CAPACITY = 10;
        private static final int MAX_ARRAY_SIZE = Integer.MAX_VALUE - 8;

        private Object[] elements;
        private int size;
        private int modCount;            // structural modifications, for fail-fast iteration

        MyArrayList() {
            this(DEFAULT_CAPACITY);
        }

        MyArrayList(int initialCapacity) {
            if (initialCapacity < 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Illegal capacity: " + initialCapacity);
            }
            elements = new Object[initialCapacity];
        }

        public void add(E e) {                               // amortized O(1)
            ensureCapacity(size + 1);
            elements[size++] = e;
            modCount++;
        }

        public void add(int index, E e) {                    // O(n): shifts the tail right
            if (index < 0 || index > size) {
                throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException("Index: " + index + ", Size: " + size);
            }
            ensureCapacity(size + 1);
            System.arraycopy(elements, index, elements, index + 1, size - index);
            elements[index] = e;
            size++;
            modCount++;
        }

        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        public E get(int index) {                            // O(1)
            Objects.checkIndex(index, size);
            return (E) elements[index];
        }

        public E set(int index, E e) {                       // O(1), not structural
            E old = get(index);
            elements[index] = e;
            return old;
        }

        public E remove(int index) {                         // O(n): shifts the tail left
            E old = get(index);
            int moved = size - index - 1;
            if (moved > 0) {
                System.arraycopy(elements, index + 1, elements, index, moved);
            }
            elements[--size] = null;                         // avoid memory leak
            modCount++;
            return old;
        }

        public boolean remove(Object o) {
            int i = indexOf(o);
            if (i < 0) {
                return false;
            }
            remove(i);
            return true;
        }

        public int indexOf(Object o) {
            for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
                if (Objects.equals(o, elements[i])) {        // null-safe
                    return i;
                }
            }
            return -1;
        }

        public boolean contains(Object o) { return indexOf(o) >= 0; }
        public int size()                 { return size; }
        public boolean isEmpty()          { return size == 0; }
        int capacity()                    { return elements.length; }

        public void clear() {
            Arrays.fill(elements, 0, size, null);
            size = 0;
            modCount++;
        }

        private void ensureCapacity(int minCapacity) {
            if (minCapacity <= elements.length) {
                return;
            }
            if (minCapacity < 0 || minCapacity > MAX_ARRAY_SIZE) {
                throw new OutOfMemoryError("Required array size too large");
            }
            int oldCapacity = elements.length;
            int newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1);   // grow by 1.5x
            if (newCapacity < minCapacity) {                       // covers capacity 0/1 and int overflow
                newCapacity = minCapacity;
            }
            if (newCapacity > MAX_ARRAY_SIZE) {
                newCapacity = MAX_ARRAY_SIZE;
            }
            elements = Arrays.copyOf(elements, newCapacity);
        }

        @Override
        public Iterator<E> iterator() {
            return new Iterator<>() {
                private int cursor;
                private int lastReturned = -1;
                private int expectedModCount = modCount;

                @Override
                public boolean hasNext() {
                    return cursor < size;
                }

                @Override
                public E next() {
                    checkForComodification();
                    if (cursor >= size) {
                        throw new NoSuchElementException();
                    }
                    lastReturned = cursor++;
                    return get(lastReturned);
                }

                @Override
                public void remove() {
                    if (lastReturned < 0) {
                        throw new IllegalStateException("next() not called, or remove() already called");
                    }
                    checkForComodification();
                    MyArrayList.this.remove(lastReturned);
                    cursor = lastReturned;
                    lastReturned = -1;
                    expectedModCount = modCount;
                }

                private void checkForComodification() {
                    if (modCount != expectedModCount) {
                        throw new ConcurrentModificationException();
                    }
                }
            };
        }

        @Override
        public String toString() {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("[");
            for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
                if (i > 0) {
                    sb.append(", ");
                }
                sb.append(elements[i]);
            }
            return sb.append(']').toString();
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyArrayList<String> list = new MyArrayList<>(2);
        for (String s : new String[] {"a", "b", "c", "d", "e"}) {
            list.add(s);
        }
        System.out.println(list + " size=" + list.size() + " capacity=" + list.capacity());
        // [a, b, c, d, e] size=5 capacity=6      (2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 6)

        list.add(1, "X");
        System.out.println(list);                                     // [a, X, b, c, d, e]
        System.out.println("removed " + list.remove(2) + " -> " + list);   // removed b -> [a, X, c, d, e]
        System.out.println("remove(\"X\") = " + list.remove("X") + " -> " + list); // remove("X") = true -> [a, c, d, e]
        System.out.println("set(0) replaced " + list.set(0, "A") + " -> " + list); // set(0) replaced a -> [A, c, d, e]
        System.out.println("contains d? " + list.contains("d") + ", indexOf zz = " + list.indexOf("zz"));
        // contains d? true, indexOf zz = -1

        for (String s : list) {                                       // Iterable -> for-each
            System.out.print(s + " ");
        }
        System.out.println();                                         // A c d e

        Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();
        while (it.hasNext()) {
            if (it.next().equals("d")) {
                it.remove();                                          // safe removal during iteration
            }
        }
        System.out.println("after iterator remove -> " + list);      // after iterator remove -> [A, c, e]

        try {
            list.get(10);
        } catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
            System.out.println("IndexOutOfBoundsException: " + e.getMessage());
            // IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 10 out of bounds for length 3
        }

        try {
            for (String s : list) {
                if (s.equals("A")) {
                    list.remove(s);                                   // structural change mid-iteration
                }
            }
        } catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
            System.out.println("ConcurrentModificationException caught");
        }

        MyArrayList<Integer> nums = new MyArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
            nums.add(i);
        }
        long sum = 0;
        for (int n : nums) {
            sum += n;
        }
        System.out.println("sum of 1,000,000 ints = " + sum);        // sum of 1,000,000 ints = 499999500000
    }
}

Complexity.

Operation Cost
get, set, size O(1)
add(e) at the end amortized O(1)
add(index, e), remove(index), indexOf, remove(Object) O(n), because of shifting or scanning
Space O(capacity), which is at most about 1.5 × size after growth

Why add is amortized O(1). A resize copies every element, which costs O(n). But resizes happen at geometrically increasing sizes (c, 1.5c, 2.25c, …). Over n adds, the total copying is bounded by n × (1 + 1/1.5 + 1/1.5² + …) = 3n. That makes the average cost per add O(1), even though a single add can occasionally be O(n). If the array grew by a constant amount instead, say +10 each time, total copying would be O(n²).

Edge cases.

  • Initial capacity: capacity 0 or 1 still grows, because newCapacity < minCapacity falls back to the minimum. A negative capacity is rejected.
  • Indexes: add(size, e) is valid and appends. get(size) throws.
  • null elements are allowed, and indexOf uses Objects.equals to handle them.
  • Overloaded remove: on a MyArrayList<Integer>, remove(1) removes index 1, while remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the value. The same trap exists in java.util.ArrayList.

Design notes.

  • Null out removed slots. Clearing elements[--size] is essential. Otherwise the array keeps references to removed objects and leaks memory.
  • Fail-fast iteration. modCount lets the iterator detect structural changes made outside it and throw ConcurrentModificationException. This is best-effort detection, not a thread-safety guarantee. Inside an iterator, remove must be qualified as MyArrayList.this.remove, because an unqualified call would resolve to Iterator.remove().
  • Thread-safety. The class isn't thread-safe. Wrap it with external locking, or compare with CopyOnWriteArrayList.
  • Going further. To get the full List<E> contract (equals, hashCode, subList, ListIterator) almost for free, extend java.util.AbstractList<E> and implement just get, size, set, add(int, E) and remove(int).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not E[] elements = new E[n]? Generics are erased at runtime, so the JVM doesn't know what E is when creating the array. (E[]) new Object[n] compiles, but it throws ClassCastException if the array ever leaks out as E[].
  • ArrayList vs LinkedList? ArrayList has O(1) random access and is cache-friendly. LinkedList inserts in O(1) only when you already hold the node, and it uses far more memory. ArrayList wins in almost every real workload.
  • How do you shrink the backing array? Add a trimToSize() that calls Arrays.copyOf(elements, size). Optionally shrink automatically when the list drops to a quarter of its capacity. Shrinking at half would cause thrashing near the boundary.
G34 Sort a list of objects using a custom comparator (including multiple criteria).

Build the comparator with Comparator.comparing, add more sort keys with thenComparing, and use reverseOrder() to sort a key descending.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

public class G34 {
    record Emp(String name, String dept, int salary) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Emp> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
                new Emp("Ravi", "IT", 50000), new Emp("Asha", "HR", 60000),
                new Emp("Kiran", "IT", 70000), new Emp("Meena", "HR", 60000)));

        list.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.salary(), b.salary()));   // single criterion
        System.out.println(list.stream().map(Emp::name).toList());

        Comparator<Emp> multi = Comparator.comparing(Emp::dept)          // dept asc
                .thenComparing(Emp::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())  // salary desc
                .thenComparing(Emp::name);                              // name asc
        list.sort(multi);
        list.forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.dept() + " " + e.salary() + " " + e.name()));
    }
}
// Output:
// [Ravi, Asha, Meena, Kiran]
// HR 60000 Asha
// HR 60000 Meena
// IT 70000 Kiran
// IT 50000 Ravi

Note: List.sort is a stable merge sort (TimSort), O(n log n). Use Integer.compare rather than a - b, which can overflow.

Approach. Build the comparator from small pieces: Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor) gives the primary key, and each thenComparing(...) adds a tie-breaker that is only used when the earlier keys are equal. If only one key should be descending, reverse just that key's comparator. Calling .reversed() at the end of the chain reverses every key. Comparable defines the type's single natural order. A Comparator is an external order, and you can have as many as you like.

import java.util.*;

public class CustomSortDemo {

    // Natural order = by name (Comparable). Other orders come from Comparators.
    record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary) implements Comparable<Employee> {
        @Override
        public int compareTo(Employee other) {
            return name.compareTo(other.name);
        }
        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return name + "/" + dept + "/" + salary;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
                new Employee("Ravi", "ENG", 95_000),
                new Employee("Asha", "ENG", 120_000),
                new Employee("Meera", "HR", 70_000),
                new Employee("Kiran", "ENG", 120_000),
                new Employee("Zoya", "HR", 85_000)));

        // 1. Natural order (Comparable)
        List<Employee> byName = new ArrayList<>(staff);
        Collections.sort(byName);
        System.out.println("By name     : " + byName);

        // 2. Multiple criteria: dept ASC, salary DESC, name ASC
        Comparator<Employee> multi = Comparator
                .comparing(Employee::dept)
                .thenComparing(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary).reversed())
                .thenComparing(Employee::name);
        List<Employee> sorted = new ArrayList<>(staff);
        sorted.sort(multi);
        System.out.println("Multi       : " + sorted);

        // 3. reversed() at the END reverses the whole chain
        sorted.sort(multi.reversed());
        System.out.println("Multi rev   : " + sorted);

        // 4. Null-safe key: employees with no department first
        List<Employee> withNull = new ArrayList<>(staff);
        withNull.add(new Employee("Neel", null, 50_000));
        withNull.sort(Comparator
                .comparing(Employee::dept, Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder()))
                .thenComparing(Employee::name));
        System.out.println("Nulls first : " + withNull);
    }
}
// Output:
// By name     : [Asha/ENG/120000, Kiran/ENG/120000, Meera/HR/70000, Ravi/ENG/95000, Zoya/HR/85000]
// Multi       : [Asha/ENG/120000, Kiran/ENG/120000, Ravi/ENG/95000, Zoya/HR/85000, Meera/HR/70000]
// Multi rev   : [Meera/HR/70000, Zoya/HR/85000, Ravi/ENG/95000, Kiran/ENG/120000, Asha/ENG/120000]
// Nulls first : [Neel/null/50000, Asha/ENG/120000, Kiran/ENG/120000, Ravi/ENG/95000, Meera/HR/70000, Zoya/HR/85000]

Complexity. List.sort uses TimSort: O(n log n) comparisons, O(n) extra space. It is stable, so elements that compare equal keep their original relative order.

Edge cases.

  • A null key throws NullPointerException unless you wrap the key comparator in nullsFirst/nullsLast. A null element also needs Comparator.nullsFirst(multi).
  • List.of(...) is immutable, and calling sort on it throws UnsupportedOperationException. Copy it into an ArrayList first.
  • With lambdas, type inference can fail: Comparator.comparing(e -> e.dept()).thenComparing(...) doesn't compile because e is inferred as Object. Use method references or write Comparator.<Employee, String>comparing(...).

Design notes.

  • Never write (a, b) -> a.salary - b.salary. The subtraction can overflow. Use Integer.compare or comparingInt.
  • Use comparingInt, comparingLong and comparingDouble to avoid boxing.
  • Make compareTo consistent with equals. Sorted collections rely on that (see G46).

Likely follow-ups:

  • Comparable vs Comparator? Comparable is one natural order built into the class (compareTo). A Comparator is an external, pluggable order, and you can define many of them.
  • How do you make only one key descending? Reverse that key's comparator: thenComparing(comparingInt(f).reversed()), or thenComparing(f, Comparator.reverseOrder()).
  • Is the sort stable? Yes. List.sort and Collections.sort are stable merge sorts (TimSort). Arrays.sort on primitives is dual-pivot quicksort and is not stable, but stability doesn't matter for primitives.
G35 Find the frequency of words in a text file using a HashMap.

Stream the lines, lowercase them, split on non-word characters, and count each word with Map.merge.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class G35 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path p = Path.of("words.txt");
        Files.writeString(p, "the cat and the hat\nThe end.");
        Map<String, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(p)) {
            lines.flatMap(l -> Arrays.stream(l.toLowerCase().split("\\W+")))
                 .filter(w -> !w.isEmpty())
                 .forEach(w -> freq.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum));
        }
        System.out.println(new TreeMap<>(freq));   // sorted only for display
    }
}
// Output: {and=1, cat=1, end=1, hat=1, the=3}

Note: O(n) in the number of words. Files.lines is lazy and must be closed, so it goes in try-with-resources.

Approach. Stream the file line by line with Files.lines so the whole file never has to sit in memory. Lower-case each line, split it on runs of non-word characters (\\W+) and drop the empty tokens. Count each word with map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum). To get the top N, sort the entries by count (descending) and then by word, and take the first N. The stream equivalent is groupingBy(..., counting()). The same counting idea is used on a string in B42.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class WordFrequency {

    // Classic HashMap + merge
    static Map<String, Integer> countWords(Path file) throws IOException {
        Map<String, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(file)) {          // closes the file handle
            lines.forEach(line -> {
                for (String w : line.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).split("\\W+")) {
                    if (!w.isEmpty()) {                            // leading punctuation -> ""
                        freq.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);
                    }
                }
            });
        }
        return freq;
    }

    // Stream version
    static Map<String, Long> countWordsStream(Path file) throws IOException {
        try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(file)) {
            return lines
                    .flatMap(l -> Arrays.stream(l.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).split("\\W+")))
                    .filter(w -> !w.isEmpty())
                    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));
        }
    }

    static List<Map.Entry<String, Integer>> topN(Map<String, Integer> freq, int n) {
        return freq.entrySet().stream()
                .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Integer>comparingByValue().reversed()
                        .thenComparing(Map.Entry.<String, Integer>comparingByKey()))
                .limit(n)
                .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path file = Files.createTempFile("words", ".txt");
        Files.writeString(file, "The quick brown fox. The lazy dog!\nThe fox jumps; the DOG sleeps.");

        Map<String, Integer> freq = countWords(file);
        System.out.println("All   : " + new TreeMap<>(freq));     // TreeMap only for stable printing
        System.out.println("Top 3 : " + topN(freq, 3));
        System.out.println("Stream: " + new TreeMap<>(countWordsStream(file)));

        Files.deleteIfExists(file);
    }
}
// Output:
// All   : {brown=1, dog=2, fox=2, jumps=1, lazy=1, quick=1, sleeps=1, the=4}
// Top 3 : [the=4, dog=2, fox=2]
// Stream: {brown=1, dog=2, fox=2, jumps=1, lazy=1, quick=1, sleeps=1, the=4}

Complexity. Counting takes O(W), where W is the number of words, with average O(1) per HashMap operation. Space is O(U) for U unique words. A full sort for top-N costs O(U log U). A min-heap (PriorityQueue) of size N brings that down to O(U log N).

Edge cases.

  • An empty file gives an empty map.
  • A line that starts with punctuation produces a leading "" token, so filter it out.
  • \\W is ASCII-only, so "café" splits into caf. Use (?U)\\W+ or [^\\p{L}\\p{N}']+ for Unicode, and to keep don't as one word.
  • Files.lines decodes as UTF-8 and throws MalformedInputException on badly encoded input. Pass a Charset explicitly if you need a different encoding.
  • Lower-case with Locale.ROOT. Otherwise the Turkish locale turns I into a dotless ı.

Design notes.

  • merge replaces the old containsKey/get/put pattern.
  • For concurrent counting, use ConcurrentHashMap.merge or a ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder>.
  • Always close Files.lines (try-with-resources). It holds an open file handle.

Likely follow-ups:

  • File too large for memory? Files.lines already streams the file. Only the map grows, and it is bounded by the number of unique words. If even that is too large, shard words by hash into separate files, or use an external sort.
  • How do you exclude stop-words? Add .filter(w -> !STOP_WORDS.contains(w)) with a Set.of(...) of the stop-words.
  • How do you get the counts sorted by word? Collect into a TreeMap: groupingBy(identity(), TreeMap::new, counting()).
G36 Generic class that stores any type of data.

Add a type parameter <T>. The compiler then checks the type on set and get, so no casts are needed. A bounded type (<T extends Number>) limits which types are allowed.

public class Box<T> {
    private T value;
    public Box(T value) { this.value = value; }
    public T get() { return value; }
    public void set(T value) { this.value = value; }

    static <N extends Number> double doubled(Box<N> b) { return b.get().doubleValue() * 2; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Box<Integer> i = new Box<>(42);
        Box<String> s = new Box<>("hello");
        int n = i.get();                       // no cast needed
        System.out.println((n + 1) + " " + s.get().toUpperCase() + " " + doubled(i));
        // s.set(5);  // compile error: type safety
    }
}
// Output: 43 HELLO 84.0

Note: type erasure removes generics at runtime, so new T() and T[] creation are not allowed.

Approach. Declare a type parameter T on the class and use it for the field, the constructor and the accessors. The compiler then checks every use, and no casts are needed at the call site. A bounded type parameter (<T extends Number>) restricts the allowed types, and in return you can call the bound's methods (doubleValue()) on T. The diamond operator (new Box<>(...)) lets the compiler infer the type argument.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class GenericDemo {

    static class Box<T> {
        private T value;

        Box(T value) { this.value = value; }
        T get() { return value; }
        void set(T value) { this.value = value; }
        boolean isEmpty() { return value == null; }

        // generic method on a generic class: transform Box<T> into Box<R>
        <R> Box<R> map(Function<? super T, ? extends R> fn) {
            return new Box<>(value == null ? null : fn.apply(value));
        }

        @Override public String toString() { return "Box[" + value + "]"; }
    }

    // Bounded type: only Number subtypes are allowed, so we can call doubleValue()
    static class NumberBox<T extends Number> {
        private final T value;
        NumberBox(T value) { this.value = value; }
        double doubled() { return value.doubleValue() * 2; }
        boolean isBiggerThan(NumberBox<? extends Number> other) {
            return value.doubleValue() > other.value.doubleValue();
        }
    }

    record Pair<K, V>(K key, V value) { }          // generic record, two type params

    static double sum(List<? extends Number> nums) { // wildcard: read-only "producer"
        double s = 0;
        for (Number n : nums) s += n.doubleValue();
        return s;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Box<String> s = new Box<>("hello");          // diamond infers <String>
        System.out.println(s.get().toUpperCase());   // no cast needed

        Box<Integer> i = new Box<>(42);
        System.out.println(i.map(x -> x * 2));
        System.out.println(i.map(n -> "n=" + n).get());

        NumberBox<Double> nb = new NumberBox<>(2.5);
        System.out.println(nb.doubled());
        System.out.println(nb.isBiggerThan(new NumberBox<>(1)));
        // NumberBox<String> bad = new NumberBox<>("x");   // compile error: String is not a Number

        Pair<String, Integer> p = new Pair<>("age", 30);
        System.out.println(p);
        System.out.println(sum(List.of(1, 2.5, 3L)));

        // Type erasure: both are the same runtime class
        System.out.println(s.getClass() == i.getClass());
        System.out.println(s.getClass().getName());
    }
}
// Output:
// HELLO
// Box[84]
// n=42
// 5.0
// true
// Pair[key=age, value=30]
// 6.5
// true
// GenericDemo$Box

Type erasure. Generics exist only at compile time. The compiler checks the types, inserts casts, and then erases T to its bound: Object for Box, Number for NumberBox. As a result:

  • You cannot write new T(), new T[n], instanceof Box<String> or T.class.
  • You cannot declare a static T field.
  • You cannot overload m(List<String>) with m(List<Integer>), because both erase to the same signature.
  • Primitives are not allowed (Box<int>). Use the wrapper types, which means boxing.

Edge cases.

  • Null values are allowed. map guards against them.
  • Raw types (Box b = new Box("x")) compile with an "unchecked" warning and lose all the type safety. Never use them in new code.

Design notes.

  • Follow PECS for wildcards: Producer extends, Consumer super. sum only reads from the list, so it takes ? extends Number.
  • If you really need the runtime type, pass a Class<T> token into the constructor.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why does List<Integer> not count as a List<Number>? Generics are invariant. If it were allowed, you could add a Double to a list of Integers through the List<Number> reference. Arrays are covariant, and that is exactly why ArrayStoreException exists.
  • What does <T extends Comparable<? super T>> mean? T must be comparable to itself or to one of its supertypes. This is the signature of Collections.max and sort.
  • How do you create a generic array? Cast: (T[]) new Object[n] (an unchecked cast), or use Array.newInstance(clazz, n) with a Class<T> token.
G37 Generic method to swap two elements in an array.

Declare the type parameter before the return type (<T> void swap(T[] ...)). The method then works for an array of any reference type.

import java.util.Arrays;

public class G37 {
    static <T> void swap(T[] arr, int i, int j) {
        T tmp = arr[i];
        arr[i] = arr[j];
        arr[j] = tmp;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Integer[] nums = {1, 2, 3, 4};
        String[] words = {"x", "y", "z"};
        swap(nums, 0, 3);
        swap(words, 0, 2);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nums) + " " + Arrays.toString(words));
    }
}
// Output: [4, 2, 3, 1] [z, y, x]

Note: O(1). It does not accept primitive arrays such as int[], because generics only work with reference types.

Approach. Declare the type parameter on the method, static <T> void swap(T[] a, int i, int j), so the method works for String[], Integer[], Employee[] and any other reference-type array. It validates the indices up front with Objects.checkIndex and swaps through a temporary variable. Generics can't range over primitives, so int[] needs its own overload. Java is pass-by-value, so you can't write a swap(a, b) that swaps two variables. You can only swap the slots of a container.

import java.util.*;

public class GenericSwap {

    static <T> void swap(T[] arr, int i, int j) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(arr, "array");
        Objects.checkIndex(i, arr.length);           // IndexOutOfBoundsException with a clear message
        Objects.checkIndex(j, arr.length);
        if (i == j) return;
        T tmp = arr[i];
        arr[i] = arr[j];
        arr[j] = tmp;
    }

    // Primitives need their own overload: int[] is NOT a T[] for any T
    static void swap(int[] arr, int i, int j) {
        Objects.checkIndex(i, arr.length);
        Objects.checkIndex(j, arr.length);
        int tmp = arr[i];
        arr[i] = arr[j];
        arr[j] = tmp;
    }

    // Generic method with a bound, for comparison: reverse using swap
    static <T> void reverse(T[] arr) {
        for (int l = 0, r = arr.length - 1; l < r; l++, r--) swap(arr, l, r);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] names = {"a", "b", "c"};
        swap(names, 0, 1);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(names));

        Integer[] boxed = {1, 2, 3};
        GenericSwap.<Integer>swap(boxed, 0, 2);     // explicit type witness (optional)
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(boxed));

        int[] prim = {10, 20, 30};
        swap(prim, 0, 2);                            // resolves to the int[] overload
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(prim));

        Double[] ds = {1.1, 2.2, 3.3, 4.4};
        reverse(ds);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(ds));

        List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
        Collections.swap(list, 0, 2);                // built-in for lists
        System.out.println(list);

        try {
            swap(names, 0, 5);
        } catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
// Output:
// [b, a, c]
// [3, 2, 1]
// [30, 20, 10]
// [4.4, 3.3, 2.2, 1.1]
// [z, y, x]
// Error: Index 5 out of bounds for length 3

Complexity. O(1) time and O(1) space per swap.

Why int[] does not work. A type variable can only stand for a reference type. int[] is an array of primitives, not Integer[], so no T makes T[] match, and the call fails with "no suitable method found". There is no autoboxing for arrays. The JDK writes a separate overload for each primitive array type (see Arrays.sort, Arrays.fill), and so should you.

Edge cases.

  • If i == j, the method does nothing.
  • A null array gives an NPE with a clear message.
  • Negative or too-large indices throw IndexOutOfBoundsException before any element is changed, so the array is never left half-modified.
  • Null elements swap fine.
  • Arrays are covariant (Object[] o = new String[2]), but swap can never cause an ArrayStoreException, because both values already came from the same array.

Design notes.

  • The XOR swap trick works only for integers and fails when i == j without the guard. The temporary-variable version is clearer and just as fast.
  • Collections.swap(List<?>, i, j) uses a wildcard and a private helper method. That technique is called wildcard capture.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Can you write swap(T a, T b) to swap two variables? No. Java passes references by value, so the method only swaps its local copies. You need a container: an array, a holder object or a list.
  • Where do you put <T> for a generic method? Before the return type: public static <T> void swap(...). It is independent of any type parameter on the class.
  • How do you call it with an explicit type? GenericSwap.<Integer>swap(arr, 0, 1). This is called a type witness.
G38 Multi-threaded program to count prime numbers in a range (with synchronization).

Split the range into chunks, one per thread. Each thread counts into a local variable, then adds its total to the shared counter through a synchronized method. join() waits for every thread before the total is printed.

public class G38 {
    private static int count = 0;
    private static synchronized void add(int n) { count += n; }   // guarded shared state

    static boolean isPrime(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        for (int i = 2; (long) i * i <= n; i++) if (n % i == 0) return false;
        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        int max = 100_000, threads = 4, chunk = max / threads;
        Thread[] ts = new Thread[threads];
        for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++) {
            int lo = t * chunk + 1, hi = (t == threads - 1) ? max : lo + chunk - 1;
            ts[t] = new Thread(() -> {
                int local = 0;
                for (int n = lo; n <= hi; n++) if (isPrime(n)) local++;
                add(local);                                         // one locked update per thread
            });
            ts[t].start();
        }
        for (Thread th : ts) th.join();
        System.out.println("Primes up to " + max + ": " + count);
    }
}
// Output: Primes up to 100000: 9592

Note: O(n·√n / threads). Without synchronized, count += n would be a race condition. AtomicInteger or ExecutorService with Futures are alternatives.

Approach. Split [from, to] into chunks. Each chunk becomes a Callable<Long> that counts the primes in its sub-range in a local variable and returns the count. The main thread sums the Future.get() results. Nothing is shared, so no locking is needed, and that is the best design. To show synchronization, the same work is also done with a single shared counter, in three versions: a synchronized method, an AtomicLong (CAS) and a LongAdder (striped cells, best when many threads write). An unsynchronized long[] shows the race condition. A parallel stream is the one-liner alternative.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;
import java.util.stream.LongStream;

public class PrimeCounter {

    static boolean isPrime(long n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        if (n < 4) return true;
        if (n % 2 == 0 || n % 3 == 0) return false;
        for (long i = 5; i * i <= n; i += 6) {               // 6k ± 1 trial division
            if (n % i == 0 || n % (i + 2) == 0) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    static long countRange(long lo, long hi) {
        long c = 0;
        for (long n = lo; n <= hi; n++) if (isPrime(n)) c++;
        return c;
    }

    // Approach 1: no shared state, Callable + Future
    static long countWithCallables(long from, long to, int threads)
            throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads);
        try {
            int chunks = threads * 4;                          // more chunks than threads -> better balance
            long size = Math.max(1, (to - from + chunks) / chunks);   // ceiling division
            List<Future<Long>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
            for (long lo = from; lo <= to; lo += size) {
                final long start = lo, end = Math.min(to, lo + size - 1);
                Callable<Long> task = () -> countRange(start, end);
                futures.add(pool.submit(task));
            }
            long total = 0;
            for (Future<Long> f : futures) total += f.get();  // get() also gives happens-before
            return total;
        } finally {
            pool.shutdown();
        }
    }

    // Approach 2: shared counter, onPrime must be thread-safe
    static void countWithSharedCounter(long from, long to, int threads, Runnable onPrime)
            throws InterruptedException {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads);
        long size = Math.max(1, (to - from + threads) / threads);
        for (long lo = from; lo <= to; lo += size) {
            final long start = lo, end = Math.min(to, lo + size - 1);
            pool.execute(() -> {
                for (long n = start; n <= end; n++) if (isPrime(n)) onPrime.run();
            });
        }
        pool.shutdown();
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) throw new IllegalStateException("timeout");
    }

    static class SyncCounter {
        private long count;
        synchronized void increment() { count++; }            // mutual exclusion + visibility
        synchronized long get() { return count; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        long from = 1, to = 1_000_000;
        int threads = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();

        System.out.println("Callable/Future : " + countWithCallables(from, to, threads));

        SyncCounter sync = new SyncCounter();
        countWithSharedCounter(from, to, threads, sync::increment);
        System.out.println("synchronized    : " + sync.get());

        AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong();
        countWithSharedCounter(from, to, threads, atomic::incrementAndGet);
        System.out.println("AtomicLong      : " + atomic.get());

        LongAdder adder = new LongAdder();
        countWithSharedCounter(from, to, threads, adder::increment);
        System.out.println("LongAdder       : " + adder.sum());

        long[] unsafe = {0};
        countWithSharedCounter(from, to, threads, () -> unsafe[0]++);   // data race!
        System.out.println("Unsynchronized  : " + unsafe[0]);

        long viaStream = LongStream.rangeClosed(from, to).parallel().filter(PrimeCounter::isPrime).count();
        System.out.println("Parallel stream : " + viaStream);
    }
}
// Output (typical; the unsynchronized number varies run to run):
// Callable/Future : 78498
// synchronized    : 78498
// AtomicLong      : 78498
// LongAdder       : 78498
// Unsynchronized  : 78231
// Parallel stream : 78498

Complexity. Trial division costs O(√n) per number, so about O(N√N) in total, divided across P cores. For large ranges, a (segmented) Sieve of Eratosthenes at O(N log log N) beats any amount of threading.

Why the unsynchronized counter is wrong. x++ is three steps: read, add and write. Two threads can read the same value and both write back value+1, and one increment is lost. Without a happens-before edge, a thread may also not see the other threads' writes at all. volatile alone does not fix this, because it gives visibility but not atomicity.

Synchronized vs AtomicLong vs LongAdder.

  • synchronized: takes a lock on every increment, so threads queue up.
  • AtomicLong: a lock-free compare-and-swap, but every thread retries on the same memory location (cache line).
  • LongAdder: spreads the increments across per-thread cells and adds them up in sum(). It is the fastest when many threads write often. sum() is not an atomic snapshot while writers are still running.

Edge cases.

  • from > to gives 0. Values below 2 are not prime.
  • The chunk size is clamped to at least 1.
  • Higher numbers cost more to test, so equal-sized chunks finish unevenly. That is why the Callable version uses threads * 4 chunks.
  • Use shutdown() together with awaitTermination(). Otherwise the pool's threads keep the JVM alive.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Which design is best? The local count plus a final reduce (Callable/Future, or a parallel stream). There is no contention at all. A shared counter only makes sense when you need live progress.
  • What is invokeAll for? It submits a collection of Callables and returns all their Futures once they are complete. It is a tidier way to write the same fan-out.
  • How about CompletableFuture? Use supplyAsync(() -> countRange(a, b), pool) per chunk, then allOf(...).join(), and sum the results with join().
G39 Producer-consumer problem with threads and a shared buffer (wait/notify, plus the BlockingQueue alternative).

In the bounded buffer, both methods are synchronized. Each one calls wait() inside a while loop until its condition holds, and calls notifyAll() after changing the buffer. With ArrayBlockingQueue, put and take do the blocking for you.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Queue;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;

public class G39 {
    interface Task { void run() throws InterruptedException; }
    static Thread start(Task t) {
        Thread th = new Thread(() -> { try { t.run(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } });
        th.start();
        return th;
    }

    static class Buffer {
        private final Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private final int cap;
        Buffer(int cap) { this.cap = cap; }
        synchronized void put(int v) throws InterruptedException {
            while (q.size() == cap) wait();          // full -> wait
            q.add(v); notifyAll();
        }
        synchronized int take() throws InterruptedException {
            while (q.isEmpty()) wait();              // empty -> wait
            int v = q.poll(); notifyAll(); return v;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Buffer buf = new Buffer(2);
        Thread p = start(() -> { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) buf.put(i); });
        Thread c = start(() -> { int s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) s += buf.take(); System.out.println("wait/notify sum = " + s); });
        p.join(); c.join();

        BlockingQueue<Integer> bq = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);
        Thread p2 = start(() -> { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) bq.put(i); bq.put(-1); });   // -1 = poison pill
        Thread c2 = start(() -> { int s = 0, v; while ((v = bq.take()) != -1) s += v; System.out.println("BlockingQueue sum = " + s); });
        p2.join(); c2.join();
    }
}
// Output:
// wait/notify sum = 15
// BlockingQueue sum = 15

Note: call wait() in a while loop, not an if, because of spurious wakeups. wait/notify must be called while holding the object's monitor.

Approach. The shared bounded buffer is guarded by one lock. put waits while the buffer is full, and take waits while it is empty. Both call notifyAll() after changing the state. The waits must be inside while loops, not if: a thread can wake up spuriously, or another thread can grab the slot first, so the condition has to be re-checked after every wake-up. In production code you would use ArrayBlockingQueue, which implements this logic for you. To shut down, the producer sends a poison pill: a sentinel value, one per consumer.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class ProducerConsumer {

    // Version 1: hand-written bounded buffer with wait/notifyAll
    static class BoundedBuffer<T> {
        private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private final int capacity;
        private final Object lock = new Object();     // private lock: outsiders can't interfere

        BoundedBuffer(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

        void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
            synchronized (lock) {
                while (items.size() == capacity) {    // WHILE, not if (spurious wakeups)
                    lock.wait();                      // releases the lock while waiting
                }
                items.addLast(item);
                lock.notifyAll();                     // wake consumers waiting on "empty"
            }
        }

        T take() throws InterruptedException {
            synchronized (lock) {
                while (items.isEmpty()) {
                    lock.wait();
                }
                T item = items.removeFirst();
                lock.notifyAll();                     // wake producers waiting on "full"
                return item;
            }
        }
    }

    private static final int POISON = -1;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        waitNotifyDemo();
        blockingQueueDemo();
    }

    static void waitNotifyDemo() throws InterruptedException {
        BoundedBuffer<Integer> buffer = new BoundedBuffer<>(2);

        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
                    buffer.put(i);
                    System.out.println("Produced " + i);
                }
                buffer.put(POISON);                   // signal "no more data"
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // restore the flag
            }
        }, "producer");

        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                while (true) {
                    int item = buffer.take();
                    if (item == POISON) break;
                    System.out.println("  Consumed " + item);
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }, "consumer");

        producer.start();
        consumer.start();
        producer.join();
        consumer.join();
    }

    // Version 2: BlockingQueue, 1 producer, 2 consumers, one poison pill each
    static void blockingQueueDemo() throws InterruptedException {
        BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(3);
        int consumers = 2;
        AtomicInteger total = new AtomicInteger();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1 + consumers);

        pool.execute(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) queue.put(i);         // blocks when full
                for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) queue.put(POISON);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        });

        for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) {
            pool.execute(() -> {
                try {
                    while (true) {
                        int item = queue.take();                     // blocks when empty
                        if (item == POISON) break;
                        total.addAndGet(item);
                    }
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                }
            });
        }

        pool.shutdown();
        pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        System.out.println("Total consumed: " + total.get());
    }
}
// Output (the interleaving varies; the final total is always 55):
// Produced 1
// Produced 2
//   Consumed 1
//   Consumed 2
// Produced 3
// Produced 4
//   Consumed 3
// Produced 5
//   Consumed 4
//   Consumed 5
// Total consumed: 55

Key rules for wait/notify.

  1. You must hold the monitor of the object you call wait/notify on. Otherwise the call throws IllegalMonitorStateException.
  2. wait() atomically releases the lock and sleeps. It takes the lock back before it returns.
  3. Always check the condition in a while loop. Wake-ups can be spurious, and another thread may have consumed the slot before this one got the lock back.
  4. Prefer notifyAll here. Producers and consumers wait on the same monitor, so notify() can wake a thread of the wrong kind (a producer waking another producer), and then everyone ends up waiting.

Edge cases.

  • Interruption: catch InterruptedException and restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Don't swallow it.
  • With N consumers, send N poison pills. The pill must be a value that real data can never have.
  • A capacity of 0 would deadlock the hand-written buffer. For a direct hand-off, use SynchronousQueue instead.

Design notes.

  • ReentrantLock with two Conditions (notFull, notEmpty) lets you signal() only the right side. ArrayBlockingQueue is built exactly this way.
  • LinkedBlockingQueue uses separate put and take locks, which gives higher throughput. If no limit is given it is unbounded, which risks running out of memory.
  • offer(e, timeout, unit) and poll(timeout, unit) let you give up instead of blocking forever.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why are wait/notify defined on Object, not Thread? Every object can be a monitor (a lock), and waiting is tied to the lock, not to a particular thread.
  • sleep vs wait? sleep keeps every lock it holds. wait releases the monitor and has to be called while holding that monitor.
  • How do you stop without a poison pill? Call shutdownNow(), which interrupts the workers, or have consumers poll with a timeout and check a volatile boolean running flag.
G40 Singleton pattern.

Make the constructor private and add a static accessor. Double-checked locking with a volatile field gives thread-safe lazy creation. A single-element enum is the simplest version and also holds up against serialization and reflection.

public class Singleton {
    private static volatile Singleton instance;      // volatile: safe publication
    private Singleton() {}

    public static Singleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {                      // 1st check, no lock
            synchronized (Singleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) instance = new Singleton();   // 2nd check
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(getInstance() == getInstance());
        System.out.println(Config.INSTANCE.url());
    }
}

enum Config {                                        // Effective Java's preferred form
    INSTANCE;
    String url() { return "jdbc:mysql://localhost/db"; }
}
// Output:
// true
// jdbc:mysql://localhost/db

Note: another option is the holder idiom (private static class Holder { static final Singleton I = new Singleton(); }), which is lazy and needs no locking.

Approach. A singleton makes sure only one instance of a class exists and gives global access to it. There are five common implementations, which trade off laziness, thread-safety and robustness:

  • Eager: created when the class is initialized.
  • Lazy synchronized: simple, but every call takes a lock.
  • Double-checked locking (DCL): needs volatile.
  • Bill Pugh holder: lazy and lock-free, thanks to the JVM's class-initialization guarantees.
  • Enum: Joshua Bloch's recommendation. The JVM blocks the reflection and serialization attacks automatically.
import java.io.*;
import java.lang.reflect.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

// 1. Eager: thread-safe because class init is thread-safe; not lazy
final class EagerSingleton {
    private static final EagerSingleton INSTANCE = new EagerSingleton();
    private EagerSingleton() { }
    public static EagerSingleton getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }
}

// 2. Lazy + synchronized: correct but every call takes a lock
final class LazySyncSingleton {
    private static LazySyncSingleton instance;
    private LazySyncSingleton() { }
    public static synchronized LazySyncSingleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) instance = new LazySyncSingleton();
        return instance;
    }
}

// 3. Double-checked locking: volatile is MANDATORY
final class DclSingleton {
    private static volatile DclSingleton instance;
    private DclSingleton() {
        if (instance != null) throw new IllegalStateException("Use getInstance()"); // reflection guard
    }
    public static DclSingleton getInstance() {
        DclSingleton local = instance;                 // one volatile read on the fast path
        if (local == null) {
            synchronized (DclSingleton.class) {
                local = instance;
                if (local == null) instance = local = new DclSingleton();
            }
        }
        return local;
    }
}

// 4. Bill Pugh holder: lazy, lock-free; readResolve keeps it singleton across serialization
final class HolderSingleton implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
    private HolderSingleton() { }
    private static class Holder {                      // loaded on first getInstance() call
        static final HolderSingleton INSTANCE = new HolderSingleton();
    }
    public static HolderSingleton getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
    private Object readResolve() { return getInstance(); }  // replace the deserialized copy
}

// 5. Enum: serialization-safe and reflection-proof for free
enum EnumSingleton {
    INSTANCE;
    private final AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
    public int next() { return counter.incrementAndGet(); }
}

public class SingletonDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("Eager same?  " + (EagerSingleton.getInstance() == EagerSingleton.getInstance()));
        System.out.println("Lazy same?   " + (LazySyncSingleton.getInstance() == LazySyncSingleton.getInstance()));
        System.out.println("Holder same? " + (HolderSingleton.getInstance() == HolderSingleton.getInstance()));
        System.out.println("Enum next:   " + EnumSingleton.INSTANCE.next() + ", " + EnumSingleton.INSTANCE.next());

        // Reflection attack on Eager: succeeds -> second instance
        Constructor<EagerSingleton> ec = EagerSingleton.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
        ec.setAccessible(true);
        System.out.println("Eager broken by reflection? " + (ec.newInstance() != EagerSingleton.getInstance()));

        // Reflection attack on DCL: blocked by the constructor guard
        DclSingleton.getInstance();
        Constructor<DclSingleton> dc = DclSingleton.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
        dc.setAccessible(true);
        try {
            dc.newInstance();
        } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
            System.out.println("DCL reflection blocked: " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        }

        // Reflection attack on enum: the JVM refuses
        Constructor<?> enumCtor = EnumSingleton.class.getDeclaredConstructors()[0];
        enumCtor.setAccessible(true);
        try {
            enumCtor.newInstance("FAKE", 1);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Enum reflection blocked: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        // Serialization round trip: readResolve preserves identity
        ByteArrayOutputStream bos = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (ObjectOutputStream oos = new ObjectOutputStream(bos)) {
            oos.writeObject(HolderSingleton.getInstance());
        }
        try (ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bos.toByteArray()))) {
            Object copy = ois.readObject();
            System.out.println("Holder same after deserialization? " + (copy == HolderSingleton.getInstance()));
        }
    }
}
// Output:
// Eager same?  true
// Lazy same?   true
// Holder same? true
// Enum next:   1, 2
// Eager broken by reflection? true
// DCL reflection blocked: Use getInstance()
// Enum reflection blocked: Cannot reflectively create enum objects
// Holder same after deserialization? true

Why DCL needs volatile. instance = new X() is not atomic: memory is allocated, the constructor runs, and the reference is assigned, and the JIT or CPU may reorder those steps. Without volatile, another thread can see a non-null reference to an object whose constructor hasn't finished. volatile creates a happens-before edge that prevents this. It has worked correctly since the Java 5 memory model (JSR-133).

Breaking a singleton and how to defend it.

  • Reflection: setAccessible(true) lets anyone call the private constructor. Defend with a guard in the constructor, or use an enum.
  • Serialization: every readObject creates a new instance. Defend with readResolve(), or use an enum.
  • Cloning: don't implement Cloneable, or have clone() throw.
  • Multiple class loaders: each class loader gets its own copy.

Spring difference. Spring's default singleton scope means one instance per bean definition per ApplicationContext, not one per JVM. The class can still be created with new elsewhere, and two contexts give you two instances. Spring does not make the bean thread-safe either. Keep singleton beans stateless.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Which singleton would you choose? An enum, unless the class has to extend another class. If it does, the holder idiom. In a Spring app, simply a Spring-managed bean.
  • Why is the singleton called an anti-pattern? It is hidden global state. It makes unit testing hard (you can't mock it easily) and couples classes tightly. Dependency injection solves the same problem more cleanly.
  • Is the eager one lazy at all? Partly. It is created when the class is initialized, which happens on first use of the class, not at JVM start. Any other static member access also triggers that initialization.
G41 Observer pattern.

The subject keeps a list of observers and calls each one when its state changes. Observers can subscribe and unsubscribe at runtime, which keeps them loosely coupled to the subject.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface Subscriber { void update(String news); }

class NewsAgency {                                   // the Subject
    private final List<Subscriber> subscribers = new ArrayList<>();
    void subscribe(Subscriber s)   { subscribers.add(s); }
    void unsubscribe(Subscriber s) { subscribers.remove(s); }
    void publish(String news)      { subscribers.forEach(s -> s.update(news)); }
}

public class G41 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NewsAgency agency = new NewsAgency();
        Subscriber a = n -> System.out.println("A got: " + n);
        Subscriber b = n -> System.out.println("B got: " + n);
        agency.subscribe(a);
        agency.subscribe(b);
        agency.publish("Java 17 released");
        agency.unsubscribe(a);
        agency.publish("Spring Boot 3");
    }
}
// Output:
// A got: Java 17 released
// B got: Java 17 released
// B got: Spring Boot 3

Note: java.util.Observer is deprecated since Java 9, so you write your own interface. Event listeners and pub/sub systems are real-world examples of this pattern.

Approach. A Subject keeps a list of Observers and calls each one when its state changes. Observers register and unregister at runtime, and the subject knows them only through an interface. This is loose coupling: the subject is closed for modification, and you add new behaviour by adding new observers. In modern Java, an observer is just a Consumer<T> lambda, and a generic event bus replaces the hand-written interfaces.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

public class ObserverDemo {

    // Classic GoF version
    interface Observer {
        void update(String symbol, double price);
    }

    interface Subject {
        void register(Observer o);
        void unregister(Observer o);
        void notifyObservers();
    }

    static class StockTicker implements Subject {
        // CopyOnWriteArrayList: safe if an observer unregisters during notification
        private final List<Observer> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
        private String symbol;
        private double price;

        public void register(Observer o)   { observers.add(Objects.requireNonNull(o)); }
        public void unregister(Observer o) { observers.remove(o); }

        public void notifyObservers() {
            for (Observer o : observers) {
                try {
                    o.update(symbol, price);
                } catch (RuntimeException e) {             // one bad observer must not break the others
                    System.out.println("Observer failed: " + e.getMessage());
                }
            }
        }

        void setPrice(String symbol, double price) {
            this.symbol = symbol;
            this.price = price;
            notifyObservers();
        }
    }

    static class PriceDisplay implements Observer {
        private final String name;
        PriceDisplay(String name) { this.name = name; }
        public void update(String symbol, double price) {
            System.out.println(name + ": " + symbol + " = " + price);
        }
    }

    static class AlertService implements Observer {
        private final double threshold;
        AlertService(double threshold) { this.threshold = threshold; }
        public void update(String symbol, double price) {
            if (price > threshold) System.out.println("Alert: " + symbol + " crossed " + threshold + " -> " + price);
        }
    }

    // Functional version: listeners are just Consumer<T>
    record PriceChanged(String symbol, double price) { }

    static class EventBus<T> {
        private final List<Consumer<? super T>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

        /** Returns a handle that unsubscribes the listener. */
        Runnable subscribe(Consumer<? super T> listener) {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () -> listeners.remove(listener);
        }

        void publish(T event) {
            listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(event));
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StockTicker ticker = new StockTicker();
        PriceDisplay display = new PriceDisplay("Display-1");
        ticker.register(display);
        ticker.register(new AlertService(1450.0));

        ticker.setPrice("INFY", 1500.0);
        ticker.unregister(display);
        ticker.setPrice("INFY", 1600.0);

        EventBus<PriceChanged> bus = new EventBus<>();
        bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("LOG " + e));
        Runnable cancel = bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("UI  " + e.symbol() + " @ " + e.price()));

        bus.publish(new PriceChanged("TCS", 3900.0));
        cancel.run();                                        // unsubscribe the UI listener
        bus.publish(new PriceChanged("TCS", 3950.0));
    }
}
// Output:
// Display-1: INFY = 1500.0
// Alert: INFY crossed 1450.0 -> 1500.0
// Alert: INFY crossed 1450.0 -> 1600.0
// LOG PriceChanged[symbol=TCS, price=3900.0]
// UI  TCS @ 3900.0
// LOG PriceChanged[symbol=TCS, price=3950.0]

Push vs pull. Here the subject pushes the data (symbol, price) to the observers. In the pull model, the subject passes itself (update(Subject s)) and each observer queries only what it needs. Push is simpler. Pull decouples the observers from the shape of the data.

Edge cases and pitfalls.

  • Lapsed listener (memory leak): an observer that is never unregistered stays reachable through the subject forever. Return an unsubscribe handle, as EventBus does, or use weak references.
  • Concurrent modification: if an observer unregisters itself while notifications are running, a plain ArrayList throws ConcurrentModificationException. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates over a snapshot, which suits lists that are read often and written rarely.
  • Exceptions: one throwing observer would stop the loop. Catch errors per observer.
  • Slow observers block the subject. Dispatch through an Executor to make notification asynchronous, but then the order of events is no longer guaranteed.
  • Registering the same observer twice gives duplicate notifications. Use a LinkedHashSet if that matters.

Spring note. Spring has the Observer pattern built in. You publish events with ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(...)) and listen with @EventListener methods. Add @Async for asynchronous listeners, and use @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) to react only after the transaction succeeds. java.util.Observable has been deprecated since Java 9.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Observer vs Pub/Sub? In Observer, the subject knows its observers directly, and the calls are synchronous and in-process. In Pub/Sub, a broker (Kafka, a message bus) sits between publishers and subscribers, so they don't know about each other and are often asynchronous and distributed.
  • Where does the JDK use it? Swing/AWT ActionListener, PropertyChangeListener, and java.util.concurrent.Flow (reactive streams) for back-pressured asynchronous streams.
  • How do you guarantee ordering? Notify synchronously in registration order (a List), or use a single-threaded executor.
G42 Lambdas to sort a list of strings, and a stream pipeline to filter and map a list.

list.sort takes a lambda or comparator chain. A stream pipeline is filter, then map, then a terminal operation such as toList() or Collectors.joining.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class G42 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("kiran", "Asha", "bob", "Meena"));
        names.sort((a, b) -> a.compareToIgnoreCase(b));
        System.out.println(names);
        names.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.<String>naturalOrder()));
        System.out.println(names);

        List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8);
        List<Integer> evenSquares = nums.stream().filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).map(n -> n * n).toList();
        System.out.println(evenSquares);

        String longUpper = names.stream().filter(s -> s.length() > 3)
                .map(String::toUpperCase).collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
        System.out.println(longUpper);
    }
}
// Output:
// [Asha, bob, kiran, Meena]
// [bob, Asha, Meena, kiran]
// [4, 16, 36, 64]
// ASHA, MEENA, KIRAN

Note: intermediate operations are lazy, and nothing runs until the terminal operation. Natural order puts uppercase letters before lowercase, which is why "Meena" sorts before "kiran".

Approach. Lambdas replace the anonymous Comparator classes: list.sort((a, b) -> ...). The Comparator factory methods (comparingInt, thenComparing, CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER) make the intent clearer still. A stream pipeline has three parts: a source (list.stream()), lazy intermediate operations (filter to keep elements, map to transform them, sorted) and one terminal operation (collect or toList()) that runs the whole pipeline. B5 covers the lambda and functional-interface theory.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class LambdaStreamDemo {

    static List<String> sortedCopy(List<String> src, Comparator<String> cmp) {
        List<String> copy = new ArrayList<>(src);   // List.of(...) is immutable, so copy before sorting
        copy.sort(cmp);
        return copy;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> fruits = List.of("banana", "Apple", "cherry", "date", "Fig", "elderberry");

        // Before Java 8: anonymous class
        List<String> old = new ArrayList<>(fruits);
        Collections.sort(old, new Comparator<String>() {
            @Override public int compare(String a, String b) { return Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length()); }
        });
        System.out.println("Anon by length  : " + old);

        // Lambdas / Comparator factories
        System.out.println("Natural         : " + sortedCopy(fruits, Comparator.naturalOrder()));
        System.out.println("Case-insensitive: " + sortedCopy(fruits, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER));
        System.out.println("Length, then A-Z: " + sortedCopy(fruits,
                Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)));
        System.out.println("Reverse (lambda): " + sortedCopy(fruits, (a, b) -> b.compareToIgnoreCase(a)));

        // Stream pipeline: filter -> map -> sort -> collect
        List<String> longUpper = fruits.stream()
                .filter(f -> f.length() > 4)          // keep
                .map(String::toUpperCase)             // transform
                .sorted()
                .collect(Collectors.toList());
        System.out.println("Long, upper     : " + longUpper);

        List<Integer> nums = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).boxed().toList();
        List<Integer> evenSquares = nums.stream()
                .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
                .map(n -> n * n)
                .toList();                            // Java 16+, unmodifiable
        int oddSquareSum = nums.stream().filter(n -> n % 2 != 0).mapToInt(n -> n * n).sum();
        System.out.println("Even squares    : " + evenSquares);
        System.out.println("Odd square sum  : " + oddSquareSum);

        String initials = fruits.stream()
                .map(f -> f.substring(0, 1).toUpperCase())
                .collect(Collectors.joining(",", "[", "]"));
        System.out.println("Initials        : " + initials);

        Map<Integer, List<String>> byLength = fruits.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length, TreeMap::new, Collectors.toList()));
        System.out.println("Grouped         : " + byLength);
    }
}
// Output:
// Anon by length  : [Fig, date, Apple, banana, cherry, elderberry]
// Natural         : [Apple, Fig, banana, cherry, date, elderberry]
// Case-insensitive: [Apple, banana, cherry, date, elderberry, Fig]
// Length, then A-Z: [Fig, date, Apple, banana, cherry, elderberry]
// Reverse (lambda): [Fig, elderberry, date, cherry, banana, Apple]
// Long, upper     : [APPLE, BANANA, CHERRY, ELDERBERRY]
// Even squares    : [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]
// Odd square sum  : 165
// Initials        : [B,A,C,D,F,E]
// Grouped         : {3=[Fig], 4=[date], 5=[Apple], 6=[banana, cherry], 10=[elderberry]}

Complexity. Sorting is O(n log n). Each filter or map step is O(n), but the stream fuses them into one pass: each element flows through the whole chain before the next one starts. sorted() is a stateful operation that has to buffer every element.

Edge cases.

  • The natural order of strings is by Unicode code unit, so all uppercase letters sort before lowercase ones ("Fig" < "banana").
  • Use a Collator for locale-aware ordering of accented text.
  • Calling sort on List.of(...) throws UnsupportedOperationException.
  • Stream.toList() returns an unmodifiable list. Collectors.toList() currently returns an ArrayList, but that is not guaranteed.
  • Null elements make String::length throw an NPE. Filter them out with Objects::nonNull first.

Design notes.

  • Lambdas can capture only effectively final local variables.
  • Keep stream lambdas side-effect free. Don't write forEach(list::add). Collect instead.
  • A stream can be consumed only once.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Is map executed if there's no terminal operation? No. Intermediate operations are lazy, and nothing runs until a terminal operation is called.
  • map vs flatMap? map turns each element into exactly one element. flatMap turns each element into a stream and flattens the results (for example, lines into words).
  • Method reference vs lambda? String::toUpperCase is shorthand for s -> s.toUpperCase(). Use it when the lambda only calls one existing method.
G43 Custom stack using an ArrayList.

Use the end of the ArrayList as the top of the stack, so push, pop and peek are all O(1) at the tail. Popping or peeking an empty stack throws EmptyStackException.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.EmptyStackException;

public class MyStack<T> {
    private final ArrayList<T> items = new ArrayList<>();

    public void push(T x) { items.add(x); }
    public T pop()  { if (isEmpty()) throw new EmptyStackException(); return items.remove(items.size() - 1); }
    public T peek() { if (isEmpty()) throw new EmptyStackException(); return items.get(items.size() - 1); }
    public boolean isEmpty() { return items.isEmpty(); }
    public int size() { return items.size(); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MyStack<Integer> s = new MyStack<>();
        s.push(1); s.push(2); s.push(3);
        System.out.println(s.pop() + " " + s.peek() + " " + s.size());
    }
}
// Output: 3 2 2

Note: all operations are O(1) (amortized for push). For production code, prefer ArrayDeque over the legacy, synchronized Stack.

Approach. Wrap a private ArrayList<T> and treat its end as the top of the stack, so push is add(e) and pop is remove(size - 1). Both are amortized O(1), because nothing has to shift. Popping or peeking an empty stack throws java.util.EmptyStackException. Composition (has-a list), rather than inheritance, hides the list's index methods, so callers can't break the LIFO order. That is the mistake java.util.Stack extends Vector made.

import java.util.*;

public class StackDemo {

    static class ArrayListStack<T> {
        private final List<T> items = new ArrayList<>();

        void push(T item) {
            items.add(item);                              // amortized O(1)
        }

        T pop() {
            if (items.isEmpty()) throw new EmptyStackException();
            return items.remove(items.size() - 1);        // O(1), no shifting
        }

        T peek() {
            if (items.isEmpty()) throw new EmptyStackException();
            return items.get(items.size() - 1);
        }

        boolean isEmpty() { return items.isEmpty(); }
        int size()        { return items.size(); }

        @Override public String toString() { return "bottom" + items + "top"; }
    }

    // Classic use: balanced brackets
    static boolean isBalanced(String s) {
        ArrayListStack<Character> st = new ArrayListStack<>();
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            switch (c) {
                case '(', '[', '{' -> st.push(c);
                case ')', ']', '}' -> {
                    if (st.isEmpty()) return false;
                    char open = st.pop();
                    if ((c == ')' && open != '(') || (c == ']' && open != '[') || (c == '}' && open != '{'))
                        return false;
                }
                default -> { }                            // ignore other characters
            }
        }
        return st.isEmpty();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ArrayListStack<Integer> stack = new ArrayListStack<>();
        stack.push(10);
        stack.push(20);
        stack.push(30);
        System.out.println(stack);
        System.out.println("peek = " + stack.peek());
        System.out.println("pop  = " + stack.pop());
        System.out.println("size = " + stack.size() + " " + stack);
        stack.pop();
        stack.pop();
        System.out.println("empty? " + stack.isEmpty());
        try {
            stack.pop();
        } catch (EmptyStackException e) {
            System.out.println("pop on empty -> EmptyStackException");
