        }

        System.out.println("{[()]} balanced? " + isBalanced("{[()]}"));
        System.out.println("([)]   balanced? " + isBalanced("([)]"));

        // Preferred built-in: ArrayDeque as a stack
        Deque<String> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();
        deque.push("a");
        deque.push("b");
        System.out.println("ArrayDeque pop = " + deque.pop() + ", peek = " + deque.peek());
    }
}
// Output:
// bottom[10, 20, 30]top
// peek = 30
// pop  = 30
// size = 2 bottom[10, 20]top
// empty? true
// pop on empty -> EmptyStackException
// {[()]} balanced? true
// ([)]   balanced? false
// ArrayDeque pop = b, peek = a

Complexity.

Operation Time
push amortized O(1), O(n) only when the array resizes
pop / peek / size / isEmpty O(1)
Space O(n)

If you used index 0 as the top, add(0, e) and remove(0) would shift every element, making each operation O(n).

Edge cases.

  • Pop or peek on an empty stack: you must choose between throwing an exception (as here, and Stack) and returning null (as ArrayDeque.peek and poll do). Document which one you chose.
  • Null elements are allowed here. ArrayDeque rejects them with an NPE.
  • This class is not thread-safe. Wrap the methods in synchronized, or use ConcurrentLinkedDeque or LinkedBlockingDeque.

Design notes.

  • Prefer Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(). It is faster than Stack, has no synchronization overhead, and push, pop and peek operate on the head.
  • On an empty deque, ArrayDeque.pop() throws NoSuchElementException, not EmptyStackException.
  • When iterating, Stack goes from bottom to top, while ArrayDeque goes from top to bottom.
  • Add a clear() method, and implement Iterable<T> if callers need to traverse the stack.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not use java.util.Stack? It extends Vector: every method is synchronized (slow), and it exposes get(i), add(i, e) and remove(i), which break the LIFO abstraction.
  • How do you implement getMin() in O(1)? Keep a second stack of running minimums, and push and pop it in step with the main stack.
  • How do you build a stack from two queues (or a queue from two stacks)? For a queue from two stacks, push onto an "in" stack. On dequeue, if the "out" stack is empty, move everything from "in" into it, then pop from "out". This is amortized O(1).
G44 Check whether a string is a palindrome using a LinkedList.

Load the letters and digits, lowercased, into a LinkedList. Then keep removing the first and last characters and comparing them until one or zero are left.

import java.util.LinkedList;

public class G44 {
    static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        LinkedList<Character> list = new LinkedList<>();
        for (char c : s.toLowerCase().toCharArray())
            if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) list.add(c);
        while (list.size() > 1)
            if (!list.removeFirst().equals(list.removeLast())) return false;
        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(isPalindrome("Madam") + " "
                + isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama") + " "
                + isPalindrome("hello"));
    }
}
// Output: true true false

Note: O(n) time and O(n) space. LinkedList is a doubly linked list, so removing from either end is O(1). Compare with equals, not ==, because the elements are boxed Character objects.

Approach. Put the normalized characters into a LinkedList<Character>: letters and digits only, lower-cased. LinkedList implements Deque, so both ends are O(1). Repeatedly remove the first and last characters with pollFirst() and pollLast() and compare them. The first mismatch means it is not a palindrome. If at most one character is left at the end, it is a palindrome. A two-pointer scan does the same work with O(1) extra space and is shown for comparison.

import java.util.*;

public class PalindromeLinkedList {

    static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        LinkedList<Character> chars = new LinkedList<>();
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) chars.addLast(Character.toLowerCase(c));
        }
        while (chars.size() > 1) {                       // stop when 0 or 1 chars remain
            if (!chars.pollFirst().equals(chars.pollLast())) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    // Same idea programmed to the Deque interface (ArrayDeque is the faster implementation)
    static boolean isPalindromeDeque(String s) {
        Deque<Character> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
        s.chars().filter(Character::isLetterOrDigit)
                 .forEach(c -> dq.addLast((char) Character.toLowerCase(c)));
        while (dq.size() > 1) {
            if (dq.pollFirst() != dq.pollLast().charValue()) return false;  // unbox to compare chars
        }
        return true;
    }

    // Baseline: two pointers, O(1) extra space
    static boolean isPalindromeTwoPointer(String s) {
        int l = 0, r = s.length() - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            char a = s.charAt(l), b = s.charAt(r);
            if (!Character.isLetterOrDigit(a)) { l++; continue; }
            if (!Character.isLetterOrDigit(b)) { r--; continue; }
            if (Character.toLowerCase(a) != Character.toLowerCase(b)) return false;
            l++;
            r--;
        }
        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] tests = {"racecar", "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama", "hello", "", "a",
                          "No 'x' in Nixon", "12321", "ab"};
        for (String t : tests) {
            System.out.printf("%-34s %-5b %-5b %b%n", "\"" + t + "\"",
                    isPalindrome(t), isPalindromeDeque(t), isPalindromeTwoPointer(t));
        }
    }
}
// Output:
// "racecar"                          true  true  true
// "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"   true  true  true
// "hello"                            false false false
// ""                                 true  true  true
// "a"                                true  true  true
// "No 'x' in Nixon"                  true  true  true
// "12321"                            true  true  true
// "ab"                               false false false

Complexity.

Version Time Extra space
LinkedList O(n) O(n): one node per char, about 40+ bytes each, plus boxing
ArrayDeque O(n) O(n), but a compact array
Two pointers O(n) O(1)

In the LinkedList version, pollFirst and pollLast are O(1) because LinkedList is doubly linked and keeps both first and last references.

Edge cases.

  • An empty string, or one with only punctuation, counts as a palindrome by convention. Say so explicitly in an interview.
  • A single character is a palindrome.
  • Case and punctuation are normalized away. Ask the interviewer whether they should be.
  • Characters outside the BMP (emoji, some CJK) are surrogate pairs. Comparing chars splits them, so work with s.codePoints() and a Deque<Integer> instead.
  • A null input returns false. Throwing IllegalArgumentException is another reasonable choice.

Design notes.

  • Compare Character objects with .equals(), not ==. == happens to work for cached values (0–127), but it compares object references.
  • Never index a LinkedList with get(i). Each call is O(n), so a loop of them is O(n²).
  • new StringBuilder(clean).reverse().toString().equals(clean) is the one-liner alternative.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you check whether a singly linked list (of nodes) is a palindrome in O(1) space? Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half, compare the two halves, then reverse it back to restore the list.
  • LinkedList vs ArrayDeque for a deque? ArrayDeque: better cache locality, no per-node allocation, generally faster. LinkedList accepts nulls and also implements List.
  • What if the input is a huge stream? You can't do it in one pass without storing the data. Use rolling hashes (forward and reverse) for a probabilistic check, or buffer the input.
G45 Phonebook using a HashMap.

Map each name, lowercased, to its number. put adds or updates an entry, get wrapped in Optional does the lookup, and remove deletes. A TreeMap copy prints the entries in sorted order.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class G45 {
    private final Map<String, String> book = new HashMap<>();

    void add(String name, String phone)  { book.put(name.toLowerCase(), phone); }   // add or update
    Optional<String> find(String name)   { return Optional.ofNullable(book.get(name.toLowerCase())); }
    boolean delete(String name)          { return book.remove(name.toLowerCase()) != null; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        G45 pb = new G45();
        pb.add("Ravi", "98450-11111");
        pb.add("Asha", "99000-22222");
        pb.add("Ravi", "98450-33333");                 // overwrites
        System.out.println(pb.find("RAVI").orElse("Not found"));
        System.out.println(pb.delete("Asha") + " " + pb.find("Asha").orElse("Not found"));
        new TreeMap<>(pb.book).forEach((n, p) -> System.out.println(n + " -> " + p));
    }
}
// Output:
// 98450-33333
// true Not found
// ravi -> 98450-33333

Note: add, find and delete are O(1) on average. To keep several numbers per name, use Map<String, List<String>> with computeIfAbsent.

Approach. Wrap a map from name to phone numbers in a small class with add, update, search, delete and list operations, and validate the input on the way in. There are two refinements over a naive HashMap<String, String>:

  • Case-insensitive names. Either normalize the key (toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)) before using a HashMap, or use a TreeMap with String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER. The TreeMap keeps the original spelling and lists names alphabetically.
  • Several numbers per name. Store Map<String, List<String>> and fill it with computeIfAbsent.

putIfAbsent gives you "add only if new" in a single call.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

public class PhoneBook {

    private static final Pattern PHONE = Pattern.compile("\\+?[0-9][0-9 -]{2,19}");

    // Case-insensitive keys, sorted listing, original casing of the first insert is kept
    private final Map<String, List<String>> contacts = new TreeMap<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);

    boolean add(String name, String number) {
        validate(name, number);
        List<String> numbers = contacts.computeIfAbsent(name.trim(), k -> new ArrayList<>());
        if (numbers.contains(number)) return false;      // no duplicate numbers
        numbers.add(number);
        return true;
    }

    boolean updateNumber(String name, String oldNumber, String newNumber) {
        validate(name, newNumber);
        List<String> numbers = contacts.get(name);
        if (numbers == null) return false;
        int idx = numbers.indexOf(oldNumber);
        if (idx < 0) return false;
        numbers.set(idx, newNumber);
        return true;
    }

    List<String> search(String name) {
        return List.copyOf(contacts.getOrDefault(name, List.of()));   // defensive, unmodifiable copy
    }

    List<String> searchByPrefix(String prefix) {
        return contacts.keySet().stream()
                .filter(n -> n.regionMatches(true, 0, prefix, 0, prefix.length()))
                .toList();
    }

    boolean deleteNumber(String name, String number) {
        List<String> numbers = contacts.get(name);
        if (numbers == null || !numbers.remove(number)) return false;
        if (numbers.isEmpty()) contacts.remove(name);    // don't keep empty contacts
        return true;
    }

    boolean deleteContact(String name) {
        return contacts.remove(name) != null;
    }

    void printAll() {
        if (contacts.isEmpty()) System.out.println("  (empty)");
        contacts.forEach((n, nums) -> System.out.println("  " + n + " -> " + nums));
    }

    private static void validate(String name, String number) {
        if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name required");
        if (number == null || !PHONE.matcher(number).matches())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid number: " + number);
    }

    static String key(String name) { return name.trim().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PhoneBook pb = new PhoneBook();
        System.out.println("add Asha #1  : " + pb.add("Asha", "+91-98450 11111"));
        System.out.println("add asha #2  : " + pb.add("asha", "+91-98450 22222"));
        System.out.println("add Ravi     : " + pb.add("Ravi", "080-2222333"));
        System.out.println("add ASHA dup : " + pb.add("ASHA", "+91-98450 11111"));
        System.out.println("search ASHA  : " + pb.search("ASHA"));
        System.out.println("update ravi  : " + pb.updateNumber("ravi", "080-2222333", "080-4444555"));
        System.out.println("prefix 'r'   : " + pb.searchByPrefix("r"));
        System.out.println("del number   : " + pb.deleteNumber("ASHA", "+91-98450 22222"));
        System.out.println("All contacts :");
        pb.printAll();
        System.out.println("delete ravi  : " + pb.deleteContact("ravi"));
        System.out.println("search Ravi  : " + pb.search("Ravi"));
        try {
            pb.add("Bob", "abc");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Error        : " + e.getMessage());
        }

        // Simple HashMap<String,String> variant with normalized keys + putIfAbsent
        Map<String, String> simple = new HashMap<>();
        System.out.println("putIfAbsent bob : " + simple.putIfAbsent(key("Bob"), "111"));  // null = inserted
        System.out.println("putIfAbsent BOB : " + simple.putIfAbsent(key("BOB"), "222"));  // existing value
        System.out.println("simple map      : " + simple);
    }
}
// Output:
// add Asha #1  : true
// add asha #2  : true
// add Ravi     : true
// add ASHA dup : false
// search ASHA  : [+91-98450 11111, +91-98450 22222]
// update ravi  : true
// prefix 'r'   : [Ravi]
// del number   : true
// All contacts :
//   Asha -> [+91-98450 11111]
//   Ravi -> [080-4444555]
// delete ravi  : true
// search Ravi  : []
// Error        : Invalid number: abc
// putIfAbsent bob : null
// putIfAbsent BOB : 111
// simple map      : {bob=111}

Complexity.

Map Lookup / insert / delete Listing
HashMap average O(1) unsorted
TreeMap O(log n) sorted, O(n)

Prefix search here scans all keys, which is O(n). A trie, or TreeMap.subMap(prefix, prefix + Character.MAX_VALUE) on lower-cased keys, makes it O(log n + k) for k results.

Edge cases.

  • Blank names and malformed numbers are rejected.
  • Null keys: HashMap allows one null key, but a TreeMap with a comparator throws an NPE. Validate before the lookup.
  • Leading and trailing spaces are trimmed on add, so do the same on lookup in production code.
  • When the last number is deleted, the contact is removed too.
  • search returns a copy, so callers can't change the internal list.
  • With the toLowerCase approach, "İstanbul" behaves differently under the Turkish locale, so always pass Locale.ROOT.

Design notes.

  • Store numbers in E.164 format (+919845011111) so that 98450-11111 and 9845011111 are recognized as duplicates.
  • For caller ID, add a reverse index Map<String number, String name>.
  • For concurrent use, switch to ConcurrentHashMap with computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()).
  • Persistence would go through JSON or a database. See G48 for why Java serialization is a poor choice.

Likely follow-ups:

  • put vs putIfAbsent vs computeIfAbsent? put always overwrites. putIfAbsent inserts a ready-made value only if the key is missing. computeIfAbsent builds the value lazily, only when the key is missing, which makes it ideal for "get or create the list".
  • Why choose TreeMap with CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER over lower-casing the keys? It keeps the user's original spelling ("Asha") and lists names alphabetically, at the cost of O(log n) per operation.
  • What happens if two keys have the same hashCode? They land in the same bucket and are told apart by equals. Since Java 8, a bucket that grows past 8 entries becomes a red-black tree, so even heavy collisions cost only O(log n) per lookup.
G46 Sort objects by multiple criteria using a TreeSet.

Pass a chained Comparator to the TreeSet constructor. The set stays sorted by marks descending, then name, then age.

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;

public class G46 {
    record Student(String name, int marks, int age) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Comparator<Student> cmp = Comparator.comparingInt(Student::marks).reversed()
                .thenComparing(Student::name)
                .thenComparingInt(Student::age);
        Set<Student> set = new TreeSet<>(cmp);
        set.add(new Student("Ravi", 85, 20));
        set.add(new Student("Asha", 92, 21));
        set.add(new Student("Kiran", 85, 19));
        set.add(new Student("Ravi", 85, 20));          // compare == 0 -> treated as duplicate
        set.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s.name() + " " + s.marks() + " " + s.age()));
    }
}
// Output:
// Asha 92 21
// Kiran 85 19
// Ravi 85 20

Note: add is O(log n). A TreeSet decides duplicates with the comparator, not equals. Without enough tie-breakers, two different objects that compare as equal are silently dropped.

Approach. Pass a multi-key Comparator to the TreeSet constructor, and the set stays sorted on every insert. The trap: a TreeSet decides uniqueness with the comparator, not equals. If compare(a, b) == 0, the set treats b as a duplicate of a and silently refuses to add it (add returns false). Every comparator used in a sorted set must therefore end with tie-breakers that tell apart any two elements you consider different, ideally down to a unique field.

import java.util.*;

public class TreeSetMultiSort {

    record Player(String name, int score, int age) {
        @Override public String toString() { return name + "(" + score + "," + age + ")"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Player> players = List.of(
                new Player("Asha", 90, 25),
                new Player("Ravi", 85, 30),
                new Player("Kiran", 90, 22),
                new Player("Meera", 70, 28),
                new Player("Dev", 85, 27));

        // BROKEN: compares only the score -> equal scores are "duplicates"
        TreeSet<Player> broken = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Player::score).reversed());
        for (Player p : players) {
            if (!broken.add(p)) System.out.println("Dropped as 'duplicate': " + p);
        }
        System.out.println("Broken (" + broken.size() + "): " + broken);
        System.out.println("broken.contains(Zed(90,99))? " + broken.contains(new Player("Zed", 90, 99)));

        // FIXED: score DESC, then age ASC, then name ASC (tie-breakers)
        Comparator<Player> byRank = Comparator.comparingInt(Player::score).reversed()
                .thenComparingInt(Player::age)
                .thenComparing(Player::name);
        TreeSet<Player> ranked = new TreeSet<>(byRank);
        ranked.addAll(players);
        System.out.println("Fixed  (" + ranked.size() + "): " + ranked);

        // NavigableSet operations
        System.out.println("Top      : " + ranked.first());
        System.out.println("Bottom   : " + ranked.last());
        System.out.println("Top 3    : " + ranked.stream().limit(3).toList());
        System.out.println("Reverse  : " + ranked.descendingSet());
        Player probe = new Player("", 85, 0);            // sorts just before every score-85 player
        System.out.println("Score>85 : " + ranked.headSet(probe));
        System.out.println("Score<=85: " + ranked.tailSet(probe));

        // Updating a sort key: remove, then re-insert (never mutate in place)
        ranked.remove(new Player("Dev", 85, 27));
        ranked.add(new Player("Dev", 95, 27));
        System.out.println("Dev -> 95: " + ranked);
    }
}
// Output:
// Dropped as 'duplicate': Kiran(90,22)
// Dropped as 'duplicate': Dev(85,27)
// Broken (3): [Asha(90,25), Ravi(85,30), Meera(70,28)]
// broken.contains(Zed(90,99))? true
// Fixed  (5): [Kiran(90,22), Asha(90,25), Dev(85,27), Ravi(85,30), Meera(70,28)]
// Top      : Kiran(90,22)
// Bottom   : Meera(70,28)
// Top 3    : [Kiran(90,22), Asha(90,25), Dev(85,27)]
// Reverse  : [Meera(70,28), Ravi(85,30), Dev(85,27), Asha(90,25), Kiran(90,22)]
// Score>85 : [Kiran(90,22), Asha(90,25)]
// Score<=85: [Dev(85,27), Ravi(85,30), Meera(70,28)]
// Dev -> 95: [Dev(95,27), Kiran(90,22), Asha(90,25), Ravi(85,30), Meera(70,28)]

Complexity.

Operation Time
add / remove / contains / first / ceiling O(log n) (red-black tree)
In-order iteration O(n)
Building the set O(n log n)
headSet / tailSet O(log n), because they return views, not copies

Edge cases.

  • The broken set lies to you: contains(Zed) returns true for a player who was never added, just because his score matches.
  • Mutating a field that the comparator uses, while the element is in the set, corrupts the tree, and later remove or contains calls fail. Use immutable records, and update by removing and re-adding.
  • Null elements throw an NPE unless the comparator is wrapped in nullsFirst.
  • If the comparator is consistent with equals (it returns 0 exactly when equals is true), TreeSet and HashSet agree on what counts as a duplicate. That is the ideal.

Design notes.

  • If duplicates by rank are legitimate (two players with identical data), either add a unique id as the final tie-breaker or use a List and call sort.
  • TreeMap has the same comparator-equality rule for its keys.
  • PriorityQueue does keep elements that compare as 0, but it only gives an ordered poll(), not an ordered iteration.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why did add return false? TreeSet is backed by a TreeMap, which calls compare and finds an existing key where the result is 0. It then treats the new element as already present and never calls equals.
  • How do you get the top K quickly? ranked.stream().limit(k), or iterate the set. Each next element in the in-order iteration costs amortized O(1).
  • TreeSet vs sorting a List? TreeSet stays sorted under continuous inserts and deletes and supports range queries. A sorted List is cheaper if you sort once, and it keeps duplicates.
G47 Store student records (name, roll number, marks) in a TreeMap sorted by roll number.

Use the roll number as the TreeMap key, so the map keeps entries sorted by key. Navigation methods such as firstKey and tailMap support range queries.

import java.util.TreeMap;

public class G47 {
    record Student(String name, int marks) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TreeMap<Integer, Student> map = new TreeMap<>();
        map.put(103, new Student("Kiran", 78));
        map.put(101, new Student("Asha", 92));
        map.put(102, new Student("Ravi", 85));

        map.forEach((roll, s) -> System.out.println(roll + " " + s.name() + " " + s.marks()));
        System.out.println("First: " + map.firstKey() + ", roll >= 102: " + map.tailMap(102).keySet());
        System.out.println("Roll 102: " + map.get(102).name());
    }
}
// Output:
// 101 Asha 92
// 102 Ravi 85
// 103 Kiran 78
// First: 101, roll >= 102: [102, 103]
// Roll 102: Ravi

Note: put and get are O(log n) because TreeMap is a red-black tree. Iteration is always in key order.

Approach. Model a student as an immutable record Student(int roll, String name, double marks) and store the students in a TreeMap<Integer, Student> keyed by roll number. The map stays sorted by key automatically, whatever the insertion order. On top of the usual map operations you get NavigableMap queries: firstKey and lastKey, the range views headMap, tailMap and subMap, the nearest-key lookups floorKey and ceilingKey, and descendingMap. Each is O(log n). Marks-based questions (topper, average) are answered with streams over values().

import java.util.*;

public class StudentRecords {

    record Student(int roll, String name, double marks) {
        Student {                                           // compact constructor = validation
            Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name");
            if (marks < 0 || marks > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("marks out of range: " + marks);
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return name + " (" + marks + ")"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TreeMap<Integer, Student> students = new TreeMap<>();
        for (Student s : List.of(
                new Student(105, "Ravi", 78.5),
                new Student(101, "Asha", 91.0),
                new Student(110, "Zoya", 66.0),
                new Student(103, "Kiran", 84.0),
                new Student(108, "Meera", 88.5))) {
            students.putIfAbsent(s.roll(), s);              // key derived from the value, so they stay consistent
        }
        boolean dupAdded = students.putIfAbsent(103, new Student(103, "Dup", 50)) == null;
        System.out.println("Duplicate 103 added? " + dupAdded);

        students.forEach((roll, s) -> System.out.println(roll + " -> " + s));   // ascending roll order

        System.out.println("firstKey=" + students.firstKey() + ", lastKey=" + students.lastKey());
        System.out.println("firstEntry  : " + students.firstEntry());
        System.out.println("headMap(105): " + students.headMap(105).keySet());              // < 105
        System.out.println("tailMap(105): " + students.tailMap(105).keySet());              // >= 105
        System.out.println("subMap 102..108: " + students.subMap(102, true, 108, true).keySet());
        System.out.println("descending  : " + students.descendingMap().keySet());
        System.out.println("floor(104)=" + students.floorKey(104) + ", ceiling(104)=" + students.ceilingKey(104)
                + ", higher(110)=" + students.higherKey(110));

        // Marks-based queries: streams over the values
        Student topper = students.values().stream()
                .max(Comparator.comparingDouble(Student::marks)).orElseThrow();
        System.out.println("Topper      : " + topper);
        System.out.println("By marks    : " + students.values().stream()
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Student::marks).reversed())
                .map(Student::name).toList());
        System.out.printf("Average     : %.2f%n",
                students.values().stream().mapToDouble(Student::marks).average().orElse(0));

        // Update (records are immutable -> replace) and delete
        students.computeIfPresent(110, (roll, s) -> new Student(roll, s.name(), 72.0));
        System.out.println("Updated 110 : " + students.get(110));
        System.out.println("Removed 105 : " + students.remove(105));
        System.out.println("Rolls now   : " + students.keySet());
    }
}
// Output:
// Duplicate 103 added? false
// 101 -> Asha (91.0)
// 103 -> Kiran (84.0)
// 105 -> Ravi (78.5)
// 108 -> Meera (88.5)
// 110 -> Zoya (66.0)
// firstKey=101, lastKey=110
// firstEntry  : 101=Asha (91.0)
// headMap(105): [101, 103]
// tailMap(105): [105, 108, 110]
// subMap 102..108: [103, 105, 108]
// descending  : [110, 108, 105, 103, 101]
// floor(104)=103, ceiling(104)=105, higher(110)=null
// Topper      : Asha (91.0)
// By marks    : [Asha, Meera, Kiran, Ravi, Zoya]
// Average     : 81.60
// Updated 110 : Zoya (72.0)
// Removed 105 : Ravi (78.5)
// Rolls now   : [101, 103, 108, 110]

Complexity.

Operation Time
put / get / remove / firstKey / floorKey / ceilingKey O(log n) (red-black tree)
Full iteration O(n)
Creating a range view O(log n), then O(k) to iterate it
Topper / average O(n)

For comparison, a HashMap gives O(1) get but no ordering, and a LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order, not key order.

Edge cases.

  • An empty map: firstKey() and lastKey() throw NoSuchElementException, while firstEntry() returns null. Pick the method based on how you want to handle the empty case.
  • floorKey and ceilingKey return null when nothing matches. Use Integer, not int, to hold the result, or you get an NPE when it unboxes.
  • A duplicate roll number: put silently overwrites, while putIfAbsent keeps the existing entry.
  • Range views are live. Writing through headMap(105) with a key ≥ 105 throws IllegalArgumentException.
  • TreeMap does not accept null keys.

Design notes.

  • The roll number lives in both the key and the value. Always insert through s.roll() so the two can't drift apart.
  • Records give you immutable value objects with equals, hashCode and toString built in.
  • For thread-safe sorted access, use ConcurrentSkipListMap.

Likely follow-ups:

  • How do you sort by marks instead? A map is ordered by its key, so either sort values() with a comparator (as above) or keep a secondary TreeMap<Double, List<Student>> as an index.
  • TreeMap vs HashMap internals? TreeMap is a red-black tree that uses compareTo/compare, O(log n) and sorted. HashMap is an array of buckets that uses hashCode/equals, average O(1) and unordered.
  • How do you get the student with the next roll number after 103? students.higherEntry(103), which returns 105=Ravi (78.5).
G48 Serialize a custom object to a file and deserialize it.

The class implements Serializable. Write the object with ObjectOutputStream and read it back with ObjectInputStream, both over NIO streams. Fields marked transient are not saved.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.ObjectInputStream;
import java.io.ObjectOutputStream;
import java.io.Serializable;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class G48 {
    static class Employee implements Serializable {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        String name; int id;
        transient String password;                     // not serialized
        Employee(String name, int id, String password) { this.name = name; this.id = id; this.password = password; }
        @Override public String toString() { return "Employee[" + name + ", " + id + ", pwd=" + password + "]"; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
        Path file = Path.of("emp.ser");
        try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(file))) {
            out.writeObject(new Employee("Ravi", 101, "secret"));
        }
        try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(Files.newInputStream(file))) {
            Employee e = (Employee) in.readObject();
            System.out.println(e);
        }
    }
}
// Output: Employee[Ravi, 101, pwd=null]

Note: declare serialVersionUID so that a changed class version fails clearly with InvalidClassException. Deserialization does not call the class's constructor. Static fields are not serialized.

Approach. The class implements the marker interface Serializable and declares a private static final long serialVersionUID. Fields marked transient (passwords, caches, live connections) are not written. Write the object with ObjectOutputStream.writeObject and read it back with ObjectInputStream.readObject plus a cast, both inside try-with-resources. Since Java 9, attach an ObjectInputFilter that allow-lists the expected classes, because deserializing untrusted bytes can execute attacker-chosen code paths.

import java.io.*;
import java.nio.file.*;

class Account implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;    // version of the serialized form

    private final String owner;
    private final double balance;
    private transient String password;                  // never written to the stream
    private transient int loginCount = 5;               // initializer is NOT re-run on deserialization

    Account(String owner, double balance, String password) {
        System.out.println("Constructor called for " + owner);
        this.owner = owner;
        this.balance = balance;
        this.password = password;
    }

    @Override public String toString() {
        return "Account{owner=" + owner + ", balance=" + balance
                + ", password=" + password + ", loginCount=" + loginCount + "}";
    }
}

public class SerializationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
        Path file = Files.createTempFile("account", ".ser");
        Account original = new Account("Asha", 2500.75, "s3cr3t");
        System.out.println("Before: " + original);

        try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(file))) {
            out.writeObject(original);
        }

        Account copy;
        try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(Files.newInputStream(file))) {
            // Allow-list: only Account and JDK classes; reject everything else
            in.setObjectInputFilter(ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter("Account;java.base/*;!*"));
            copy = (Account) in.readObject();
        }

        System.out.println("After : " + copy);
        System.out.println("Same object? " + (original == copy));
        Files.deleteIfExists(file);
    }
}
// Output:
// Constructor called for Asha
// Before: Account{owner=Asha, balance=2500.75, password=s3cr3t, loginCount=5}
// After : Account{owner=Asha, balance=2500.75, password=null, loginCount=0}
// Same object? false

What happens during deserialization.

  • The constructor of a Serializable class is not run. That is why "Constructor called" appears only once. The JVM calls the no-arg constructor of the first non-serializable superclass (here Object) and then fills in the fields from the stream.
  • transient fields get their default values (null, 0, false). Field initializers don't run either, so loginCount comes back as 0, not 5.
  • Static fields are never serialized.

serialVersionUID. When you read an object, the stream's UID must match the class's UID. If it doesn't, readObject throws InvalidClassException. If you don't declare one, the JVM computes it from the class structure, so adding a single method breaks compatibility with files you already have. Declare it explicitly. Then compatible changes, such as adding a field (it is read as its default value), keep working.

Edge cases.

  • A non-serializable field, or a superclass field without a no-arg constructor, throws NotSerializableException or InvalidClassException. Make those fields transient or serializable.
  • Object graphs with cycles and shared references are handled. Each object is written once and later references point back to it.
  • A singleton needs readResolve (see G40).
  • To restore transient state, write private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in): call in.defaultReadObject() first, then recompute the derived fields.

Security warning. Never deserialize data from an untrusted source without a filter. "Gadget chains" (Apache Commons Collections and others) have turned readObject into remote code execution. Defend with an allow-list via ObjectInputFilter, or the JVM-wide jdk.serialFilter property. Better still, don't use Java serialization for data that crosses a trust boundary at all.

JSON alternative. In practice, use Jackson (new ObjectMapper().writeValue(file, account) and readValue(file, Account.class)) or Protobuf. The output is human-readable, works across languages, can be versioned explicitly, and goes through constructors and setters, so validation runs. Java records serialize through their canonical constructor, which makes them safer if you must use Java serialization.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Serializable vs Externalizable? Serializable is automatic and reflection-based, and you can customize it with writeObject/readObject. With Externalizable you write every field yourself in writeExternal/readExternal, and the class needs a public no-arg constructor, which is called.
  • How do you exclude a field without transient? Declare serialPersistentFields, or write a custom writeObject. In Jackson, use @JsonIgnore.
  • Is a subclass serializable if its parent is? Yes, it inherits the interface. If the parent is not serializable, the parent's fields are not saved, and the parent must have an accessible no-arg constructor.
G49 Read and write data with RandomAccessFile.

Open the file in "rw" mode. seek(byteOffset) jumps to any position, so you can read or overwrite fixed-size records in place and append at length().

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.RandomAccessFile;

public class G49 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        try (RandomAccessFile raf = new RandomAccessFile("data.bin", "rw")) {
            raf.setLength(0);                                   // start fresh
            for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) raf.writeInt(i * 10); // 5 ints x 4 bytes
            raf.seek(2 * Integer.BYTES);
            System.out.println("3rd int: " + raf.readInt());
            raf.seek(2 * Integer.BYTES);
            raf.writeInt(99);                                   // overwrite in place
            raf.seek(raf.length());
            raf.writeUTF("end");                                // append (2-byte length + 3 bytes)

            raf.seek(0);
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) sb.append(raf.readInt()).append(' ');
            System.out.println(sb + raf.readUTF() + " (length=" + raf.length() + ")");
        }
    }
}
// Output:
// 3rd int: 30
// 10 20 99 40 50 end (length=25)

Note: seek is O(1). This is useful for fixed-length record files and indexes. For very large files, FileChannel with memory mapping is the NIO alternative.

Approach. RandomAccessFile treats a file as a large byte array with a movable file pointer. seek(pos) jumps anywhere, and then readX/writeX work at that position. Open it in "rw" mode to read and write (it creates the file if needed). The key to random access is fixed-size records: if every record is exactly RECORD_SIZE bytes, record i starts at byte i * RECORD_SIZE. You can then read or update it in place in O(1), without rewriting the file. To get fixed-length strings, pad or truncate them to N chars. writeUTF is variable-length, so it breaks the offset arithmetic.

import java.io.*;
import java.nio.file.*;

public class RandomAccessDemo {

    static final int NAME_CHARS = 20;
    // int id (4) + 20 chars (40) + double salary (8) = 52 bytes per record
    static final int RECORD_SIZE = Integer.BYTES + NAME_CHARS * Character.BYTES + Double.BYTES;

    record Emp(int id, String name, double salary) { }

    static void write(RandomAccessFile raf, long index, Emp e) throws IOException {
        raf.seek(index * RECORD_SIZE);
        raf.writeInt(e.id());
        writeFixed(raf, e.name(), NAME_CHARS);
        raf.writeDouble(e.salary());
    }

    static Emp read(RandomAccessFile raf, long index) throws IOException {
        if (index < 0 || index >= count(raf)) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException("No record " + index);
        raf.seek(index * RECORD_SIZE);
        int id = raf.readInt();
        String name = readFixed(raf, NAME_CHARS);
        double salary = raf.readDouble();
        return new Emp(id, name, salary);
    }

    static long count(RandomAccessFile raf) throws IOException {
        return raf.length() / RECORD_SIZE;
    }

    // Update one field in place: jump straight to the salary offset
    static void updateSalary(RandomAccessFile raf, long index, double salary) throws IOException {
        raf.seek(index * RECORD_SIZE + Integer.BYTES + NAME_CHARS * Character.BYTES);
        raf.writeDouble(salary);
    }

    static void writeFixed(RandomAccessFile raf, String s, int len) throws IOException {
        for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
            raf.writeChar(i < s.length() ? s.charAt(i) : '\0');   // pad with NULs / truncate
        }
    }

    static String readFixed(RandomAccessFile raf, int len) throws IOException {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(len);
        for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
            char c = raf.readChar();                             // always consume all len chars
            if (c != '\0') sb.append(c);
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path path = Files.createTempFile("emp", ".dat");

        try (RandomAccessFile raf = new RandomAccessFile(path.toFile(), "rw")) {
            raf.setLength(0);
            write(raf, 0, new Emp(101, "Asha", 50000));
            write(raf, 1, new Emp(102, "Ravi", 65000));
            write(raf, 2, new Emp(103, "Meenakshi", 72000));
            System.out.println("Record size = " + RECORD_SIZE + " bytes, file length = " + raf.length()
                    + ", records = " + count(raf));
            for (long i = 0; i < count(raf); i++) System.out.println("#" + i + " " + read(raf, i));

            updateSalary(raf, 1, 99000);                                  // in-place update
            System.out.println("After update #1: " + read(raf, 1));

            write(raf, count(raf), new Emp(104, "A very long name that will be truncated", 40000)); // append
            System.out.println("Appended #3: " + read(raf, 3));
            System.out.println("File length now = " + raf.length());

            StringBuilder ids = new StringBuilder("IDs in reverse:");
            for (long i = count(raf) - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
                raf.seek(i * RECORD_SIZE);                                // read just the id field
                ids.append(' ').append(raf.readInt());
            }
            System.out.println(ids);
        }

        // Why writeUTF breaks fixed offsets: 2-byte length + variable-length modified UTF-8
        try (RandomAccessFile raf = new RandomAccessFile(path.toFile(), "rw")) {
            raf.setLength(0);
            raf.writeUTF("Asha");
            long a = raf.getFilePointer();
            raf.writeUTF("Meenakshi");
            long b = raf.getFilePointer();
            System.out.println("writeUTF sizes: " + a + " and " + (b - a) + " bytes");
            raf.seek(a);
            System.out.println("Read back 2nd UTF: " + raf.readUTF());
        }
        Files.deleteIfExists(path);
    }
}
// Output:
// Record size = 52 bytes, file length = 156, records = 3
// #0 Emp[id=101, name=Asha, salary=50000.0]
// #1 Emp[id=102, name=Ravi, salary=65000.0]
// #2 Emp[id=103, name=Meenakshi, salary=72000.0]
// After update #1: Emp[id=102, name=Ravi, salary=99000.0]
// Appended #3: Emp[id=104, name=A very long name tha, salary=40000.0]
// File length now = 208
// IDs in reverse: 104 103 102 101
// writeUTF sizes: 6 and 11 bytes
// Read back 2nd UTF: Meenakshi

Complexity. Reading or updating record i is O(1): one seek and a fixed number of bytes. Appending is O(1). Deleting from the middle would need an O(n) shift, so use a "deleted" flag (tombstone) and compact later. The reads and writes here are unbuffered, so each writeChar is a system call. For bulk I/O, assemble a record in a byte[] or ByteBuffer and write it in one call.

Modes.

Mode Behaviour
"r" Read-only. Throws FileNotFoundException if the file is missing.
"rw" Read and write. Creates the file if it doesn't exist.
"rws" Like "rw", plus every write of content and metadata is synced to disk.
"rwd" Like "rw", plus content writes are synced to disk.

The sync modes are slower, but no data is lost on a crash.

Edge cases.

  • Reading past the end of the file throws EOFException. The index check guards against it.
  • Seeking beyond the end and then writing extends the file. The gap's contents are unspecified (often zeros).
  • Names longer than 20 chars are truncated. Validate them or document the limit.
  • writeChar stores UTF-16 code units, 2 bytes each. For mostly-ASCII data, a fixed byte[] in UTF-8 halves the size, but then multi-byte characters need careful truncation.
  • Always close the file (try-with-resources). On Windows an open handle blocks deletion.

Design notes.

  • This is how simple database pages and index files work.
  • The modern alternative is FileChannel with ByteBuffer, which supports positional read(buf, pos) without moving a shared pointer, so several threads can use it. MappedByteBuffer (memory-mapped I/O) is better still for large files.
  • A RandomAccessFile is not thread-safe, because the file pointer is shared state.

Likely follow-ups:

  • Why not just use writeUTF? Its length varies with the content (2-byte length prefix plus modified UTF-8), so you can't compute where record i starts. You would need a separate index of offsets.
  • How do you find a record by id quickly? Keep the records sorted by id and binary-search with seek, which is O(log n), or keep an in-memory Map<id, index>.
  • RandomAccessFile vs FileInputStream? Streams are sequential and read-only or write-only. RandomAccessFile supports seeking and reading and writing in the same file.
